The events are: | Event | Fields | |---|---| | emergency.revocation (the header, one per row) | reason (compromised, lost, offboarding or incident), keys, sessions (counts) | | api_key.revoked | as for an ordinary revocation, with cause {"kind":"emergency"} | | session.revoked | session id, user, cause "emergency" (one per named session) | | user_sessions.revoked | user, cause "emergency", count (all sessions of a user) | Core code calls erp_security::auth::emergency::revoke(tx, &Target, EmergencyReason) in a read-committed transaction opened for the core System principal with an OperationIdentity, then commits. The call refuses before any deletion when the principal is not the core System principal, when the audit store cannot take the row (Transaction::audit_store_state) and when current_user does not own res_users_apikeys, erp_session and erp_event.ir_audit_entry. On an error the caller rolls the transaction back. Addon code does not call it. The owner role can rewrite its own rows: the row is evidence, not a defence against a hostile owner.

No constructor accepts a string that could carry a credential: events are made of ids, closed enums, flags and counts. A new kind of event is a new AuthEvent variant added by the slice that owns it, with its own validated payload. Addons cannot suppress, rewrite or delete a row: the request role holds INSERT on the columns it supplies and nothing else, the table is in the closed event namespace (every ORM and RPC operation on it is refused), and no context key disables audit.

A flagged action (set by an administrator, on an action with groups) runs with superuser mode. The order is fixed: the caller's own right to run the action (group membership) is checked first, a caller who may not run it records nothing, then the transaction records the elevation (action id, root action id, groups, who last wrote the action and when) and only then does the action and its subtree run with the elevated environment. A flagged action inside an elevated subtree is recorded as its own entry. The same action twice in one transaction is one entry with a count. When the store cannot take the row the action does not run.

Opening an elevation block (Transaction::elevated, see [scoped elevation blocks](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/access.md#scoped-elevation-blocks)) calls the crate-private hook Transaction::record_elevation on block entry, after the scope was validated and before the body runs; an error aborts the block before any elevated statement, and a refused entry records nothing. The entry's grant is {"kind": "scoped", "block": <number of the first block>, "items": [...]} with each item's model, operations, fields ("*" for all) and lifted rules. The hook only buffers (no statement, no second connection), deduplicates by reason, scope (by value), original attribution and effective subject, allows 128 distinct entries per transaction attempt and keeps the evidence of an elevation whose savepoint rolled back, marked savepoint_rolled_back. The unscoped escape hatch Transaction::audited_unscoped_sudo records each call.

- The table erp_event.ir_audit_entry is installed by every runtime grant publication (erp db publish-grants) and by erp audit maintain, with today plus 31 UTC daily partitions. A missing partition fails the insert; the server therefore refuses to start with no partition ahead of today and logs an error with one day left. The server creates the missing days itself at every start and once an hour on every node (Orm::maintain_event_partitions); a failed hourly run is logged and retried, and erp audit maintain repairs the window by hand. - Runtime contract version 8 (erp db runtime-grant-contract) preserves the insert-only runtime right and adds isolated SELECT-only reader publication/admission. Restoring an older publisher is refused before publication or pointer switching; old binaries do not implement this reader contract. - Configuration refuses identical runtime and owner roles. A configured reader must also differ from runtime, owner and heartbeat roles.

The test harness installs the real table in every database that builds its tables; there is no recording sink in any build. Read rows over an owner connection. HarnessBuilder::without_audit_store() starts from an empty event namespace, for tests of the event schema or of the refusal while the store is missing.

erp_orm::audit::seal provides pure format-1 canonical values, complete schema-1 row digests, ordered batch digests and validated seal envelopes (ADR 0039). These helpers do not write audit events, connect to a database, publish a witness or verify history. Supply already-redacted values; encoding is not redaction. RowDigest::schema1 requires every persisted column name, including generated columns, and sorts them bytewise. The database adapter remains responsible for SQL types, actual schema versions and (xid,id) ordering. Use CanonicalValue::numeric with an exact decimal token, never a value rounded through floating point; timestamp_micros takes integral UTC microseconds and xid preserves unsigned xid8. Structured values are built from typed children, not parsed with the ordinary f64 JSON parser. The codec bounds each encoded value/row to 8 MiB, each collection/batch to 65,536 members, decimal input/output to 4,096 bytes, and nesting to 16 containers. These are safety limits; batch defaults are a separate policy described in the owner-side sealing section below. Rejections are typed CodecError values with no payload in their messages; CanonicalValue debug output omits content. Raw encoded bytes still contain the input and must not be logged. The row adapter and owner-side batch operation are described below. Verification and CLI/configuration remain separate chain packages. The external witness library is described below. No new operator command, configuration or installation step is provided by the codec alone. Its serving integration and screen remain pending.

ADR 0167 defines three dedicated read-only methods on ir.audit.entry: audit_search, audit_read and audit_export. They are not available yet. Do not route audit storage through generic ORM methods or an owner connection while waiting for this work. The request role remains INSERT-only; the reader will use a separate restricted SELECT role. The typed engine requires both audit.read and audit-model read permission. Current target model, record and company rules still apply. The initial reader returns only entry identity/time, kind/outcome, model, method/effect and target ids. It conceals whole rows with any inaccessible or deleted target, unknown metadata or no target; it also conceals argument digests, raw events and identity/correlation aggregates. Search and export use the same projection, including their filters and continuation. This is a bounded view of currently authorized history, not recovery of deleted data or a complete forensic export. The native audit_reads = true declaration and its owned equivalent compose monotonically: an extension cannot disable another declaration's true value. Operator policy may additionally select all users or members of named groups. It cannot disable mandatory attempts, model opt-in or elevation recording, and request context cannot override it. A selected successful read remains READ ONLY and its result is withheld until the independent read_ok attempt commits. No audit history is seeded during installation: rows describe real operations. Capability and model ACL defaults belong in base. The audit.read mapping already exists; dedicated audit-model ACL installation, serving binders and JSON-2 tests remain obligations of INTEGRATE. Optional reader credential admission is described below. This engine does not make the serving API available or claim Agent/Service RPC admission. The internal erp_orm::audit::reader service provides validated AuditQuery, ReadRequest and composite EntryKey types. AuditReader::search, read and export use the transaction's original caller, with all elevation removed, on the primary. Field groups apply to requested fields and continuation keys. The registered capability is erp_security::audit::AUDIT_READ; its existing base data mapping is reused. A System-only transaction cannot supply reader authority. Generic event ORM operations still refuse. Queries require one known model and a positive UTC interval of at most 31 days. Page size defaults to 100 and cannot exceed 1,000; direct reads accept at most 1,000 composite keys. Candidate scans are bounded to 4,096 rows and 16 MiB of payload; each stored target set expands to at most 4,096 IDs. Continuations are at most 1 KiB and bind the query, caller, companies and current generations. A full page's continuation does not promise another eligible row. Scan, output and deadline limits return errors without partial success. The engine has no public enabled-pool constructor in shipped builds. AuditReader::unavailable() fails explicitly; for_tests exists only with test-faults and uses real restricted-role storage. INTEGRATE must compose the admitted reader handle with this service and serving-generation wiring before enabling any endpoint. The reader authority facility below supplies credential admission and shared connection-budget configuration. No owner-connection fallback is provided. Engine tests do not establish installed defaults, JSON-2 behavior or two-node admission. Dedicated reader methods and their RPC tests remain pending; the operational reader authority below does not open the current API or claim Agent/Service RPC admission.

The optional server [audit_read_policy] table accepts exactly one mode: [audit_read_policy] user_groups = ['base.group_system'] Alternatively use all_users = true. Omit the table, use all_users = false, or use user_groups = [] for defaults-only selection. Both mode keys together, an empty table, unknown keys, wrong types and group expressions are errors. Supply at most 256 positive group XML IDs, each at most 256 UTF-8 bytes. Duplicate names and order do not affect the shared configuration digest. Group matching uses the caller's current transaction-bound effective memberships, including implied groups, independently of request debug mode. Unresolved group references fail the operation, even when another group matches or the model already requires auditing. Fix the operator configuration or restore the group; an unknown group never silently disables recording. Subsequent operations use refreshed membership under the normal authorization invalidation contract. Model opt-in, observed elevation and mandatory denial/failure/replay/commit-unknown attempts cannot be disabled by this configuration. Nodes must agree on its canonical value before serving together. The normal native startup and lifecycle recomposition use the same RPC settings construction.

The optional audit_reader_database_url_file names a mode-600 regular file containing a PostgreSQL URL for a dedicated login on the same database endpoint. Relative paths resolve next to the server configuration. Symlinks, malformed files, another endpoint/database and a reused role are refused. Connection material is node-local and omitted from configuration Debug, shared settings digests and reader admission errors. The credential can read raw audit storage: keep it in the trusted platform boundary, never in addon state, RPC input or client configuration. Transaction::grant_audit_reader_role publishes schema USAGE and SELECT on the audit parent only. It reconciles direct event table, column, partition and sequence ACLs for this role, then verifies its effective privileges. Inherited or PUBLIC excess privileges, unsafe role attributes, ownership, role-switch paths, schema creation, database CREATE/TEMPORARY and executable application SECURITY DEFINER functions are refused. Operator remediation must remove the source of those privileges; publication does not rewrite unrelated roles or shared PUBLIC grants. New event partitions remove non-owner default ACLs so upkeep cannot grant direct partition access. Existing partition drift is caught by reader admission and reconciled by publication where directly granted to the reader. AuditReaderRoles::new declares the other deployment identities. AuditReaderConnection::open constructs its own private single-slot pool from the reader credential. It verifies the actual login, effective rights and a random live-session challenge against the trusted primary's pg_stat_activity. Every new connection is admitted; verify rechecks pooled role/privilege state before generation publication. No raw pool or SQL operation is exposed by the public handle. A query/projection service will be attached by the reader integration slice. With reader configuration absent, the server retains eight request slots and no reader pool. When configured, it reserves one of those slots: seven request slots and one reader slot, reused across registry generations. Policy and independent attempt-writer facilities retain their existing budgets. Invalid supplied credentials fail startup without trying owner/runtime/node credentials. Absence preserves ordinary writes; dedicated reader methods and their unavailable response remain pending.

erp_orm::audit::seal::{Anchor, AnchorRange, AuditWitness} describes operator-side external anchors. Anchor carries a validated SealIdentity, SHA-256 seal hash and format version 1. Construction validates these types; callers must separately establish that the database seal is valid and its transaction committed. The trait's synchronous publication and scoped fetching must never run inside an ordinary request transaction. erp_cli::audit::FileWitness implements this contract and supplies inventory() independently of database rows, heads or epoch lists. Inventory retains anchors for database history that has since disappeared, sorts by incarnation/epoch/batch identity and collapses identical duplicates. Scoped fetch validates the entire file before filtering; corruption outside its range still fails. An empty inventory provides no external assurance. Database comparison and recovery orchestration remain pending. use erp_orm::audit::seal::{Anchor, AnchorRange, SealIdentity}; let identity = SealIdentity::new([1; 16], 1, 1)?; let anchor = Anchor::new(identity, [9; 32], 1)?; let range = AnchorRange::new(1, 100)?; assert!(range.contains(anchor.identity().batch_no()));

FileWitness requires an existing trusted operator directory and a regular single-link file; publication creates a missing file with owner-only permissions. Reads never create evidence. Each operation opens fresh descriptors and uses an operating-system advisory lock. A competing operation (file creation or locking) returns typed WitnessError::Busy; callers may retry under their own bounded policy. Publication validates existing records, appends only a new identity, then synchronizes the file and directory. Identical retries also synchronize, so an earlier synchronization failure can be reconciled without duplicate records. Conflicting identities fail without rewriting history. I/O failures preserve the operation and OS error kind without echoing paths or JSON. The closed JSONL format contains only incarnation, epoch, batch number, seal hash and format version. Unknown/duplicate/missing fields, wrong types, malformed identities and unsupported versions are refused. Bounds are 1,024 bytes per physical line including LF, 16 MiB per file and 65,536 physical records. Blank lines and a final line without LF fail; CRLF is accepted. Exceeding a bound refuses operation rather than silently dropping evidence. There is no automatic truncation, rotation or torn-record repair, and file storage provides no database verification by itself. No witness command or server configuration key is introduced by this library delivery.

Transaction::install_audit_chain_schema installs or validates the unpartitioned erp_event.ir_audit_chain, ir_audit_seal and seal sequence. It requires the System principal with full elevation and the database owner connection. Existing objects must match the closed catalog declaration; drift requires explicit owner recovery. The installer creates no epoch. The caller commits or rolls back its transaction. Use EpochReason::new with an identifier of 1 to 128 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens. initialize_audit_chain explicitly creates epoch 1; new_audit_chain_epoch preserves its incarnation and links the next epoch to the current final seal. An empty predecessor epoch is refused. Both operations require Read Committed isolation and share a transaction advisory lock with sealing. EpochChange::Busy means another maintenance transaction holds that lock; retry in a new transaction. Created describes an insertion awaiting the caller's commit. EpochState reports the inherited lower-exclusive cursor and predecessor hash. A new epoch cannot reset either. These metadata operations do not seal audit rows, publish an external witness or establish verified history. The file witness library is described above; SEALER, VERIFY and INTEGRATE provide the remaining database orchestration. No operator CLI for these new operations is delivered by the schema package. Runtime roles receive zero table, column or sequence authority on chain storage under contract v6.

Transaction::seal_audit_batch(&SealOptions) reads the next committed safe prefix of persisted audit rows and inserts one immutable seal/checkpoint in the caller's transaction. Initialize the chain explicitly with initialize_audit_chain first. Use the database owner connection, System/full authority and Read Committed isolation, as for epoch maintenance. SealOptions::default() admits at most 10,000 rows and 8 MiB of cumulative stored encoded_bytes. SealOptions::new(rows, bytes) accepts 1..=65,536 rows and 1..=8 MiB. Stored estimates do not authorize unbounded decoding: transport is limited to 8 MiB per row and 16 MiB per batch, with the existing canonical depth, member, number and byte bounds applied independently. Invalid estimates, unsupported schema/value shapes and an oversized first row are explicit errors. The operation returns SealOutcome::Busy when another maintenance transaction holds the shared epoch/sealer lock, NoWork when no safe row is available, or Staged(SealReport). **Staged still requires the caller to commit.** Rollback discards both seal and checkpoint; sequence-generated seal ids may have gaps. After an error, roll back the transaction. Confirm commit before publishing an external witness anchor. A failed or uncertain commit requires reconciliation by identity; the report alone does not prove persistence or external assurance. The prefix is ordered by (xid,id) and lies strictly below snapshot xmin from the selection statement. A long-running writer can delay sealing, so NoWork is not a declaration that all history has been sealed. The first seal of a linked epoch inherits the preceding epoch's cursor and final hash. Every persisted schema-1 column contributes to the row digest, including generated ids, timestamp, xid and the stored byte estimate. JSONB numbers retain exact decimal tokens; SQL integers, UUIDs, bytea, SQL NULL and timestamp microseconds use their own canonical types. Transport JSON text is never hashed as the row encoding. This component is an owner-side library operation. The erp audit seal command, configuration and commit-to-witness recovery are planned; row verification is described in the next section. Retention and the audit-log serving UI retain their separate obligations.

Transaction::verify_audit_chain(&VerifyScope, &WitnessEvidence) re-reads rows, seals and epoch links and recomputes every digest and seal hash. Use an owner System/full transaction opened with **REPEATABLE READ** (one snapshot for the whole walk; Read Committed is refused). It writes nothing and takes no lock, so a running sealer never blocks it. WitnessEvidence::NotConfigured means no witness; WitnessEvidence::Inventory takes an AnchorInventory built from anchors your witness returned (at most 65,536; identical duplicates collapse; two anchors for one identity with different hashes are refused at construction). VerifyScope::full() walks everything; `VerifyScope::range(epoch, first, last)` verifies inclusive batches of one epoch, checks the stored predecessor boundary, compares anchors inside that range only, and marks the report partial. The result is a value, not an error: VerifyOutcome::Failed(VerifyFailure) names the first defect in (epoch, batch_no) order (FailurePoint plus a stable VerifyProblem; no row payload). It covers changed or deleted rows, edited seal columns, broken links, a missing anchored seal (deleted middle seal, suffix or epoch), a hash that differs from its anchor, anchors of another incarnation and anchors with no chain. Err only means the verifier could not run (not System/full, wrong isolation, catalog drift, SQL failure). VerifyReport::assurance() states what the success means. NoWitness and NoAnchors are internal consistency only. AnchoredThrough { epoch, batch_no } is the last anchored seal; the chain links cover every earlier seal. Seals after it (unanchored_tail) and rows after the head's last cursor (unsealed_tail, full scope only) are counted with their create_date bounds in UTC microseconds and are not verified. Deleting seals from the end cannot be seen without an anchor for them. The erp audit verify command and its exit codes are planned.

The accounting policy records AuthEvent::AccountLockDateChanged through the same transaction buffer. Its validated payload contains a positive company id, an exhaustive AccountLockField, and old/new optional dates encoded as integer days since 1970. Actor and time come from the existing row attribution and database timestamp. No free-text reason or arbitrary JSON is accepted. A no-op emits no event. Savepoint rollback drops the event describing the rolled-back mutation; a failed audit INSERT rolls back the company date and fiscal-period changes. This does not widen the audit reader's permitted projection fields or expose event payloads through its existing API.

erp_security::auth::apikey provides the native format and keyed-digest building blocks defined by ADR 0037. GeneratedApiKey::generate() returns redacted, zeroizing secret text; expose() explicitly borrows that text for the eventual one-time response. NativeApiKey::parse() validates a borrowed canonical token. ApiKeyHasher, derived from DatabaseSecret, produces the digest and key id for storage. These primitives do not authenticate a user, grant access or persist a key. Addon business code uses the authorized erp_sdk::auth::apikey_manage API, rather than inserting key rows directly. The apikey module's rustdoc contains a compiling example of generation and digest preparation. Never log the exposed text or serialize the hasher. A display prefix is only a label; it cannot identify or authenticate a credential. What an addon can use and extend in password login and sessions (design: docs/design/m3-auth.md §14). Everything is in erp_sdk::auth. Native API key verification and browser HTTP routes are described here; programmatic native key management is described below; MFA and SSO remain separate deliveries.

| Piece | Where | What it does | |---|---|---| | res.users.password | addons/base/src/res_users_auth.rs | write it in clear, it is stored hashed (Argon2id by default), it always reads empty. An empty password and one over 1,024 bytes ("A password may have at most 1024 bytes.") are refused. Setting it ends every session of the user at once, with the session-end hooks. | | res.users.login | same | unique ("You can not have two users with the same login!") | | res.users._check_credentials(credential, env) | same | verifies a credential for one user; the base implementation checks the password | | res.users.context_get() | same | {lang, tz, uid} of the calling user (JSON-2, read effect) | | res.users.log | addons/base/src/res_users_log.rs | one row per successful login (create_uid, create_date) | | ir.config_parameter | addons/base/src/ir_config_parameter.rs | database-wide settings with a typed API | Logins themselves run in the framework (Auth::authenticate, erp-security), not in an addon: the server calls it, and it calls _check_credentials through dispatch, so an addon override takes part. A login is two short transactions with no database connection held in between: one flight reads the throttle rows, the user and the installed languages; the password is hashed on the hashing pool; one flight writes the verdict (the failure count, or the session). The success is written only if the user's stored password and active flag are still the ones the first flight read: a password changed while the login was verified makes it fail with "Access Denied", and nothing is written.

- **Cancellation.** Dropping the authenticate future (a client that hangs up, a deadline) is safe: after the first flight the rest runs in a task of its own, so a guess is verified and counted even when its caller is gone, and a success leaves a session row nobody holds (idle collection ends it). Call it inside a Tokio runtime. - **Client address.** LoginRequest::new(login, password, client) takes the address explicitly: ClientAddr::Known(addr) (the address after the trusted-proxy rule) from every HTTP route, ClientAddr::InProcess("reason") only for tools, jobs and tests. In process there is no address cooldown, no pre-filter and no trusted pair, so an HTTP route must never use it. Debug of a request prints neither the login nor its length (users type passwords into the login field). - **Admission.** At most min(2 × hashing permits, primary pool size / 2) logins are in progress per ORM lineage, shared by every Auth handle and retained through detached work. The half-pool reservation also applies before an addon installs a credential override. A login that waits longer than the hashing pool's queue wait fails with LoginError::Overloaded { retry_after } (503 with Retry-After). A login can wait for the admission, for the settings (only after they changed: another request's reload, or its own; both share one deadline of the queue wait, and the reload's statement carries the same limit), and for its hashing permit, each up to the queue wait: three queue waits and one hash, and four queue waits and two hashes when the credential changed while it was verified (the login reads phase A again and verifies once more, once). A rehash of a correct password, or the cost floor's dummy after a wrong one, adds one queue wait and one hash to the verify it follows (so up to six waits and four hashes for a login restarted between two rehashes). The database statements of the login are bounded by the ORM's transaction limits, not by the queue wait: per try, and the failure count and the success statement each run up to three tries after a deadlock (5 – 25 ms apart), with the admission permit held. A session check that cannot read the settings within the queue wait fails with ResourceExhausted and Condition::Overloaded (503 too); a check whose keys changed while it ran reads them a second time, so it waits up to two queue waits for them. The hashing pool refusing one attempt's hash before it was verified (its own wait expired) answers "Access Denied" and is not counted; once the stored hash was verified, a wrong password is always counted. - **Denial cost.** A wrong password on a hash cheaper than the current parameters, or of another scheme (an imported Odoo PBKDF2 hash), also runs a dummy verify at the current parameters, so no denial is cheaper than an unknown login's. It is a floor: such a denial may take longer, which is accepted (BUG-082's residual; a later change may close it). - **Hashing settings.** password.hashing.argon2_memory_kib above what a hashing permit reserves (admission.hash_memory_kib) is refused when written (checked against the writing node's pool) and stops Auth::new. It can still reach a running node: one whose admission.hash_memory_kib is smaller than the writing node's, or any node after password.hashing.scheme is switched to argon2id over a larger memory value written earlier. That node logs the settings at error once per settings generation (AuthStats::settings_over_reservation) and keeps answering: unknown and inactive logins still verify a dummy (made within its reservation) and are counted; a correct password whose stored hash fits logs in without the rehash (AuthStats::rehash_skipped); a user whose stored hash another node made over this node's reservation is refused through this node like a wrong password, "Access Denied" and counted, logged at error naming admission.hash_memory_kib. Give every node the same admission.hash_memory_kib. - **Sessions per user.** A user keeps at most 100 sessions; the login past that ends the oldest, with the session-end hooks. - **Trusted address.** The per-login cooldown (failures of one login from any address) never refuses the correct password from an (address, login) pair that logged in successfully within the last 30 days; any other address stays under the cooldown, and wrong passwords from the trusted pair still count. The address cooldown applies to everyone. A login keeps at most 16 trusted pairs: the oldest go first. A success clears no failure counter: they decay. - **Throttle rows.** Their keys are an HMAC under a key derived from database.secret, never a plain hash of the login or the address; Auth::throttle_key gives the key of a row. Rotating the secret resets the counters. - **Password and login changes end sessions.** Setting a password, or renaming the user's login, ends every session of the user at once, with the hooks, the caller's own included (a planned change_password will keep the current one). A login that rehashes the stored password (an imported Odoo hash, or raised hashing parameters) sweeps obsolete tokens against the current user fields and trusted key source in independently committed batches of at most 1,000 sessions. Concurrent valid sessions survive, including credentials that cycle back to a previous value. Each batch locks user, key source, then sessions; malformed tokens, missing/malformed keys or an unknown key id stop that batch without deleting any of its rows. Earlier batches may already have committed. The sweep stops with a counted/logged error after 100 full batches; token validation still governs access. Writing passwords for many users hashes them on every permit of the pool but one at once (the one left keeps logins going), inside the writing transaction. - **Logout takes an id, which is not a secret.** Auth::logout(id) ends the session id. Session ids appear in CSRF tokens and audit rows, so pass only the id of the session the request just checked, or, on a devices page, an id you have checked belongs to the requesting user; never an id the client merely sends.

Override it to add a condition to every login of a user, and call super for the check itself. The method runs as the user being logged in, in superuser mode, in a REPEATABLE READ transaction of its own that the login keeps open through the check (it commits with a success, so the override's writes stand, and rolls back with a refusal); return an error to refuse. Without an override the login checks the password with no transaction at all, so an override costs a held connection for the length of the hash: keep the check itself cheap. use erp_sdk::auth::{AuthInfo, CheckEnv, Credential, access_denied}; use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

impl ResUsersLoginHours { #[method(override)] async fn _check_credentials( this: &RecordSet<ResUsers>, tx: &mut Transaction, credential: Arc<Credential>, env: CheckEnv, sup: Super, ) -> Result<AuthInfo> { let info: AuthInfo = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), (credential, env)).await?; if !within_login_hours(tx, info.uid()).await? { // the same refusal as a wrong password: the client cannot tell them apart return Err(access_denied()); } Ok(info) } } Rules: - Refuse with access_denied() (kind AccessDenied, text "Access Denied"): the attempt counts as a failure for the cooldown. Any other error fails the login with that error and rolls its transaction back; it is not counted as a failed attempt. - Never log or put into an error the password, the stored hash or the Credential (its Debug is redacted). - Credential is #[non_exhaustive]: match it with a _ arm. Only Credential::Password exists today; other credential types are planned. - The failure counting, the cooldown and the timing of unknown logins are the framework's; an override does not need to (and cannot) change them.
Override res.users._on_login_cooldown(context) to ask for a *stricter* cooldown than the base.login_cooldown_* settings (ADR 0076). Call super, then add rules to the policy it returns:

async fn _on_login_cooldown(this: &RecordSet<ResUsers>, tx: &mut Transaction, context: LoginCooldownContext, sup: Super) -> Result<LoginCooldownPolicy> { let policy: LoginCooldownPolicy = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), (context,)).await?; policy.with_login_rule(3, Duration::from_secs(300)) } - The attempt is refused when the core rule **or** an added rule is in force, using the same shared failure counters; a policy cannot disable a core rule, accept a credential or keep a counter. Rules combine along a super chain by keeping the stricter threshold and the longer duration. Bounds: address threshold 1..=1_000_000, login threshold 1..=4_000_000, whole seconds 1..=604_800; anything else is a Validation error naming the field. - An added login rule keeps the trusted-pair exception; an added address rule applies only with an actual client address. - The hook runs once per attempt (and again before a restart), before any credential work, as the superuser in a **read-only** transaction that is always rolled back. It is told only the submitted login (which may name no user), the client address and the current settings, never a user id, hash or password. A hook that looks the login up in the database makes known and unknown logins take different times: that is yours to avoid. Do not make external calls and keep it short: it holds a login admission permit and a connection while it runs. One call has a deadline (AuthConfig::cooldown_hook_deadline, default 5 s, 10 – 60,000 ms): past it the task is aborted and the attempt refused like any hook failure. Await, do not block the thread: a blocking call is not interrupted. - A hook error, panic or invalid rule refuses the attempt (LoginError::Failed); nothing is verified or counted. The caller gets a fixed text; your error goes to the erp::auth log. - The pre-filter and over-long credentials are refused before any database work and never call the hook.

ADR 0075 defines these hooks; docs/adr/0126-login-rollout-admission.md (ADR 0126) defines serving admission. Auth::new refuses a registry that overrides either selection hook with ErrorKind::Programming and custom login selection requires an active membership-bound rollout. There is no exact-login fallback. Served composition uses `Auth::with_membership(orm, config, pool, member.admission())`, derived from an actual registered membership. It validates helper publication, schema, database, binary declaration and registry association. Starting membership may compose Auth; authentication still requires live serving admission and an enabled rollout. The native binary declares auth.login_principal, version 1, as part of its combined identity. Registration precedes composition, and a changed catalogue requires membership restart. Operators follow the [rollout procedure](/en/next/developer/installation/login-selection-rollout.md) to publish isolated NOLOGIN-owned helpers, approve exact eligible digests and confirm legacy-service fencing. An ordinary node rollout window never enables this feature. Every attempt retains its original feature generation through hashing, restart and detached verdicts. Successful finalization revalidates it under protection held through session commit; disable waits for earlier protected commits. New custom authentication refuses while disabled. While enabled, a bound base-only peer also applies principal accounting, and an unbound base service refuses before real verification. Failed guesses remain counted after disable/disconnect; pre-disable sessions retain normal session semantics. Selection plus credential overrides preserve the SESSION refusal. Membership-bound credential overrides also refuse until SESSION, including when disabled, to avoid acquiring feature protection after an override's user locks. This is an explicit native compatibility limit; the existing unbound inactive base path retains its query/flight contract. Integration fixtures can explicitly call erp_security::auth::test_support::login_selection_auth when the default-off test-support feature is enabled. This helper bypasses only the rollout refusal; model, schema, settings, pool and unsupported credential-composition checks still apply. Enabling that feature alone does not change Auth::new. The helper is fixture-only, is not re-exported through the SDK and is not an activation mechanism. Plan construction and candidate execution are internal to the service; addon hooks produce raw domain/order values which the framework admits before compiling or executing them.

The hook receives LoginLookup, not a String. It returns LoginDomain; the framework admits the returned AST against the pinned registry before compiling SQL. Native hooks are trusted deterministic metadata functions. ORM database, record, transaction and changed-environment effects are forbidden in their scope; this does not sandbox native Rust's direct I/O. The following integration fragment uses the checkpoint's actual API. The addon must declare login_alias as a stored char field on res.users; imports and its model declaration are omitted. This fragment has not independently been compiled as a guide example; the executable alias/super fixtures are in crates/erp-test-models/src/test_login_selection.rs.

async fn _get_login_domain( this: &RecordSet<ResUsers>, tx: &mut Transaction, lookup: LoginLookup, sup: Super, ) -> Result<LoginDomain> { let base: LoginDomain = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), (lookup.clone(),)).await?; let alias = Domain::condition("login_alias", Operator::Eq, lookup.as_str()) .map_err(|_| Error::validation("invalid alias selection domain"))?; Ok(LoginDomain::custom(Domain::or([base.domain().clone(), alias]))) } Supported fields are physical local stored id/integer, boolean, char and static selection columns. Related/computed/search-callback, inherited, translated, company-dependent and relational fields are refused. Supported operators are =, !=, <, <=, >, >=, in, not in with scalar operands; membership requires a collection. The ordinary domain optimizer/compiler supplies null and Boolean semantics. No raw SQL, dynamic time/context expression or pattern operator is admitted. Base domain construction is fallible: LoginDomain::exact_login(...) returns Result<LoginDomain>. Default ceilings derive from QueryLimits: 65,536 plan bytes, depth 16, 512 conditions, 128 distinct fields and 8 effective order terms; auth also bounds AST nodes at 1,024 and membership elements at 512. Core predicates and ordering share the aggregate admission budget. Witness transfer is independently bounded. Exact aggregate-boundary proof is still pending. Normal ORM transaction deadlines apply; this checkpoint does not establish a separate 500 ms selection deadline. Core selection always enforces active = true, total ordering and LIMIT 1. Constant/empty domains retain domain semantics and the core active filter. An unknown/inactive candidate uses dummy password verification; malformed hook results return an error rather than silently selecting through the base path. No timing-equality or identical-accounting claim is made.
An addon with a stored integer login_priority may return this order. As above, this is an integration fragment whose omitted model/import context must be supplied.

async fn _get_login_order( _this: &RecordSet<ResUsers>, _tx: &mut Transaction, _sup: Super, ) -> Result<LoginOrder> { Ok(LoginOrder::custom(vec![LoginOrderTerm::desc("login_priority")])) } The framework validates the fields, refuses duplicate/empty ordering and appends id ASC when id is absent. An explicit id direction is retained. The effective order, including that tie-breaker, must fit the ceiling of eight terms.

Password hashing runs outside a database transaction. After a successful verify, custom selection opens a READ COMMITTED finalization transaction, protects its original active rollout generation, then takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on res_users, reruns the hooks and ordered selection, compares the complete plan/winner witness, and retains the guard through rehash/session persistence and commit. A mismatch restarts the entire attempt once; a second mismatch denies it. Tokens use canonical stored login, not alias. The checkpoint's focused tests prove the guard exists at session insertion and exercise a competitor reordered while hashing; broader race cases remain open. Failed guesses write address, submitted-login and selected UID counters atomically. A wrong password creates no trusted UID/address pair. The UID cooldown is checked before password verification and survives alias/address changes; only exact UID/address trust can exempt that dimension. Existing address protection remains. Old counters are retained during schema migration, and bounded GC now covers both principal kinds. The rollout report records process-level shared-budget and disable coverage; native alias HTTP acceptance, broader trust-expiry/cap coverage and whole-case certification remain open. Both constructors refuse selection overrides combined with _check_credentials overrides for now; that composition error takes precedence over the unbound custom-selection refusal. Digest-bound membership and activation are implemented. Remaining race coverage, boundary and type matrices, the full mapping, parity regeneration and compiled examples are still open. The functional page is docs/user/login-selection.md. The operator procedure is available at [Custom login selection rollout](/en/next/developer/installation/login-selection-rollout.md). This checkpoint does not establish whole-LOGIN acceptance or deployment readiness.

A session's token covers id, login, password and active of its user, so changing any of them ends the user's sessions at their next check. An addon that adds a credential factor (a TOTP secret, a linked account's token) adds the **name** of the user field to that set (H58 TOKEN, SPEC-AUTH-041 and SPEC-AUTH-042; decision: ADR 0155). Override res.users._get_session_token_fields, call super, and add names:

async fn _get_session_token_fields(this: &RecordSet<ResUsers>, tx: &mut Transaction, sup: Super) -> Result<SessionTokenFields> { let fields: SessionTokenFields = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), ()).await?; fields.with_field("totp_secret") } - **Names only.** The result is a bounded set of names: at most 16 added fields, each [a-z_][a-z0-9_]* of at most 63 bytes. The hook returns no SQL, no value and no per-user decision; the framework reads the values in the statements that already read the base fields (no extra round trip) and encodes them. The type cannot remove a base field, and a duplicate (a base field, or a name added twice along the chain) is a Validation error, not a silent merge. - **Resolved once per registry.** The hook runs once, when the Auth service of the registry is built, as the superuser in a read-only transaction that is always rolled back, where any query or write is refused, with a bound (AuthConfig::with_token_plan_hook_deadline_ms, default 10 s, 10 – 60,000 ms). It is not called per login or per request. The service is not built, and nothing is issued or checked, when the plan is refused. There is no fallback to the base fields: a hook error or panic, a name that is no field of res.users, a field that is not stored or is translated or company dependent, a type other than boolean, integer, selection, many2one (the id) and char with a size of at most 16,384 (so float, monetary, date, datetime, text and a char without a size are refused: their text form depends on session settings or their size is not bounded), and any one2many or many2many field, give a Programming error naming the field. Odoo's auth_totp declares totp_secret as a non-stored computed Char over a hand-made column (odoo/addons/auth_totp/models/res_users.py:33, :40-41); that shape is refused, a native TOTP addon declares a stored, sized char. An install-time check of the plan is planned. Relation fields (a passkey list) are **not supported yet**. - **What changes a token.** A change of an added field's value, including NULL to a value and back, ends the user's sessions at their next check, on any node, with the same SessionExpired answer ("user is not connected") as any other mismatch. A field that is NULL adds nothing to the token (Odoo's rule), so installing an addon does not log anyone out until a value is set. Values are read from the primary at every check; nothing caches them, so another node sees a change at its next request. A value over 64 KiB is refused with an error, never cut. - **Everywhere the same plan.** Login issuance (a factor changed while the password was being verified makes the login restart and read it again), the session check (also the cookie checked beside an API key), the current session after the user's own password change or an administrator reset, and the cleanup after a password rehash all use it. - **Who may write the field.** Anyone allowed to write an added field can end that user's sessions (and a write by the session's own user changes the token under it). Give the field restrictive groups, as Odoo does for its secrets. Do not add a field the framework updates on every write, such as write_uid: any write to the user, by anyone, would then end all of that user's sessions. - **Not combined with custom login selection yet.** An addon that overrides _get_login_domain or _get_login_order together with a plan that adds fields makes the service refuse to start with an error saying that token fields and custom login selection cannot be combined yet. - **Mixed versions.** A node whose plan differs from the one a session was issued under computes a different token for users whose added fields are not NULL and refuses the session like any mismatch (the row is deleted; the user logs in again). Upgrade all nodes of a database together.

Writing password on res.users hashes it. When an addon stores another secret the same way, use hash_password(tx, password) (the database's current parameters, on the database's hashing pool: the one handed to its Auth, so every hash of the ORM lineage shares one bound). For direct verification, retain auth::pool::for_env(env) and use its PoolBinding::run around StoredHash::parse(..)?.verify(..). That lease survives cancellation until the blocking hash finishes, including data loading before the first Auth. Never hash on the async runtime; the pool bounds concurrent CPU and memory use.

An addon that keeps rows per session (push subscriptions, devices, websocket presence) registers a hook. It runs in the transaction that deletes the session rows, for every reason: logout, archiving or deleting the user, setting the user's password, a rehash at login (sessions with obsolete tokens), the per-user cap of 100, a refused check, collection of expired sessions. Delete your rows there; returning an error fails the whole deletion, so the session survives with your rows. Use raw statements only (query, execute, batch), never the record API. The dispatcher enforces this for every caller with Transaction::raw_statements_only(), including user changes inside REPEATABLE READ transactions. Record access fails with Programming; READ COMMITTED retains its existing isolation-specific diagnostic. Cached reads, prebuilt query execution, stream advancement, method continuations and explicit ORM flushes are restricted too. The caller's prior restriction is restored when the hook returns, errors or is cancelled; existing transaction cancellation and rollback requirements still apply. Transaction metadata and projections of values already held by native code remain available. This is a consistency contract for trusted native addons, not a Rust or SQL sandbox (ADR 0078). use erp_sdk::BoxFuture; use erp_sdk::auth::SessionEnd; use erp_sdk::prelude::*; erp_sdk::auth::session_end_hook!(DROP_DEVICES, addon = "my_addon", run = drop_devices); fn drop_devices<'a>(tx: &'a mut Transaction, ended: &'a SessionEnd) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<()>> { Box::pin(async move { let ids: Vec<String> = ended.sessions().iter().map(|s| s.id().to_text()).collect(); tx.execute("DELETE FROM my_addon_device WHERE session_id = ANY($1)", &[&ids]) .await?; Ok(()) }) } ended.reason() tells why (EndReason::Logout, Revoked, Expired, CredentialChanged for a password set or a rehash at login, OverCap for the per-user cap). The hook of an addon that is not installed in the database never runs. Keep the work set-based: one statement for all ended sessions, never a loop of per-session queries (collection ends up to 1,000 sessions per transaction).

Use the typed API, as Odoo 20 does: get_str, get_int, get_float, get_bool and set_str, set_int, set_float, set_bool, from Rust (records("ir.config_parameter")?.call(tx, "get_int", (key, default))) or over JSON-2. A missing key or an empty value gives the default; a value of the wrong type is a Validation error naming the key (Odoo returns the default and logs a warning; we fail loudly, BUG-083 for the setter). Setters return the previous value only after model and existing-row write **and read** authorization, including a no-op. Missing keys still require normal create permission. Malformed-value errors name the key and expected type and never include the stored value. - database.secret cannot be read, searched, exported or written by any caller without full elevation, whatever the groups (ADR 0037 decision 8): it signs the session tokens. In-process code that needs it runs in superuser mode. Never copy it into another record, a log or a response. - The keys base creates (database.secret, database.uuid, database.create_date, base.login_cooldown_after, base.login_cooldown_duration) cannot be renamed or deleted. - Every write invalidates the authentication settings cache on every node, so a changed cooldown or session limit applies to the next login or check without a restart.

Auth::begin_session(&secret, CredentialOptions::new()) (erp_orm::CredentialOptions, re-exported) opens the request's transaction with the session check in its opening flight (CredentialOptions carries the context, limits and read intent; nothing else is accepted). Auth::rotate and Auth::touch(&[Touch::new(id).addr(ip).agent(ua)]) are one READ COMMITTED round trip each, outside the request's transaction; a touch skips rows another transaction holds, and two rotations of one secret converge on one successor (the second returns None). A row whose key id this node does not hold is refused but kept (another node may hold the key during a rollout).

erp_testkit::Harness creates the core tables of the crates linked into the test, the session and throttle tables among them, as Orm::sync_schema does on a real server. The helpers in crates/erp-test-models/tests/auth_support/mod.rs show a database ready for logins (the init hooks of ir.config_parameter and res.users, an administrator, users with passwords).

Trusted composition can call Auth::check_session_in(&mut tx, &secret) when ModuleSystem owns the primary transaction. Its opaque SessionAuthorization exposes the current human principal/session and has_groups; the policy is compiled from that transaction's rows, even when the engine's root policy is System-only. It does not change transaction authority. Only the native lifecycle engine binds the validated actor before schema/data effects. Addon RPC code must use its existing caller transaction and must never use this seam as an elevation or install API.

Auth::check_identity(Some(cookie_secret)) checks the current HTTP session's identity window. IdentityCheck::Required.action() returns the typed res.users.identitycheck window descriptor; the adapter renders confirmation and resubmits its fixed operation. None is refused with the SEC-041 no-HTTP error. An identity observation is never authority to skip the operation's own check. Auth::confirm_identity(cookie_secret, password, client) verifies that session's user through the existing credential-dispatch and shared-throttle path and stores confirmation in PostgreSQL. Pass ClientAddr::Known from an HTTP adapter. Confirmation is per session, not per user, and expires at ten minutes; future timestamps are not accepted. It does not create a login session or upgrade a legacy hash. Failed guesses are recorded even when the caller disconnects during verification. Auth::change_password(Some(cookie_secret), new_password) takes the same admission before opening any transaction. A stale identity returns IdentityCheck::Required without mutation. Success returns Verified after committing the password, the current session's refreshed token and the revocation of other sessions together. The cookie and stable session id survive. A session-end hook failure rolls all of that back. Concurrency errors require retrying the complete service operation. This service owns its transactions: invoke it before opening an ordinary RPC transaction. It is a dedicated self-service path, not a call to the password field's inverse. Credential-check overrides participate in confirmation and session-end hooks participate in revocation; password-field inverse overrides do not participate. Ordinary password-field writes retain their revoke-all behavior. The HTTP/RPC adapter, transient wizard model and rendered UI are not supplied by this typed API. Identity confirmation and password change reject more than 100 stored sessions for the current user with Validation, including expired/pending rows. End excess sessions and retry. The bound is checked under the user lock before confirmation/password/token mutation; password change revokes every other admitted session and runs its hooks in the same transaction.

erp_sdk::auth::IssueRequest::new validates a typed subject, name, kind, scope and optional naive-UTC expiry. The store currently admits only KeyKind::User and KeyScope::Rpc: unrestricted models and methods, writable access, subject capabilities. There is no JSON-to-authority deserializer. Agent and service requests return the ADR 0037 principal gate; MCP user requests are refused. Labels are nonempty after trimming and at most 128 bytes. Addons that renew or create keys for the current user should call erp_sdk::auth::apikey_manage::generate, which validates the presented key, scope and policy and then delegates here. erp_sdk::auth::issue itself audits in the caller's transaction: it writes one api_key.issued event built from the inserted row, and the transaction needs an OperationIdentity, otherwise the commit fails with an audit error and no key survives. There is no unaudited issuance path. Pass the tenant's ApiKeyHasher to erp_sdk::auth::issue in the caller's transaction. Rebuild the hasher after database.secret rotation; never reuse another tenant's material. A subject-row version fence precedes policy/count reads. The database supplies the clock and effective groups. Non-system subjects must supply an expiry within their groups' maximum duration (one day when the maximum is zero or absent). Persistent keys are reserved for system subjects. The native store handles issuance. Programmatic management delegates to it after validating the current user and the supplied key; native verification and scheduled collection use the same database expiry semantics. Use Orm::run for whole-transaction serialization/deadlock retry. Construct the one-time secret inside each attempt; never produce a response, log or external effect within that retryable closure. Only return the IssuedApiKey from the committed attempt. Explicit transactions surface Concurrency unchanged: roll back and retry the complete unit of work, never only its INSERT. The issuance result and its secret have no Debug, Display, Clone or serialization implementation. After commit succeeds, consume the result with into_secret(), then explicitly borrow expose() for the one-time response. Do not expose any secret before successful commit. Rollback or connection loss revokes pending issuance automatically. Secret storage zeroizes on drop. base.programmatic_api_keys_limit imposes a tenant-local active-key cap per subject, defaulting to 10 when absent; a present value must be positive. The predicate includes persistent keys and expiration_date >= database time. Malformed configuration refuses issuance. The caller must belong to base.group_system, or the strictly parsed base.enable_programmatic_api_keys setting must be true. Delegation requires actual system group membership; sudo/core elevation alone does not grant it. Public management endpoints and credential checks are planned. Generic ORM create/write cannot bypass issuance. Issuance, revocation and expired-key collection are recorded in the audit trail with typed events (erp_sdk::audit::AuthEvent) in the same transaction as the change; see [the audit trail](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/audit.md). The events carry key ids and enums, never a key, a digest, a display prefix or a key name.

Transport integrations authenticate with Auth::begin_api_key(ApiKeyRequest, CredentialOptions). Construct the request with the submitted credential, exact KeyScope and the client IP resolved by the trusted proxy boundary. Optional .uid(...) constrains the expected subject; optional .session(...) checks cookie precedence. Keep the input out of diagnostics and retain it only for the request and its bounded RPC retries. The returned transaction is authorized by the key row and the current subject's groups and companies. Finish it with commit or rollback. A user key's validated scope also supplies Actor::ApiKey; a human session without a key has no key actor. Native user keys currently use the subject's capabilities and unrestricted model and method scope. Agent and service keys are refused until scoped principals exist. Imported legacy 40-hex credentials (rows carrying legacy_index and legacy_hash, ADR 0037 decision 5) verify with their original PBKDF2-SHA512 hash under the same route audience, expiry, active-user, uid and kind rules as native keys. Re-issue a native key to stop paying the hash cost; deleting the row (erp auth emergency-revoke --key <id>) refuses the key on the next request on every node. res.users.apikeys.last_used_at records when a key was last accepted. It is a coarse signal, not an access log: it moves at most once an hour per key across the whole cluster, using the database clock (naive UTC), and a key never used has it empty. The write is bookkeeping. It runs outside the request transaction, never touches write_date, and a failure is logged at warn with the key id and counted, never raised to the request. ApiKeyBegin.last_use carries the work for a caller of begin_api_key. It is Some only when the key is due, and it is an ApiKeyLastUse ticket: **dropping it launches the write**, so hold it until the request transaction has ended (commit or rollback), then drop it. Dropping it earlier is safe except for one case: the request transaction is REPEATABLE READ, so any such transaction that took its snapshot before a write of this key committed, and then updates, deletes or locks (FOR UPDATE) that key row, gets a serialization failure (40001). That is the same request when it dropped the ticket early (a key revoking itself), and also another request that revokes or changes this key while a write from a different request commits in between; the RPC layer retries such a failure as a whole attempt. If you call begin_api_key more than once for one request (a preflight, then the real opening), keep the first ticket and call ApiKeyLastUse::discard on the others: it throws a ticket away without writing. A ticket dropped while the runtime shuts down may record nothing. Ignoring the field entirely is also fine; the ticket is dropped with the ApiKeyBegin. One write per process and ORM lineage runs at a time; a ticket dropped while another write runs is skipped (AuthStats::last_use_skipped) and the key's next use is due again. Outcomes are in AuthStats::last_use_writes, last_use_noops (not due any more, row locked or deleted) and last_use_errors. Verification reads tenant-primary PostgreSQL in the opening transaction flight. Acceptance is never cached: revocation, expiry and user deactivation apply to the next transaction on another node too. Only tenant settings and cryptographic derivation are cached by settings generation. A stale or invalid optional cookie does not grant authority and does not extend or delete its session. A valid cookie belonging to another user raises Access with Session user does not match the used apikey. A failed key never falls back to cookie access. The HTTP adapter first uses the existing bounded process address prefilter once per external bearer request; RPC rechecks do not consume additional flood tokens. The shared tenant address throttle covers invalid native bearer attempts. Cooldown and database failures propagate; they cannot turn into authorization. ApiKeyCooldown is the typed error source used by the HTTP adapter to return 429 and Retry-After. Malformed, unknown, revoked, inactive-user, expired and wrong-scope native keys return AccessDenied with Invalid apikey. The HTTP adapter returns 401 and WWW-Authenticate: bearer. Submitted credentials are never included in errors. The canonical HTTP entry point is POST /erp/json/2/<model>/<method> with a single Bearer Authorization header. Native bearer requests are stateless. Cookie JSON-2 requests retain their same-origin checks. Bearer requests with an Origin must name the configured public origin; no cross-origin allowlist is configured by this slice. Module installation continues to require a human session and its existing CSRF checks. No legacy XML-RPC or JSON-RPC endpoint is added.

The browser password operations are a closed, request-local interface. They run after RPC parsing, exposure and binding but own their sensitive authentication transactions. Never call the Auth service from an ordinary model transaction. Identity authority is the presented browser cookie; context, caller-supplied user IDs, API keys and a prior principal snapshot do not replace it. Own changes call Auth::change_password after Auth::confirm_identity when required. The legacy res.users.change_password(old_passwd, new_passwd) explicitly verifies its old password on every call. Administrator resets use validated PasswordReset inputs and a fresh manager authorization. They do not grant general user-write permission. Every target must be visible to the actor under res.users' generated company restriction with all of the actor's companies active (through its share escape this scopes portal users only); an actor without base.group_system also needs every target, internal users included, to share one of its companies; a target holding base.group_system needs an actor holding it; the superuser row is never a target (ADR 0138 Amendment 1). These run through SessionAuthorization::check_reset_targets when the wizard opens, in Auth's preflight and after the final locks; a refused target answers like a missing one (erp_security::auth::missing_reset_target). Reset lines (change.password.user) are created only by the wizard open, in superuser mode: the line model's create refuses every other creation with the same answer, so addon code cannot add a line through create. The visibility call underneath, Transaction::visible_under_company_restriction (ADR 0190), takes an explicit policy, principal and company set; it is a check for core services, not an addon API. An empty administrator line skips mutation; password byte and selected-user/session limits fail before partial effects. The current actor's cookie is retained when its own password changes; affected other sessions end through the existing transactional hooks. Wizard secret fields are nonstored and read empty. Do not generically save them: send only the fixed operation parameters documented in ADR 0138. No password enters a persisted replay request, action context, tracking or debug output. Managed submissions refuse Idempotency-Key explicitly; a missing commit answer is uncertain and must never trigger automatic replay. The web client implements this in addons/web/static/src/client/password-flow.ts. The three submissions (res.users.identitycheck.run_check, change.password.own.change_password, change.password.wizard.change_password_button) skip the save: the wizard dialog validates the form and sends the typed values as operation parameters (password; new_password and confirm_password; changes as {line_id, new_passwd} per selected-user line). The four password models never send an edit to onchange. When an operation answers with the identity confirmation, the client keeps that operation in memory and sends it again, once, after the confirmation succeeds; the server stores no callback. The set is closed: an addon cannot add a password submission to it. Native base-only managed entry implementations are the initial supported composition. A hidden entry stays hidden; additional implementation overrides are refused explicitly, rather than silently skipped. Credential and session-end hooks retain their current dispatch. As in the existing self-change service, Auth-owned password mutation does not dispatch _set_password overrides. No broader addon parity is claimed.

erp_sdk::auth::apikey_manage::generate(tx, key, scope, name, expiry) verifies an active native user key owned by the transaction's current user, with the requested scope, then returns IssuedApiKey. Commit before exposing its secret. It creates a replacement without deleting the old key: store the new credential securely, verify it, then call revoke(tx, old_key). Revocation deletes the row atomically; every replica rejects it on its next authenticated transaction. Deletion invalidates the apikeys named cache; signal-enabled commits publish that generation atomically. Generic create, write and unlink cannot bypass these APIs, including under sudo. Only native unrestricted user keys with rpc scope are admitted in this slice. Agent/service and imported legacy credential support retain their existing future-task gates. The public model methods are `res.users.apikeys.generate(key, scope, name, expiration_date) and res.users.apikeys.revoke(key)`. Generation returns the new credential string once; revoke returns true. A refused key answers AccessDenied: "The provided API key is invalid or does not belong to the current user." from generation (Odoo's text), "The provided API key is invalid." from revoke. Revoke deletes only an rpc key of the current user and gives that one answer for an unknown, foreign, expired, wrongly scoped or malformed key. This differs from Odoo on purpose (ADR 0037 decision 5): Odoo lets a system user revoke any key, ignores the scope and answers a foreign key with a different error; one uniform answer tells a caller nothing about other users' keys. Generation also checks the presented key before the active-key limit, where Odoo checks the limit first. expiration_date accepts a UTC Odoo date/datetime string, or null for a system subject's persistent key. Invalid dates, wrong argument types, unknown arguments and invalid metadata fail. Body size, argument binding, authenticated principal scope and write-effect admission remain the normal RPC boundaries. Idempotency-Key is explicitly refused for generation before execution: the generic replay store must never persist a credential response. Other methods retain their existing replay behavior. Management requires base.enable_programmatic_api_keys unless the actual current user belongs to base.group_system. Malformed present configuration fails loudly. The tenant-wide active-key limit and subject lifetime policy apply to replacements as they do to issuance; renewal therefore needs one free slot before revoking the old key. Possession of another user's credential does not confer ownership. A user may revoke their current key; its current request commits and subsequent requests fail. No accepted-credential cache or plaintext key store is introduced. Never log request bodies or credential responses; server responses use `Cache-Control: no-store`. collect_expired(tx, limit) is a core-System-only raw-SQL primitive, with a bound of 1 through 1000 rows. The existing authentication collector invokes one batch per run, under its durable scheduling fence, and reports GcReport.api_keys. A partial expiration index supports selection. Concurrent collectors skip locked rows; rollback makes work available to a later collector. Persistent keys and keys at or after the inclusive database expiry boundary remain untouched. No additional service or per-node accepted-key cache is needed. Product performance evidence is DEFERRED_PERFORMANCE under ADR 0065.

Every key lifecycle change writes a typed event into the transaction's audit row (erp_event.ir_audit_entry), so the event commits or rolls back with the key itself and never needs a hand-written audit statement. The events are built only from ids, closed enums, flags and counts (erp_orm::audit::AuthEvent); no constructor takes a key string, digest, display prefix or key name, so none of them can reach the trail. | Operation | Event | Notes | |---|---|---| | apikey_store::issue (so also apikey_manage::generate) | api_key.issued | key id, owner, creating user, kind, route, expiry, built from the inserted row; allowlist lengths are null for user keys; exactly one event per key | | apikey_manage::revoke | api_key.revoked | cause is self when the transaction's own key is the revoked one, programmatic (naming the revoking key) when another key revoked it, owner for a session without a key actor (an impersonation chain is looked through to the original actor) | | apikey_manage::collect_expired | api_keys.collected | one event per committed batch naming exactly the deleted ids (at most MAX_COLLECTED_KEYS, 1000), row origin auth; an empty batch writes nothing. The collector loops batches until a short one, bounded by its per-run row cap | An operator can also end keys and sessions on the owner connection with erp auth emergency-revoke ([cli.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cli.md#auth-emergency-revoke)). That path writes an emergency.revocation header and one api_key.revoked event per key with cause emergency, in its own cli row, and it works while the runtime role cannot write audit rows; every revocation made through the runtime role still fails when audit is unavailable. See [the audit trail](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/audit.md#emergency-revocation-by-the-owner). A renewal is two operations and therefore two events: generate records the issuance, and the later revoke of the old key records its own event (cause self or programmatic; the renewed cause is reserved for a single-call replacement flow that this slice does not provide). Audited writes need an OperationIdentity on the transaction (RPC and the collector supply one; test harnesses opt in with identify_transactions). If the audit store is not ready or the audit row cannot be written, the operation fails as a whole and the key change rolls back; there is no silent fallback. Collection keeps its cluster-wide exclusion from the existing authentication collector's durable PostgreSQL fence plus FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; the audit event is written in the same batch transaction. Missing functional page: docs/user/api-keys.md (the audit trail reader is separate planned work).

AuthConfig now holds six node admission/execution options, loaded from server [auth] TOML. The actual served constructor and registry rebuilds receive the validated node configuration. The three former session timing builders/getters are removed: use the database's validated AuthSettings::session_policy() snapshot, with SessionPolicy timing getters. Do not construct a node-specific session policy or cache one beyond its config_parameter generation. Database System Parameters (whole seconds, changed by a Settings administrator in Technical → System Parameters): | Key | Default | Minimum | Maximum | |---|---:|---:|---:| | sessions.touch_interval_seconds | 60 | 1 | 3600 | | sessions.rotation_interval_seconds | 10800 | 60 | 86400 | | sessions.rotation_grace_seconds | 120 | 5 | 600 | Touch must be shorter than effective sessions.max_inactivity_seconds; grace must be shorter than rotation. A refusal names both keys and values. Missing, null and empty values restore defaults; clearing or deleting a key also checks the resulting pair. Change the longer interval first when increasing both, or the shorter one first when decreasing both. Node settings (quoted dotted keys in server [auth] TOML, applied after restart): | Key | Default | Minimum | Maximum | |---|---:|---:|---:| | limits.credential_bytes | 1024 | 64 | 4096 | | throttle.login_burst | 20 | 5 | 1000 | | throttle.login_rate_per_sec | 2.0 | 0.1 | 1000 | | throttle.table_entries | 4096 | 64 | 1048576 | | limits.cooldown_hook_deadline_ms | 5000 | 10 | 60000 | | limits.token_plan_hook_deadline_ms | 10000 | 10 | 60000 | Only the refill rate may be fractional. These values bound input before database work, local prefilter memory/work and local hook execution; they may differ across nodes. Shared database cooldown remains authoritative. Wrong types, unknown keys, non-finite rates and out-of-range values stop startup by name, without raw input in diagnostics. Zero never means unlimited. Upgrade: remove startup_limits."session.touch_interval_secs" from every node file before the restart. Use the database touch parameter instead; there is no automatic import. Restart nodes together; mixed-version policy compatibility is not claimed. Restore the previous binary and configuration together if admission fails. Existing auth hooks and hash parameters are unchanged. Standalone Auth callers still supply AuthConfig for local admission; session timing is read from the database even for these callers. Scalar validate_setting checks individual ranges; the base parameter model additionally validates the effective correlated policy under a transaction advisory lock and repeatable-read conflict fence, including create batches, writes, renames, clearing and unlink. Direct SQL bypasses write validation but invalid stored values are refused at startup/reload/touch. Touch loads the four non-secret policy parameters in its update transaction. Normal session checks reuse the existing validated settings cache and generation retry; lifecycle and identity checks use their transaction's policy. This changes touch batch query work; latency and allocation evidence is deferred to milestone end. The grace floor is five seconds so overlapping requests have a positive predecessor window. The database remains authoritative when a node dies.

Native clients without a browser session obtain an rpc-scoped user API key by posting a closed JSON object { "db", "login", "password", "device_name" } (Content-Type: application/json, optional charset=utf-8, body <= 16 KiB, device_name non-empty trimmed and <= 128 bytes) to POST /erp/session/api-key. - **Authentication & cooldowns:** runs non-interactively (interactive = false) through the same Auth::authenticate pipeline, pre-filter, dummy hash, and shared address/login cooldowns as POST /erp/login. Accounts requiring a second factor or pending MFA are refused (403). - **Session & quota hygiene:** authentication, key issuance (IssueRequest::at_policy_maximum, AuditOrigin::Auth, correlated with the HTTP request id), and logout of the temporary browser session run inside one cancellation-safe task. If the client disconnects before issuance, no key is issued and the temporary session is still ended. - **Response & revocation:** returns 200 JSON { "api_key", "expires_at", "uid" } with Cache-Control: no-store and no Set-Cookie. Cross-origin browser requests are refused (403). Clients revoke their own key on logout via res.users.apikeys/revoke.

A binary field keeps file content on a record. An image field is a binary field that accepts pictures only and can store them scaled down. Odoo calls them fields.Binary and fields.Image. The design is ADR 0089 (docs/adr/0089-model-binary-field-and-bytea-column-storage.md); this page describes its column-backed mode: the content is stored in a bytea column of the model's table. Status: the field kinds, the image checks, the image mixin and the company logo fields are delivered by task IMG.FIELD. In views, show a binary field with the image widget (an image_url widget shows a char field that holds a URL). A form sends a chosen picture as base64 inside the record's write, so the request body limit (limits.rpc_body_bytes) bounds it; the widget refuses a larger file and SVG before it reads anything. The Rust examples on this page are not compiled as doctests.
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

pub struct Book { #[field(char, required = true)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, /// any file #[field(binary, string = "Scan")] pub scan: Option<Blob>, /// a picture, stored at most 1024 x 1024 pixels #[field(image, max_width = 1024, max_height = 1024, string = "Cover")] pub cover: Option<Blob>, } - The Rust type is Option<Blob>. Blob (erp_sdk::Blob, in the prelude) is shared, immutable bytes. It dereferences to [u8]; build one with Blob::from(vec). Empty content is no value. - max_width and max_height are pixels. Leave one out, or give 0, and that edge has no bound. A bound is between 16 and 4096; a value outside that range refuses the registry and names the field. An image field with no bound at all checks the picture and stores the bytes as they came. - Both kinds report the field type binary. - The content is not loaded with the other columns of a record. It is read when a caller asks for that field. A binary or image field cannot be indexed, translated or made company-dependent: the registry refuses such a declaration and names the field. A search cannot order by it and a grouped read cannot group by it; both are refused by name (Cannot order by the binary field library.book.cover). A domain can still test whether a value is set (('cover', '!=', False)).

| Surface | Write | Read | |---|---|---| | Typed Rust (Vals, RecordSet::get) | Option<Blob>, Vec<u8> or &[u8] | Option<Blob> | | Dynamic values and RPC | standard padded base64 text; false clears the value | the bytes; base64 text over RPC | - The dynamic write also accepts a map with a content key in base64 (the {filename, content} form of Odoo clients). The file name is not stored. - Text that is not valid base64 is refused with a message that names the model and field (for example library.book.scan) and the defect (here, a length that is not a multiple of four), never the content. - With bin_size true in the context, a read returns the size as text in place of the content (two decimals and a unit out of bytes, Kb, Mb, Gb, Tb, for example 4.88 Kb), and false for an empty value. read, search_read, web_read, web_search_read and web_save answer the same way. The web client reads its views like this: see [Views and bin_size](#views-and-bin-size). - A read that names no fields returns every readable field except binary and image fields.
