Name the field to read its content. - Export writes the content as base64 and import reads base64 back. - An addon built for the WASM ABI 1 cannot read or write these fields: a call that names one is refused, as for the other native kinds.

The web client adds bin_size: true to the record reads of its views: the list and card reads (web_search_read), the form read (web_read) and the answer of a save (web_save). A view therefore never carries file content it does not draw: - A binary field in a view arrives as its size text, or false when it is empty. - The image widget reads the picture it draws itself, with one read of that field without bin_size (addons/web/static/src/client/binary-content.ts). The cells of one list column, or the cards of one page, travel as one request. With options="{'preview_image': 'image_128'}" the widget draws the smaller field and reads the field itself only when the user enlarges (zoom) or downloads the picture. Name the smallest stored size that fits in lists and cards. - Until the picture arrives the widget shows the size; when the view moves on first, the read is cancelled; Download saves through a Blob, shows that it is reading, ignores a second press meanwhile and says when the file was removed; a read that fails leaves the placeholder and says why under the field. A record that is not saved yet has no stored picture to read, and a picture the user just picked is shown from the form itself. - A size is never written back: onchange and web_save leave out a binary field whose value is still the size text, so the stored file stays as it is. A picked file travels as base64, and Clear sends an empty value. - onchange and default_get are called without bin_size; a binary value they set arrives as content. Calls from your own client code are not changed: a read that names a binary field without bin_size in its context answers the content.

Every write of an image field checks the content, from typed Rust and from RPC alike: - **Type.** The content must be PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP. The type is read from the bytes, never from a file name or a declared media type. SVG and other markup is refused for every user. - **Bytes.** The content must not be larger than the system parameter base.image_max_bytes. - **Pixels.** Width times height, read from the file header before any pixel is decoded, must not exceed the system parameter base.image_max_pixels. Every frame of a GIF must lie inside the screen its header declares, so no frame is larger than the checked size. - **Size.** A PNG or JPEG larger than the field's bounds is scaled down to fit them. The aspect ratio is kept and a picture is never enlarged: a 400 x 200 picture in a 128 x 128 field is stored as 128 x 64, and in a 1024 x 1024 field as 400 x 200. - **Encoding.** A PNG or JPEG in a bounded field is decoded, turned upright by its orientation and encoded again in its own format, so the metadata of the uploaded file is not stored. JPEG uses the quality of base.image_jpeg_quality. A JPEG that already fits and carries no metadata is kept as it is. - **GIF and WebP** that fit the field's bounds are stored as they came, so an animation stays whole. A larger one is decoded (its first frame), scaled down to the bounds and stored as a PNG: a bounded field never holds a picture larger than its bounds. An unbounded field keeps every GIF and WebP as it came. - **Colour profile.** The re-encoded picture carries no ICC profile, as in the reference: the colours of a wide-gamut photograph can shift slightly. - **Decoding.** Decoding and scaling run on the server's blocking pool, at most attachments.image_decode_permits pictures at once on a node. A write waits for a free decode and for its result no longer than base.image_decode_timeout_secs; then it fails with an error that names the field and the setting, and nothing is stored. A computed or related image field with bounds must be stored (store = true): the registry refuses bounds on one that is not. A refused picture gives a validation error that names the field and the reason, for example: Invalid image for res.partner.image_1920: the file is not a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP image Invalid image for res.partner.image_1920: SVG and other markup is not accepted; use PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP A picture above the byte or pixel limit is refused the same way and the message names base.image_max_bytes or base.image_max_pixels. When no decode becomes free in time the error is a resource error: res.partner.image_1920: no picture decode became free within 10 s (base.image_decode_timeout_secs; this node decodes 2 pictures at once, attachments.image_decode_permits); try again

A stored related image field with smaller bounds is a stored size of its source. It is filled from the source when the source is written, and cleared when the source is cleared: #[field(image, max_width = 1920, max_height = 1920, string = "Cover")] pub cover: Option<Blob>, /// the cover at most 256 x 256 pixels, stored #[field(image, max_width = 256, max_height = 256, related = "cover", store = true)] pub cover_256: Option<Blob>, The source can be on another record: res.company.logo_web (at most 180 pixels wide, any height) is a stored size of partner_id.image_1920. Lists and cards read the small field, so the server does not scale a large picture on every read.

Addon base ships the abstract model image.mixin (erp_addon_base::ImageMixin), the same set of fields as Odoo's image.mixin: | Field | Bounds | Kind | |---|---|---| | image_1920 | 1920 x 1920 | the picture you write | | image_1024 | 1024 x 1024 | stored size of image_1920 | | image_512 | 512 x 512 | stored size of image_1920 | | image_256 | 256 x 256 | stored size of image_1920 | | image_128 | 128 x 128 | stored size of image_1920 | Inherit it as an Odoo addon writes _inherit = ['image.mixin']: use erp_addon_base::ImageMixin; use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

pub struct Author { #[field(char, required = true)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, } To add the fields to a model of another addon, use `#[extend(TheirModel, addon = "my_addon", inherit = [ImageMixin])]. Write image_1920` only; the four sizes follow. In base, contacts (res.partner) inherit the mixin. In product, products (product.template) inherit it, and a variant shows its template's picture unless it has its own ([Product pictures](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/product.md#product-images)). The company logo res.company.logo is a writable related field of the company contact's image_1920: writing the logo writes the contact's picture. The server never draws a picture: a contact without one reads false, and there is no generated avatar.

The limits are declared technical parameters of base (ADR 0227), edited in **Technical → System Parameters**. A missing or empty value is the default. A value outside the range is refused by name on write, and a stored value outside the range refuses the write of a picture. Zero never means unlimited. | Parameter | Meaning | Default | Floor | Hard bound | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | base.image_max_pixels | the most pixels (width x height) an image field accepts | 40,000,000 | 1,000,000 | 100,000,000 | | base.image_max_bytes | the most bytes of a picture an image field accepts | 10,485,760 | 65,536 | 134,217,728 | | base.image_jpeg_quality | the quality of a JPEG the server encodes | 95 | 1 | 100 | | base.image_decode_timeout_secs | how long a write waits for a free decode and its result, in seconds | 10 | 1 | 120 | The default byte limit is the most a report prints for one picture (its image_bytes limit), so a stored logo always prints. A higher value is allowed; a picture above 10 MiB is then stored but a report that prints it stops with its image_bytes limit. The number of decodes a node runs at once is node configuration, in the [attachments] table of the server configuration file, read at start: | Key | Meaning | Default | Floor | Hard bound | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | attachments.image_decode_permits | picture decodes one node runs at once | 2 | 1 | 64 | The limits are read once per transaction, on the first admission of a picture (create, write, onchange, new(), defaults, upsert and the stored sizes a flush computes). An onchange admits the pictures the form sends. The pictures the edited record already holds in the database start its draft as they are stored: they were admitted when they were saved, are not decoded again on every onchange, and a picture saved under an earlier, wider limit does not stop the form from changing other fields. In Rust the names and bounds are in erp_sdk::image (ImagePolicy::PARAMETERS, DecodePool), next to probe, which returns the format and header size of image content.

- Storage is the column-backed mode of ADR 0089 only. The attachment-backed mode of that ADR (content in the blob store, read as a handle, upload ids instead of base64) is not built yet. - The node rule of ADR 0089 B9 (a pixel cap derived from process.memory_soft_bytes and the permits) is not built: the pixel limit is base.image_max_pixels alone. - bin_size asks the database for the length (octet_length) when the transaction holds no value for the records; a value already in the transaction is sized from it. A stored file named in such a read is not fetched, for any user: the record checks are decided without its column. A computed picture is still computed to be sized, so its sources are read. - A draft (new) record keeps a picture as it was given; the checks and the scaling run when the record is created or written. - The image limits are read from the system parameters by create and write. A recompute of a stored size that runs in a transaction which wrote no picture uses the declared defaults; its source was already checked when it was written.

base supplies res.partner with name, email, active and optional company, and the nullable res.users.partner_id relation. New administrator activation must create a real contact and link it in the same ORM transaction; base seed files contain no credentials or active default administrator. The nullable field preserves old user rows. User/contact field delegation is not implemented by this minimum foundation. The real base manifest loads groups before capabilities and loads the main company after currencies. Native policy identifiers are base.group_user, base.group_user_regular, base.group_portal, base.group_public, base.group_erp_manager, base.default_user_group and base.group_system. The initial company is base.main_company, referencing base.USD. Group/company seed records are noupdate for normal upgrades; explicit reinitialization retains the existing module lifecycle contract. No public/portal permission is supplied. Configuration administration is limited to the listed base models in addons/base/security/ir.access.csv; internal access is read-only for selected metadata and allowed companies. An addon grants its own model rights through its security data, never through an unconditional ORM bypass. Raw parameter/session/audit write access is not granted by these seeds. Effective authenticated access is an integration acceptance requirement, not implied by loading the seed rows successfully.

Status: implemented. You can declare a capability, map it to groups (the ir_capability table) and check it with Transaction::has_capability. The design is in ADR 0035 decision 7 and docs/design/m3-access-engine.md §2.1. Some checks are not about records but about *who may do an admin action*: switching to another user, explaining another user's access, approving above a limit. Odoo writes these as hard-coded group checks (user.has_group('base.group_system')). In ERPForAll you give the check a **name**, a capability. A database then decides which groups hold it, and you can change that later without touching code (fine-grained admin roles are planned for M7).

Declare a capability once, at the top level of your addon crate, with erp_sdk::capability!: erp_sdk::capability!( /// Approve sale orders above the company's approval limit. pub APPROVE_ABOVE_LIMIT = "my_sale.approve_above_limit" ); fn main() { assert_eq!(APPROVE_ABOVE_LIMIT.name(), "my_sale.approve_above_limit"); } - The name has dot-separated parts made of lowercase ASCII letters, digits and _, and is at most 64 bytes long. Start it with your addon's name, so two addons never pick the same name. - The macro makes a static of type erp_sdk::Capability and registers it at link time. There is no other way to make a Capability value, so a check can only name a declared capability. - The server checks every linked capability when it builds the ORM of a database. A malformed name, or the same name declared twice (in your addon or in another one), stops it with an error that names both declarations: capability 'my_sale.approve_above_limit' is declared twice (in erp_addon_my_sale and in erp_addon_other).

The ir.capability model has one row per capability: its name and a groups text in the same syntax as a field's groups ([field-access.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/field-access.md#what-a-groups-text-means)): base.group_system, a.x,b.y (any of them), a.x,!b.y. base ships rows for its own capabilities, for example principal.impersonate; an addon ships its rows in its data files. principal.impersonate is the one the engine asks itself: a with_user switch to another user by a principal that is not System is admitted only when that principal's own user holds it (ADR 0164 A4, SPEC-PRIN-029; see [models.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md), environments). erp-security declares it (erp_security::principal::PRINCIPAL_IMPERSONATE) and the binary names it to the ORM with OrmBuilder::impersonate_capability; an ORM built without it refuses every such switch.

use erp_sdk::prelude::*; erp_sdk::capability!(pub APPROVE = "capability_guide.approve"); async fn approve(tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<()> { let env = tx.env(); if !tx.has_capability(&env, &APPROVE).await? { return Err(Error::access("You may not approve.")); } Ok(()) }

- The answer is about the user the environment is for. Superuser mode (sudo()) and elevation blocks never grant a capability. - It costs no statement for the transaction's own user. - A capability linked into the server but missing its row is an error when the policy is built (the build report lists it), and so is checking it: a check never quietly answers "no". The same for a row whose group text names a group that does not exist: the check fails with an AccessError that names the text, and the report lists it. - A row naming no linked capability (an uninstalled addon's) grants nothing and is reported as a warning.
The erp CLI tool provides developer utilities for scaffolding new addons, managing module installation, upgrade, and uninstallation, and running the local development environment.
The CLI is compiled as part of the ERPForAll workspace: cargo build -p erp-cli --bin erp

The erp scaffold command creates a complete addon skeleton conforming to the ERPForAll addon architecture (ADR 0001, ADR 0005, ADR 0009). Scaffolding generates files atomically into a temporary directory sibling, guaranteeing that failures leave no partial trees on disk. Destination paths that are symlinks, existing files, or non-empty directories are strictly refused.

By default, erp scaffold generates a compiled Rust addon crate: erp scaffold my_addon --summary "My custom sales module" --author "Your Name" This creates the following directory layout under ./addons/my_addon: my_addon/ ├── Cargo.toml               # Addon crate depending on erp-sdk ├── manifest.toml            # Strict TOML manifest ├── src/ │   ├── lib.rs               # Library root with erp_sdk::addon! declaration │   └── models.rs            # Models declared with #[model] ├── views/ │   └── my_addon_views.xml   # Form and list view architectures (<erp> root) ├── data/ │   └── my_addon_data.xml    # Initial seed data (<erp> root) └── tests/ └── test_my_addon.rs     # Integration test suite The generated Cargo.toml explicitly sets edition = "2024", license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0", and depends directly on erp-sdk = "0.1". src/lib.rs registers the addon via erp_sdk::addon!(name = "my_addon", depends = ["base"]);. src/models.rs imports erp_sdk::prelude::* and provides a model declaration template using #[model]. Summary and module name attributes are escaped so that quotes or non-ASCII characters never break the generated crate.

The generated Cargo.toml references erp-sdk = "0.1", which is the intended published crate name on crates.io once ERPForAll reaches release. Until erp-sdk is published: - **In-tree / CI tests (test_scaffold_build_cargo_check)**: Tests patch Cargo.toml with a local workspace path dependency (erp-sdk = { path = "../../crates/erp-sdk" }) and copy the workspace's [patch.crates-io] entries (absolute paths) before invoking cargo check --offline. Required registry crates must already be available in Cargo's local cache; a missing crate fails the test with Cargo's offline resolution error. - **External developers outside the repository**: To build a scaffolded addon outside the main repository, adjust Cargo.toml to point to the local checkout path or git repository: [dependencies] erp-sdk = { path = "/path/to/ERPForAll/crates/erp-sdk" } # or via git dependency: # erp-sdk = { git = "https://github.com/IndoERP/ERPForAll.git" } # Required in both cases: ERPForAll builds against vendored, patched copies of two crates # (vendor/README.md), and Cargo applies [patch] only from the top-level workspace, never from a # dependency. Copy the [patch.crates-io] entries of ERPForAll's Cargo.toml with paths into your # checkout; without the tokio-postgres entry erp-orm does not compile (ADR 0055). [patch.crates-io] hyper = { path = "/path/to/ERPForAll/vendor/hyper" } tokio-postgres = { path = "/path/to/ERPForAll/vendor/tokio-postgres" } The generated manifest.toml is pre-configured with: - Valid technical module name my_addon matching ^[a-zA-Z0-9_]{1,256}$. - Initial version 1.0.0 (semver compatible per ADR 0009 §5). - License set to MIT OR Apache-2.0. - Core dependency depends = ["base"]. - Declared data and view files that exist on disk.

To create a data-only addon without a Cargo.toml or Rust code (ADR 0001, ADR 0009 §1), use the --data-only flag: erp scaffold custom_tags --data-only --summary "Declarative tags for partner records" This creates: custom_tags/ ├── manifest.toml            # Addon manifest ├── views/ │   └── custom_tags_views.xml └── data/ └── custom_tags_data.xml Data-only addons declare views and data in XML/CSV per ADR 0019, requiring no Rust compilation step.

The erp module command coordinates module lifecycle operations against a target PostgreSQL database. Without --dry-run it runs the operation through the module system (ADR 0022): one transaction per operation, as the superuser, with the same rules as button_immediate_install, button_immediate_upgrade and button_immediate_uninstall. Live runs need: - **DATABASE_URL** in the environment (URL or key=value form) for the credentials. The database is the one named by -d; the database in the URL is ignored. Credentials never come from the command line, and error messages never echo the connection string. Use the role that owns the database (it may create the trusted extensions the modules need), not a PostgreSQL superuser: module operations run hooks and data loaders as that role, and a superuser would give them rights they do not need. - A database the module system already initialized (it lists the addons, installs base). On an empty database the command fails with Database <name> not initialized and exit code 1; it never initializes a database for you. - Addons the erp binary can load: data-only addons (manifest, models in models/*.toml, data files). A manifest that names a hook (pre_init_hook and the like) needs the hook implementation linked into the binary; until you build a binary that links your addon, a hook-carrying addon is refused with no #[hook] implementation of it is linked. export DATABASE_URL="postgres://erp@db.internal/postgres" erp module install -d production_db sale --addons-path ./addons prints what the operation did: Install completed: installed: base_setup, sale post-commit steps run: 0 The first line of work is a plain load of the database (it also finishes an operation a crashed run left pending); the operation follows.

| Code | Meaning | |---|---| | 0 | Done. | | 1 | The request was refused: unknown module, module not installed (upgrade), incompatible modules, protected module (base), uninitialized database, missing DATABASE_URL, invalid arguments, unresolvable dependencies. Nothing changed. | | 2 | System error: database or I/O failure, broken invariant. | | 3 | The database is busy: another module operation runs, or a lock or statement timeout hit. Run it again later. Nothing changed. | | 4 | A step of the operation failed (hook, schema update, init(), data file, purge) and the operation was rolled back; the message names the module, the step and the cause. Nothing persists. | | 5 | The operation committed, but its post-commit phase (index builds and the like) did not finish: the report lists the failed steps; they run again after the next module operation. |

erp module install -d production_db sale account --addons-path ./addons --dry-run Options: - -d, --database <DB>: Target PostgreSQL database name (required, 1..=63 ASCII alphanumeric or underscore characters). - --addons-path <PATHS>: Comma-separated paths containing addon directories [default: ./addons]. - --dry-run: Compute and display the resolved topological load order without applying database changes. Needs no connection. - --with-demo / --without-demo: the demo data choice. Without either, the install follows the choice the database was initialized with. --with-demo on a database without demo data first loads the demo data of every installed addon (as "Load demo data" in the browser does; it cannot be undone), then installs. --without-demo on a database with demo data is refused: demo data cannot be switched off. Upgrade and uninstall refuse both options. A live install marks the named modules and their uninstalled dependencies, then the auto_install modules their installation triggers; the report lists every module installed, in order.

erp module upgrade -d production_db sale --addons-path ./addons Upgrades the named installed modules and, as in Odoo, the installed modules that depend on them. A module that is not installed is refused (exit 1). Without a database, --dry-run has no module states to inspect: the plan conservatively marks dependencies of upgraded modules ToInstall.

erp module uninstall -d production_db sale --addons-path ./addons Uninstalling cascades to the installed modules that depend on the named ones (Odoo's behavior); the report lists everything removed, so read it. Modules base, rpc and web cannot be uninstalled. A module whose records would be orphaned (records in models that stay installed) is refused until the data loader's purge handles them. --dry-run has no database state: it conservatively refuses an uninstall when another addon *on disk* depends on the target.

Upgrade and uninstall require an installed per-addon content receipt matching the admitted files. An unknown receipt refuses with identity unknown, run identity-enroll first; unchanged manifest versions do not approve changed bytes. Install creates a receipt atomically and uninstall removes it atomically. These rules also apply to protected/native addons; there is no legacy addon-name exemption. After reviewing an existing database's artifact provenance, the operator explicitly enrolls its installed addons using the protected server configuration and owner connection: erp module identity-enroll --config /protected/server.toml \ --operator operator@example.test --note "Reviewed installed release provenance" base acceptance_notes Unlike ordinary module commands, this administration command takes the target and owner connection from --config; it does not take -d or --addons-path. Keep the configuration and owner credentials outside git and readable only by the operator. Enrollment requires between one and 64 unique installed addon names, an operator identity of one to 256 bytes and a reason of one to 4096 bytes. Identity and audit changes commit together; the audit records operator, timestamp, note and per-addon hashes. Enrollment is deliberate recovery authority, never a routine retry for a mismatched or unknown file. For the first identity-aware release over a legacy prepared release, use the candidate binary with `identity-enroll --config /protected/server.toml --legacy-release /path/to/old-release --installed --operator operator@example.test --note "Reviewed installed old release"`. --installed and --legacy-release are paired and replace explicit addon names. This explicit bootstrap hashes the old release's installed addon files, including files changed in the candidate, and records an atomic audit. It refuses an identity-aware previous release and a conflicting existing receipt. The ordinary enrollment command retains its native artifact attestation rules. Rehearse enrollment and forward upgrade on an isolated clone before performing the same steps on the target database; investigate any uncertain commit before retrying. A forward upgrade must select every installed addon whose candidate content differs from its installed receipt; omitting a changed addon refuses during lifecycle admission before upgrade effects or publication. identity-activate is the release helper's internal publication command. It validates the explicit candidate and previous release receipts and a protected successful forward migration receipt; the candidate must already be active. After successful migration, switch and health, one lifecycle transaction retains unchanged identities and transitions changed ones. Runtime upgrade does not re-stamp. Automatic restore and manual rollback never re-stamp. If publication fails or its commit outcome is uncertain, inspect and reconcile the release and database state before another lifecycle operation; a failed command is not proof the transaction rolled back. Per-addon file identity is separate from the node configuration/build digest and from database schema compatibility. File-content identity authorizes lifecycle operations on addon artifacts; it is not a database schema-version check (that admission check is planned). See [the lifecycle engine guide](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/human-lifecycle-engine.md) for the integration and recovery boundaries. Deployment operators should follow their protected release runbook.

Module operations perform strict validation before making any changes: 1. All technical module names are validated at CLI argument parsing time. 2. Database names are validated against identifier constraints. 3. Database connection credentials come exclusively from the DATABASE_URL environment variable, never from command-line arguments (argv). 4. An AddonIndex scans the configured search paths. 5. Transitive dependencies are computed and ordered using ModuleGraph in LoadMode::Update. 6. If any dependency is missing or a dependency cycle is detected, the command fails loudly with exit code 1 and displays the cycle members or missing dependency. 7. In --dry-run mode, the plan is returned without calling any database executor. 8. A live run asks the module system, which checks the plan against the database's own module states.

The erp dev command validates configuration and discovers addons: erp dev -d dev_db --addons-path ./addons --port 8069 > [!NOTE] > The development server HTTP runtime and live reload are scheduled for M3 (erp-server). Running erp dev currently validates the configuration and addon paths and fails loudly naming M3. With -d, erp dev first registers in that database as a **dev node** (ADR 0057). When live non-dev nodes already serve the database it refuses with exit code 1 and names them (`erp dev refuses to join a database served by live non-dev nodes: app-1 (host h1, pid 4242, app)`), so a development process never joins a production cluster: use a development database. Until the HTTP server exists, the dev node leaves again at once.

Every server process registers a row in its database and keeps it alive with a heartbeat (ADR 0057, spec docs/specs/node-registry.md). A node becomes ready only when its configuration, build and addons match the nodes that are already ready; otherwise it stays unready and says what differs. These commands connect with the DATABASE_URL role (the database owner) to the database named by -d: erp cluster nodes -d prod                     # one line per node: name, role, state, fresh, host, pid, build, digest, lease end, id erp cluster rollout open -d prod --to <digest> --for 30m   # let <digest> become ready next to the current one erp cluster rollout status -d prod erp cluster rollout close -d prod - A rolling upgrade opens a window from the running digest (--from; when omitted, the one digest the ready nodes run) to the new one (--to, the 64-hex digest the new node prints in its unready reason). Opening a window closes the one that was open. While the window is open, exactly those two digests may be ready side by side; when it ends or is closed, newcomers must match again. - --for takes <n>s, <n>m or <n>h, from 1 minute to 24 hours. A rollback is a window with --from and --to swapped. - Malformed digests and durations exit with code 1 before any connection. A refused window (the duration is out of bounds, --from equals --to, or --from is omitted while no node or nodes of several digests are ready) exits with code 1; a missing node table or a database fault exits with code 2.

Two commands read and repair the access policy of a database, as the System principal (ADR 0035). The connection credentials come from DATABASE_URL (URL or key=value form, never echoed), the database from -d: DATABASE_URL="postgres://erp@db.internal/postgres" erp access report -d prod report prints the policy generation and the build report of compiling the database's rules: counts, every rule that cannot be compiled (it denies the operations it covers), capabilities declared in the binary without an ir_capability row (asking for them fails), rows naming no declared capability, and group implication cycles. erp access disable-rule -d prod sale.sale_order_rule_portal disable-rule sets active = false on the rule with that external id, through the ORM (audit fields written, the policy change recorded for every process), and prints access rule <id> '<name>' on <model> disabled, or ... was already disabled when it was. An unknown external id, or one naming a record of another model, exits with code 1. ir.access itself is governed by permissions only, so this always works for an administrator. > [!NOTE] > The registry is composed from the addons linked into the erp binary (base and the external-id > model); composing the registry of a given database (its installed modules and custom fields) > comes with the HTTP server (planned).

erp db build-object -d prod --model booking.booking --object _no_double_booking \ [--lock-timeout <secs>] [--build-timeout <secs>] Builds an exclusion constraint or WITHOUT OVERLAPS key on a table above large_table_rows, where the install refuses it (the build holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the table: run it in a maintenance window). Credentials come from DATABASE_URL, as for erp access. - --lock-timeout is 1 to 3600 seconds (default 30). While the build waits for its ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, every new reader and writer of the table queues behind it, so choose a short timeout on a busy table. - --build-timeout is 60 to 86400 seconds (default 21600, six hours) and must be longer than the lock timeout. A statement that runs past it is stopped, nothing is changed, and the message names the object, the table and the limit. Prints a report with the statements that ran, or says the object is already present; exit code 1 for an unknown model or object, conflicting rows or a lock timeout. Details: docs/addon-guide/exclusions.md.

erp db init --config server.toml --admin-login admin --admin-password-file /private/admin-password [--with-demo | --without-demo] Installs base and web into the empty database of the configuration and creates the administrator from the login and the mode-600 password file; no default credential exists. --with-demo makes it a demo database: base gets demo data and every addon installed later gets its own ([demo data](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/demo-data.md)). The default is --without-demo. The choice is stored on the database; on an initialized database the other choice is refused.

erp db dump       --config server.toml -d erpforall      --file /backups/erpforall.dump [--force-live] erp db restore    --config server.toml -d erpforall_copy --file /backups/erpforall.dump [--replace] [--force-live] erp db neutralize --config server.toml -d erpforall_copy --password-file /private/throwaway [--physical-copy] [--unrecorded-identity] [--force-live] erp db drop       --config server.toml -d erpforall_copy [--force-live] Each command acts on the one database named by -d. It connects with the owner connection of the deployment configuration (the same file as erp server --config); the configuration's own database is not used, so one configuration serves for the database and its copies. Nothing these commands print contains a connection URL or a password, also not in an error. - **A live database is refused.** When a node of the database is running (its row in the node registry is not stopped and its lease has not expired), the command refuses and names the database and the nodes. Stop the server first. --force-live acts anyway; a drop then also ends the open sessions. - **dump** writes the PostgreSQL custom archive format to a new file created with mode 600. It never replaces a file; a failed dump removes what it wrote. Attachment content in the attachment store is not part of the archive. - **restore** first reads the archive's table of contents; a file that is not an archive, or one this pg_restore cannot read, is refused and nothing changes. It then restores the archive into a new temporary database <name>_erp_restore (created like every ERPForAll database: from template0, encoding UTF8, collation C) and gives it the target name only when the restore succeeded. An existing database is refused unless --replace. After the archive restored (and the live check on the existing database passed again), the existing database is renamed to <name>_erp_replaced, the restored one takes the target name, and only then is the replaced one dropped; if the second rename fails, the existing database gets its name back. A bad archive therefore never costs you the existing database: a restore that fails drops the temporary database and leaves the existing one untouched. The name can have at most 50 bytes, so that both reserved names fit. When a database already exists under <name>_erp_restore or <name>_erp_replaced, the restore refuses and names it: a restore stopped before it finished, or one is running now. If none is running, drop the temporary one, and either drop the replaced one or rename it back to the target name, then restore again. When the target name itself is missing, the replaced database is the only copy of the original: the refusal tells you to rename it back to the target name, never to drop it. A failure message says what happened to the existing database: left untouched, its sessions ended by --force-live, or renamed away and back. Owners and grants of the source are not restored: the owner role of the configuration owns everything, so run erp db publish-grants with a configuration of the restored database before serving it. When an installed addon declares a SECURITY DEFINER function, publish-grants refuses it after a restore (its owner is then the owner role, not the definer role); no addon declares one yet. - **drop** removes the database. The attachment store, roles and other files of a deployment are not touched. - dump and restore run pg_dump and pg_restore (PostgreSQL 18 client programs, at least the server's version). --pg-bin <dir> or the environment variable ERP_PG_BIN names their directory; without it they are looked up on PATH. A program that fails is reported with its own error and a pointer to these two settings (an older client than the server is the usual cause). The credential reaches them through their environment, never their argument list, and no PG* variable of your shell reaches them. - postgres, template0 and template1 are refused. erp db neutralize makes a copy safe to test on, in one transaction, and can be repeated: | What | Why | |---|---| | Scheduled actions switched off | they would run the copy's business logic as if it were the original | | Every job held, except the job queue's own clean-up of old dead letters and run history | scheduled messages and attachment store jobs must not act from a copy; the attachment store may be shared with the original | | Sessions removed | they were issued by the original | | API keys removed | integrations of the original must not reach the copy | | Login throttle rows cleared | they are keyed with the database secret that is replaced | | Every password replaced by the throwaway password | nobody's real password is kept in a copy; testers sign in with the throwaway one | | Database secret replaced | a copy never shares the signing secret of the original | | database.neutralized = true | marks the database as a neutralized copy for you and your tools; nothing reads it yet, so a held job or a scheduled action can still be started again by hand | neutralize refuses the database a copy was made from. A database records its physical identity (cluster and database number) the first time its attachment ownership work runs (the owner heartbeat, for example); a restored copy has another database number. When the recorded identity is the database's own, the command refuses and changes nothing. A physical copy of the whole cluster (a base backup or a volume snapshot) carries the original's identity: pass --physical-copy for it. A database without a recorded identity cannot be told from the original it may have been copied from, so the command refuses it too and says so. Pass --unrecorded-identity only when you know the database is a copy; the command then prints a line saying the identity check was skipped. The throwaway password is read from a mode-600 regular file (--password-file, at least 12 bytes) and is never printed. Users without a password stay without one. The table is the whole list: an addon cannot add a neutralize step of its own yet, and outgoing mail servers are not part of the list.

- 0: Success (including --help and --version). - 1: User, argument, and validation errors (including invalid database identifier syntax -d, invalid module names, missing modules, dependency resolution failures, or invalid input values). Both CLI argument parsing of an invalid -d and programmatic validation via DatabaseName consistently exit with code 1. - 2: Command-line usage errors (unknown flags, missing required arguments such as omitted -d), system I/O errors, or unimplemented runtime/execution errors.

Start the linked native application with one explicit deployment configuration: erp server --config /private/deployment/server.toml The command uses the existing application listener, registry and authentication services. It registers an application node and checks its build, addon and shared-setting identity before admitting work. Use prepared runtime addon trees; package-manager links and build caches are not runtime artifacts. Probe GET /erp/health/ready and require HTTP 200 before routing application traffic. A listener accepting connections does not establish readiness. See [server lifecycle](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/server-lifecycle.md). The configuration is strict TOML: unknown keys and invalid supplied values are refused. Relative file and addon paths resolve from the configuration file's directory. Each connection URL and proxy token is read from a private, mode-600 regular file; symlinks and insecure secret files are refused. Keep those files outside version control. This direct-access example binds only to loopback: database = 'erpforall' database_url_file = '/private/deployment/request-url' owner_database_url_file = '/private/deployment/owner-url' node_database_url_file = '/private/deployment/node-url' node_name = 'app-1' shutdown_deadline_secs = 45 bind = '127.0.0.1:8069' public_origin = 'http://127.0.0.1:8069' proxy_mode = 'direct' addons_path = ['/srv/erp/addons'] assets_manifest = '/srv/erp/assets/manifest.json' [startup_limits] 'http.max_connections' = 8192 'process.memory_soft_bytes' = 4294967296 database is a nonempty ASCII alphanumeric/underscore name of at most 63 bytes. The request, owner and node connections target that same database and endpoint, with distinct roles. A serving command requires node_database_url_file; it is optional only for configuration consumers such as database initialization. The node name defaults to erp-server and accepts one to 63 ASCII alphanumeric, dot, underscore or hyphen bytes. The shutdown deadline defaults to 45 seconds and accepts 5 to 3600 seconds; HTTP drain, node departure and runtime shutdown use the remaining absolute budget. For an external HTTPS service, use proxy_mode = 'authenticated', an HTTPS public_origin, a trusted_proxies list of allowed peer IP addresses, and proxy_token_file pointing to a protected shared token. Direct mode requires a loopback bind and refuses proxy peers/token configuration. Configure the proxy to supply one actual client IP in X-Forwarded-For; without it, the peer IP becomes the throttle address and users behind that proxy share its address bucket. The canonical public origin is shared across replicas even when their bind addresses differ. The live HTTP/1 connection timers use the optional top-level keys http_header_deadline_secs (default 5, range 1–60), http_keep_alive_idle_secs (default 30, range 5–600), and http_max_connection_age_secs (default 120, range 10–3600). They require header deadline < idle limit < maximum age. The separately validated [startup_limits] keys http.header_read_secs and http.keepalive_idle_secs currently do not override these live timers; their aliasing is pending. [startup_limits] accepts quoted dotted keys with integer values. Missing values use the defaults below; wrong types, unknown keys, out-of-range values and incompatible byte budgets refuse startup. These are admission settings, not a claim that pending websocket, streaming, cache or cancellation facilities are implemented or that actual memory use has been measured. http.max_connections is live: it caps concurrent HTTP connections. Give the process a descriptor limit (ulimit -n, systemd LimitNOFILE) above that cap plus the database pools and open files. When accept() still runs out of descriptors, socket buffers or memory, the server stops taking new connections for 100 ms at a time, so existing connections can finish, and logs one warning when the episode starts and one when it ends; it does not exit. A handshake the peer aborted, or a pending network error of the new connection (Linux accept(2) retry list), is skipped. Any other listener error stops the server. | Keys | Defaults | |---|---| | http.max_connections, http.keepalive_idle_secs, http.header_read_secs, http.body_read_secs | 8192 connections; 60, 10 and 30 seconds | | http.body_min_bytes_per_sec, http.response_min_bytes_per_sec | 8192 and 16384 bytes/s | | db.cancel_concurrency, limits.header_bytes, limits.header_count | 4; 16384 bytes; 100 | | admission.inflight_bytes, admission.ws_inflight_bytes | 536870912 and 67108864 bytes | | buffers.thread_cache_bytes, assets.memory_bytes, rpc.spec_cache_bytes | 4194304, 268435456 and 16777216 bytes | | limits.rate_table_entries, session.touch_queue_entries | 65536 entries each | | ws.read_buffer_bytes, ws.message_read_secs, ws.min_bytes_per_sec, ws.max_message_bytes | 4096 bytes; 30 seconds; 8192 bytes/s; 1048576 bytes | | limits.rpc_body_bytes, limits.rpc_result_bytes, process.memory_soft_bytes | 2097152, 16777216 and 4294967296 bytes | Session timing is database policy under ADR 0200; remove the retired startup touch key before restarting. The [authentication configuration table](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/auth.md#authentication-configuration) lists all database timing and node [auth] settings with defaults and bounds. Inflight capacity must cover twice the maximum RPC body, the maximum result and the websocket share; the websocket share must cover a maximum message. Inflight capacity and the checked configured reservation sum, including the actual hashing pool, must fit the process soft cap. The hashing pool must fit one quarter of that cap. The cap must fit reported physical host RAM. The current check uses host RAM rather than a container's cgroup limit; the default cap refuses a host with less than 4 GiB. Choose an explicit compatible cap and reservation configuration for smaller deployments. A passing startup check is not performance acceptance.

erp audit maintain --config /private/deployment/server.toml Runs as the owner role. It installs the audit table erp_event.ir_audit_entry when it is missing, checks an existing one against its fixed definition (it never adopts or repairs a table of another shape) and creates the missing daily partitions of the window (today plus 31 UTC days). It is idempotent and changes no grants; every erp db publish-grants does the same and then grants the request role its insert-only rights. When the event outbox table erp_event.ir_event_outbox is installed, the command also creates its missing daily partitions (today plus 7 UTC days); when it is not installed the output says so and nothing else happens. The output names both tables. The server keeps both windows itself: it runs the same partition upkeep at every start and then once an hour on every node, so this command is for repairs and for an immediate refresh. When another session holds the outbox table's lock longer than the partition lock timeout, the command stops with an error that says so; run it again. See [the audit trail](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/audit.md).

erp auth emergency-revoke --config /private/deployment/server.toml --reason compromised --key 41 42 erp auth emergency-revoke --config /private/deployment/server.toml --reason lost --session 0193f2c4-8a1e-7b3d-9c2a-5e6f70819a2b erp auth emergency-revoke --config /private/deployment/server.toml --reason offboarding --user 17 --keys --sessions Use it when a credential must end now and the normal path cannot do it: the runtime role cannot write audit rows (its insert right was revoked), or a person or service has to lose its keys and sessions at once. Ordinary revocation (the key's own revoke, a logout, the devices page) stays the normal way; it commits with its audit row and fails when the audit store is unavailable. The command ends the keys and sessions that exist when it runs. It does not archive the user, reset the password or block a later login or a new key. To cut a person off, the operator also archives the user or resets the password. A key issued for the user while the command runs waits for it on the user's row: it is either deleted by the run or issued after it commits. The command runs on the owner connection of the configuration (owner_database_url_file) as the core System principal. It writes its own audit row in the same transaction as the deletions, so there is no unaudited revocation. | Option | Meaning | |---|---| | --config FILE | Deployment configuration; its owner connection is used. Required. | | --reason REASON | Why: one of compromised, lost, offboarding, incident. Closed list; recorded in the audit row. Required. | | --key ID... | API key ids, at most 500 per run. Every id must exist. | | --session UUID... | Session ids, at most 500 per run. Every id must exist. | | --user UID with --keys, --sessions or both | All keys (500 per transaction, each its own audit row) and/or all sessions of one user. | Give exactly one of --key, --session and --user. The command never takes a key secret, a key prefix or a key name. Its output lists ids and counts only. A user with nothing to revoke is a success: it prints 0 revoked and writes no row. It refuses before any deletion when: - the connected role does not own res_users_apikeys, erp_session and erp_event.ir_audit_entry. The message names the first table it does not own and says that emergency revocation runs only on the owner connection. A superuser that is not the owner is refused too; - the audit store cannot take the row on the owner connection: the table is missing, has another shape or has no partition day left. The message names the state and erp audit maintain; run that first. The command does not install partitions itself; - a named key, session or user does not exist. The message lists the missing ids and nothing is revoked. Exit codes: 0 success (including 0 revoked); 1 the request was refused (wrong owner role, unknown id, bad argument value); 2 a failure (the audit store cannot take the row, a database error, a usage error such as a missing option). A later chunk of --user --keys that fails leaves the earlier chunks revoked and audited; the error says how many were committed. If the connection drops during a commit, the message says the outcome is unknown: check the keys and sessions before you run the command again. Session-end hooks run in the same transaction on the owner connection, but only the hooks linked into the erp binary. When installed addons exist beyond the ones the CLI links, the output says so (decision D6 of ADR 0151). The owner role can rewrite its own audit rows. The row this command writes is evidence for the operator and for the audit reader; it does not defend against a hostile owner. Keep the owner credential to the people who may run this command. See [the audit trail](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/audit.md#emergency-revocation-by-the-owner).

A native deployment uses separate owner and runtime roles. CLI module operations use DATABASE_URL as owner and do not know the deployed runtime identity. After a successful install or upgrade, use the candidate binary with the protected deployment configuration: erp db publish-grants --config /private/deployment/server.toml Run the release's schema/module upgrade before publication, then publish grants before starting or activating the candidate server. Publication does not create missing node or authentication collector tables. The command reads owner/request credentials from the configuration's protected files, publishes the same grants as native initialization/browser install, and verifies the server's schema, table and sequence privilege check as the request role. It preserves the restricted signal, post-commit and installation-audit privileges. The request role receives SELECT and UPDATE on the durable erp_auth_gc_state singleton, while INSERT, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER privileges are revoked. Collection needs no table ownership or CREATE privilege. The request role receives no access to erp_node, erp_node_detail or erp_node_rollout. When node_database_url_file is configured, publication also grants the separate heartbeat role its restricted node-table privileges and schema usage. Publication and server startup refuse any request/heartbeat role membership in either direction, including reachable NOINHERIT/SET/ADMIN paths; a request role with reachable node-table privileges is refused. A heartbeat role with reachable business or authentication table privileges, or the checked administrative role attributes, is also refused. Revoke the offending source of effective access instead of granting either role ownership or broader privileges. Repeated publication is safe. It does not run module hooks, initialize the database or recover pending operations. A busy lifecycle lock returns exit 3; pending recovery, unsafe roles, database errors and failed verification return nonzero. Failed verification after commit explicitly says the grants were committed; fix the runtime connection or finish the concurrent operation and rerun. No success is reported until runtime verification completes. erp db runtime-grant-contract reports this binary's compiled privilege contract as {"version":16,"ui_assets":"read-only","node_features":"execute-only","event_outbox":"insert-only","uom_references":"guarded-monotone","job_queue":"column-grants","audit_trail":"insert-only","attachment_usage":"append-only","audit_reader":"select-only","attachment_owner":"read-only","attachment_pending":"guarded-create","attachment_peer":"read-only","attachment_recovery":"owner-write, progress-read","sql_objects":"exclusive-id-sequences"}. It needs no configuration or database connection, performs no publication, and does not verify an existing database's grants. Version 1 declares only read-only UI assets; version 2 adds execute-only node-feature access; version 5 adds the job queue's column-level grants (ADR 0150). The unmerged historical outbox-only version-2 shape is unsupported. Version 3 combines both guarantees with the dedicated event-schema insert allowlist (ADR 0136). Version 4 adds the UoM permanent-reference grant and admission matrix (ADR 0144). Version 15 added declared SQL-object role bindings. Version 16 also protects explicitly exclusive named id sequences during grant publication, startup and recovery. See [SQL-object database roles](/en/next/developer/installation/sql-object-roles.md). Version 6 adds the insert-only audit trail (ADR 0151): the request role may insert the columns it supplies into erp_event.ir_audit_entry and use its sequence, and nothing else. A release restore or grant reassertion with an older publisher over a version-6 release is refused before any grant is published, because an older publisher revokes the audit insert right and every call that changes data would then fail closed. Version 8 adds isolated reader publication and admission (ADR 0167); restore to an older publisher is likewise refused because it does not implement that contract. Operators restore from backup or move forward. The request role can read markers, update only the fence's singleton column and execute bounded id-only registration. It cannot mutate markers or use their sequences/internal functions. Missing guard infrastructure and leaked effective privileges refuse publication/startup; neither path repairs history. Release recovery probes verified source and target binaries before the target publisher runs. Equal contracts recover normally. Version 3 may recover to version 2: that publisher leaves the erp_event schema untouched. Versions 12 and 13 recover to each other in both directions: version 13 only relabels the attachment recovery capability and both publish the same grants. Recovery from version 2 or 3 to version 1 requires disabled, unapproved login-feature state and its private durable rollback fingerprint before broad grants. Roll-forward validates that fingerprint before and after narrowing. Other unequal recovery contracts, unsupported output and probe failures refuse before target publication or switching. The existing identity-aware-to-legacy refusal also remains. Use ordinary forward activation for upgrades, or explicit operator reconciliation when recovery is refused. By contract declaration (ADR 0136), v2 promises the same node-feature and UI-asset fences as v3; the pinned v2 literal SQL exercises only the node-feature and event halves. --activate refuses, before any publication, a pre-contract candidate over a supported-contract active release and any candidate whose contract is older than the active one (use --rollback for a recorded previous release). From version 4, every older target refuses before publication or switching, including the otherwise allowed v3-to-v2/v1 cases. This applies even without UoM installed. Failed v4 activation can therefore require backup/operator recovery; an attempted recovery does not establish that a previous release is healthy. The translation verification table erp_translated_verified, when present, is owner-only. Publication removes the runtime role's direct grants and verifies its effective privileges, including access inherited from another role or PUBLIC. If access remains, revoke that source and publish again. Run publication as part of upgrading an existing deployment before serving requests; a node refuses publication when its runtime role can still access the table. scripts/human-release.py --activate runs this command using the packaged candidate before switching the active release. Run the schema upgrade first; activation does not migrate the database. A publication failure leaves the active release unchanged and reports a safe child exit code, timeout or spawn failure. Child stdout/stderr remain suppressed. Deploying older binaries without this command requires their historical release procedure; automatic activation with the new script refuses them. Rollback remains the existing explicit --rollback operation.

Tenant bundle hashes and installed-addon static declarations are served from verified resident identity, gzip and Brotli forms. The host supplies one shared AssetStore to release-bundle and tenant publication, using the validated startup_limits.assets.memory_bytes setting. That setting already participates in the configured process reservation. It does not disable limits when zero; startup refuses invalid settings. Admission includes live representation payloads and conservative resident bookkeeping, plus separate owned publication metadata. Identical complete content entries can share across tenant snapshots, while each snapshot pays for its own declarations. Active snapshots, response bodies and detached clones of response header values keep their allowance until their last owner drops. Cache eviction reclaims only idle entries; a detached header can retain its charge after eviction. A candidate that cannot fit fails loudly with asset publication refused: assets.memory_bytes admission limit exceeded. The logical admission charge is not a measured process RSS value. Bounded database decoding and codec scratch are separate transient work; retained-load preflight applies the lower host/hard cap. A rollout can temporarily hold old and new generations. Provide enough allowance for that overlap; otherwise a newly authoritative generation can answer maintenance/503 until an operator adjusts capacity or reduces declared assets through the normal lifecycle. Do not delete manifests, remove admission checks or grant broader database rights to work around the refusal. Read the server log for the failed admission boundary, then retry through the normal startup/publication path. When a running replica refuses to re-admit a newer generation on a request, it logs UI asset re-admission failed; web assets answer 503 with the cause and answers clients only the fixed text "UI assets are unavailable; the operator must check the server log". It remembers that refusal for the same generation and retention list for 30 seconds, so requests in between get the 503 at once instead of repeating the reload. After 30 seconds, or as soon as the published generation changes, one request tries again; this lets the replica recover once older generations drain. /erp/assets/<hash>.* uses private, max-age=31536000, immutable; a declared /<module>/static/... uses exactly no-cache. Available encoded forms are negotiated with Accept-Encoding; ETags identify the actual selected bytes. Conditional GET can answer an empty 304. An unacceptable encoding set gives 406/no-store; malformed negotiation gives 400. The current durable authority query remains: a memory hit never proves tenant authorization or compatible runtime. Unchanged admitted generations do not reload blob payloads. Operator client.<hash>.js/css release manifests remain schema-1 identity-only in this delivery. Release compressed sidecars and the older large-static streaming design remain open scope; there is no directory mount or request-time compression. The source repository records this contract in ADR 0122 and the ASERVE specification. Product performance acceptance is DEFERRED_PERFORMANCE under ADR 0065. Version 7 adds append-only attachment usage, a read-only compacted base and column-limited attachment writes (ADR 0165). An older publisher cannot safely restore over this contract. Apply the authorized base schema upgrade before publishing these grants.

Set audit_reader_database_url_file='audit-reader-url' in the deployment TOML to enable reader connection admission. Store the reader URL in that protected mode-600 file; do not pass it as a CLI argument. Provision a distinct login without SUPERUSER, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION or BYPASSRLS, and without memberships leading to runtime, owner, node or administrative roles. Use erp db publish-grants --config <protected-config> as the owner. It publishes parent-only audit SELECT for the reader, preserving runtime INSERT-only rights, and verifies the actual reader login after the grant transaction commits. Initial administrator activation and native addon lifecycle publication also verify a configured reader. A configured bad credential produces a nonzero failure; startup never falls back to another credential. Repeated publication restores the same intended ACLs. The reader must not inherit PUBLIC TEMPORARY on the database, PUBLIC CREATE on a schema, unrelated table/column/sequence rights or executable application SECURITY DEFINER functions. The operator must reconcile those sources deliberately before publication; the tool does not revoke shared grants for other roles. Parent SELECT covers future partitions without direct partition grants. erp audit maintain continues to refresh partitions; newly created event partitions discard non-owner default ACLs. The exact compiled publisher contract is version 13 with attachment_recovery: owner-write, progress-read, attachment_peer: read-only, attachment_owner: read-only, audit_reader: select-only and audit_trail: insert-only, plus the earlier capabilities. Version 12 added attachment recovery (ADR 0183) under the label owner-only; version 13 grants exactly the same and relabels it, because the owner connection writes the claim and the runtime role reads its progress. Automatic restore to versions 1–11 or a pre-contract binary is refused before grants, login-state changes or pointer switching. Use a compatible candidate or the documented backup/recovery path. No audit reader RPC method or audit-log UI is supplied by role publication alone. Publisher contract version 9 retains the audit reader and accounting capabilities and adds attachment_owner: read-only: request roles read ownership health but cannot mutate identity, pending intents, heartbeat, contest or observation state. Publication refuses a partially installed ownership schema or inherited/PUBLIC write rights. Restoring a pre-v9 publisher requires operator reconciliation before any grant publication; automatic restore/reassert refuses it.

erp attachments probe-store --peer --config <protected-server.toml> --store <key> start --timeout 120 starts a bounded two-host attempt; join <session-uuid> joins from the second host and status reports current durable state. It uses the owner connection and linked raw registry without loading pending module work, running hooks, upgrading addons or starting jobs. The configuration must select a registered shared local store. See the installation attachment-store runbook. Publisher contract version 11 retains every version-10 capability and adds attachment_peer: read-only. The publisher excludes peer evidence from blanket CRUD, requires its schema and checks effective privileges, including PUBLIC and inherited roles. A version-10 or older publisher cannot be restored over this authority. Upgrade base before publishing version-11 grants. Publisher contract 10 additionally declares attachment_pending: guarded-create (ADR 0176). After the base upgrade, request roles may SELECT/INSERT pending guard rows and UPDATE only their generation. Startup rejects missing schema and effective unsafe rights. A pre-10 publisher can restore blanket CRUD on the retained table, so automatic restore/reassert refuses it before effects.

After a native addon operation, erp db publish-grants --config <protected-server.toml> reconciles runtime access against the installed addon set without running hooks or recovering pending operations. Restricted SQL-object tables retain their declared operations; ordinary tables receive CRUD access. An unsafe role or an unresolved declaration refuses publication. If an addon operation already committed, correct the reported cause and retry publication without repeating the addon operation.

docs.title: Client registries, environments, services and patches

sections.text: UI4 BASE API under ADR 0030; implementation and validation evidence is in the slice review report. Register contributions from an addon's exported synchronous register(ctx) callback. The assembler supplies callbacks in the server module load order; importing a module alone must never patch or register anything. UI3 owns connecting that callback list to bundle output. Define each category once with a runtime type guard, then use its typed registry. Guards run on every insertion and forced replacement, including production mode. Addon types extend Registries in @erpforall/elang; service aliases extend Services. Executable examples are in web/tests/extensions.test.ts; final validation evidence is recorded in docs/design/m4-ui4.md. import { RegistryHub } from "@erpforall/elang"; declare module "@erpforall/elang" { interface Registries { badges: { title: string }; } } const registry = new RegistryHub(); const badges = registry.define("badges", (value: unknown): value is { title: string } => typeof value === "object" && value !== null && "title" in value && typeof value.title === "string"); badges.add("my_addon.ready", { title: "Ready" }, { sequence: 20 }); getEntries() and getAll() participate in reactive bindings. Adding/removing an entry updates a mounted consumer without reloading. Returned arrays and entry pairs are copies. The payload is shared: publish a replacement with force: true to notify consumers. Sequences default to 50, forced replacement preserves the previous sequence, and equal sequences retain insertion order. Duplicate keys, missing keys and missing categories have typed ExtensionError codes; `get(key, fallback)` explicitly opts into an optional lookup. An omitted schema is an error. Create one ServiceContainer and createEnv({services}) per mounted application. Register classes with add(Class, alias?), await services.start(env), then pass env to mount. A class declares static dependencies = [OtherService] and a static start(env, dependencies) returning its instance (or a promise). The resolver's get(Class) returns typed dependency instances. A dependency may be used only if declared. Startup validates missing dependencies and cycles before starting anything; independent services start in parallel. Failure rejects with a service-named error and original cause; retry needs a fresh container. In component setup(), useService(Class) returns an instance-shaped facade; useService("alias") is typed through Services. Methods keep the original instance receiver. Declare static asyncMethods = ["read", "save"] (or static readonly asyncMethods = true to inspect every method result) for async protection: pending results and errors stop reaching the component when it is destroyed; later calls reject with service-destroyed. This suppresses delivery and does not abort the service's underlying remote work. The service must own any transport cancellation it needs. Synchronous errors and live async failures propagate to the caller. useEnv() returns the component's environment; Component.env exposes it after construction. useSubEnv({context: ...}) creates a shallow frozen environment inheriting from the current one. The component and descendants see that scope; siblings and other mounted applications retain their own scope. All hooks above require setup. The environment holds services, an EventTarget bus, debug, isSmall and action context; freezing the container does not deeply freeze service instances or other supplied objects. Use ctx.patch(Class, sup => ({ method() { return sup.method.call(this); } })) for instance methods and ctx.patchStatic(Class, factory) for static members. Plain objects are also supported. Override signatures must match the target; augment the target interface first when declaring new members. Constructors and ES class fields cannot be intercepted: initialize patchable state in setup(). Each call returns an idempotent undo function. Undoing a middle patch keeps other patches in their original order. Factories may run again when an earlier patch is removed, so keep factories free of side effects and put work in the returned methods. Descriptors and symbol members are preserved; a getter-only patch keeps the existing setter. Within a patched getter, use Reflect.get(sup, "name", this) to evaluate the predecessor getter against the live receiver. Non-configurable members cannot be patched reversibly and fail loudly. registerAddons returns a read-only map from addon id to its PatchSet. Its context's patch functions are bound to that set, so host addon removal can call sets.get(addonId).unpatchAll(). It removes that addon's patches in reverse order, preserving other addons' layers. A standalone new PatchSet(addonId) offers the same typed patch and patchStatic functions. Each set admits 4096 active patches; addon ids contain 1..256 UTF-16 code units. getPatches() copies the active (addon,target,member) metadata without executing factories. Class instance targets appear as their prototypes; symbol member identity is retained. UI6 still owns automatic rollback for its test harness. Default business services are outside this API. unpatchAll() closes the set to further installation, including saved context functions and late asynchronous code. Repeated removal is safe. When a factory rebuild refuses removal, the failed handles remain available for retry. If both registration and cleanup fail, AddonRegistrationError retains the original cause, all errors, and a patchSets index for explicit cleanup retry. The build-host conflict lint is run with the pinned Node toolchain: node web/scripts/lint-patches.mjs path/to/tsconfig.json path/to/patches.json The JSON manifest is an ordered array of {"addon":"my_addon","file":"./register.ts"} entries, with files relative to the manifest. Supply server/assembler load order; the lint does not infer dependencies. It prints JSON diagnostics and exits 1 on conflicts or unanalysable syntax, 2 on malformed inputs or syntax/project failures, and 0 on a clean analysis. It resolves imported class/object aliases, distinguishes static and instance targets, and flags later addon replacements without a sup call to the same member. A mention in a comment or string is insufficient. This tooling uses the pinned TypeScript 7 native API; it is not in browser bundles. Use direct ctx.patch / ctx.patchStatic statements in a named register(ctx) function with inline factories returning object literals. Dynamic execution, computed symbol keys, spread descriptors, aliased patch functions and indirect factory returns produce explicit unanalysable diagnostics. This conservative lint is not a proof that arbitrary JavaScript delegates on every execution path. UI3 owns emitting the final bundle's ordered manifest; no automatic bundle lint integration is claimed by this runtime helper. Registries allow 4096 entries/category and 256 categories/hub. Names and keys contain 1..256 UTF-16 code units; sequences are integers in -1000000..1000000. Bounds reject before publishing; replacing an existing entry at capacity works. The service container accepts at most 256 classes; registration closes when startup begins. A lazy bundle must import the canonical service class from the same defining module as the host. Two separately evaluated classes sharing a name are different keys. String aliases are unique typed lookup keys, not class-name matching or automatic deduplication. Patches refuse the shared Object, Function and Array prototypes and the reserved keys constructor, prototype and __proto__. Override descriptors must be configurable to permit removal. Factory failures retain the current chain. Addon registration failure stops the sequence and removes its owned patches. Already published registry contributions still require the host to abort/rebuild its app; there is no transaction across all addon side effects. Removal failures surface to the caller and retain failed patch ownership for retry. Async protection preserves synchronous return values and synchronous throws; it wraps actual thenables only. Declaring asyncMethods=true does not turn synchronous methods into Promise-returning methods. The facade forwards property reads and method calls, but raw own-field reflection (Object.keys, object spread and own fields checked with in) is not forwarded by BASE. Use service methods/property reads for component access rather than assuming raw-instance reflection.

docs.title: Companies in addons: the active companies and company consistency

sections.text: Status: implemented (ADR 0044, design note docs/design/m3-company.md). Section 1 is the active companies of an environment, sections 2 to 4 are company-scoped models, what is checked by default and the messages and cost, section 5 is related fields and section 6 the multi-company hint. Section 7 is the company_access declaration (ADR 0044 amendment A1, design note docs/design/m3-company-a1.md). Every Rust example on this page is compiled as a doctest of erp-test-models.

An environment has **one** company context, validated against the companies of the user. It is what record rules see (company_ids, company_id in an ir.access domain), what company-dependent cache keys use, and what ir.default and ir.sequence use. There is no second, unchecked copy in the context: env.company() and a record rule can never disagree. use erp_orm::{CompanyId, Env}; use erp_sdk::Value; fn report(env: &Env) -> erp_sdk::Result<()> { // the active companies, the current one first; no statement is issued let companies: &[CompanyId] = env.companies()?; // the current company: the first of them let current: Option<CompanyId> = env.company()?; assert_eq!(current, companies.first().copied()); // move company 5 to the front (Odoo's with_company); 0 changes nothing let in_five = env.with_company(5)?; // the same through the context let _also = env.with_context([("allowed_company_ids", Value::list([Value::Int(5)]))]); let _ = in_five; Ok(()) } Where the companies come from: | The context says | env.companies() is | |---|---| | no allowed_company_ids, False or [] | the user's default order: the main company (res.users.company_id) first, then the others in res.company order (sequence, name, id); archived companies are left out, except an archived main company | | a list [A, B] | exactly that list, in that order (A is current); with_company(C) gives [C, A, B] | | System principal with a list | the list as given (system code names the companies it works for) | The list is checked against the user's companies **every time the companies are used**, not when the environment is built, as in Odoo, where with_company(x) of a company the user is not in succeeds and the first read of env.companies fails. Unlike Odoo, sudo() does not skip the check: an elevated environment is refused the same way, and so is every ORM operation on it (search, read, write, create, unlink). Code that really works for another company states it with a principal that is a member (or System); sudo().with_company(other) on a user who is not in other fails with the error below. | Mistake | Error | |---|---| | a company the user is not in, a list that is not company ids, an archived company | Access: One of the selected companies does not exist or is not one of yours. | | a company listed twice | Validation: context key 'allowed_company_ids': company 5 is listed twice (the same text the RPC layer returns for a call's context) | | with_company(-1) | Programming: with_company: invalid company id -1 | Notes for Odoo developers: - env.company is env.company()? and env.companies is env.companies()?; both return a Result, because the check can fail. - A user's company list is read once per transaction by the principal resolver. If the user loses a company inside the transaction, the next ORM operation of an environment that still names it fails with the same Access error. - The resolver installed with erp_security::resolver::Resolver::for_registry(&registry) orders the companies by sequence, name, id and skips archived ones when res.company stores active and sequence; Resolver::id_order() does not know the registry and uses the id order. - A duplicate id in allowed_company_ids is an error here; Odoo accepts it. This is a recorded divergence (ADR 0044, "Lead decisions" in the design note).

A model is **company-scoped** when it has a stored, not company-dependent many2one company_id to res.company (scope *single*), or a stored many2many company_ids to res.company (scope *many*); res.company itself is its own scope. Abstract models are never scoped. You write nothing: the registry finds the scope. Other records that link to a scoped model must fit its **company match**, the rule that says which records of this model a record of company R may use: | company_match | A target is allowed when | Default for | Odoo's _check_company_domain | |---|---|---|---| | "exact" | it has no company, or its company is one of R | company_id models | the default [('company_id', 'in', companies + [False])] | | "parent_of" | it has no company, or its company is a company of R or one of their parents | none | check_company_domain_parent_of | | "any_of" | R is empty, or its company_ids meet R | company_ids models (res.users) | the res.users override | | "parent_of_any" | R is empty, or one of its company_ids is a company of R or a parent | none | check_companies_domain_parent_of | parent_of and parent_of_any need res.company to keep a parent path (parent_store = true with an indexed parent_path field, as Odoo's does); a model that asks for them without it makes the registry refuse to build. A match has to fit the scope (any_of needs company_ids), and company_match on a model that is not company-scoped is an error too. Those four forms are all there is: a catalogue shared with the branches of a company is parent_of, a record that lists its own companies is any_of.
use erp_sdk::prelude::*; /// A catalogue entry of one company that the company's branches may use as well.

pub struct Product { #[field(char, required)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, } /// A record that lists the companies it belongs to (any_of is the default for company_ids).
pub struct Channel { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2many, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_ids: Vec<RecId>, }

An unknown value is a compile error (`company_match must be one of "exact", "parent_of", "any_of", "parent_of_any"). In a model file (models/*.toml`) the same key is spelled the same way, and an unknown value is an error with the file and line: [[model]] name = "x_catalogue" company_match = "parent_of"

In Odoo a link is checked only when the model sets _check_company_auto and the field sets check_company=True; every flag an author forgets is a silent cross-company link.
