Here the check is **on by default**: a field of a company-scoped model is checked unless it opts out, when - it is a many2one or many2many, stored (a column or a relation table); - it is neither computed nor related, not an _inherits field or its delegate many2one, and not one of the four audit fields (create_uid, create_date, write_uid, write_date); - its comodel is company-scoped (so a link to res.company itself is not checked, nor a link to a model without a company). One2many fields are not checked (their lines carry the inverse many2one, which is). A model with at least one checked field has its check on. The check runs where Odoo's does: after create, for every checked field of the new records, and after write, for the written checked fields, or for all of them when company_id or company_ids is written. It runs under every elevation, sudo() and System included; it reads company ids without access rules and returns nothing to the caller but its error. A company-dependent field is compared with the current company (env.company()), not the record's; writing a value of one without a current company is an error that names the field. The two opt-outs keep Odoo's behaviour exactly. Use them when a link across companies is the point (an inter-company flow, a shared catalogue kept with a company):
use erp_sdk::prelude::*; /// Opted out as a whole: no field is checked.

pub struct Mirror { #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "shop.order")] pub source_id: Option<RecId>, } /// Opted out for one field; the others stay checked.

pub struct Order { #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, /// Checked: a contact of this order's company, a parent company's, or none. #[field(many2one, comodel = "shop.contact")] pub contact_id: Option<RecId>, /// Not checked: the mirrored order may belong to another company on purpose. #[field(many2one, comodel = "shop.order", check_company = false)] pub mirror_of_id: Option<RecId>, }
pub struct Contact { #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, }

In a model file the model-level opt-out is a key of the model, the field-level one a key of the field: [[model]] name = "x_mirror" check_company_auto = false [[model.field]] name = "source_id" type = "many2one" comodel = "x_order" check_company = false Writing check_company (true) on a field, or check_company_auto = true on a model, works as in Odoo and checks that field even where the default would not. Unlike Odoo, which logs and skips it, doing so on a model without company_id/company_ids makes the registry refuse to build: `shop.mirror.source_id declares check_company, but shop.mirror has no company_id or company_ids field linked to res.company`. Abstract mixins may declare checks; they apply to the models that use them.

An inconsistency is a UserError with Odoo's text, at most five lines: These values link records of different companies: - “Order 7” is in company “Company B”, and “Contact” (contact_id: 'Ada') points to a record of another company. - The record is company “Company A”, and “Default Contact” (contact_id: 'Ada') points to a record of another company. Choose records of the same company, or records shared by all companies. The second form is a res.company record (its own company). Targets are shown as Python reprs ('Ada', "O'Neil"). **Names are read as the caller**: a record or company the caller cannot read is written shop.contact(12,) instead of its name, so the error cannot be used to read names; Odoo reads them as superuser. The typed error is erp_sdk::CompanyError (the source of the returned Error, total counts every inconsistency, also those the text does not list). A linked record that does not exist is a Missing error: `Record does not exist or has been deleted: shop.contact,12 (linked by shop.order.contact_id)`. The check reads company ids only for what the transaction cache lacks, in **one** statement per call (one per 100,000 distinct ids on very large batches) and decides in memory. Values written in the same transaction are in the cache and win over the database, so nothing is flushed for the check, and when everything is cached it costs no statement. Odoo's check costs two reads per call plus a loop in Python. | Operation | Odoo 20 | Here | |---|---|---| | company check of a create/write call, cold cache | 2 reads | at most 1 | | company check, values cached | 2 reads | 0 | | a batch of 1,000 rows over several checked fields | 2 reads and 1,000 Python checks | 1 statement |

A related field reads through records: partner_id.country_id.name. In Odoo such a field is read as superuser unless it says related_sudo=False, so a user in company A reads a value through a record of company B without any check. Here a related field that **does not declare compute_sudo** is *company-bound*: - permissions and non-company rules do not apply to the path, as in Odoo (a salesman still reads the credit limit of the partner through a related field); - but every record reached through a hop of a **company-scoped** model must belong to the reader's active companies (env.companies()), by that model's own company_match, or have no company. When the last field of the path is a relational one, the records it points to are one more hop; - a company-bound related field met on the path is followed along its own path with the same bound, so a field cannot reach through another field what the reader could not reach directly; - a hop outside the active companies fails the read with Access; there is no silent empty value. A record read ahead with the ones you asked for (the prefetch set) that fails the bound does not fail your read: it stays unread, and raises only when you ask for it. | Declaration | The path is read | Company check | |---|---|---| | nothing (the default) | as superuser for permissions | every company-scoped hop must be in the active companies | | compute_sudo = true | as superuser (Odoo's default) | none: this is the opt-out | | compute_sudo = false | as the caller (Odoo's related_sudo=False) | the caller's own rules decide |
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

pub struct Line { #[field(many2one, comodel = "shop.order")] pub order_id: Option<RecId>, /// Company-bound: fails when the order belongs to a company outside the active ones. #[field(char, related = "order_id.reference")] pub order_reference: Option<Arc<str>>, /// Odoo's superuser read, for a value every company may see. #[field(char, related = "order_id.reference", compute_sudo = true)] pub order_reference_any: Option<Arc<str>>, /// Read as the caller: the caller's rules decide. #[field(char, related = "order_id.reference", compute_sudo = false)] pub order_reference_mine: Option<Arc<str>>, }
pub struct Order { #[field(char)] pub reference: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, }

Reading order_reference of a line whose order belongs to a company the user is not working in fails with, for example: You cannot read “Order Reference” (shop.line.order_reference) of Order Line (shop.line: 7): it is read through Sales Order (shop.order: 12), which belongs to a company outside your active companies. To open the record, switch to its company: Company B. The hop's id is shown for the first hop only, the one read on the record itself; a hop reached through another hop is named by its model, since you may not be allowed to see that record. The second paragraph is the hint of the next section: the company to switch to when it is one of the user's, the "no access" note when it is not (a company the user is not in is never named). The error carries the suggested_company context in the first case. A label is read the same way: the name shown for a many2one value is the target's record name, and when that is a company-bound field it is read with your companies, however many links deep the chain goes. If one target fails the bound, the read of the whole set fails with the same error, without the hop's id (you reached the record through a link and may not read the record behind its hop); the read never substitutes a placeholder name. A search on a company-bound field that ends on an x2many leaves out every record with a target outside your active companies (the read of such a record fails, so a search must not find it by one of its own-company targets or probe the foreign ones). A one-segment related field (related = "partner_id") is bound like the longer ones: the record it points to counts as a hop. The registry checks, when it assembles the graph, that a company-bound related field can drop its cached value when a hop changes company. A path that ends on a relational field that is computed, not stored and not related is refused (the ORM cannot tell which records to invalidate): store that field, make it related, or declare compute_sudo on the related field. What is not bound: - a sudo() read and a System read keep Odoo's value (elevation is explicit, and a read for a system job states its company through the principal); - a stored related field is filled at write time and read as any stored column; the write-time consistency check of sections 2 to 4 covers its sources. **Search and group-by** on a non-stored company-bound field add the same company condition to each company-scoped hop of the sub-query, so the field cannot be used to learn values of other companies: a search for a value only a foreign hop holds finds nothing, and a group-by puts the records behind a foreign hop into the empty group. A search is still one statement. **Cost.** The company of an exact or any_of hop is a column of the row that is fetched for the hop anyway, so such a read costs the same statements as the compute_sudo = true read of the same data. A parent_of or parent_of_any hop adds one statement for the active companies' parent paths (once per transaction), and a hop scoped by company_ids one for its link rows. The company of each hop is a dependency of the value: a hop that moves to another company drops the cached value. The cached value of a company-bound field that goes through a company-scoped hop is kept per set of active companies (and apart for superuser reads), so a value read for one company context is never served to another within a transaction. For Odoo developers: a related field that really must show a value across companies (a partner's country, a product's name on a document of another company) declares compute_sudo = true; every other related field keeps working in the user's own companies and fails loudly outside them.

When a record-level access error is caused by a rule that names the company (a global rule such as ['|', ('company_id', '=', False), ('company_id', 'in', company_ids)], or one that tests user.company_id), the message ends with Odoo's multi-company texts, computed from the companies of the (at most six) denied records: | The denied records | The message adds | |---|---| | belong to several companies | The records belong to several companies: switching the current company may help. | | belong to one company the user is in | To open the record, switch to its company: Company B. and the error context {"suggested_company": {"id": 2, "display_name": "Company B"}} | | belong to one company the user is not in | The record belongs to a company outside your allowed companies. The company is never named | | have no company, or the model has no company field | nothing | A model with a company_ids field suggests the first of its companies that the user is in (Odoo's (company_ids & user.company_ids)[:1]); when there is none, nothing is said. In the debug listing (an internal user with the technical-features group in debug mode) a record line carries , company=Company B when the rule names the company and the record's company is one of the user's. **Difference from Odoo:** the listing shows a record's display name only when the record has no company or a company among the user's *active* companies; any other record is listed by model and id (- Sales Order (shop.order: 12, company=Company B)), and its name is never read. This keeps the error from being a way to read the names of records of other companies. The listing decides on the record's own company_id / company_ids: a model without one lists its names, as Odoo does, so a model whose names must stay inside a company declares its own company field. The hint costs no statement: the companies of the denied records are read by the one statement that already evaluates the rules on them. The company of a related-field hop (section 5) uses the same texts and context.

company_match (section 2) says which records a record of company R may *link to*. Which records a user may *see* is a separate declaration: company_access says how the user's active companies restrict the model's records. In Odoo an addon writes this by hand as a global restriction row in its security file, and nothing notices a model that has none; here the model declares it once, the registry checks it when it is built, and the restriction row is generated from it. The registry refuses a concrete company-scoped model without a declaration. A concrete model without a company field must also make an explicit decision if it has a required, stored many2one to a company-scoped model. That check does not infer ownership: choose parent(edge = "…") only when that link is the owner, or unrestricted(reason = "…") when an explicit opt-out is justified. Optional, company-dependent, non-stored and inherited-copy links do not trigger this check.

| Declaration | Restricts by | Typical use | |---|---|---| | direct(field = "company_id", branch = …, empty = …) | the model's own company field (company_id, or company_ids for a model shared between companies) | documents, journals, accounts | | parent(edge = "order_id") | the record that owns it: a stored, required many2one; the record is visible when its owner passes the owner's company restriction | lines of a document that have no company of their own | | direct(…, parent = "tax_id") | both, ANDed | a child with its own company that must never be shared beyond its owner | | unrestricted(reason = "…") | nothing, said explicitly; the reason (not blank, at most 512 bytes) is listed in reports | a model reached only through another record's access (a user-type escape is the escape modifier below, not this form) | branch and empty have no default, so every direct declaration says them: | branch | A record is admitted when its company is | |---|---| | "exact" | one of the active companies | | "ancestor" | an active company or one of their ancestors (needs res.company to keep its hierarchy) | | empty | A record without company (company_id empty, company_ids empty) is | |---|---| | "deny" | refused | | "allow" | admitted, while the user has at least one active company | A nullable company field never implies "allow": write it when you mean it. With company_ids, a record is admitted when one of its companies matches.
use erp_sdk::prelude::*; /// A document of one company: users see the documents of their active companies.

name = "shop.order", description = "Order", company_access = direct(field = "company_id", branch = "exact", empty = "deny") )] pub struct Order { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, } /// A line has no company of its own: it is visible when its order is.

name = "shop.order.line", description = "Order Line", company_access = parent(edge = "order_id") )] pub struct OrderLine { #[field(many2one, comodel = "shop.order", required, ondelete = "cascade")] pub order_id: Option<RecId>, } /// A catalogue shared with branches, also usable without a company; each price belongs to its /// catalogue entry as well.

name = "shop.price", description = "Price", company_access = direct( field = "company_id", branch = "ancestor", empty = "allow", parent = "order_id" ) )] pub struct Price { #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "shop.order", required, ondelete = "cascade")] pub order_id: Option<RecId>, } /// Visible to every company, on purpose.

name = "shop.notice", description = "Notice", company_access = unrestricted(reason = "public notices are shown to every company") )] pub struct Notice { #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.company")] pub company_id: Option<RecId>, }
branch = "ancestor" in that example needs res.company to keep its hierarchy (parent_store with parent_path); without it the registry refuses the declaration.

Odoo's partner and user rules admit a record when it passes the company test **or** belongs to an internal user. direct(…, escape = "<field>") states that: a record whose own boolean <field> is false is admitted whatever its companies; any other record takes the company test. The generated rule is '|', ('<field>', '=', False), <company test>. company_access = direct(field = "company_id", branch = "ancestor", empty = "allow", escape = "share") The registry refuses the escape unless <field> is a boolean of the model that is **stored** (a stored compute is fine, as res.users.share is) and **required**. Required matters: the negative boolean test also matches a NULL column, so an optional field would silently admit rows with no value. A pending recompute of a stored-compute escape is applied before the restricted query of the same transaction. An extension may drop the escape but never add or change it, and escape cannot be combined with parent. With an empty active-company set nothing is admitted, escaped records included. A writable escape lets whoever can write the record make it visible in every company, so declare the escape on a computed or read-only field. Model files take escape = "share" inside direct = { … }. Base uses the escape for its two user-facing models, which is the worked example to copy: | Model | Declaration | Generated rule | |---|---|---| | res.partner | direct(field = "company_id", branch = "ancestor", empty = "allow", escape = "partner_share") | ['\|', ('partner_share', '=', False), '\|', ('company_id', '=', False), ('company_id', 'parent_of', company_ids)] | | res.users | direct(field = "company_ids", branch = "exact", empty = "deny", escape = "share") | ['\|', ('share', '=', False), ('company_ids', 'in', company_ids)] | Both escape fields are stored computes declared required with the static default true: a row that the compute has not reached yet, or that an upgrade filled when the column became NOT NULL, takes the company test instead of being shown to every company. A static default does not stop a stored compute without inverse from running after the insert, so the default is only the fail-closed starting value. share is false for an internal user; partner_share is false for the superuser's partner and for a contact with an active internal user. A contact or user of another company is therefore visible to a restricted user when it belongs to (or is) an internal user, and otherwise only through the company test. Code that reads contacts or users of other companies for its own logic (followers, notifications, pickers that must list everyone) reads them with sudo and states why; a restricted read gets the record-level access error. Ordinary writes and upsert updates check the resulting generated restriction when they change an escape or any transitive local compute input of it. A refused update poisons the transaction and cannot be committed. This covers the updated records themselves; it does not recheck other records reached through relational compute triggers. Upsert's existing required-compute/default admission rules still apply before its insert-or-update statement.

#[extend(Model, company_access = …)] declares on a model another addon owns, and an abstract mixin may declare for the models that inherit it (it is checked on each of them). Declarations compose through _inherit: the newest is effective, and **each later declaration may only narrow** the one before it: - anything narrows unrestricted; - on the same field, "exact" narrows "ancestor" and "deny" narrows "allow"; - adding the other half narrows: direct(…, parent = "x") narrows direct(…) and parent(edge = "x"); - the same owner edge narrows itself. Everything else is refused: switching between direct and parent, dropping a half, unrestricted after a restriction, and naming another owner edge (a record has one owner). _inherits delegation is not inheritance: a delegating model takes nothing from its parent's declaration.
/// A hardening addon: orders without a company are no longer visible.
pub struct StrictOrder {}

[[model]] name = "x_contract" [model.company_access] direct = { field = "company_id", branch = "ancestor", empty = "allow" } parent = "partner_id"          # with direct: the owner as well; alone: the owner only
Unknown keys, a missing field, branch or empty, an unknown branch or empty value and unrestricted combined with another form are errors with the file and line.

The registry refuses a missing required company-access decision. An extension may narrow an existing core declaration; it cannot widen it. An explicit unrestricted(reason = "…") is an opt-out and must be justified independently of ordinary model permissions.

When the registry is built (also for model files and per-database overlays), a declaration fails with a Programming error naming the model and the declaring definition (addon, file and line) when: - a direct declaration is on a model without company field, or names another field than the model's company field; - it is declared on res.company (which keeps its own base policy); - branch = "ancestor" is used while res.company keeps no hierarchy; - parent(…) alone is declared on a model that has its own company field (declare both); - the owner edge is not a field, not a many2one, not stored (computed, related, company-dependent, or a copy from an _inherits parent), optional, or links to res.company; - an owner chain ends in a model that is unrestricted, declares nothing, or has no company field; loops back to a model of the chain; or is more than 8 edges deep; - unrestricted is declared on a model with neither a company field nor a qualifying required stored link to a company-scoped model, or its reason is empty or longer than 512 bytes; - a later declaration widens an earlier one, or names another owner edge. For example: shop.order.line: company_access parent(edge = "order_id") names the owner 'order_id', but shop.order.line.order_id is optional: an owner edge is required (required = true), so every record has an owner (declared by model definition 'shop.order.line' of addon 'shop' (src/lib.rs:20)) A syntax error in #[model(company_access = …)] (an unknown form or parameter, a missing branch or empty, an empty name, a reason that is blank or longer than 512 bytes) is a compile error on the offending token.

A row of ir.access marked generated belongs to the model's company_access declaration. ORM write and unlink reject these rows, including archived rows and mixed batches, even under System or sudo(). Explicitly supplying generated to create or write is refused, including false; addon data files use the same boundary. A default cannot manufacture an enabled generated marker either. Use copy() without a generated override to make an ordinary restriction; generated has copy = false. Ordinary restrictions remain editable and are combined with generated restrictions by the access engine. Change the model declaration to change its generated restriction. Lifecycle emission, the tamper ledger and explicit restoration are planned separately; this protection alone does not install restrictions or prevent raw SQL from changing the database.

Every module operation (install, update, uninstall, reinit) ends by writing the company restriction of each model whose company_access declaration generates one: a group-less, active crud row in ir.access marked generated. You write nothing; the row follows the declaration. When upgrading an existing database to these base declarations, update base before serving users. The update installs the generated restrictions and fills the company hierarchy paths. A missing generated restriction fails closed; a cycle in the company hierarchy refuses the update. Plan and verify this database update as part of deployment. **Ledger.** ir.model.company_restriction holds the domain text the last operation emitted for the model. The next operation compares the stored row with it before writing anything. **What an update refuses.** If a generated row was deleted, archived, given a group, given another operation or another domain, or if a generated row exists without a ledger entry, the update fails and writes nothing: Module operation refused: the generated company restriction of <model> (<declaration>) was archived since it was generated; run the update with --restore-generated-restrictions to rewrite it erp addon update --restore-generated-restrictions (upgrade only) rewrites those rows from the declaration and lists each one (generated restriction restored: <model>: <what>; programmatically OperationOutcome::restored_restrictions). Nothing is rewritten unless you pass the flag. **Other refusals.** - … the generated company restriction of <model> (<declaration>) <problem>: the read-back after writing did not match the declaration (for example another database trigger altered the row). The operation rolls back. - <model> restricts by its owner '<edge>', but N record(s) have no owner: ids …: a model newly restricted through an owner edge has records without an owner (at most 20 ids are listed). Give them an owner, then update again. **Declarations that leave.** When a declaration is removed or a model is uninstalled, its generated row and ledger entry go in the same operation. A database that predates generated restrictions has neither; the first update only inserts. Not here: the ORM refuses to create, archive, change or delete a generated row from code or data files (ir.access guards); that is a separate protection.

res.company.parent_id is assigned during create and is immutable afterward. Every write containing it fails, including no-op assignments and relational commands that would move an existing branch. Create nested branches with a one2many Create command or an explicit/default parent; do not create a root and reparent it later. child_ids contains active direct branches. all_child_ids uses inactive-inclusive relation context and contains archived direct branches as well. Neither relation is recursive. The existing company contact creation and mirrored contact fields remain in the normal method chain; default_parent_id is removed from the new contact's environment. Missing branch currency inherits from the root; explicit mismatches are validation errors. Root currency writes propagate to every descendant, including archived records. Archive cascades; unarchive does not. Propagated writes use the actor's ordinary ORM method chain. Addon overrides still run and may refuse; the operation then rolls back atomically. Required inaccessible descendants cause a whole-operation refusal rather than partial propagation. action_all_company_branches is a read RPC on one existing readable company. It returns list/form current-window navigation with the direct-parent domain, default_parent_id and boolean active_test=false. Authority-bearing context keys remain refused. Modal action context remains defaults-only. The client preserves the initial parent filter when clearing user search. The private lifecycle row-version fence serializes creation, deletion, archive/currency writes and relevant active-user/default-company transitions. It is PostgreSQL state, not a process lock. Preserve the original retryable serialization error and retry the whole transaction through the established unit-of-work boundary. There is no public skip flag or new delegated-field API. Operation admission is bounded to 256 nested lifecycle entries and 4096 distinct companies. For binaries linking base, retain .require_core_tables(erp_addon_base::partner_hierarchy::core_tables()); this existing requirement list now covers both partner hierarchy and company lifecycle fences. Publish runtime grants after upgrading base before starting the candidate. See ADR 0137 and the release note for migration and verification status.

res.company.root_id is a readonly, nonstored relation to the topmost company (ADR 0225). Saved-company reads validate the full path against the parent links before returning a root. Drafts resolve their live parent chain; a parentless draft resolves to itself. Search, grouping and ordering on this computed relation are refused with its field name; use the stored company hierarchy for filters. No new database column or migration is needed; update base metadata when shipping the new native registry. Native callers can call _accessible_branches on one readable company. It returns the selected companies reachable through active child edges, using Transaction::companies to validate the selection. An unselected intermediate parent does not hide its selected descendant; an archived intermediate parent stops the traversal. The source itself remains eligible even when archived. Only a core-created System principal without an impersonator may fall back to the source when there is no intersection. Ordinary elevation does not grant that fallback, and switching a user to the superuser is refused by the existing principal guard. _all_branches_selected compares a readable input recordset with the complete active membership of its roots. Empty input is complete; duplicate identities do not affect the comparison; an archived input makes it incomplete. The internal completeness query ignores record rules, so a hidden sibling cannot disappear and make an incomplete selection look complete. It returns only a boolean. This reveals one fact: an omitted active company exists under a selected root, possibly one the caller cannot read. No hidden identity or name is returned. Neither helper is an RPC endpoint, and neither bypasses access checks on later record reads or writes. All discovery is local to a call and follows flushed ORM state. A subsequent call after a membership change or savepoint rollback rereads that state. These helpers add no configuration, no default records and no separate closure cache. Database state remains authoritative across nodes; existing snapshots keep their transaction isolation.

Use erp_addon_base::company_calendar::business_date(tx, company_id) for effective accounting dates. For a multi-company operation use business_days(tx, env, ids) to read the dates together. Each entry includes the local date and the first valid instant of that date in ERPForAll's UTC timestamp representation. The instant comes from PostgreSQL's current transaction. Zone rules come from the base addon's Jiff timezone database. Supply the caller environment when a service operates on behalf of another principal. Business dates are resolved from the document's company, even when a different company is active. Use the explicit Env argument of business_days when the recordset and transaction principals differ; business_date uses the transaction environment. The helper authorizes company and timezone-field reads, flushes pending timezone values, and refuses missing or invalid configuration. Do not replace a refusal with UTC. The fiscal service uses the same pure conversion after its own company admission because its separate transaction boundary permits raw SQL only. Accounting draft and payment dates, undated customer invoices, posting lock decisions, lock-date validation, journal dashboard windows, and stock confirmation share this calendar. Explicit document dates retain their meaning; the posting lock policy may still shift an accounting date. Batch work must resolve each record's company separately. Audit timestamps remain UTC instants. Journal dashboards preserve the ancestor-journal access contract: after reading journal fields under the caller's rights, they may read calendar configuration for those journal companies with elevated record access. Time-zone field permission is still checked as the caller. Ledger figures remain under the caller's rights; this exception does not grant a general parent-company read. Account's company write override invalidates journal dashboard cards when tz changes. A dotted compute dependency would prefetch a parent company under the branch reader before the narrow metadata admission, so the dashboard deliberately does not declare that path. Native SQL writers that change tz must also invalidate account.journal's dashboard_card cache in the same transaction.

A company-dependent field keeps one value per company. The same record reads one value in company A and another in company B; a company without a value of its own reads the default configured for it. Odoo calls these fields properties. The design is ADR 0163. Status: the generic ORM support is delivered (storage, create, read and write, defaults, search, ordering, grouping, drafts and onchange, deletion of referenced records, migration of existing scalar columns). The operations under [What is refused](#what-is-refused) return a named error. Fields in use today: property_account_position_id on contacts (account), property_stock_customer and property_stock_supplier on contacts and property_warehouse_id on users (stock). The product cost is not company-dependent yet; its adoption is separate work. Do not enable the flag on an existing scalar business field without the migration under [Existing data](#existing-data).
Add company_dependent = true to the field. The Rust type stays the scalar type:

pub(crate) struct StockPartner { /// Destination used when shipping goods to this contact in the active company. #[field( many2one, comodel = "stock.location", company_dependent = true, check_company = true, string = "Customer location" )] pub property_stock_customer: Option<RecId>, } Reading and writing use the ordinary record API. Every value is the value of the environment's current company. The public API never accepts or returns the map of all companies. A field cannot be both translated and company-dependent.

- A write stores the value for the current company only. The other companies' values stay. - A company without a stored value reads the fallback: the ir.default value of that field for the company, or the global one. Defaults are looked up by model and company, not by record. - An explicit null on a nullable field is a value: it suppresses a non-null fallback. - Writing a value equal to the company's fallback removes that company's stored value. A record without any stored value has SQL NULL in the column. - Boolean and numeric nulls follow their normal conversion (false, zero). - A required company-dependent field is checked on its effective value. The column stays nullable. - HTML policy, precision and monetary rounding apply to the scalar before it is stored. - Exact numbers (a Float with digits, Monetary) are stored as decimal text and never pass through a binary float. Reads of an existing record use the fallback a superuser would see for the caller's company. This grants the caller no access to the record or the field. Ordinary creation defaults (default_get) keep their usual precedence and the caller's identity. Fallbacks are read in the caller's transaction and kept for that transaction only; they are never shared between transactions, so an older snapshot never receives a newer fallback. A change of an ir.default row through the ORM clears them and the computed fields that depend on the company context; a pending default write is flushed before the lookup. The fallbacks of a model for a company are read once per transaction and reused by every later create, read, write and query. The first use sends the default lookup, plus one existence statement per target model when a many2one fallback names a record. They are read again after any of these in the same transaction: - a change of ir.default, ir.model.fields or decimal.precision records through the ORM, or through the ir_default functions; - records created or deleted in a model that a many2one fallback points to; - a statement that names the table it writes (INSERT INTO …, UPDATE …, DELETE FROM …, MERGE INTO …) when that table holds defaults or a fallback's target, including rows a database cascade removes; and any raw TRUNCATE, COPY, CALL, DO, DDL or Transaction::batch; - Transaction::invalidate_all, invalidate_model of the target model without a field list, a rollback to a savepoint. An operation that is already running keeps the fallbacks it started with; the next read, write, create or query reads them again. Raw SQL the ORM cannot read this way owns its invalidation: after a raw data-changing WITH (WITH … INSERT, WITH … UPDATE, WITH … DELETE), a SELECT that calls a writing function, or a trigger that changes ir_default or a fallback's target table, call tx.invalidate_ormcache("ir.default") (defaults changed), tx.invalidate_model(<target>, None) (target rows changed) or tx.invalidate_all().

A System environment without a current company can create a record when every company-dependent field stays unset after the creation defaults. The columns stay SQL NULL and no company is inferred. A supplied value, including null, false or zero, and a context, field or overridden creation default that supplies one, needs a validated company; otherwise the call returns Validation with company-dependent fields require a current company. Reading or writing such a field needs a current company too.

"tested" means at least one test in the binaries listed under [Tests](#tests) exercises that kind in that column. "untested" means composition admits it and no test in those binaries covers it. No cell is a performance statement. | Field kind | Create, read, write | Search, order, group | Drafts and onchange | Migration helper | |---|---|---|---|---| | Char | tested | search, order and group key tested | tested | tested | | Text | tested | untested | untested | tested | | Html | tested | untested | tested | tested | | Boolean | tested | search tested | read from an origin tested | tested | | Integer | tested | search and sum tested | tested | tested | | BigInt | untested | untested | untested | untested | | Float | tested | search tested | untested | tested | | Float with digits (exact) | tested | sum tested | untested | tested | | Monetary | tested | equality search and sum tested | untested | tested | | Selection | tested | search and order tested | untested | tested | | Date | tested | search tested | untested | tested | | Datetime | tested | search tested | untested | tested | | Many2one | tested | search, path, hierarchy and group key tested | tested | tested | Every other field kind, and a field that is not stored, computed, related, generated, tracked or has an inverse, is refused when the registry is composed.

Each of these returns an error whose text names the follow-up work that will add it. None is silently ignored. | Operation | Error kind | |---|---| | A declaration outside the matrix (other kinds; computed, inverse, related, generated or tracked company-dependent fields) | Programming | | Upsert on a model that has a company-dependent field | Programming | | A write hook registered on a company-dependent field | Programming | | A compute that reads a company-dependent field and is stored, or does not depend on the company context | Programming | | A native selection catalog expression over a company-dependent field | Programming | | Keyset pagination ordered by a company-dependent field (use offset pagination) | Programming | | A company-dependent many2one of a draft that points at an unsaved record | Validation | A non-stored compute that reads a company-dependent field and declares the company context dependency is supported. A stored output is refused because it would keep the value of whichever company computed it last. One further limit is open: the company-setting adapters of SPEC-FIELD-084 (a company field kept in step with a company-dependent default) are not built. A restrict reference written while its target is being deleted is covered, see [A write and a deletion at the same time](#a-write-and-a-deletion-at-the-same-time).

A flush sends only the changed companies' entries, and the database merges them into the stored map in one statement. A mutation keeps the company and the environment it was made in; flushing through another environment does not move it to that environment's company. Changing the origin flushes the earlier pending mutation before the new one is staged. A rollback (of the transaction or of a savepoint) discards the pending entries and their baselines. Two transactions that write the same row conflict, also when they write for different companies: the row is one row. The later one fails with kind Concurrency and SQLSTATE 40001, the database's serialization failure. Nothing of it is stored. Retry the complete transaction; after the retry both companies' values are stored. Orm::run and Orm::run_with_options do this: they roll back, discard the cache and run the unit of work again in a new transaction, within a bounded number of attempts. Code that opens a transaction by hand retries by hand. Writers of different rows do not conflict. Nothing here uses a process-local lock, so the rule is the same on one node and on several.

New records (Transaction::new_record, the records of a form's onchange) support company-dependent fields. A draft keeps a company map in its cache, like a stored record, and nothing of it reaches the database: - An explicit value, or a field default, is the environment's company value. Another company reads its own fallback. - A draft without value or origin reads the company fallback (the ir.default value for that company). A first onchange call returns it as the default, the same value default_get gives. - A draft with an origin (an edit form) reads the origin's value in every company. Writing on the draft, also from an onchange method, changes the writing environment's company only, in the cache. - Switching the environment's company on a draft is allowed: the read projects that company's entry. - A non-stored compute over the field that depends on the company context recomputes in the draft when the value changes. Onchange values have the same wire shape as web_read of a stored record. - Saving goes through create or write, which store the caller's company value only. Write commands of draft lines (x2many_commands) carry that scalar, never a map. - A draft's read is checked on its origin like a read of the stored record: an origin the reader may not read refuses with the same Access error. - A company-dependent many2one cannot point at an unsaved record (Validation): a map stores database ids only. Reading the company-dependent fields of a draft from its origin uses the stored record's prefetch read; the test prints both statement counts.

A company-dependent many2one is a reference inside a JSON map, not a foreign key, so the ORM runs the referential action itself when it unlinks the target. This happens for every caller, not only an elevated one, and it looks at the rows of all companies whatever the caller may see. - Every refusal is decided first, then every cleanup runs; a refused deletion changes nothing. - A restrict field with a reference stored for any company refuses the deletion. The message ("You cannot delete a record used by a company-dependent field") names neither the holder nor the company, because the caller may not be allowed to see either. - A fallback set in ir.default for a company-dependent many2one to the record refuses it too, naming the field. An ordinary many2one default does not block: it is discarded with the record. The force_delete context key skips both refusals and the references are then cleared, but only for an elevated environment (the module loader's purge). Any other caller's force_delete is ignored and the refusals apply, and the RPC layer refuses the key from clients outright (Odoo honours it from any context; this is deliberate). - Every other reference is set to null in its map. The other companies' entries stay. cascade on a company-dependent field behaves as set null: the holder row is never deleted. - Fields that depend on a cleared reference recompute on the next read, and cached maps are dropped. - A target removed by a database cascade (its parent was deleted) does not run these checks, as in Odoo. References to it read as empty from then on. A reference whose target no longer exists reads as empty (an empty recordset, False, None), and a search for an empty value finds it. It never falls back to the default: a missing override means "no value", not "use the default". The same holds when the default itself names a missing record. A default that names a missing record is not a creation default either: default_get does not offer it and a create does not store it, so the new record reads like every record without a value of its own. When the missing record was a user's own default, the company's fallback is offered instead. Reads do not rewrite the stored map; a dangling entry is simply not reported. A record rule on the target does not change this; existence is checked directly in the database.

A restrict field also holds when one transaction stores a reference while another deletes the target (SPEC-CRUD-068; Odoo checks without a lock, BUG-147). Nothing is declared for it: the ORM does the work for every company-dependent many2one with ondelete = "restrict". - Storing a reference (create or write) locks the target row the way a foreign key does and records the reference in two ORM tables, erp_company_ref_guard and erp_company_ref_link. This costs one extra statement per such field in each INSERT or UPDATE batch that changes it. Removing the value, or deleting the holder with unlink, removes the recorded reference. - Deleting the target locks it first, so it waits for a write in flight. When a reference was committed after the deletion's snapshot, the deletion fails with a Concurrency error (SQLSTATE 40001). Orm::run and the RPC layer retry that error; the retry sees the reference and returns the usual refusal. Code that opens a transaction by hand handles Concurrency as for any other statement. - A write that waits for a deletion which then commits fails with Concurrency too. Its retry stores the id of a record that no longer exists, unless the code reads the target first; that is allowed for any id and reads as empty (above). - The first reference a record ever gets creates its guard row. A second transaction that stores a reference to the same record, and whose snapshot is older than that first commit, fails once with Concurrency and succeeds on its retry. Later references to the record do not conflict with each other. - Limits: set null and cascade fields are not guarded; a reference stored there while its target is being deleted reads as empty, as after the cleanup. A map written with SQL outside the ORM has no link row, so only the scan protects it. A target removed by a database cascade runs none of this (above). A default in ir.default committed while the record is being deleted is not seen by that deletion. Link rows of holders that a database cascade removed stay until their target is deleted; they change no result.

Search and count evaluate the current company's effective scalar value. Ordering, group keys, aggregates and HAVING use the same expression and logical SQL type. Missing company keys inherit prepared defaults, while explicit JSON null suppresses them. A missing row on an optional relation join stays absent; it does not inherit the missing model's defaults. Relation traversal and principal user paths use the effective many2one ids, and a dangling target compares as absent. Exact values cast to PostgreSQL numeric without passing through binary floats. A query that touches only ordinary fields prepares nothing. The ORM prepares defaults for the models the expression reads and binds company and fallback values per query component. Bound values are not stored in shared filter or order caches. Default changes, rollback and separate transaction snapshots follow the read rules above. Orders over a company-dependent field are compiled per query; ordinary orders keep the existing order memo.

Direct erp_sql callers use company::CompanyValues with compile_where_with_company or the context-aware order entry points. Supply normalized typed fallback cells after company authorization and the field's ordinary precision/HTML admission. Positive-ID validation in this pure compiler is not authorization. Context-free compiler entry points still support ordinary fields and refuse a referenced company-dependent field with a Programming error naming its missing prepared company values. Constant DDL predicates also refuse them because they have no current-company context. The context and its individual values share a 16 MiB payload admission limit. This is a resource limit, not a measured memory cost. Values remain parameters; query text contains registry-derived identifiers and fixed logical casts. A btree_not_null prefilter is added only when conservative fallback evaluation proves it cannot remove matches. Unknown relation visibility or patterns omit that prefilter. No index-performance claim is made.

erp_orm::company_dependent provides pure scalar encode/decode, effective project, single-company apply and map delta functions. They perform no database access and grant no access to another company. Runtime callers must authorize the company, record and field and admit precision/HTML policy before encoding. Public record values remain scalar; raw maps are an internal storage format. Maps use positive canonical company IDs as keys. Missing keys inherit the supplied fallback; explicit JSON null suppresses it. Fallback-equal updates remove their key, and empty maps become SQL NULL. Decimal values use normalized decimal text and never pass through f64. Fractional JSON numbers are refused for Decimal storage; migrate such legacy values through exact PostgreSQL text. Dates use canonical four-digit-year date strings. Datetimes use canonical UTC strings, with a six-digit fractional suffix when microseconds are nonzero. Storage decoding rejects abbreviated or trailing date/time strings; dynamic input conversion remains the caller's responsibility. A map admits at most MAX_COMPANIES entries and MAX_MAP_BYTES key/scalar payload bytes, charging 64 bytes per entry in addition to key and string lengths. These are safety limits, not measured memory-use claims. Direct scalar decoding also enforces the byte ceiling. Map mutation validates before cloning; a delta can contain removals from the old map plus changes from the new map, so its entry/payload upper bound is the sum of two admitted maps. Invalid map keys, nested values and wrong scalar kinds return errors without including hidden company values. delta returns [value] for a set (including null) and [] for removal. Pass these validated deltas to erp_sql::version::VersionedUpdate::merge_company; translation merge_json has different null semantics. The statement atomically patches the existing database map and has its own cache identity. A SQL NULL patch is empty, not a request to clear every company. Company merge takes precedence if a caller names the same column in both merge lists; callers should select exactly one operation.

Do not change a populated scalar column to a company map with an implicit type cast. Its adoption must define the companies owning the old value. The installer's current company is not a data-ownership policy. Existing JSONB columns are not proof of compatible storage. Schema initialization validates all non-null values against the field's map codec before applying schema changes, including on repeat initialization. Incompatible shapes, keys, scalar types or exceeded admission limits return Validation naming the field and an explicit migration requirement. Values are not included in the error. Valid maps and SQL NULL remain unchanged. An operator must migrate incompatible data with an explicit ownership policy before retrying; neither a translation marker nor the installer's company establishes that policy.

Changing an existing scalar business field requires a native **pre** migration in a newer addon version. Use erp_sdk::migrations::CompanyMigrationPolicy with tx.migrate_company_dependent(model, field, &policy). An explicit company set assigns each existing non-null scalar to those companies; row_company("company_id") uses a stored ordinary Many2one to res.company on the same table. Shared rows with a non-null scalar and no owner refuse. SQL NULL stays SQL NULL. The installer's active/allowed companies do not select owners. The helper is trusted native migration code; it is not an RPC operation. It runs under the upgrade transaction and schema/table locks. Never commit inside a migration. Exact numeric values remain exact JSON strings; false, zero and empty text remain explicit historical overrides. Conversion does not prune values against current defaults. Existing valid maps keep their owners on repeat; explicit helper normalization changes an empty map to SQL NULL. Ordinary schema admission keeps valid maps unchanged. Invalid maps and populated reverse conversion refuse; there is no automatic conversion from a company map back to a scalar.

1. Inventory custom constraints, indexes and dependent views on the column. Known ORM scalar foreign keys are removed when a Many2one becomes a company map. Unsupported custom dependencies refuse and must be handled by a separately reviewed migration; the helper never drops their rules silently. 2. Keep a backup and rehearse the version upgrade on a disposable clone. 3. Run the upgrade. A lock or validation failure is an upgrade failure: the previous data and schema are kept. Resolve the cause and retry the whole upgrade from the retained predecessor. 4. Coordinate runtime activation through the existing deployment procedure; the helper alone cannot make an older binary compatible with the new storage format.

Lookup costs, bytes per row and index gains of this feature are not measured. Performance acceptance is DEFERRED_PERFORMANCE until the milestone end (ADR 0065). Tests print statement counts where that helps a reader; one count is asserted. A create on a model with a company-dependent many2one sends one statement, the INSERT, once one create in the same transaction has warmed the caches, with or without an ir.default for the field (SPEC-FIELD-087, asserted by tests). The first create of a transaction also sends the default lookups, and one existence statement per target model when a fallback names a record, because fallbacks are not shared between transactions (see [Values and fallbacks](#values-and-fallbacks)).

- crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_acceptance.rs: values and fallbacks per company (the whole SPEC-FIELD-075 case), product-like exact cost, partner-like relation, a real user's company isolation, concurrent writers with retry, rollback, statements of a create. - crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_create_queries.rs: one statement for a warmed create, and every way the prepared fallbacks are read again (defaults changed through the functions, the ORM or raw SQL, a target removed by raw SQL or a cascade, savepoint rollback, a second company, another transaction's commit, a restricted read). - crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_runtime.rs: create, read, write, defaults, cache, access, drafts and onchange. - crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_query.rs and crates/erp-sql/tests/company_dependent_query.rs: search, order, grouping, the direct compiler. - crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_relations.rs: deletion and dangling references. - crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_restrict_lock.rs: a restrict reference stored while its target is deleted. - crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_schema.rs, crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_schema_migration.rs and crates/erp-modules/tests/company_dependent_migration.rs: existing data and migration. - crates/erp-orm/tests/company_dependent_codec.rs and crates/erp-test-models/tests/company_dependent_delta_sql.rs: the codec and the merge statement. Spec cases: SPEC-FIELD-075, 076, 085, 086, 106 to 110, SPEC-REL-015, SPEC-CRUD-035, SPEC-CRUD-068 and SPEC-COMPMIG-001 to 004. SPEC-FIELD-075, SPEC-FIELD-076, SPEC-FIELD-087, SPEC-FIELD-108, SPEC-FIELD-109 and SPEC-CRUD-035 carry a whole-case test tag; the others are covered in part. SPEC-FIELD-084 is not implemented.

Use @erpforall/elang-test from a workspace test to exercise the real component runtime. Keep every test's work inside withTestScope; it tears down mounted roots and restores registry and patch mutations even when the callback rejects. The package is test infrastructure and must not be imported by a production addon entry point. import { withTestScope } from "@erpforall/elang-test"; const model = { label() { return "original"; } }; await withTestScope(async scope => { scope.patch(model, sup => ({ label() { return ${sup.label.call(this)} patched; }, })); // Assert the component's behavior while this patch is installed. }); // model.label() is restored here. scope.patch and scope.patchStatic explicitly give the scope ownership of a patch; teardown removes it. To own a synchronous addon registration or PatchSet operation, wrap it in scope.manage(() => { /* register here */ }). The callback must be synchronous; Promise-returning callbacks are rejected by the type boundary and unexpected runtime thenables remain observed during cleanup. An outstanding patch installed directly through the runtime without scope ownership is reported as a leaked patch: the scope fails the test boundary, then attempts restoration. Calling its returned unpatch function before teardown avoids the leak. This catches accidental patches while allowing intentional scoped overrides. scope.mount(ComponentClass, options) returns the real component instance and an attached root. Supply the same props and compiled templates that the runtime expects. Scope teardown unmounts the component and removes the root; a failed mount also cleans its target. Use semantic DOM assertions across the entire mounted app, including portals and overlays where the component creates them. A small fixture establishes only the behavior it exercises. Before mounting, call scope.mockService(CanonicalServiceClass, mockInstance) to replace that service's instance while keeping its canonical class identity. Register other required services on scope.services. Startup uses the real container: dependency errors, cycles and startup failures still reject. Every scope gets a fresh environment, service container and registry hub. Registry mutations made during the scope are restored with their original sequence, ordering and value identity. Rollback restores registrations, not arbitrary in-place mutations to an entry's payload object. Only one scope may own runtime mutation tracking in a test realm at a time. Overlapping or nested scopes fail explicitly, including while another scope is disposing. Do not use concurrent tests for shared patch/registry state. Disposal keeps ownership until known service-startup and component lifecycle work settles; when testing a deliberately deferred operation, begin disposal, release that operation, and then await disposal. Arbitrary detached asynchronous callbacks are not canceled by the harness: the test author must await or stop them before the scope ends. createTestScope() is available when lifecycle control is required; always await scope.dispose() in finally and preserve both the test error and cleanup errors. withTestScope handles that combination. Do not call scope.dispose() from a component teardown callback; the harness rejects that reentry instead of making cleanup await itself. While a returned asynchronous teardown callback is pending, additional disposal calls are refused even from outside that callback. Keep and await the first disposal promise. Ordinary repeated disposal calls during pending service startup share that first promise when no teardown callback is pending.

MockRpc<Contract> accepts caller-owned operation types with request and response members. Import response/request DTOs from their generated owner; TypeScript checks handler arguments and results. Register each operation with on, call it with call, and inspect calls. An operation without a handler rejects rather than silently returning an empty value. Handler errors propagate. The harness does not invent production view request types or a universal model/method map. UIX supplies generation tooling and its test-only schema; production view slices own their DTOs. The harness suite checks the generic boundary against generated declarations, including the human client's generated company DTO. Mock success establishes neither HTTP transport nor authorization acceptance. Keep live server and browser tests for those boundaries.

Place workspace harness suites under web/packages/*/tests/*.test.ts or addon suites under addons/<name>/static/tests/*.test.ts; the shared Vitest configuration discovers them. Use the pinned web toolchain and the normal TypeScript checks. Builds and tests run on an approved build host through the documented sync path, never on the editing laptop. A leaked-patch error identifies remaining members. Restore manual patches or move intentional registration into scope ownership. A cleanup error remains a failure even when another cleanup succeeded; inspect all errors in an aggregate before retrying. Do not turn these errors into ignored teardown warnings.

web/scripts/browser-human-ui.mjs exercises the compiled client in an isolated Chrome profile against loopback HTTP protocol fixtures. It checks login rendering, list and form interactions, search, Settings, Addons, confirmation, loading and permission-dialog recovery at desktop and narrow widths. The fixture supplies its own records and denied responses: it does not establish real authentication, authorization grants, database persistence, multi-node behavior or deployment acceptance. The full CI browser stage runs this fixture as web-browser-human-ui. It builds erp-ui-compiler-cli's erp-ui-compile executable from the same revision, through the build gate with cargo build --locked, and honors CARGO_TARGET_DIR. It then sets ERP_UI_COMPILER to that executable and runs node web/scripts/build-human-ui.mjs --addons web,acceptance_notes. The explicit addon list is required because the fixture exercises the acceptance-notes title widget; the asset builder's default selects only web. Run the full check from a clean, committed task worktree. Have the operator set ERP_CI_HOST to an approved build host: CI_HOST="${ERP_CI_HOST:?Select an approved build host}" scripts/ci-remote.sh --no-wait <slice> The wrapper syncs the revision, starts CI under nohup, and prints the remote location. Follow that existing run with --wait; do not launch a duplicate run while it is active. Standalone scripts/ci.sh --lane web retains its cargo-free TypeScript/Vitest checks and does not run this compiler-dependent fixture. Use the pinned web toolchain on the build host. Chrome must already be installed; CHROME_BIN can select its executable. On macOS the default is /Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome. A missing or non-executable browser fails the check with its path. Report that prerequisite to the operator rather than installing software or skipping the browser step. CI runs the complete default/light fixture with its diagnostic and reduced-scope options disabled. Each run gets a fresh directory under logs/browser-human-ui-<revision>-<timestamp>.*, with evidence/result.json and screenshots. Keep the surrounding CI log as well. A successful result records the source revision, asset hashes, browser version, host and capture time. A missing, failed, mismatched-revision or diagnostic-only result cannot satisfy the gate. For a focused rerun after building the compiler from the same revision on the approved build host, choose a new output directory rather than reusing an old receipt. The wrapper sync can remove generated assets, so rebuild them inside the wrapped command: scripts/mini-build.sh <slice> 'set -eu eval "$(scripts/web-toolchain.sh env)" target_dir="${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-target}" case "$target_dir" in /*) compiler="$target_dir/debug/erp-ui-compile" ;; *) compiler="$PWD/$target_dir/debug/erp-ui-compile" ;; esac ERP_UI_COMPILER="$compiler" node web/scripts/build-human-ui.mjs --addons web,acceptance_notes mkdir -p logs capture=$(mktemp -d "$PWD/logs/browser-human-ui-focused.XXXXXX") env -u CLIENT_BROWSER_CDP CLIENT_BROWSER_OUTPUT="$capture/evidence" CLIENT_BROWSER_THEME=light CLIENT_BROWSER_OFFICE_BLUE=0 CLIENT_BROWSER_LIST_ONLY=0 CLIENT_BROWSER_DIALOG_PROBE=0 CLIENT_BROWSER_VIEWPORT_ONLY=0 node web/scripts/browser-human-ui.mjs' Preserve the complete failure log before diagnosing a stale assertion or client defect. A missing browser, failed asset build or fixture setup error is not proof of a product regression. The functional browser checks do not enable the deferred product performance inventory.

Keep extension fixtures under an addon's test directory (or the test package's tests/fixtures/ directory); do not import them from production addon entry points. The UI6 completion fixture in web/packages/elang-test/tests/fixtures/extension-test-addon.ts is a small copyable example. It adds one validated registry entry and patches one component method. Define the typed category in the scope, register addons through the normal loader, and keep registration inside scope.manage so the harness owns the patch handles: import { registerAddons } from "@erpforall/elang"; import { withTestScope } from "@erpforall/elang-test"; import { extensionTestAddon } from "./fixtures/extension-test-addon.js"; class Heading { label(): string { return "Base"; } } await withTestScope(async scope => { scope.manage(() => { scope.registries.define("extensionTemplate", (value): value is string => typeof value === "string"); }); scope.manage(() => registerAddons([ extensionTestAddon({ id: "first", label: "First", target: Heading.prototype }), extensionTestAddon({ id: "second", label: "Second", target: Heading.prototype }), ], { registry: scope.registries })); expect(new Heading().label()).toBe("Base / First / Second"); }); After the scope closes, check that the component returns its original value and that the scope's registry hub no longer contains the test category. The fixture proves this small composition and cleanup path; it does not replace addon installation or browser end-to-end tests.

The opt-in Contacts List test logs into the existing reference, switches the real Contacts action to List mode, and asserts that the rendered table contains at least one row. It reads the view only and writes a redacted JSON receipt (row count and route, no record values) with mode 0600: set -a && . "$HOME/.config/erpforall/odoo-ui-ref.env" && set +a && eval "$(scripts/web-toolchain.sh env)" && node web/scripts/odoo-reference-view-test.mjs --origin http://127.0.0.1:18369 --output /tmp/ui6-odoo-list The operator-managed file must be outside the checkout, mode 0600, and export ODOO_UI_REF_PASSWORD; never pass the value on the command line or save it in the repository. HTTP is allowed only on loopback; use HTTPS for network hosts. The output directory must not already exist; choose a fresh path for each run. The Odoo demo must already be running. A missing credential, unsafe origin, authentication error, HTTP failure or empty list fails the test with a clear error. The receipt is an observation of this one list flow; it does not establish backend authorization parity, form behavior or full view parity. Keep the receipt with the slice evidence. Playwright fixtures belong to the shell tests.

The focused runner (run-focused.sh) exercises the shared Rust/browser URL corpus and mounted-app search integration. The native runner (run-native.sh http) runs the actual CLI server HTTP boundary; run-native.sh browser additionally builds the compiler/client at the synced revision and drives web/scripts/browser-shell-url.mjs. Run these only through the build gate on an approved host, with a clean scripts/sync.sh revision and its protected .env. Before invoking either runner, include $HOME/.cargo/bin in PATH and evaluate eval "$(scripts/web-toolchain.sh env)" in that same remote shell. The SSH login shell's default Node is not the pinned web toolchain and can fail driver syntax before any test runs. Use an approved remote build host under its build gate. Historical receipts retain their original host and source; new runs need their own exact-source receipts. Initialize the pinned toolchain in the same gated invocation as the runner, before its syntax check or builds. The internal deployment and development setup documents own host selection. The browser mode reuses the installed-fixture private handoff in support/wizard_browser.rs, starts the real native server/database, and checks source/asset revision plus manifest hashes. It requires the operator-owned Playwright installation at ~/.local/share/erpforall-qa and an installed Chrome (CHROME_BIN, default /usr/bin/google-chrome for this Linux runner). Credentials remain in a mode-600 temporary fixture contract and must never be copied to evidence. Only credential-free result JSON, screenshots and command output belong in the branch. The native HTTP assertions run with the ordinary human_runtime suite. Browser mode is explicit installed acceptance for the shell; the broader browser-stage and retention work remains open. Protocol fixtures alone do not prove native acceptance.

docs.title: Countries, Federal States, and Country Groups

sections.text: The base addon supplies res.country, res.country.state, and res.country.group.

Country records represent sovereign nations or autonomous territories. - name: Required country name (e.g. "Indonesia", "United States"). - code: Required, unique 2-letter uppercase ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code (e.g. "ID", "US"). Lowercase inputs are sanitized to uppercase on create and write. - address_format: Report address presentation template string, defaulting to: '%(street)s
%(street2)s
%(city)s %(state_code)s %(zip)s
%(country_name)s'. - currency_id: Foreign key to res.currency. - phone_code: International telephone dialing prefix integer. - country_group_ids: Many-to-many relationship linking member res.country.group records. - state_ids: One-to-many relationship linking subdivision res.country.state records. The helper method get_address_fields extracts all interpolation field placeholders from address_format.

Federal states represent first-level administrative subdivisions of countries (states, provinces, cantons). - country_id: Required many-to-one link to res.country (indexed, ondelete restrict). - name: Required state name (e.g. "California", "West Java"). - code: State code, unique per country (unique (country_id, code)).

Country groups represent trade, tax, or regional country clusters (such as "EU", "SEPA", "GCC"). - name: Group name. - code: Optional unique uppercase code. - country_ids: Many-to-many link to constituent countries.

res.partner integrates geographic addressing via: - country_id: Many-to-one to res.country. - state_id: Many-to-one to res.country.state, dynamically filtered by the partner's country_id. - country_code: Related read-only ISO code from country_id.code. - _address_fields: Address propagation includes state_id and country_id. Contact children automatically synchronize their country and state with their parent company address.

docs.title: Extending other addons, data-only models and custom fields

sections.text: Status: implemented. Native extension across crates, models/*.toml of data-only addons and custom x_ models and fields reach the registry and the database schema. Installing a data-only addon (module state, data records) is covered by the module lifecycle; turning ir.model/ir.model.fields rows into an overlay comes with the work that adds those models (ADR 0026). Every example here is taken from code that builds and runs in CI: crates/erp-test-models/addons/test_ext_* (native crates), crates/erp-modules/tests/fixtures/test_data_only (data-only addon) and the tests crates/erp-test-models/tests/cross_addon.rs, crates/erp-registry/tests/overlay.rs, crates/erp-modules/tests/model_files.rs. For an overview of how Odoo concepts map to ERPForAll and a complete worked example, see [Odoo compatibility](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/odoo-compatibility.md).
Your addon is its own crate. It depends on the crate of the addon it extends, and its manifest and addon!() name that addon:
[dependencies] erp-sdk = { workspace = true } erp-addon-test_ext_a = { workspace = true }

name = "Test Ext B" depends = ["base", "test_ext_a"] // addons/test_ext_b/src/lib.rs use erp_addon_test_ext_a::Book; use erp_sdk::prelude::*; erp_sdk::addon!(name = "test_ext_b", depends = ["test_ext_a"]);
pub struct BookPages { #[field(integer)] pub pages: i32, #[field(char, string = "ISBN")] pub isbn: Option<Arc<str>>, }

impl BookPages { #[method(override)] async fn describe(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, sup: Super) -> Result<String> { let pages = this.get(tx, BookPages::PAGES).await?; Ok(format!("{}, {pages} pages", sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), ()).await?)) } } - Inside your crate, #[extend] and #[methods] need no addon = "...": they belong to the addon your crate root declares with addon!(). - test_ext_a does not know test_ext_b. Any number of addons extend the same model and the same method; test_ext_c does it too, independently of test_ext_b. - Overrides run newest first in load order (dependency depth, then name): with a, b and c installed, describe runs C, then B through sup, then A, and returns "book Dune, 412 pages [3/5]". - Field handles of your extension (BookPages::PAGES: Field<Book, i32>) work on Book recordsets and in Vals<Book>, like the defining addon's own. - Linking a crate does not install its addon. Only addons in the database's addon set contribute fields, columns and overrides. A handle of a linked addon that is not installed fails with Programming: Invalid field 'rating' on 'test_ext.book'.

When an extension adds values to an existing selection field (via selection_add), each added value can declare an ondelete policy that specifies what happens to records holding that value when the extending addon is uninstalled (SPEC-FIELD-034, SPEC-FIELD-035, SPEC-DATA-029): use erp_registry::decl::{FieldDecl, SelectionOnDeleteDecl}; FieldDecl::selection_add_ondelete( "state", &[("archived", Some("Archived"))], &[("archived", SelectionOnDeleteDecl::Cascade)], ) Native #[field] declarations can bind the existing cleanup metadata directly, for example #[field(selection, selection_add = [("archived", "Archived")], ondelete = [("archived", "set default")])]. The attribute accepts set null, cascade and set default; required selections must choose a non-null policy, and set default requires a declared default. Unknown policies and duplicate cleanup keys are compile errors. The lower-level registry API below also supports explicit replacement values and callbacks. This native attribute binding does not add selection support to the WASI descriptor loader, which continues to refuse unsupported selection declarations. The supported ondelete policies are: - "set null" (SelectionOnDeleteDecl::SetNull): Resets the selection field to NULL / False on affected records (the default when no policy is specified). If the selection field is marked required, "set null" is rejected at setup with a Programming error (Odoo parity: fields_selection.py:151). - "cascade" (SelectionOnDeleteDecl::Cascade): Deletes records holding this selection value via ORM unlink (with force_delete=true), executing unlink hooks and cleaning up external IDs. - "set default" (SelectionOnDeleteDecl::SetDefault): Resets affected records to the field's default value. Setup fails loudly if the field defines no default. - "set <value>" (SelectionOnDeleteDecl::SetValue("val")): Resets affected records to <value>. Setup fails loudly if <value> is not an existing valid option in the field's final selection. - Callable / Callback (SelectionOnDeleteDecl::Callback("callback_name")): Dispatches to an async callback registered on OrmBuilder::selection_callback / Transaction::call_selection_callback(name, ids). Setup fails loudly if the callback name is empty or duplicate.

- **Multi-addon preservation**: If multiple addons add the same selection value, records are only purged when the last addon providing that value is uninstalled. If another installed addon retains the value, records remain untouched. - **Savepoint isolation and SQL fallback (safe_write)**: Selection updates are attempted via the ORM inside a savepoint so model write overrides can execute. If an override raises an error, the savepoint rolls back cleanly and a direct parameterized SQL update (UPDATE ... WHERE id = ANY($1)) is performed. This guarantees that custom write overrides cannot block module uninstallation. - **Company-dependent selections**: Company-dependent selection fields stored as JSONB dictionaries are cleaned across all company keys using batch SQL.
An addon without Rust (a folder with manifest.toml, data files and models/*.toml) declares and extends models in TOML. The result is the same registry metadata as #[model]/#[extend].

[[model]] name = "test_data_only.tag" description = "Tag" order = "sequence, name" [[model.field]] name = "name" type = "char" string = "Tag Name" required = true [[model.field]] name = "sequence" type = "integer" default = 10 [[model.field]] name = "color" type = "selection" selection = [["red", "Red"], ["green", "Green"]] default = "red"

[[model]] extend = "res.users" [[model.field]] name = "tag_id" type = "many2one" comodel = "test_data_only.tag" ondelete = "set null" [[model.field]] name = "tag_name" type = "char" related = "tag_id.name"

| Key | Meaning | |---|---| | name | a new model (_name) | | extend | extend an existing model in place (_inherit of itself); exactly one of name/extend | | inherit | parent models: prototype inheritance for a new model, extra mixins for an extension | | description, order, rec_name | _description, _order, _rec_name | | table | _table (new models only) | | transient, abstract | the model class of a new model (default: regular). Leave them out on extend: the extension takes the kind of the model it extends (abstract and transient models included); if you state one, it must match | | field | the fields, as [[model.field]] tables |
