Static groups/invisible prune its subtree on the server. Unknown attributes, nested/duplicate asides and service-form asides refuse. Ordinary field permissions remain authoritative. Inherited views can insert an aside with an XPath after //sheet or extend its groups. Both appearances place it beside the sheet on wide screens and stack it on narrow screens. Fields share the parent record's draft/save and validation lifecycle. The four fields in this example require model log access and are record information, not a complete event audit or approval workflow.

<form> <sheet>...</sheet> <chatter reload_on_post="1" open_attachments="0"/> </form> <chatter/> belongs directly to a record form, at most once, and may sit beside an aside. It has no children and takes only the flags reload_on_post, reload_on_attachment, reload_on_activity, reload_on_follower and open_attachments (default false). Each flag accepts only 1, 0, true, false, True or False; any other text refuses, unlike Odoo, which treats any non-empty text as true. groups and invisible are not accepted. The model must inherit mail.thread, otherwise get_views fails with View element <chatter> requires model '<model>' to inherit 'mail.thread'. The server sets has_activities from mail.activity.mixin; it is never written in the XML. Refusals appear when views are served, not when the XML view is saved. Placement under sheet, aside, group or page and in service forms refuses. This slice delivers the node and an empty slot only (side column under the aside on wide Office Blue, after the sheet on narrow screens and the Default theme; none in dialogs, x2many forms or the relation editor). Messages, followers and activities are planned, and no registered model inherits mail.thread yet. Older clients refuse the unknown chatter node, so ship the client with the server. A <chatter> inside a conditional wrapper (<t groups="...">) is refused. The side-column placement (wide Office Blue only) has no browser check yet: Playwright check not run. Spec cases: SPEC-FORMXML-008, -009, -010; ADR 0104 addendum. Sheet belongs directly to form. Groups accept optional name/string and static col/colspan. Columns are even label/control track counts2..12; two tracks make one field column. Default col is4 when a group has child groups, otherwise2. Default colspan2 applies inside parent groups; top-level groups occupy the sheet row. Put groups inside one outer group for side-by-side sections. Phone layout becomes one column. Notebook contains page elements only. A page needs name or string; an absent caption uses its name, and visible names within one notebook must be unique. Static groups and invisible on containers are evaluated server-side before descendant field lookup. A separator has optional string/name and occupies its group's row. Arbitrary HTML, classes, odd track counts and dynamic layout modifiers remain explicitly unsupported. List and service views retain their existing closed grammar. The first name/char field remains the human client's prominent title; registered custom widgets continue to render inside the declared container. Field widgets retain required, readonly and native validation behavior. Notebook changes preserve draft edits and selected page through onchange; they do not save. On save, the first invalid field's page opens before native validity feedback. Existing save/discard/navigation rules still apply. This is not whole Odoo form parity. The smart-button subset below is supported; broader statusbar, arbitrary templates, chatter and relational subview behavior remains subject to the individual form slices.

Static per-view field modifiers are part of the human metadata contract (ADR 0091). Declare readonly, required, invisible and force_save on each field occurrence. The existing static boolean spellings are 0, 1, false, true, False, True. Omitted readonly/required inherit model presentation metadata; explicit false overrides it in that view. Omitted invisible/force_save are false. Record forms also accept dynamic readonly, required and invisible expressions (ADR 0124); force_save stays a literal. List views refuse dynamic field expressions until rows evaluate them ([views guide](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/views.md#field-widget-presentation-contract)). These field rules do not alter the container pruning rules above. <field name="reference" readonly="1" force_save="1"/> <field name="note" required="0"/> <field name="internal_token" invisible="1"/> An invisible authorized field keeps its read/default/onchange/draft values, with no rendered control/column. Hiding it does not make it secret. Group and server field access are the security boundary. View required false removes client validation only; server ORM requirements still apply. Readonly prevents control edits; it does not grant or revoke write permission. force_save lets present readonly defaults/onchange/draft changes participate in save/create; it never makes the control editable. Without force_save readonly changes are omitted from save, while onchange still includes readonly state. id always stays readonly and is never written. Repeated nodes keep individual presentation, while the view's record policy combines readonly and invisible with AND, required and force_save with OR. Use consistent required flags where possible: any required occurrence makes the combined visible field required. Form/list and relational line policies are independent. Existing relation command/value normalization applies. Functional documentation gap: docs/user/forms.md does not yet exist; a user page should explain required markers, readonly values, hidden values, server save refusals and draft retention. This authoring guide does not establish a delivered user-facing capability.

A one2many in a form shows its lines with the comodel's default list and edits a line in the comodel's default form. When two fields of one form point at the same comodel and must show different columns (the product lines and the journal items of an invoice are both account.move.line), a field names the views of its lines in its context, with the keys Odoo uses: <field name="invoice_line_ids" context="{'list_view_ref': 'account.view_invoice_line_list', 'form_view_ref': 'account.view_invoice_line_form'}"/> The values are qualified XML ids of views of the comodel. The client asks the comodel's views with these keys, the server selects the named views, and a name that does not resolve is refused by the server. A field without them keeps the default views. The context must be a constant: one that reads a record value is not used for the views. A group of amounts (<group string="Totals"> with monetary fields) is an ordinary leaf group: one field per row, label and value on the group's two tracks.

Declare

inside a record form or sheet. Field names are ordinary model metadata, not a reserved convention. h2 is also supported; title children can be ordinary fields or headings, and headings contain fields. The div accepts only exact class oe_title, name, groups and static invisible; headings accept name, groups and static invisible. Normal XML inheritance and field authorization still apply. Titles remain inside their declared form/sheet, group or page scope. Main record routes keep the editable title out of the command header and preserve native form ownership and validation. A view without this declaration keeps its previous title fallback at the existing field occurrence. Spans, literal text, extra classes, dynamic labels and richer upstream title markup are not supported and fail explicitly. See ADR 0106. This does not add field permissions.

A named area belongs directly inside a record-form sheet. Addons may insert into it with or alter a button's attributes using normal view inheritance. The combined arch determines ordering and placement.
The example requires an actual model integer/float line_count and an RPC-exposed open_lines method. Neither is generated by XML. The server applies groups to containers, buttons and fields. Record-dependent button invisible expressions can only use fields admitted in this view. The button caption comes from its explicit string or the first statistic field's explicit string. Statistics are readonly; zero is displayed as zero and missing values as an em dash. Do not add required, readonly or force_save attributes to statistic fields. Clicks use the existing object-button path: confirmation, save for a dirty/new record, public method RPC and the normalized action-result handler. type="action", contexts, icons, percent widgets and arbitrary nested HTML remain unsupported with an explicit error. A data-only addon needs a real supported action/field provider before it can show a counter; XML never invents values from relation lengths or labels. Buttons wrap within their sheet; the Odoo overflow menu and dialog-specific hiding are not implemented. Operations: install/upgrade changed view XML through the normal addon lifecycle; no new server settings or services. Functional-page gap remains docs/user/forms.md: the future page must explain related-record action values, save-before-action, access filtering and error behavior.

ADR 0108 adds the ERPForAll-specific read-only record method relation_count. For a registered direct one2many loan_ids on an installed book model, send: {"ids": [42], "field": "loan_ids"} Use /erp/json/2//relation_count. The response is a nonnegative integer counting target records visible to the caller, including model/field, record/company and active filtering. Target ACL is checked even at zero. Errors remain errors. No schema, settings, grants or data migration is introduced. Only a stored direct O2M with a stored M2O inverse is supported. Computed, related, inherited, nonstored, field-domain/context relations and other relation types refuse explicitly. Dirty unsaved relations are not counted. Every call reads its transaction snapshot; later navigation can see concurrent committed changes. This method is an ERPForAll extension, with no standard Odoo method/widget parity claim. It does not change numeric statinfo behavior or register a fake count field. Use the explicit ERPForAll provider inside a smart button:
The object method must be genuinely exposed by the installed addon. Count-only relations are excluded from normal record reads/defaults/onchange/write payloads. If another occurrence is an ordinary sublist, it retains its own read/edit policy. The component shows loading and error states, guards old responses and refetches on render after save/reload/action return. New forms display an em dash and disable this related action until saved. Dirty unsaved relation edits are counted after save. Error details stay visible in the existing error surface and statistic tooltip. Library's base1.0.3 adds the named empty box; optional package1.3.6 inserts the Loans button and an exposed open_loans action through XPath. Stage the matching server/client first, then perform the coordinated native sample_library update with the verified previous release identity before upgrading the stored package. Only then reopen human forms and activate the release under the existing lifecycle procedure. The prior base lacks the XPath target; upgrading only the package is unsupported and must fail, rather than silently inserting a second region. No schema/grants/settings change is needed; installed-content identities and addon version/source receipts must follow the standard upgrade path. Browser/package acceptance status is recorded in docs/design/relation-count.md.

Native composition can call ModuleSystem::upgrade_authorized with the same trusted InstallAuthorizer adapter used by installation. The historical adapter name remains for compatibility. It checks the primary session, active user and current system authority in the supplied transaction after the module lifecycle lock; adapters must not commit or open a separate transaction. The engine binds that human as the actor while running elevated module work. The request contains between one and 64 unique module names. Every target must be installed. Every upgraded target and installed reverse dependent must have a known matching installed artifact receipt. Linked native code also needs matching build provenance. Known data-only addons can participate in upgrades; newly installed dependencies still use the existing human-install data-only allowlist. Unattested, replaced or missing content refuses before effects. Unrelated pending CLI operations are refused and preserved. Both authorized install and upgrade write erp_module_lifecycle_audit inside the lifecycle transaction: actor, session, operation, requested names, sorted resolved names, separate installed and upgraded sets, and committed outcome. Installation also preserves its existing install audit. A failed operation or audit insert rolls back together. Runtime credentials have no access to the new table or its sequence. Post-commit failures remain explicit in OperationOutcome; they do not mean that committed state or audit rolled back. Callers must use the returned ORM generation. The sealed POST /erp/module/upgrade adapter accepts exactly {modules:["addon_name"]}. It requires the active primary administrator session and the accepted same-origin JSON protocol, then uses the same authorizer under engine ownership. API keys cannot authorize the route. Success contains separate upgraded and newly installed name sets, registry_version and asset_version, after runtime grants and complete Auth/RPC/assets publication. Native POST /erp/module/uninstall validates the primary administrator session and delegates to ModuleSystem::uninstall_authorized with its trusted session authorizer. It preserves the engine's refusal, unknown commit outcome and committed recovery distinctions. The shipped composition has configured Signal, a package runtime and a host asset lifecycle service. Under ADR 0186, configured Signal stores backed by verified native storage are safely opened before lazy BEGIN and generation reads; complete package/host effects and the preview bridge are planned. ModuleSystem::uninstall_composition_blocker() reports the first static blocker in order: package runtime, custom data loader, registered lifecycle services. Configured Signal is safely admitted when backed by verified native storage (ADR 0186). The typed UninstallCompositionBlocker::message() returns a fixed diagnostic. This inspection performs no SQL or callbacks and grants no authority. None means that further transaction-bound admission is required, including schema, installed artifact identity, current authority and confirmed membership; it never establishes that uninstall will succeed. | Composition | Confirmed-impact engine admission | |---|---| | Minimal callback-free, unconfigured system | Continues transaction-bound schema, identity, authority and fingerprint checks; existing supported subset can succeed | | Configured Signal | Safely admitted when backed by verified native storage (ADR 0186); non-native storage types or aggregate overloads refuse during idle source preflight | | Package runtime, including an empty runtime | Refuses undescribed package callbacks; CONFIRMED-EFFECTS prerequisite | | Custom data loader | Refuses undescribed purge callbacks; CONFIRMED-EFFECTS prerequisite | | Registered host lifecycle service | Refuses before effects rather than skipping the service; CONFIRMED-EFFECTS prerequisite | | Full base addon schema/model composition | Independent unsupported schema, model and callback effects still refuse; absence of a static blocker does not admit them | Authorized addon detail and ir.module.module.erp_preview_uninstall report that composition reason. Preview returns no successful fingerprint. If a custom composition has no static blocker, the native JSON-2 preview binder still refuses because it lacks a trusted-session confirmed-impact bridge. It does not start an owner lifecycle operation inside the existing request transaction. The existing callback-free minimal engine seam remains separately callable through its trusted native API. ir.module.module.erp_addon_detail is an authorized Read RPC taking name, optional limit (default 50, maximum 100), and optional dependencies_cursor, dependents_cursor, menus_cursor and views_cursor. Its collections carry items and explicit nullable next_cursor. Installed metadata ownership comes from durable module provenance, and descriptions remain plain text. Cursors bind the addon, collection and metadata revision; changed or malformed cursors refuse. The complete response is limited to 65,536 bytes. These are admission bounds, not measured performance. The metadata snapshot additionally refuses more than 10,000 entries or more than 1 MiB before paging; per-field text bounds also apply. The Rust wire declarations and generated TypeScript own the contract. ADR 0120 preserves commit certainty through managed lifecycle execution. A typed unknown commit answer requires reconciliation and bypasses cleanup that assumes rollback. After known commit, failed post-commit work or publication returns a committed recovery error with a stage. Neither error is permission to replay the write. There is no addon-overridable lifecycle mutation RPC. Legacy bootstrap with no active administrator may predate private lifecycle audit storage. Grant publication permits complete absence until an authorized lifecycle operation creates it, revokes both private objects when present, and refuses an incomplete table/sequence pair with operator recovery. It does not silently grant audit access or perform a schema migration under the users-table lock.

Lifecycle operations bind each installed addon to a durable content receipt, separate from the available catalog and the whole build identity. An unknown legacy receipt refuses upgrade/uninstall with identity unknown, run identity-enroll first; replacing files without changing the manifest version also refuses. A snapshot admitted within the operation supplies the consumed bytes; symlinks and hard-link aliases are refused. Device/inode checks apply only within that operation, so a copied release with identical content retains its identity. The confirming uninstall (ModuleSystem::uninstall_authorized) runs its operation transaction at READ COMMITTED, while preview stays at REPEATABLE READ. Confirmation takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE membership locks after its opening statements, and a REPEATABLE READ snapshot taken before that wait would not see a writer that committed during it. A fixed snapshot would then pass the fingerprint check and drop the writer's row. With every writer fenced out by the lock, per-statement snapshots are current and consistent. An InstallAuthorizer used for confirmation therefore runs raw statements only; record-API calls fail loudly with a Programming error. The authorizer's session check also reads current state after the lock wait. An operator reviews the existing database's artifact provenance before using erp module identity-enroll --config <protected-server.toml> --operator <identity> --note <reason> <addon>.... Enrollment is explicit and audited, including operator, database timestamp, note and per-addon hashes. No installed addon receives an automatic legacy exemption. Protect the owner credentials and enrollment command as database administration authority. A successful forward release activation can transition changed per-addon receipts atomically after migration, pointer switch and health verification. Unchanged receipts remain unchanged. Ordinary native runtime upgrade never re-stamps. A successful authorized forward package upgrade is a separate transition point: under the existing package lifecycle lock and fresh authorization, validate the old receipt against the current verified installed package and stored archive digest before applying the candidate. Commit its new verified archive digest with package storage, lifecycle effects and audit in the same transaction. Failed upgrades retain the prior receipt. Neither automatic restore nor manual rollback re-stamps. A receipt mismatch following recovery requires an explicit operator decision; do not treat enrollment as a substitute for reviewing database compatibility. File-content identity authorizes lifecycle operations on addon artifacts; it is not a database schema-version check (that admission check is planned). These changes do not widen the impact planner's supported effect subset. The full base composition and unsupported effects retain their named refusals; no successful configured native uninstall is implied. Identity storage is owner-only: installed_addon_identity, installed_addon_identity_audit and the latter's sequence are excluded from request-role grants. Schema-sync creates empty storage on an older database; it does not approve whichever files happen to be present. A first install creates its receipt atomically with installation, and uninstall removes it atomically with lifecycle effects. The release helper uses the candidate binary's identity-activate administration command after a matching successful migration receipt, active-pointer verification and health check. Candidate migration uses the verified previous release to validate the installed preimage; it does not stamp new content early. An identity-publication error can mean that the transaction outcome is uncertain: keep the reported candidate state, inspect the owner-side outcome and reconcile before retrying. Do not infer rollback from an error returned after commit. An explicit native candidate upgrade with identity_previous commits per-addon migration evidence in installed_addon_identity_audit with operation forward-migrate, binding each changed upgraded addon's previous installed hash and exact candidate hash. The installed receipt remains unchanged until activation. Activation requires that committed evidence for every changed installed addon; upgrading only selected modules does not authorize a changed sibling omitted from that upgrade. Durable receipts and lifecycle locking coordinate cooperating instances. Node admission/rollout integration remains subject to the actual serving path; a lifecycle lock does not fence older nodes that do not participate. Do not treat successful single-instance enrollment as proof of a safe mixed-version rollout. Product performance evidence is deferred under ADR 0065; the snapshot limits are safety admission bounds. Operator composition resolves configured search-directory prefixes once, including the release current pointer and a host temporary-directory alias. It preserves the final configured directory and every discovered addon root for no-follow admission; linked addon roots and descendants still refuse. Identity administration verifies stored packages into a fresh process without loading/replaying pending lifecycle work, then rechecks their stored archive identity under lifecycle ownership. Artifact identity follows release packaging: dependency/build caches and repository/desktop metadata named node_modules, target, .git, __pycache__ or .DS_Store are excluded. Do not reference these paths from lifecycle data; the engine refuses them. Ship generated runtime assets outside those reserved paths. Symlinks at excluded entries themselves still refuse, and excluded contents are never used as a fallback data source.

The web client's addon administration panel (addonsView) implements lifecycle interactions over the authorized transport: 1. **Authorized Detail View**: Clicking any addon tile outside of direct action buttons navigates to an in-place authorized detail view. It queries ir.module.module.erp_addon_detail and displays complete manifest metadata, technical name, lifecycle state badge, icon, summary, rich description, and key facts (Author, Version, Installed version). Dependencies, reverse dependents, created menus, and created views are presented in separate sections with cursor pagination ("Load more"), querying the server with collection-specific cursors without reloading the view. The Back button and Escape restore the catalog grid and refocus the triggering card. 2. **Upgrade Confirmation Flow**: Triggering the Upgrade button (from either the catalog tile or the detail header) displays a native confirmation dialog asking for explicit confirmation. On confirmation, it issues POST /erp/module/upgrade with { modules: [name] } and write: true. On successful upgrade publication, it alerts the user and reloads the application. When upgrade is refused by server metadata (e.g. unavailable source or transitional state), the button is disabled and displays the refusal reason note. 3. **Destructive Uninstall Modal**: Clicking Uninstall first queries ir.module.module.erp_preview_uninstall to compute impacted reverse dependents, dropped models, and exact database record counts. It opens an accessible modal <dialog> with: - Warning alert regarding data deletion; - Complete list of resolved affected modules; - Dropped models table displaying Model name, SQL Table name, and exact Record count; - Total affected record count summary; - Accessible keyboard focus trap (Tab / Shift+Tab constrained between Cancel and Confirm) and Escape / Cancel dismissal restoring focus to the opener button. Confirming uninstallation submits the preview fingerprint to POST /erp/module/uninstall. If the database state changed between preview calculation and confirmation, the server responds with 409 Conflict; the client traps this condition, alerts the user that database state changed, and prompts for a fresh preview confirmation.

In a multi-node topology where multiple application servers connect to a shared PostgreSQL database and shared addon repository: 1. **Global advisory lock serialization**: ModuleSystem serializes lifecycle mutations using PostgreSQL transaction-bound advisory locks. Concurrent upgrade, install, or uninstall requests across different nodes are serialized in the database: a request that overlaps a running operation is refused with 422 UserError ("ERPForAll is currently processing another module operation. ...", SPEC-MOD-028), and the caller retries. On any individual node, re-entrant concurrent invocations are rejected immediately with a Concurrency error ("A native installation is already running"). 2. **Authority revocation across nodes**: Lifecycle administrative operations (erp_addon_detail, erp_preview_uninstall, POST /erp/module/upgrade, POST /erp/module/uninstall) require an active primary administrator session belonging to base.group_system. When administrative group membership or session validity is revoked in the database, all cluster nodes immediately deny subsequent operations with 403 AccessError or 401 Unauthorized, leaving durable database records, audit entries, and identities intact. 3. **Stale impact confirmation refusal**: Uninstall execution recomputes the exact impact fingerprint within the lifecycle transaction under the database lock. If concurrent changes occur between preview and confirmation, or if an invalid/mismatched fingerprint is submitted, confirmation is refused across all nodes with 409 Conflict (or 422 ValidationError under configured Signal compositions), ensuring no unverified or widened schema/data deletion occurs. 4. **Node loss resilience**: If an application node holding or waiting on a lifecycle lock terminates or crashes (SIGTERM/SIGKILL), PostgreSQL automatically closes the backend connection and releases all transaction and advisory locks. Surviving peer nodes proceed with lifecycle queries and operations without deadlocks or lingering orphaned locks. 5. **Survivor maintenance and refresh**: When any node commits a lifecycle operation that advances erp_signal_generation(key='registry'), surviving peer nodes observe the superseded signal upon their next request. The request layer triggers NativeLifecycle::refresh to reload the updated registry, recompile runtime Auth/RPC services, and publish fresh assets. A POST that met the superseded registry (a JSON-2 call, a lifecycle request) is refused with 503 ("Server busy; retry later.", Retry-After) and never replayed; a safe GET navigation is retried once on the new services (SPEC-HUMAN-006). If a survivor cannot complete publication (e.g. a module left in to upgrade, or runtime grants not published), it stays in maintenance and answers 503 until a rebuild succeeds; failed rebuilds back off from 1 s, doubling up to 60 s. It never serves inconsistent or corrupt state.

Status: implemented (ADR 0040 D5, design docs/design/m3-ormx.md §6). Field indexes brin and gin, typed model-level indexes with include and a constant filter (a partial index such as `WHERE state = 'open'), from native addons and from models/*.toml`. Every Rust example in this page is compiled and run as a doctest of erp-test-models (`cargo test --doc, part of scripts/ci.sh`), through the same registry checks a server runs at startup. Lines starting with #  are hidden setup.

index on a field takes Odoo's three kinds and two more: | index = | Index | For | |---|---|---| | true, "btree" | USING btree (f) | equality, ranges, ordering (the default for many2one fields) | | "btree_not_null" | USING btree (f) WHERE f IS NOT NULL | columns that are mostly empty | | "trigram" | USING gin (f gin_trgm_ops), accent-folded like ilike when that is indexable | ilike substring search; needs the pg_trgm extension | | "brin" | USING brin (f) | date, datetime and integer fields whose values follow the insert order | | "gin" | USING gin (f jsonb_path_ops) | json fields searched by containment (@>) or JSON path (@?, @@) |
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

pub struct EventLog { #[field(integer, index = "brin")] pub seq: i32, #[field(json, index = "gin")] pub payload: Option<erp_sdk::serde_json::Value>, } /// The audit field create_date of the log gets a BRIN index too: an #[extend] may set index /// on a field it does not declare, like any other attribute.
pub struct EventLogDates { #[field(datetime, index = "brin")] pub create_date: Option<DateTime>, }

**When BRIN helps.** A BRIN index stores the smallest and largest value of each block range of the table (128 pages by default), so it is thousands of times smaller than a btree and costs almost nothing to maintain. It only narrows a search when the values in each block range are close together, i.e. when the column follows the order rows are inserted in: creation dates and sequence numbers of append-mostly tables (logs, outbox, audit, posted journal items). On a column that is updated freely, or filled in random order, use a btree. **When GIN helps.** jsonb_path_ops indexes the paths and values of a JSON document, so a containment filter (payload @> '{"tag": "t42"}') reads only the matching rows. It does not serve key-existence (?) or ordering. The domain operators that use it on json fields arrive with properties (M4); the index can be declared now. A kind on a field type it does not fit is refused when the registry is built (and, for #[field], at compile time):
pub struct EventCode { // error: index = "brin" is for date, datetime, integer and bigint fields (this field is char) #[field(char, index = "brin")] pub code: Option<Arc<str>>, }

trigram needs the pg_trgm extension in the database (erp db create installs it). Without it the install fails before any table is touched, naming the field: field '<model>.<field>' declares index = "trigram", which needs the PostgreSQL extension pg_trgm; it is not installed. Changing a field's kind (say from true to "brin") rebuilds its index under the same name at the next schema sync; an index that already matches is left alone, so a sync that changes nothing issues no DDL. Removing index keeps the existing index in the database, as Odoo does. **Runtime extension limits.** A runtime extension (models/*.toml or overlay) can add an index to an unindexed native field (one where no index attribute was specified in native code) or declare typed indexes ([[model.index]]), but it cannot change or drop the index kind of a field already carrying an index in native code, nor add an index to a field that explicitly declared index = false (which records kind none). Likewise, a runtime extension cannot change the field type of a natively indexed field or make it non-stored via store = false, compute, or related. Attempting to violate these limits fails at registry build with a Programming error naming both declarations and both index kinds (SPEC-ORMX-034).

An index over several fields, with another access method or with covering columns, is declared on the model with index(...) in indexes = [...], next to the raw ("_name", "(a, b)") tuples Odoo ports use:
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

name = "booking.slot", description = "Booking slot", indexes = [ // key (state, start), resource_id stored in the index: a list of a resource's open slots // by date is answered from the index alone (an index-only scan) // only open slots are indexed: a smaller index, and the planner uses it for queries that // filter on state = 'open' index( name = "_open_by_date", fields = ["state", "start"], include = ["resource_id"], filter = "[('state', '=', 'open')]" ), index(name = "_by_stop", fields = ["stop"], method = "brin"), ] )] pub struct Slot { #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.users")] pub resource_id: Option<RecId>, #[field(datetime)] pub start: Option<DateTime>, #[field(datetime)] pub stop: Option<DateTime>, #[field(selection, selection = [("open", "Open"), ("cancel", "Cancelled")])] pub state: Option<Arc<str>>, }

| Parameter | Meaning | |---|---| | name | required, starts with _; the index is <table>_<name without _> (shortened to 63 bytes like every table object) | | fields | required, the key fields in order: stored fields of the model's own table, or id | | method | "btree" (default), "brin" (date, datetime, integer), "gin" (json, jsonb_path_ops), "gist" (scalar and range fields; needs btree_gist, which schema sync installs when the index is declared, from a model file too), "trigram" (char, text, html; needs pg_trgm) | | filter | optional constant domain in list syntax, e.g. "[('state', '=', 'open')]": only matching rows are indexed (WHERE (...)). Literal operands over the model's own stored fields, operators =, !=, in, not in; anything else is refused when the ORM is built, naming the index and the model | | include | covering fields (stored fields or id), stored in the index but not part of its key; btree and gist only, never a key field | At most 32 columns in all (PostgreSQL's limit). Everything is checked when the registry is built; the errors name the index and the model, for example `index '_by_state' of 'booking.slot': method = "brin" is for date, datetime, integer and bigint fields ('state' is char)`. **Why include.** An index-only scan answers a query from the index without visiting the table, as long as the table's visibility map says the pages are all visible (after a VACUUM; autovacuum keeps it so on tables that are not rewritten constantly). include adds the columns the query returns without making them part of the key, so the key stays small and ordered by what you filter on. **Across addons.** An addon may add typed indexes to a model it does not own, in #[extend], and may replace one by name: the composed index is the newest declaration's (load order), exactly like raw table objects.
pub struct SlotReportIndexes;

Schema sync creates a typed index with its definition (`INDEX USING btree ("state", "start") INCLUDE ("resource_id")`) as the index comment and compares that text at every sync: a changed declaration drops and recreates the index, an unchanged one issues nothing. An existing index of the same name without the ORM comment (or from an interrupted build) is compared by structure (IndexStruct::is_declared): - When the existing index matches structurally (same method, columns in order, INCLUDE columns, exact PostgreSQL canonicalised filter predicate via temporary probe index, and exact trigram key expressions), only the comment is written (COMMENT ON INDEX ... IS ...), adopting the index without rebuild. The filter comparison creates a temporary probe table, so the schema-sync role needs the TEMP privilege on the database (PostgreSQL grants it to PUBLIC by default). Without it, or when the probe cannot parse the predicate on the existing table, the sync fails with `could not canonicalise index predicate ...` and the server's message; the index is left untouched. - If it differs, a native declaration replaces it (the declaration owns the name) with a warning in the log, while a runtime declaration (models/*.toml or overlay) is refused loudly with a Programming error to avoid silently shadowing or destroying DBA-managed objects.

A data-only addon declares the same typed indexes, with field names only (no SQL), so a package loaded from the database may use them: [[model]] extend = "booking.slot" [[model.index]] name = "_by_date" fields = ["start"] method = "brin" [[model.index]] name = "_open_by_date" fields = ["state", "start"] include = ["resource_id"] Unknown keys, an unknown method, a name without _, a name declared twice in one model, and filter that is not a string are refused with the file and line; field checks happen when the registry is built, with the messages above. A model file declares at most 64 indexes per model.

Below large_table_rows (the schema-sync option) an index is built, or replaced when its kind, method, include or filter changed, inside the install transaction. Above it, a new or replaced index of any kind (field or typed) is built by a CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY step after the install commits, which does not block writes while it builds: init_models_with plans the steps (SchemaSync::steps) and sync_schema_with runs them. For a replaced index the step builds the new index concurrently under a temporary name (<name>__swap) on nonpartitioned tables, verifies it is valid, and then swaps it into place in one short transaction (DROP INDEX / ALTER INDEX RENAME or DROP CONSTRAINT / ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX): the old index keeps enforcing until the atomic swap. Partitioned-table replacement still uses its separate drop-and-rebuild path; it does not have this guarantee. If the build fails, the existing index remains in place untouched; run the step again once the failure is resolved.

A job is a row of the durable queue (ADR 0150). It is written in the same transaction as the data that caused it, so it exists exactly when that data does. A worker claims it later, under the principal that enqueued it, and runs it in short transactions called chunks. Each chunk commits its effects together with the job's own progress, so a crash repeats at most one chunk. Operators: the settings and limits are in [Background jobs for operators](/en/next/developer/installation/background-jobs.md). Odoo developers: ir.cron owns its calendar schedule fields and synchronizes the base.cron queue kind. The server has optional in-app runner composition; its activation is node configuration. Shared policy comes from the tenant database through an injected native settings source.

A kind is a name <addon>.<name>, a version, and a handler. The usual handler is a *step*: a method of one of your models that does one chunk of work. Because it is an ordinary model method, another addon can extend it with an override that calls super. use erp_sdk::jobs::{StepArgs, StepOutcome}; use erp_sdk::prelude::*; erp_sdk::addon!(name = "guide_jobs");
pub struct Recount { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, }

impl Recount { /// One chunk: count a batch, say how far it got. #[method] async fn run_step( _this: &RecordSet<Recount>, _tx: &mut Transaction, args: StepArgs, ) -> Result<StepOutcome> { let done = args.progress.as_ref().and_then(|p| p["done"].as_u64()).unwrap_or(0); let total = args.payload["total"].as_u64().unwrap_or(1); let next = done + 1; let progress = erp_sdk::serde_json::json!({ "done": next }); Ok(if next >= total { StepOutcome::done(progress, 1) } else { StepOutcome::more(progress, 1, Some(total - next)) }) } } erp_sdk::jobs::register_job_kind!( RECOUNT_KIND, erp_sdk::jobs::JobKindDecl::new( "guide_jobs", "guide_jobs.recount", erp_sdk::jobs::HandlerRef::Step { model: "guide_jobs.recount", method: "run_step" }, ) .max_attempts(5) ); fn main() {} A step returns the job's new progress (replacing the old one), how many items it did and how many are left. finished completes the job in the same commit. The payload and the progress are data: bounded JSON that is never evaluated. Do not put credentials in them; store a reference. Builder settings of a kind (all optional): version and accepts (a rolling upgrade runs jobs written by an older version), backoff, max_attempts, priority, history, timeouts (Maintenance for long upkeep), max_concurrency and elevated (core and base maintenance kinds that run as an elevated principal; a runner built with exclude_elevated never claims them). The registry refuses a malformed name, a name outside your addon's prefix, a duplicate, and principal(System) for any addon but the core and base.

use erp_sdk::jobs::{EnqueueRequest, JobKey, OnDuplicate, When}; use erp_sdk::prelude::*; use std::time::Duration; async fn schedule(tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<()> { let env = tx.env(); let request = EnqueueRequest::new("guide_jobs.recount") .payload(&erp_sdk::serde_json::json!({ "total": 3 }))? .at(When::After(Duration::from_secs(60))) .dedup(JobKey::new("recount:warehouse:3")?, OnDuplicate::Earliest); tx.enqueue(&env, request).await?; Ok(()) } fn main() {} - The job runs as the caller: the user and companies of env, resolved again at every chunk. If that user is archived or loses the company, the job becomes a dead letter; it never falls back to another principal. - dedup makes the enqueue idempotent among live jobs of the kind (Keep leaves the old one, Earliest lowers its due time). singleton lets at most one job with the key run at a time, on any node. - A dedup key does not include the principal: a second caller with the same kind and key finds the first caller's job and, with Keep, leaves it as it is, so it runs as the first caller. Put the user in the key when the work differs per user. - enqueue_many writes up to 1,024 jobs with one statement. - Running as another user needs an audited elevation; until it ships the call is refused with an error that says so. Only core code may name another user today.

When a business record has one job (a scheduled message) and the record is cancelled or rescheduled, drop the job instead of leaving a stale one that wakes up to do nothing: use erp_sdk::jobs::JobKey; use erp_sdk::prelude::*; async fn drop_job(tx: &mut Transaction, id: i64) -> Result<()> { let env = tx.env(); let key = JobKey::new(&format!("{id}:1"))?; let cancelled = tx.job_cancel_by_key(&env, "guide_jobs.recount", &key).await?; // say what you expect: zero is a count, not an error, so a missing job is yours to catch if cancelled != 1 { return Err(Error::invariant(format!("job {} was not live", key.as_str()))); } Ok(()) } fn main() {} job_cancel_by_keys(&env, kind, &[keys]) does the same for many keys in two statements (at most 10 000), for example the keys of every row of a deleted record. job_cancel_by_key needs no administrator right. It cancels the live jobs of the kind and key that **the caller's user enqueued** and returns how many; a job of another user is left alone (it counts as missing). Server code that must cancel whoever's job it is (after its own access check) passes env.sudo(true); an RPC or a client cannot. Waiting jobs leave the queue with a cancelled history row, a running job is asked to stop, dead letters stay for the operator. ADR 0150 D17. Zero cancelled has four meanings, and the caller tells them apart: the job already finished (a failed record), it is a dead letter (proceed), a non-dead job with the key exists but another transaction holds it (a claim in flight: return a serialization failure, Error::new(ErrorKind::Concurrency, ..).with_sqlstate(Some("40001".into())), and the unit of work repeats the call), or no job exists at all (the dead letter expired or an administrator discarded it: do not fail, log, and re-enqueue if the record still needs the job). Do not treat any of them as an invariant breach that sticks the record. Lock order: a cancel locks your business row first and the job row after, a running chunk the other way round, so a rare 40P01 deadlock is possible and retried.

A handler or step returns an error to say what happens next: | Error | Effect | |---|---| | a database or lock failure (the default for ? on them) | retried after a capped exponential backoff with jitter; a dead letter after max_attempts | | validation, access or programming errors | dead letter at once | | JobError::Yield { after } | run again later, the attempt is given back (a rate limit) | | JobError::item(..) inside chunk_items | that item fails alone (below) | A chunk that commits progress restarts the attempt count: a long job is not killed by failures that came before it made progress. A serialization failure inside a chunk runs the chunk again.

Core crates and native addons can implement JobHandler and drive chunks themselves, with items that fail individually and external steps such as sending mail. In a native handler: use erp_sdk::jobs::{ChunkResult, JobContext, JobError, RunOutcome}; use erp_sdk::BoxFuture; async fn run(ctx: &mut JobContext<'_>) -> Result<RunOutcome, JobError> { while !ctx.budget_exhausted() { let report = ctx .chunk(|_tx| { Box::pin(async move { Ok(ChunkResult::more(erp_sdk::serde_json::json!({}), 10, None)) }) }) .await?; if report.finished { return Ok(RunOutcome::Done); } } // the run's budget is used and work remains: go back behind the jobs that are due Ok(RunOutcome::Continue) } fn main() {} - chunk_items runs the whole batch set-based first; when an item-attributable error comes (a constraint or data error, or JobError::item), it runs the batch again with one savepoint per item. Failing items are rolled back, listed in erp_job_item_failure and counted; the others commit with the progress. A batch in which every item fails is a failure of the chunk. - external runs work outside any transaction while the runner renews the lease; poll the CancelToken between items and call checkpoint every few of them. After a crash the next run reads the stored progress and repeats at most the items after the last checkpoint, so effects must be safe to repeat. - A run stops starting chunks after both jobs.max_chunks_per_run chunks and jobs.run_budget_secs seconds, then continues in a new run. - Chunk closures return boxed futures (Box::pin(async move { .. })). This keeps handler futures Send; async closures do not yet do that reliably.

Override the step method of the owning model and call super; both effects commit in the same chunk. This is how Odoo addons change what a cron calls, and it works for native and WebAssembly addons alike because the step is an ordinary method.

| Odoo | Here | |---|---| | ir.cron record in XML | the same record; one job row per schedule will be kept for you (not delivered yet) | | _trigger(at, coalesce) | ir.cron trigger, or enqueue with dedup | | _commit_progress | a chunk boundary: progress commits with the chunk's effects, never in the middle of a call | | the server action run under the cron user | a step or handler run as the stored principal | Data-only addons can add schedules (ir.cron records calling server actions) but cannot add kinds, because a kind needs code.

A trusted composition root can call JobRunnerBuilder::maintenance_kinds with exact references to registered native System declarations using Maintenance timeouts and ReadCommitted isolation. The empty list, a copied/unregistered declaration or an incompatible handler is refused at build. The same selection applies to claims, next-due queries, reaping and direct execution; handing a claim to the wrong runner returns Access before execution or settlement. run_claimed now returns Result<()> for this admission result; handler outcomes still settle through the queue. Use additive exclude_kinds(names) or exclude_elevated() for the ordinary runner. Inclusion that conflicts with exclusions is refused. Addon data and job payloads must never supply the elevated set. Share a database_slots semaphore sized to jobs.workers_per_db and the existing process_slots semaphore sized to jobs.workers between the pair. The semaphores bound the pair; creating separate pools would give each runner a separate allowance. Native attachment composition supplies a minimal owner ORM and supervised generation replacement. Enable it explicitly per node; every external removal still requires current fence admission. Ordinary request credentials remain separate. Attachment composition keeps the existing additive exclude_kinds(names) and exclude_elevated() APIs. maintenance_kinds(declarations) adds an exact registered native System allowlist, validated for maintenance timeout and READ COMMITTED isolation; inclusion that conflicts with exclusions is refused. The effective set applies to claim, next-due, direct execution and reaping. database_slots and process_slots accept the shared pools used by the ordinary/owner runner pair; configuration must not allocate a second independent worker allowance. The server's owner allowlist is fixed in native code, not selected by payload or an addon's elevated flag.

Base publishes Shared jobs.* catalogue entries as database-global base.jobs.* declared settings. For example, jobs.chunk.default.lock_ms maps to base.jobs.chunk.default.lock_ms. The catalogue remains the source of defaults and bounds; its read-only Setting::is_shared() marks the scope. Group validation reuses JobSettings::builder() so retry backoff and timeout ordering are checked against unchanged values. workers, workers_per_db, claim_batch and run_in_app remain node configuration. The Settings service stores and audits administrator choices. New admissions read committed database policy; an active run keeps its captured limits. Saving a new value does not rewrite a granted lease or change a running handler's snapshot.

JobSettingsSource is an ORM-owned native interface; base provides DatabaseJobSettingsSource over the existing declared Settings service. Native composition gives its minimal reader a separate bounded primary pool. The source returns a validated JobSettingsSnapshot; the ORM applies only the node's local capacity. Every read is bounded by the node ORM transaction timeout, including connection acquisition. Sources must read committed revision and values consistently and must return errors for unavailable or corrupt policy. Orm::job_settings_snapshot().await is for new admission. Orm::job_node_settings() describes local capacity and explicitly static configuration; it is not a live Shared-policy getter. OrmBuilder::job_settings(...) selects static policy for isolated core fixtures. With a database source attached, explicit Shared process overrides are refused by name. Orm::rebuild retains its source; minimal owner ORMs share the authority. A claimed job retains an immutable snapshot. Native handlers use JobContext::settings() and settings_revision() rather than reloading policy. Budgets, timeouts, deadline, renewal, progress writes, retry defaults and retention stay consistent for that run. Persisted attempts and validated kind overrides retain their existing meanings. A later claim can read an older checkpoint larger than its current write limit, but must write within its newly admitted limit. New enqueue payloads use the current policy. job_settings_identity() describes provider/schema/catalogue compatibility in database mode; mutable values and revisions do not enter node identity. Static mode remains value-sensitive. Node capacities, build/addon identity, readiness, leases and epoch fencing retain their existing roles.

Status: implemented (ADR 0040 "ORM primitives for scale" D1–D3, design note docs/design/m3-ormx.md (docs/design/m3-ormx.md, not part of the published documentation) §3–§4, spec docs/specs/orm/orm-scale.md (docs/specs/orm/orm-scale.md, not part of the published documentation) SPEC-ORMX-001..015). Odoo has none of these: a stock balance there is a row lock plus a merge job, and a stale edit silently overwrites. Every Rust block below is compiled as a doctest of erp-test-models (as in [Models, fields and method overrides](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md)). Model declarations run a composition check; the async call examples are compiled but their bodies are not executed by that setup. Lines starting with #  are hidden setup.

A business key is a named UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT constraint over columns of the model's own table. A NULL part is a value ("no lot"), so two quants without a lot for the same product and location conflict:
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;
pub struct Location { #[field(char, required)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, }

name = "stock.quant", description = "Quant", row_version = true, keys = [key( name = "_quant_key", fields = ["product_ref", "location_id", "lot_ref"], message = "A quant already exists for this product, location and lot." )] )] pub struct Quant { #[field(char, required)] pub product_ref: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "stock.location", required)] pub location_id: Option<RecId>, #[field(char)] pub lot_ref: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(float, digits = 0)] pub quantity: Decimal, #[field(float, digits = 0)] pub reserved_quantity: Decimal, #[field(datetime)] pub in_date: Option<DateTime>, }

Stock quantity examples use unrounded exact decimals (digits = 0), as required by stock addon admission. - The key also becomes an associated constant, Quant::QUANT_KEY (the name without its leading _, upper-cased), for Upsert::on. - Schema sync creates it as `ALTER TABLE stock_quant ADD CONSTRAINT stock_quant_quant_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (product_ref, location_id, lot_ref)` (the table-object naming rule) and keeps the definition as the constraint's comment; a changed declaration re-creates it. - On an existing table with more rows than SchemaSyncOptions::large_table_rows (100,000 by default), a new key puts nothing in the install transaction (the ADD CONSTRAINT would hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the table while it builds the unique index). Two steps run after the commit, in order: key_index.<constraint> (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, writes go on) and key_constraint.<constraint> (ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX, a short lock, no scan). Until both have run, an upsert naming the key fails with Database "business key '<name>' of '<model>' is not usable yet: its post-commit steps have not completed (pending or failed; ...)". If rows already duplicate the key, step 1 fails with Validation "cannot add key '<name>' to '<model>': existing records conflict, e.g. (<id>, <id>)" (up to 20 pairs of ids), cleans up its invalid index and leaves the table as it was; fix the rows and sync again. - A key whose declaration *changes* on such a table is refused before any DDL (UserError): there is no online replacement that keeps the old key enforced and arbitrating correctly while the new one builds. Drop the old constraint in a window you choose and sync again; the new key is then built by the two steps. - A row that duplicates the key fails with Validation and The database refused the change: <message>, from create, write and raw SQL alike. - nulls_distinct = true gives a plain UNIQUE (rows with NULL parts never conflict). Such a key still enforces uniqueness, but it cannot arbitrate an upsert. - Key fields are stored columns of the model's own table: not inherited through _inherits, not x2many, not id or row_version, not a float without digits (inexact) and not JSON. The registry refuses anything else when it is built, naming the key and the field. - An addon adds a key to a model it does not own with #[extend(Model, keys = [...])]; a later declaration of the same name replaces the key.

records.upsert(tx, Upsert::on(KEY)...) inserts the rows whose key is new and updates the others in **one statement per batch** (1,000 distinct keys per statement, OrmConfig::insert_batch), and returns one entry per input row, in input order:

let quants = tx.env().model::<Quant>()?; let row = |product: &str, quantity: Decimal| { quants .vals() .set(Quant::PRODUCT_REF, product) .set(Quant::LOCATION_ID, stock) .set(Quant::LOT_REF, None::<Arc<str>>) .set(Quant::QUANTITY, quantity) .set(Quant::RESERVED_QUANTITY, Decimal::ZERO) .set(Quant::IN_DATE, now) }; let out = quants .upsert( &mut tx, Upsert::on(Quant::QUANT_KEY) .rows([row("P1", Decimal::from(5)), row("P2", Decimal::from(-2))]) .update([Quant::IN_DATE])                          // overwrite when it differs .accumulate(Quant::QUANTITY)                       // existing + row value .accumulate_floor(Quant::RESERVED_QUANTITY, Decimal::ZERO),  // GREATEST(0, existing + value) ) .await?; for row in out.rows() { let (_id, _outcome, _before): (RecId, UpsertOutcome, Option<i64>) = (row.id(), row.outcome(), row.previous_version()); } let _records: &RecordSet<Quant> = out.records(); // the distinct upserted records

What the call does: - **Outcomes.** Inserted for a new key, Updated when an update field differs or an accumulate delta is not zero, Unchanged otherwise (the row is not written: no new tuple, no version bump, write_date untouched). previous_version() is None for inserted rows and for models without row versions; for an unchanged row it is its current version. Without update and accumulate the call is get-or-create. - **Every row sets every key field** (a NULL part counts as set), every update field and every accumulate field (a delta, never NULL). Key fields cannot be updated on conflict. - **Duplicates in one call are merged** before the statement, as sequential calls would end: update fields take the last row's value, accumulate fields are summed with checked arithmetic, every other field keeps the first row's value. accumulate_floor cannot merge duplicates (its floor applies per call): split such rows over calls. - **Accumulation** adds to the existing value (a NULL counts as 0). A sum out of the column's range fails with Validation naming the field (`… the new value of 'Count' (count) on 'Quant' is out of range). accumulate_floor stores GREATEST(floor, existing + value)` on updates; a *new* row whose value is below the floor fails the call (nothing can be committed). - **Defaults.** Static field defaults fill the fields a row leaves out (inserted rows only). A field whose default is computed — a default function, a sequence, a default_<field> context key — must be given explicitly: the statement would evaluate it before it knows which rows are new, and a sequence would lose numbers on updated rows. Required stored computed fields must be given too. default_get overrides do not run. - **Concurrency.** Two transactions that upsert the same new key both succeed: the second waits for the first, fails with a serialization failure under REPEATABLE READ and Orm::run retries it, so accumulate ends at the sum and no duplicate row exists. - **What runs afterwards.** The cache holds the written values; stored computes of inserted rows and dependents of updated fields recompute at the next flush; #[constrains] methods run for the written fields; write hooks get the old values. **create and write overrides do not run**: that is the contract of declaring a key. Logic that must see every change overrides upsert itself, which is a dispatched method:
pub struct QuantAudit { #[field(integer)] pub upserts: i32, }

impl QuantAudit { #[method(override)] async fn upsert( this: &RecordSet<Quant>, tx: &mut Transaction, call: UpsertCall, sup: Super, ) -> Result<UpsertResult> { // before: call.rows(), call.update(), call.accumulate(); call.rows_mut() to adjust let result = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), (call,)).await?; // after: one entry per input row let touched = this.as_records().browse_ids(result.distinct_ids()); touched.write(tx, RawVals::new().set_cell("upserts", Cell::Int(1))).await?; Ok(result) } }

- **Access** follows the create and write checks of ADR 0035, through the same engine entry points: both model-level checks (an API key scoped read_only is refused here); the write rule over the existing rows of the batch's keys in one SELECT *before* the statement (no statement when no rule restricts); the create rule on the inserted rows in one SELECT *after* it. A denied row fails the whole call with the engine's record-level text; after the statement the transaction cannot commit. A denied existing row the caller may not read is never named: the call fails with the key's own message (`The database refused the change: A quant already exists for this product, location and lot.), as a create of that key would; the Access` error is raised only for rows the caller can read. An upsert on a policy table (ir.access, groups) is a policy write: pending writes are flushed first and the transaction rebuilds its policy before its next decision. A read-only transaction refuses the call. A field outside the caller's write mask is not checked yet. - **Every row the upsert matches must be readable** by the caller, including for get-or-create and an accumulate of 0, because the result reports ids, versions and values; otherwise the call fails with the key's own message and no id. Rows with one key are merged: update takes the last row's value, accumulate sums, any other field keeps the first row's value (a field only a later duplicate gives is dropped for a new key). The access pre-check also denies a row the upsert would leave unchanged. Make the leading key column required: a nullable leading column cannot use the key's index in the upsert's joins. While expect_versions expectations are pending for the model the upsert is refused. - **Server-set fields** cannot be given: id, create_uid, create_date, write_uid, write_date (on models with log access), row_version and parent_path in a row, in update or in accumulate are a Programming error such as `'stock.quant.create_date' is set by the server and cannot be written. (Odoo's create` drops such values silently; the upsert refuses them.) - **Not supported:** models with _parent_store, x2many values in rows, fields inherited through _inherits, keys declared nulls_distinct (each is a Programming error naming the reason). - **Untyped surface.** Overrides and dynamic callers use UpsertCall (UpsertCall::new("_quant_key").with_rows(..).with_update([..]).with_accumulate(..)) with Records::upsert; Records::upsert_values(tx, key, rows, update, accumulate) takes rows as {field: value} maps (Luau, data files). JSON-2 exposure is separate. Statements (ceilings, ADR 0007): 0 for an empty batch; 1 per batch without a restricting rule; +1 for a restricting write rule, +1 for a restricting create rule (a refusal adds the engine's evidence statements); then the model's normal recompute flush.

row_version = true (on the model or on an extension; it cannot be turned off later) is **opt-in**: a model that does not declare it has no column and no trigger, because the trigger costs about +10 % of a statement's executor time (docs/bench/ormx-row-version.md). It adds an int8 NOT NULL field row_version, readonly and not copied. Every UPDATE of the row bumps it by exactly one: the ORM's flush, recompute and upsert statements set row_version + 1 themselves, and a BEFORE UPDATE trigger that schema sync creates (<table>__row_version) bumps it for any other SQL — raw SQL, migrations — and corrects an explicit value. Read it like write_date, through the Base::ROW_VERSION handle or read:

let note = tx.env().model::<StockNote>()?.browse([id])?; let _version: i64 = note.get(&mut tx, Base::ROW_VERSION).await?; // optimistic concurrency: fail instead of overwriting a change someone else made meanwhile let record = note.rec_ids()[0]; note.expect_versions(&mut tx, [(record, version_the_client_read)]).await?; note.set(&mut tx, StockNote::BODY, "edited").await?; tx.flush().await?; // ErrorKind::Conflict when the stored version moved

- expect_versions sends nothing: the next flush UPDATE that writes the record also requires row_version = <expected> (0 extra statements when it matches). When it does not, one SELECT tells the two cases apart: a stale record fails with ErrorKind::Conflict (`Record 'Note' (stock.note) 7 was changed by someone else since you read it (version 2, now 3). Reload it and apply your change again.), a deleted one with Missing`. - Conflict answers JSON-2 with status 409 and the name erp.conflict. It is **never retried** by Orm::run (a retry cannot make the edit current); a concurrent change that commits while the transaction is open first surfaces as a serialization failure, the retry then reports the Conflict. - An expectation is consumed by the first flush that writes the record; later flushes in the same transaction already hold the row lock and do not check again. - A caller value for row_version — in create, write, an upsert row or an import — is a Programming error: 'stock.note.row_version' is set by the server and cannot be written. - expect_versions on a model without versions is a Programming error ('<model>' has no row version (declare row_version = true)).

A WriteHook registered on the ORM (OrmBuilder::write_hook, HarnessBuilder::write_hook in tests) receives the old and new values of the fields it names for every row a flush UPDATE or an upsert update writes, from that statement's own RETURNING (no extra statement); models nobody hooks keep the plain UPDATE. Tracking and the outbox are built on it: use erp_sdk::{BoxFuture, Result, Transaction, WriteBatch, WriteHook}; fn track_quantity<'a>(_tx: &'a mut Transaction, batch: &'a WriteBatch) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<()>> { Box::pin(async move { for row in batch.rows() { // one (old, new) pair per field of batch.fields(), for record row.id() for (old, new) in row.values() { assert_ne!(old, new, "record {} was written", row.id()); } } Ok(()) }) } const TRACK: WriteHook = WriteHook::new("stock.quant", &["quantity"], track_quantity);

docs.title: Load demo data on an existing database

sections.text: A database created without --with-demo has no demo records and every module has demo = false. Odoo's "Load demo data" (base.demo_force_install_action, ir.demo.install_demo) makes such a database a demo database afterwards. ERPForAll has the same operation as a module lifecycle operation (ADR 0153). **It cannot be undone.** Nothing removes demo records afterwards. Use it on test databases only.

1. Sets demo = true on every module row, installed or not. 2. For every installed module, in dependency order, loads the files listed in the manifest's demo key. Each module's demo files load as superuser in one savepoint, in init mode, so noupdate demo records are written the way they are at install. 3. Does not load the data files again and does not touch the schema. A record an administrator changed in a data file keeps the change. 4. Writes one force_demo row to erp_module_lifecycle_audit (actor, session, outcome). Odoo also sets the auth_password_policy.minlength parameter to 4. ERPForAll does not; an addon whose demo users need a weaker password policy sets it in its own demo file.

A module whose demo files fail on their data (a parse error, an unknown model, a refused value) is rolled back alone: none of its demo records stay, its demo flag becomes false, the other modules still load (a module that depends on it is not skipped). The operation commits and the reply names each failed module with the loader's text: {"loaded": ["base", "x", "y"], "failed": [{"module": "bad", "error": "Module \"bad\": demo file 'demo/broken.xml' failed ..."}]} The Apps page shows the list. In Rust the same data is OperationOutcome::data_notices with NoticeKind::DemoFailed, and a row in ir.demo_failure when a registry declares that model. A failure of the database itself (a refused statement) fails the whole operation and nothing persists. Odoo only logs a warning here; ERPForAll reports it to the administrator who pressed the button.

Running it twice does not duplicate anything: demo records keep their external ids and are updated in place. A module installed afterwards gets its demo files when every module it depends on has demo = true, which it has after this operation (the rule of SPEC-MOD-033).

| Caller | Entry point | |---|---| | Browser (administrator session) | Settings ▸ Addons ▸ Load demo data, which posts {"confirm":true} to POST /erp/module/force-demo. The route takes a primary browser session only (no Authorization header) and WebLifecycle::force_demo rechecks the system group under the lifecycle lock. | | Rust | ModuleSystem::force_demo(&env) (superuser environment) or ModuleSystem::force_demo_authorized(&authorizer) (browser seam). Switch to OperationOutcome::orm afterwards like any lifecycle operation. | Odoo reaches the operation through a transient model ir.demo with a confirmation form. ERPForAll has no such model: the module system holds the lifecycle lock and the new registry, which a model method cannot, so the confirmation is the dialog of the Apps page and the confirm field of the request.

- List demo records in the manifest's demo key, never in data; give every record an id, so a second run updates it. - A demo file may rely on the module's own data records and on its dependencies' records, not on demo records of a module that does not depend on yours. - Keep one module's demo files independent of another module's demo failing: the flag is forced on every module, so your demo loads even when a dependency's demo was rolled back.

docs.title: Luau scripts: code server actions and data-only addon hooks

sections.text: ERPForAll runs the Python bodies of Odoo code server actions, and the hooks and post/end migrations of data-only addons, as **Luau** (ADR 0001, ADR 0009 §6-§7). Scripts run in a sandbox (crates/erp-script, design: docs/design/m2-script.md) with the rights of the user who triggers them (ADR 0009 §10).

- Basic functions: `assert error ipairs next pairs pcall rawequal rawget rawlen rawset select tonumber tostring type typeof unpack`. - Libraries: math, string, table, utf8, bit32 (read-only: you cannot replace their functions). - What the runner injects. For server actions that is env (env.search, …), record/records, context and log. Not available: require, load/loadstring, getfenv/setfenv, setmetatable/getmetatable, coroutine, print, os, io, debug, collectgarbage, _G. Scripts are plain source text; precompiled bytecode is rejected.

A script's result is what it returns: one value (use a table for several). An Odoo-style action = {...} assignment works where the runner asks for the action global (server actions do). if record ~= nil then local data = env.read(record.model, {record.id}, {"is_company"})[1] if data.is_company then action = { type = "ir.actions.act_url", url = "https://example.com/p/" .. record.id } end end Returned tables must be plain data: arrays with keys 1..n, or records with string keys. Holes, mixed keys, functions, cycles, NaN and infinity are errors, not silently converted.

Each run has limits (defaults, which a host may only lower): 256 KiB of source, 10 million steps (an approximate measure: calls, loop iterations, pattern-matching steps), 5 seconds, 16 MiB of memory. string.find/match/gmatch/gsub accept subjects up to 64 KiB and patterns up to 256 bytes. When a limit is reached, or a host function (env.write, …) fails, the run stops for good: pcall cannot catch it, and the action fails with the real error (for example the AccessError from the ORM). pcall still catches your own error(...) calls and returns the message string.

- tostring(t) and string.format("%s", t) print table, function, … for reference values (no addresses). error(v) with a table or function raises its type name; use string messages. - table.sort and table.move count against the step limit in proportion to the table size. - A returned value (and values passed to host functions) may total at most the memory limit in string bytes: returning one big string many times in a table fails instead of copying it.

code actions execute once for the active set, including an empty set. record is the first {id, model} descriptor or nil; records is the descriptor array. Field values are explicit reads, not attributes on a descriptor. env.uid, env.context and context describe the caller. Mutating a Luau table never changes server rights. | Function | Arguments and result | |---|---| | env.search | (model, domain[, limit]) → descriptor array; domain uses Odoo list syntax, limit defaults to256, range1–256 | | env.read | (model, ids, fields) → row dictionaries; 1–32 explicit field names; relations use raw IDs | | env.write | (model, ids, values) → nil; values use ORM field conversion and x2many command arrays | | env.create | (model, values) → one descriptor | | env.unlink | (model, ids) → nil | | env.ref | (module.name) → existing descriptor after target read authorization; absent IDs fail | | log | (string) → nil; combined log text ≤64KiB, emitted through server tracing after success | All host operations use the caller's transaction, model/record rules, field groups, companies and context. IDs must be positive and unique (at most256 per call); create/write dictionaries have at most32 fields and cannot set id. Nested x2many commands are inspected before dispatch, including HTML refusal and a conservative 256-command-record work bound (multiplied by the active parent count). The sandbox provides no sudo, impersonation, arbitrary method dispatch or raw SQL API. Return one action dictionary **or** assign action; both non-nil is an error. Nil means no client action. A client action must have a nonempty string type. evaluation_type=equation evaluates its Luau expression per active record, then writes using the normal field converter; e.g. `env.read(record.model, {record.id}, {'name'})[1].name .. '-updated'`. The active context is per record for equations. The bridge accepts at most256 active records,1024 host calls per evaluation,256 context entries, and1MiB logical string/byte content per converted request/response (max100k nodes, depth32). These are admission limits, not a measured heap or wire size. Generic ORM reads may materialize stored/computed fields before the bridge's conversion refusal; no exact database-transfer ceiling is claimed. A stored action code field also observes the tree's64KiB per-field bound. A per-process semaphore admits at most the host's available CPU parallelism. Busy workers refuse immediately; replicas have independent permits (cluster ceiling is replicas × per-process permits). A permit stays owned by the blocking VM until exit. Cancellation disconnects host requests and trips a sticky VM flag. Scripts cannot continue after host failures; the primary ORM error retains its kind/message/SQLSTATE and source. **Always roll back on error, timeout or cancellation**, including after earlier successful host writes. No callback retains the transaction borrow. run_as_superuser stays refused until audited elevation exists. Sequence generation requires secured base sequence dispatch; the raw sequence access gap is not bypassed. HTML updates remain refused pending the HTML sanitizer engine, including equations. This is not complete object-write/HTML parity. Product performance remains deferred to milestone end (ADR0065).

docs.title: The shared thread, message and composer: registries and patch points

sections.text: Chatter, Discuss, chat windows and embedded comment threads show messages with the same components (ADR 0148 D1.5). Package: @erpforall/mail-thread-view (web/packages/mail-thread-view). Behavior: docs/specs/web/mail-thread-view.md. Design: docs/design/m4-mail-thread-view.md. Executable examples: web/packages/mail-thread-view/tests/ (the test addons are addon.test.ts); the snippets below are compiled from web/typechecks/mail-thread-view.ts. The components read the messaging store (messaging-store.md) and never fetch: the host gives them a ThreadTransport (posting and message operations) and a ThreadPager (the pages of the thread). A user-facing functional page for the chatter does not exist yet.

const registries = defineThreadViewRegistries(hub); registerBuiltins(registries); const transport: ThreadTransport = { async post(ref, post) { const answer = await jsonRpc(/json/2/${ref.model}/thread_post, { ids: [ref.id], post }); // applyAnswer takes the payload as text, exactly as received. return { message_id: answer.message_id, replayed: answer.replayed, store: JSON.stringify(answer.store) }; }, }; const pager: ThreadPager = { loadLatest: (ref) => fetchLatestPage(ref.model, ref.id), loadOlder: (ref, before) => fetchOlderPage(ref.model, ref.id, before), }; const common = { store, ref: { model: "sale.order", id: 42 }, registries, transport, pager, self: { partnerId: 7 }, translate: createTranslator({ language: "en_US" })._t, reportError: (error: unknown) => console.error(error), }; const thread = new Thread({ ...common, order: "desc" }); const composer = new Composer({ ...common }); host.append(thread.element, composer.element); Thread and Composer share one context per thread (the draft, the reply target and the unsent posts are local records of the store, ADR 0148 D1.3), so a host mounts the Thread of a reference wherever it mounts that reference's Composer: the unsent posts are drawn by the Thread. Thread options: order (desc newest first, the chatter; asc, Discuss), squash, threadName, scroller. Composer options: sendOnEnter, platform, silent. Shared options: allowReply, services (each optional: pickEmoji, confirm, copyText, searchPartners, fieldLabel, now, newUid, locale, timeZone, uploadAttachment), document. Call dispose() when the surface goes away: the thread releases its lease on the store, both stop following it. The thread's model must be a model of the store's schema.

Required message fields: body, message_type, date, author_id; a schema without one makes the constructor throw ThreadViewError("schema"). Optional fields are capabilities that exist only when the schema declares them: subject, is_internal, parent_id, tracking (the documented JSON text), attachments, reactions, starred, pinned_at, edited_at. capabilitiesOf(store) reports them; message.hiddenActions() and composer.hiddenActions() list actions hidden because the deployment lacks what they need, with the reason (for example "Reactions need server support"). A transport operation that does not exist is not faked: invoking the action fails with ThreadViewError("unavailable") naming the owner task. Until the server tasks land, reactions, bookmarks, pins and deletion therefore stay hidden or fail loudly; attachment upload is active when uploadAttachment is configured; and the full composer is hidden with its owner.

| Registry | Value | Built-ins | |---|---|---| | mail.messageActions | { label(ctx), glyph?, condition?(ctx), unavailable?(ctx), pressed?(ctx), run(ctx) } | reaction 10, reply 20, bookmark 80, copy-text 85, pin 90, delete 120 | | mail.composerActions | { label(ctx), glyph?, condition?(ctx), unavailable?(ctx), run(ctx) } | emoji 20, attach 30, full-composer 40 | | mail.messageRenderers | { match(message), layout: "bubble" or "row", render(ctx) } | tracking 10, notification 20, comment 90 | | mail.suggestionProviders | { delimiter, label(ctx), search(term, ctx) } keyed by the delimiter | @ 10 | Numbers are sequences (lower first); give yours with { sequence }. condition says whether the action applies to this message; unavailable returns a reason when the deployment cannot do it (checked only where condition holds). run may be async: a throw or rejection is shown on the message, announced and reported through reportError, never swallowed.
