A renderer builds DOM nodes (view.document.createElement, textContent); it must not use innerHTML or insert body markup of its own: a message body reaches the page only through renderBody. A provider's registry key must equal its delimiter, or the provider is ignored and reported. A suggestion with mention: { partnerId } becomes a structured mention; any other suggestion inserts its insert (or label) as plain text. export const acmeCalls: AddonRegistration = { id: "acme_calls", register(ctx) { ctx.registry.category("mail.messageActions").add( "acme_calls.flag", { label: (a) => String(a.view.translate("Flag")), glyph: "!", // Only offered where the schema has the field your addon adds (see "Capabilities"). unavailable: (a) => (a.view.capabilities().bookmark ? null : "Flagging needs the starred field"), run: async (a) => { await fetchFlag(a.message.id); }, }, { sequence: 15 }, ); ctx.registry.category("mail.messageRenderers").add( "acme_calls.call", { match: (message) => message.messageType === "acme_call", layout: "row", render: ({ view, message }) => { const card = view.document.createElement("div"); card.textContent = Call log #${message.id}; return card; }, }, { sequence: 5 }, ); ctx.registry.category("mail.suggestionProviders").add("#", { delimiter: "#", label: () => "Channels", search: (term) => ["general", "sales"].filter((c) => c.startsWith(term)).map((c) => ({ id: c, label: #${c} })), }); ctx.registry.category("mail.composerActions").add("acme_calls.log", { label: () => "Log call", run: (a) => a.insertText("[call] "), }); }, }; declare function fetchFlag(messageId: number): Promise<void>;

export const acmePatches: AddonRegistration = { id: "acme_patches", register(ctx) { ctx.patch(Message, (sup) => ({ authorName(message) { return ${sup.authorName.call(this, message)} (verified); }, })); ctx.patch(Composer, (sup) => ({ // Everything buildPost returns is sent, and kept with an unsent post for Retry. buildPost() { return { ...sup.buildPost.call(this), subject: "Re: order" }; }, })); ctx.patch(Thread, (sup) => ({ emptyLabel() { return ${sup.emptyLabel.call(this)} (yet); }, })); }, }; // The same, outside an addon (a host or a test): patch is the module function and returns its undo. export const undo = patch(Thread, () => ({ emptyLabel: () => "Nothing here" })); Thread: isSquashed, dayLabel, emptyLabel. Message: showSubject, authorName, timeLabel, isOwn, rendererFor. Composer: canSend, isSendChord, placeholder, buildPost. Two addons that patch the same member compose in registration order, and removing one addon's patch set unwinds only its layer. buildPost() returns the draft as a PostInput: the subject, recipients and silent flag it returns are sent and are kept with an unsent post, so a retry sends the same thing.

The composer keeps a plain-text draft and a list of mention spans; it never produces HTML. On send, the spans become UTF-8 byte offsets and the transport receives only the closed thread_post object: body, message_type, subtype (comment for Send message, note for Log note), optional parent_id, partner_ids, mentions ({ start, end, partner_id }), silent and client_uid. The answer's store payload is applied as one request and the new message id is placed in the thread's window before the request settles; when it cannot be placed the pager loads the latest page. A failed post stays as an unsent row with Retry (same client_uid, so the server replays the stored message) and Discard.

The feed is one tab stop (the current article) followed by that article's toolbar. ArrowDown/ArrowUp and PageDown/PageUp move between articles, Home and End jump, ArrowLeft/ArrowRight/Home/End move inside the toolbar, Escape returns from the toolbar to its article. In the composer Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) sends in the chatter, Enter in Discuss (sendOnEnter); the suggestion list takes ArrowUp/ArrowDown, Enter or Tab, Escape. The feed is a role="feed" of articles only; actions are text buttons; toggles use aria-pressed; failures use role="alert"; status messages are announced through a polite live region. An addon's controls must have text names and may not add positive tabindex.

ThreadViewError has a closed code: schema, unavailable, bad_option, registry, data, transport, mention, body, pending_limit, disposed. Constructor refusals are thrown; failures during use are shown in the component and passed to the reportError option.

Edit in place, the reaction list, pinned-messages panel, search, copy link, download files, translation, canned responses, emoji and command providers, roles as mention targets, and the variable-height virtual list (the thread renders its bounded window; Thread.layout is the seam). The owning slices are named in the design note.

docs.title: The client messaging store: reading records and adding typed fields

sections.text: One MessagingStore per browser tab serves the chatter, Discuss, chat windows and the messaging menu (ADR 0148 D1). Surfaces never keep message, thread, channel or partner data of their own: they read it here. Package: @erpforall/mail-store (web/packages/mail-store). Behavior: docs/specs/mail/messaging-client-store.md. Executable examples: web/packages/mail-store/tests/ (the test addon is extension.test.ts).

const message = store.record("mail.message", 5);   // a handle: (model, id) message.get("body");                                 // tracked per (record, field) inside a reactive scope message.one("author")?.get("name");                  // many2one: a handle on the target record message.many("attachments").map((a) => a.get("name")); // x2many: handles in ascending id order store.record("mail.thread", 1).counter("unread");    // { value, saturated, stale } A handle is a view, not a copy: a read that finds nothing (not loaded, evicted, deleted) is undefined, an empty list or exists === false. A model that is neither in the schema nor local, a field the model lacks, or an id of the wrong kind throws MessagingStoreError (unknown_model, unknown_field, bad_id); nothing is skipped silently. Wire records are read-only: only payloads write them (the store applies applyAnswer and applyFrame).

Types are compile-time declarations that you add to StoreModels. The runtime checks every name against the schema the server sent, so a declaration cannot invent a field. import type { Many, One } from "@erpforall/mail-store"; declare module "@erpforall/mail-store" { interface StoreModels { "mail.message": { starred: boolean };               // a field your addon's _to_store adds "acme.note": { text: string; owner: One<"res.partner">; tags: Many<"acme.tag"> }; } } Plain TS types stand for scalars; One<M>, Many<M>, Counter and Reference stand for relation, counter and polymorphic reference fields, so one(), many() and counter() are typed. Two addons declaring fields of one model merge. A model with no declaration is dynamically typed (unknown values).

store.delegate("discuss.channel", { via: "thread" }) makes the channel read fields it does not have from the record its many2one field thread names (Odoo's _inherits). Declare the delegated fields on the delegating model's StoreModels entry so they type. Delegation is read-only, follows chains, allows one rule per model, and refuses cycles and a via that is not a many2one field of the schema (delegation).

const drafts = store.defineLocalModel("acme.draft", ["text", "threadId"]); drafts.create("draft-1", { text: "" });           // ids are non-empty strings drafts.set("draft-1", { text: "hello" }); store.record("acme.draft", "draft-1").get("text"); Local records live in the same keyed tables and are reactive like server records, but they are never sent to the server and never appear in a resync request. The model name must not be a schema model (local_model_clash, also when a later schema introduces it). store.persistable(model) returns local data for your own persistence (D7) and refuses server models.

Add a read helper to every handle with patch(RecordHandle, ...) and declare it so it types: declare module "@erpforall/mail-store" { interface RecordHandle<M extends string = string> { acmeLabel(): string } } patch(RecordHandle, () => ({ acmeLabel() { return ${this.model}#${String(this.id)}; } })); The returned function removes the patch. Register patches, delegation and local models from your addon's register(ctx) callback (see client-extensions.md).

A surface that displays a record calls store.hold(model, id) and lease.release() when it leaves. collect() (also run when a request settles) drops, beyond maxThreads, the message windows of threads nobody holds (least recently used first), then messages no window or lease holds, then collectable models (default res.partner, ir.attachment; add yours through config.collectModels) that nothing retained references. Models that are neither messages nor collectable are roots and are never swept by the core. A message that only a root record's many2one field references is evicted unless a window or lease holds it (relations are followed into collectable models only). A thread's messages live in a window (store.windows): one contiguous run capped at pageSize * maxWindowPages (defaults 30 and 5). After eviction, windows.get(thread) is undefined: fetch the latest page and call windows.replace. The caps are configuration (new MessagingStore({ config })); their effect on speed and memory is measured at milestone end, not claimed here.

MessagingStoreError carries a closed code and a message naming the model, field and value. Payload refusals (WireError) are passed to the reportError you give the store, and the result of applyAnswer/applyFrame is refused with a resync request; an unknown schema generation is needs_schema.

docs.title: Migrations: upgrading an addon's data and schema

sections.text: Status: implemented. The design is in ADR 0009 §5 and §7 and docs/design/m2-s5.md; the behaviour is specified in docs/specs/modules/module-system.md (SPEC-MOD-036..039). When an installed addon is upgraded to a newer version, its migrations run inside the upgrade's transaction (ADR 0009 §2): a failing migration aborts the whole upgrade and nothing of it is kept. A migration is either a Rust function marked #[erp_sdk::migration] or a .sql file under migrations/<version>/. Odoo's migrations/<version>/<stage>-*.py modules with a migrate(cr, version) function do not exist here; the rules for selecting and ordering them are the same.

An upgrade from the installed version I to the manifest's version T runs: - every migration of a version V with I < V <= T; - every migration of version 0.0.0, on any upgrade where I < T. A fresh install runs no migration, and neither does a reinit (an upgrade that reloads the addon in init mode). Versions are compared in their semver form (ADR 0009 §5): 1.1 and 20.0.1.1 are both 1.1.0, 1.1.2 is 1.1.2. So if the installed version is 1.0.0 and the manifest now says 1.3, the migrations of 1.1, 20.0.1.2 and 1.3 run, 1.0 and 1.4 do not.

| Stage | Runs | Version order | |---|---|---| | pre | before the addon's schema is updated and its data files are loaded: its new tables and columns do not exist yet, use SQL | 0.0.0 first, then ascending | | post | after the addon's schema update and data files, on the updated registry | ascending, then 0.0.0 last | | end | after every addon of the operation was loaded (upgraded addons in load order) | ascending, then 0.0.0 last | Within one version and stage, the Rust and SQL migrations run together, ordered by name (a Rust migration's name defaults to its function name). Each migration receives the previously installed version in its semver form (1.0.0, not Odoo's '20.0.1.0'). When one operation upgrades several addons (base with yours, for example) and your addon has a pre migration selected in it, the schema update of an addon that comes earlier in the operation does not change a table your addon creates or adds a column, index or table constraint to. That table is updated at the step of the last addon of the operation that adds to it and has a selected pre migration, after that addon's pre migrations ran. So your pre migration sees the table as the installed versions left it, and can add and fill a new required column; the schema update then makes it required. Without a selected pre migration nothing waits: the table is updated at the earlier addon's step, as on any upgrade. While a table waits, every change of it waits, the new columns of the earlier addon's version included: in that operation, the earlier addon's data files and post migrations cannot write a column its new version adds to such a table.

erp_sdk::addon!(name = "library", depends = ["base"]); use erp_sdk::migrations::SemverVersion; use erp_sdk::{BoxFuture, Result, Transaction}; /// Fill the new isbn column from the old code (version 1.1, after the schema update).

async fn fill_isbn(tx: &mut Transaction, _from: &SemverVersion) -> Result<()> { tx.execute("UPDATE library_book SET isbn = code WHERE isbn IS NULL", &[]) .await?; Ok(()) } /// Runs on every upgrade (version 0.0.0), after all addons were loaded; from says which /// version the database had.

async fn recount(tx: &mut Transaction, from: &SemverVersion) -> Result<()> { if *from < SemverVersion::new(1, 1, 0) { tx.batch("REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW library_book_counts").await?; } Ok(()) } /// A plain function must already have the MigrationFn type; name sets the name that orders /// it among the steps of the same version and stage.

fn rename_code<'a>(tx: &'a mut Transaction, _from: &'a SemverVersion) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<()>> { Box::pin(async move { tx.batch("ALTER TABLE library_book RENAME COLUMN ref TO code").await }) } fn main() {} The attribute takes addon, version and stage (pre, post or end, written in lower case, bare or as a string) and an optional name. The build of the addon fails, on the offending token, for a missing, unknown, repeated or empty argument, an unknown stage, a method, a function with type parameters, an unsafe function, or an async fn that does not take (&mut Transaction, &SemverVersion). When the module system starts, a version that is not a migration version (0.0.0, x.y, x.y.z or 20.0.x.y) and two migrations of one addon with the same version, stage and name are errors naming the source locations.

Put the scripts in the addon folder, one folder per version: library/ manifest.toml migrations/ 1.1/ pre-rename.sql      runs before the schema update post-fill.sql       runs after the data files 0.0.0/ end-reindex.sql     runs on every upgrade, after all addons were loaded A file runs when its name is <stage>-<anything>.sql; other files are ignored. Its name without the .sql extension orders it (post-fill). The text is sent as one batch of statements in the upgrade's transaction. A script must not end or open that transaction. When a selected script is read, before any of it is sent, a statement that starts with BEGIN, START, COMMIT, END, ROLLBACK, ABORT, SAVEPOINT, RELEASE or PREPARE TRANSACTION refuses the upgrade with Error::MigrationSqlRefused naming the file and the statement. The same words inside strings, quoted identifiers, comments and dollar-quoted bodies are fine. A BEGIN ATOMIC function body is refused as well: write the body as a dollar-quoted string. A script that ends inside a string or comment is refused. Transaction control inside DO or a procedure fails in PostgreSQL itself (SQLSTATE 2D000). Scripts are read with standard string rules, so a script runs only while the session's standard_conforming_strings is on (PostgreSQL's default). Rust migrations follow the same rule: they run in the upgrade's transaction and never commit, roll back or open one (they are not scanned; the module system detects an ended transaction after the step, when a commit can no longer be undone). One operation selects at most max_migration_files SQL files (all its addons together, default 4096), and one addon's migrations/ holds at most that many version folders. A file past the count is refused before it is read (Error::MigrationFilesTooMany, Error::MigrationFoldersTooMany); the selected files' bytes count against max_operation_data_bytes with the data files (Error::OperationDataTooLarge). A folder named tests, hidden folders and folders whose name is not a version are not read (the last ones log Invalid version for upgrade script). Only the folders the upgrade selects are read; their files follow the data-file rules (modules.md, "Data files"): regular files only, no symbolic links, one hard link, at most max_data_file_bytes, UTF-8. SQL migrations are read from an addon's development folder; an embedded or packaged addon uses Rust migrations.

The upgrade stops, its transaction rolls back, and the modules keep their state and installed version. The error is Error::StepFailed naming the module, the stage and the step (the SQL file's path or the Rust function's file:line); its source is Error::MigrationFailed with the module, version, stage and name, whose source is the function's error or the SQL statement's (its SQLSTATE kept): Module "library": post migration 'migrations/1.1/post-fill.sql' failed caused by: Module 'library': migration 'post-fill' (version 1.1.0, stage post) failed caused by: <the database error> An upgraded addon whose stored row has no installed version (latest_version is empty) while it has migrations is refused with Error::InvalidModuleRow: the migrations cannot be selected without it.

Pre migrations run before schema synchronization and upgrade data files; Post migrations run afterward. If an old writable catalog becomes noupdate, protect its existing external IDs in Pre. Changing the new file's pragma or marking old IDs in Post cannot undo values already overwritten during the upgrade. Base1.1 uses Pre for currency/language protection and Post for company representatives that require the new schema. A failure later in the operation rolls back both stages, schema and data together. Test a genuine old installation, new missing records, tenant customizations and a later injected failure, without rewinding module version markers.
Use an explicit native pre-migration when a scalar field becomes company-dependent: use erp_sdk::{Result, Transaction}; use erp_sdk::migrations::{CompanyMigrationPolicy, SemverVersion};

async fn assign_legacy_cost(tx: &mut Transaction, _from: &SemverVersion) -> Result<()> { let policy = CompanyMigrationPolicy::row_company("company_id")?; tx.migrate_company_dependent("library.book", "cost", &policy).await }

Alternatively, CompanyMigrationPolicy::companies([1, 2]) explicitly assigns old values to both companies. Supply verified tenant identities, never an installer-context default. Missing ownership of a non-null value refuses; shared rows need an explicit company-set decision. The target registry must declare the field company-dependent. Version bump, pre-migration, schema/data loading and later steps share the upgrade transaction: a later failure rolls the conversion back. Repeating the helper on valid maps validates them without changing their company ownership. Populated reverse conversion requires a separate reviewed materialization migration.

Inventory version 1.2 installs database integrity guards and backfills missing location policy rows in the same upgrade transaction. Existing policy identities, flags and audit fields are preserved. Newly backfilled rows have NULL creating/updating users and migration-time timestamps; the migration does not attribute their creation to the historical location creator. New locations copy their insertion row's creating/updating users into the policy, retaining NULL when a SQL writer supplied none. New locations, including locations inserted through COPY, receive their policy automatically. Independent deletion of a policy is refused; deleting its location may cascade it. Stop nodes running an older registry before an upgrade that changes SQL objects, then restart them with the matching build after it commits. A failed migration rolls back its data, installed objects and version marker together. Restore the matching release and database backup when reverting an accepted upgrade; disabling triggers or editing SQL-object provenance is not an upgrade or rollback procedure.

Inventory 1.6 fills each transfer's move counters and state from its moves, and 1.7 rebuilds the transfers' reference projection. Both fills lock the transfer and move tables, but they read the upgrade transaction's snapshot, taken before the lock (the upgrade runs at REPEATABLE READ). A move or reference link that a node on the older registry commits during the upgrade is missing from the fill, and the triggers installed by the same upgrade only add later changes to the stored values. Stop every node on the older registry (or at least its ingress) before this upgrade, as for any upgrade that changes SQL objects. When that was not possible, run each fill once more after the upgrade committed, in a single READ COMMITTED transaction so the snapshot follows the lock: psql --single-transaction -f addons/stock/migrations/1.6/post-move-counters.sql <database> psql --single-transaction -f addons/stock/migrations/1.7/post-move-references.sql <database> Both files are safe to repeat: they set the stored values from the moves and write only rows that differ, so a second run on a complete fill changes nothing.

Exercise an upgrade through the module lifecycle against a disposable database, with existing rows and the relevant old schema restored. Assert the old state before upgrading: changing only an installed version can leave the new defaults, constraints or triggers in place and hide a missing migration. Check preserved record identities and administrator choices, newly filled values, named constraint refusals, and a second upgrade that preserves the resulting data. The CLI's stock integration tests use this approach for the 1.0.0 shape: missing location policies, nullable reservation lead times, and absent security data and SQL guards. They compare the upgraded security data with a fresh install, and test the shipped policy SQL in a non-UTC session so audit timestamps cannot accidentally use local wall time. A reconstructed fixture retains unrelated current metadata; compatibility with an older executable needs a separate previous-binary rehearsal.

Status: M1 slices S1 (scalar fields, create/read/write, method chains), S2 (domains on scalar fields, search, order, prefetch), S3 (relational fields, commands, _inherits, unlink), S4a (computed fields, constraints, inverses, new records, savepoints), S4b (dependencies and related fields through relations, relational fields and commands on new records, parent store) and S5 (grouped reads, the web client's methods, onchange). Every Rust example in this guide is compiled and run as a doctest of erp-test-models (cargo test --doc, part of scripts/ci.sh): the declarations go through the same registry, method-chain and dependency checks a server runs at startup, so an example that drifts from the API fails CI. Lines starting with #  in the source of this file are hidden setup (the models an example refers to, and the async fn that gives it a transaction); rustdoc compiles them, the rendered guide leaves them out. For developers coming from Odoo, see [Odoo compatibility](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/odoo-compatibility.md) for a concept map, worked example, and fail-loudly differences.
Each addon crate declares itself once, at its crate root: erp_sdk::addon!(name = "sale_stock", depends = ["sale", "stock"]);
base is always a dependency. The load order of addons is (depth, name) over the dependency graph, identical after install, upgrade and restart (ADR 0009 §3).
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

pub struct Book { #[field(char, required)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(integer, default = 1)] pub copies: i32, #[field(selection, selection = [("draft", "Draft"), ("done", "Done")], default = "draft")] pub state: Option<Arc<str>>, }

Book is a *declaration type*: it has no values and is never a record. Records are RecordSet<Book> values; the fields are associated constants (Book::NAME, Book::COPIES, Book::STATE) used to read and write typed values:

let books = tx.env().model::<Book>()?; let book = books.create(&mut tx, vec![books.vals().set(Book::NAME, "Dune")]).await?; let copies: i32 = book.get(&mut tx, Book::COPIES).await?; book.set(&mut tx, Book::COPIES, copies + 1).await?; book.write(&mut tx, books.vals().set(Book::COPIES, 5).set(Book::STATE, "done")).await?; book.unlink(&mut tx).await?;

books.vals() builds typed values for Book: only field handles of Book and of the models it inherits are accepted, and create/write validate every value against its field (selection keys, Char(size), digits) whichever API built it. Every data operation takes tx: &mut Transaction: one task owns a transaction, and its cache is shared by every environment (sudo, with_user, with_context). Run units of work through Orm::run, which commits and retries serialization failures and deadlocks (ADR 0008 §5); register side effects that must only happen after a successful commit with tx.after_commit(...).

A regular model opts into transactional event metadata with eventful = true. The default is false; enabling it on any loaded declaration or extension enables the composed model. A later eventful = false does not disable another declaration's opt-in. Rebuilding the registry after the opting-in addon is uninstalled removes that contribution; existing event rows are retained. Classical _inherit also contributes the parent declaration's opt-in through the named child's method resolution order: an eventful parent enables the named child, even if the child declares eventful = false. Delegation with _inherits does not compose this flag; the parent and child opt in independently, and a delegated-field mutation belongs to the parent model's capture.
pub struct EventfulItem { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, }

Native code may also use ModelDecl::eventful(true); owned declarations use ModelDef::eventful(true). Data-only addons set eventful = true in their [[model]] table; non-boolean values are refused. Described WebAssembly declarations preserve the same boolean. The registry refuses opt-in on abstract models, transient models and the closed event namespace, with a diagnostic naming the model and enabling addon. General auto = false and SQL-view model declarations are not supported: their attributes are refused rather than treated as ordinary tables. The current candidate captures creates, scalar writes/upserts, stored computes scheduled by admitted mutations and supported eventful-root unlinks. X2many/relation and reserved-range bulk capture remain unfinished. A persisted event-relevant mutation requires an immutable operation identity from its entry point, including a non-eventful source whose changed dependency reaches an eventful stored compute. Events contain names and identifiers, not field values. Delegated fields belong to the parent model's capture, and each model opts in independently. Delegation capture follows physical ownership even when one write supplies both inherited and local values. Each owner opts in independently. When a write also changes the delegation link, inherited values apply to the new parent; changing only the link does not invent a parent event. Equal physical business values emit nothing. Parent changes precede local child changes, and envelopes share the transaction's final outbox INSERT. Shared-parent batches capture each actual parent target once. The bounded delegation acceptance also covers an ordinary authorized writer, explicit impersonation, a different flushing environment, effective company attribution, access denials and child-constraint rollback. These are specific tested paths, rather than every authority/company combination. See the current OUTBOX report for source-qualified evidence and remaining reentrancy limitations. Write capture compares actual database OLD/NEW values. An equal business write emits no event; automatic log-access and row-version bookkeeping does not itself create a business event. Stored computed/generated changes are included. The originating actor, operation and effective companies are retained when another environment later flushes or computes. Compute execution authority and the existing recompute-only write_uid rule remain separate from event attribution. A later event-relevant operation can settle earlier pending changes before staging its values, so repeated changes to one record retain operation order. Scalar batches remain set-based; all captured envelopes still share one final transaction INSERT. Nested event-relevant side-effect mutations inside an active mutation or compute currently refuse with a named S7 reentrancy error. This includes an inverse or async compute that tries to create/write another event-relevant record; ordinary computed output assignment is supported by the candidate. This refusal is an incomplete S7 case, not full outbox acceptance. No context flag disables required capture. See ADR 0126 for the contract. Scalar upsert on a declared business key captures returned physical outcomes: new rows emit create metadata, changed existing rows emit only actual business field names, and unchanged rows emit nothing. Overwrite, accumulation and floor actions retain their existing upsert semantics. Duplicate input keys map back to every input position but produce one capture per physical row; IDs are actual returned IDs, never inferred sequence ranges. Generated changes and deferred stored-compute writes retain the upsert writer's attribution. Create/write overrides still do not run; an upsert override may wrap the base operation through super as before. Explicit input fields, conflict targets and context defaults obey the ordinary field write mask. Capture admission, callback/constraint/access failure after SQL, or cancellation prevents partial business/event commit. Envelopes split at the existing limits and share the final transaction INSERT. Relation commands, partitioned models and other pre-existing unsupported upsert shapes remain refused. See ADR 0134 and the source-qualified S9 report; this is producer support, not consumer delivery or full OUTBOX acceptance. An unlink tombstone contains only root IDs actually returned by PostgreSQL, with no field values or changed-field list. Missing rows and repeated deletions emit nothing. Batches split at 256 IDs per envelope and share the transaction's final outbox INSERT. The actor, operation and companies come from the deleting environment, even when another environment commits. cascade_models names physical FK cascade/set-null targets, following cascade edges transitively. This summary comes from the current registry snapshot, including cold-cache targets; it does not list exact child IDs. Cycles and duplicate paths are deduplicated. More than 64 affected models refuses the unlink before destructive work; metadata is never truncated. Exact child IDs are planned. The candidate still refuses non-eventful roots that could indirectly change eventful rows, and eventful x2many or ancillary company-dependent/default/follow-delete effects outside the supported FK contract. These are explicit limitations. Deletion-triggered surviving stored computes retain the deleting origin; pending computes for records being deleted are dropped. Cancellation, caught capture refusal or a failed post-delete hook prevents the deletion from committing without capture. See ADR 0133 for this unlink boundary. Consumers, notifications and retention remain unfinished; this producer API does not establish event delivery.

| Kind | Rust type | NULL reads as | |---|---|---| | boolean | bool | false | | integer | i32 | 0 | | bigint | BigInt / Option<BigInt> | bigint zero / None | | float | f64 | 0.0 | | float, digits = (p, s) / digits = 0, monetary | Decimal | 0 | | char, text, html, selection | Option<Arc<str>> (or Option<String>) | None | | date / datetime | Option<Date> / Option<DateTime> (naive UTC) | None | | json | Option<serde_json::Value> | None | | many2one, comodel = "..." | Option<RecId> or Many2one<C> | None | | one2many, comodel = "...", inverse_name = "..." / many2many, comodel = "..." | Vec<RecId> or X2many<C> | [] | | reference, selection = [...] | Option<Arc<str>> ("model,id") | None | | many2one_reference, model_field = "..." | i64 | 0 | | date_range, bounds = "[)" / datetime_range, bounds = "[]" ([exclusions.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/exclusions.md)) | Option<DateRange> / Option<DatetimeRange> | None | A mismatch between the kind and the Rust type is a compile error at the field.

#[field(bigint)] stores a signed PostgreSQL int8 using erp_sdk::BigInt (ADR 0210). Construct native values with BigInt::from_i64(value) and retrieve the exact i64 with .get(). Zero is a stored value. Option<BigInt>::None stores SQL NULL; ordinary dynamic reads map NULL to bigint zero, while typed optional reads retain None. A static default can be a safe integer such as default = 0, or canonical decimal text such as default = "9223372036854775807". Dynamic values accept tagged BigInt, safe integers and canonical decimal strings. Floats refuse. Text has no plus sign, whitespace, redundant leading zeros or negative zero. Full-width domain operands use decimal strings and compare numerically, including IN/NOT IN and keyset/order operations. Company-dependent maps store bigint values as strings, with the same exact decoder. JSON-2 emits bigint values as decimal strings at every magnitude; see [RPC](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/rpc.md#exact-bigint-values). Grouping and aggregation are unavailable in this scalar delivery. Frozen WASM ABI1 also refuses the new scalar explicitly. A browser widget is not supplied by this scalar slice. Changing an ordinary stored field declaration from integer to bigint widens its column during module upgrade. Back up the database and use the normal module upgrade operation; schema changes and data loading share its transaction. Existing values and NULLs survive; declared indexes/constraints remain. Adopting a non-integer physical column also refuses and requires an explicit migration. Reverting the declaration to integer refuses: any narrowing requires an explicit migration that first checks every value. Do not use a relation field to store an unrelated 64-bit counter or job id.

The outbox work adds purpose-neutral Uuid, Xid8 and TimestampTz scalar types and uuid, xid8, timestamptz field identities. This branch has focused prerequisite proof; it does not deliver an outbox, generated native fields, UI widgets or a complete native-field integration contract. Whole native-field integration and outbox acceptance remain incomplete. | Scalar | Value and input contract | |---|---| | Uuid | All 128-bit values, including nil; text requires lowercase canonical 8-4-4-4-12. No version, correlation or authorization policy is inferred. | | Xid8 | Exact unsigned 64-bit value; canonical decimal text, with no sign, leading zeroes (except zero itself), floating-point or signed intermediary. | | TimestampTz | Finite whole-microsecond instant with explicit Z or numeric offset, normalized to UTC. The supported range is MIN_UNIX_MICROS through max_unix_micros() in its rustdoc, bounded by the pinned time library; full PostgreSQL extremes/infinity are unsupported. | SQL NULL is distinct from nil UUID, zero xid8 and the Unix epoch. There is no implicit scalar default. Native literal field defaults refuse pending the future native static-default slice; explicit null/removal retains its meaning. A native schema type mismatch in either direction requires an explicit migration, including on an empty table. Schema sync never silently casts text to UUID/xid8 or attaches a timezone to existing naive Datetime values. Existing DateTime remains naive UTC; there is no implicit conversion to TimestampTz. Legacy RPC CorrelationId and IdempotencyKey parsers retain their existing case-insensitive UUID behavior. Frozen WASM ABI1 cannot discriminate these native kinds from ordinary strings. Explicit native fields, including NULL/empty requests, therefore refuse after the caller's existing access checks, naming a future typed ABI major. Ordinary fields on the same model remain usable. The refusal follows the method chain, not the caller: once a WASM addon overrides create or write on a model, a create or write that sets one of that model's native UUID, xid8 or timezone-aware timestamp fields is refused for every caller, native code and RPC included, because the value would have to cross the frozen ABI (a guest sees Unsupported; native code gets a Programming error naming the field and the future ABI major; an RPC client sees erp.programming). Install such an override only on models whose native fields are set elsewhere, or wait for the typed ABI major. Generic CRUD JSON, nested command ownership, compute metadata and tagged context values have separate admission boundaries; arbitrary user JSON strings are not guessed to be native values. The frozen WIT ABI remains unchanged. Native server_set, physical defaults, grant-contract publication and outbox storage remain disabled until a reviewed operational publisher identity boundary is enforced. No operational role migration or activation is authorized by this prerequisite. Kind parameters: size (char), digits (float), currency_field (monetary), selection, selection_method, selection_add, ondelete (selection: policies for added values at module uninstall; see [Extending other addons](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md#adding-selection-values-and-ondelete-policies)), comodel, ondelete (many2one, many2many), delegate, bypass_search_access (many2one), inverse_name (one2many), relation, column1, column2, ondelete (many2many), domain = [("name", "ilike", "a")], context = {...}, check_company (relational fields). Model parameters: name, description, inherit = [OtherModel], kind = "abstract" | "transient", transient_max_age_seconds / transient_max_count (transient models only; declared policy, cleanup is not active yet, see [Wizard dialogs](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/wizard-dialogs.md#cleanup-policy)), table, log_access, inherits = [("parent.model", "parent_id")], check_company_auto, parent_name, parent_store, rec_name (the field that names a record; a many2one names it by its target's name), rec_names_search = ["name", "code"] (fields a name search looks at; default: rec_name), active_name, order, `constraints = [("_name", "CHECK(...)", "message")], indexes = [("_name", "(a, b)")] (raw) or indexes = [index(name = "_name", fields = [...], method = "...", include = [...])]` (typed, [Index kinds](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/index-kinds.md)), unique_indexes = [("_name", "(a, b)", "message")], fillfactor = 80 (see below), id_sequence = "my_seq" or = MY_SEQ (a &str constant; see below), signal_triggers = [("_name", "policy")] and follow_deletes = [("_name", cache = "my_cache")] (see below), addon = "name" (only needed when one crate declares several addons in modules; by default the declaration belongs to the crate's addon!). Exclusion constraints (exclusions = [exclude(...)]), WITHOUT OVERLAPS keys (`keys = [key(..., without_overlaps = "...")]) and extensions = [...]`: see [exclusions.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/exclusions.md). **Fill factor** (ERPForAll only, ADR 0017 §1). fillfactor = N (10–100, percent) keeps 100 - N percent of each table page free so an UPDATE can put the new row version on the same page (a HOT update: no index entries written, less WAL). Without it the table keeps PostgreSQL's default (100) or whatever a DBA set; with it, schema sync creates the table WITH (fillfactor = N) and applies changes with ALTER TABLE … SET, which affects pages written afterwards (existing pages keep their layout until the table is rewritten, e.g. VACUUM FULL). Measured on a 100,000-row table (docs/bench/m1-s7-orm-perf.md): scattered updates are all HOT from 90 down; rewriting every row in one statement (a mass recompute) needs about 50 to stay HOT and then runs 3–4× faster with a quarter of the WAL. Lower values cost disk and scan time, so use them for tables whose rows are updated often (order lines, stock quants), not for append-mostly tables (logs, posted journal items). Resolution follows the model's declaration order (MRO) like order: the newest declaration that sets fillfactor wins, so an #[extend] in an addon loaded later can tune a model it does not own, and an addon loaded earlier cannot override it. **Shared id sequence** (ERPForAll only, ADR 0058). id_sequence = "ir_actions_id_seq" makes the table's id draw from that named sequence instead of its own identity; every model naming the same sequence shares it, so their ids never collide (the action models use it to share one id space, as Odoo's table inheritance does). Schema sync creates the sequence (bigint, increment 1, no cycle, owned by no column; an existing sequence of another shape is refused) and sets it as the id default of new tables. The name is checked at compile time (a PostgreSQL identifier of at most 63 bytes, given once). It is set per model, never inherited through inherit, and refused on abstract and partitioned models, on a name that is a table, a many2many relation table or a table's own identity sequence (<table>_id_seq), and on an existing table whose id is an identity or draws another sequence (converting a populated table is a data migration). It costs one shared sequence per insert batch, so keep it to low-volume tables. **Signal triggers** (ERPForAll only, ADR 0035 decision 4). The access policy every process serves is compiled from database rows (ir.access, groups, capability mappings, field groups); when one of those rows changes, every process must rebuild it. signal_triggers = [("_name", "policy")] makes schema sync put a statement-level trigger on the model's table that records one policy change per transaction, whoever writes: the ORM, raw SQL, a foreign-key action. Add relation = "<many2many field>" to put it on that field's relation table instead, and update = false to leave updates out (inserts and removals still count). The function the trigger runs belongs to the core: you name the table and the signal, never SQL. base declares them on its policy tables; an addon needs one only for a table whose rows are compiled into the policy. A table an access rule reads through a sub-select (a share table read by a grant) needs none: the predicate reads it fresh in every statement. erp_sdk::addon!(name = "library_policy", depends = ["base"]); use erp_sdk::prelude::*; /// Rows compiled into the access policy (an illustration).

name = "library.policy_row", description = "Library policy row", signal_triggers = [ ("_policy_bump", "policy"),                                   // every write ("_policy_bump_readers", "policy", relation = "reader_ids"), // the relation table ], )] pub struct PolicyRow { #[field(char, required = true)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2many, comodel = "res.users")] pub reader_ids: Vec<RecId>, } fn main() {} A relation trigger must name a stored many2many of the model itself (not one inherited through _inherits); anything else fails the registry build with a Programming error naming the field. A process that changes such rows decides correctly inside its own transaction only if the model is also registered in erp_sdk::access::POLICY_SOURCE_WRITES (see security.md). **Follow-delete triggers** (ERPForAll only, design m2-s3.md §6.1). A table whose rows are mirrored in a key table (the action types and ir_actions) or summarized in a named cache must follow every deletion, also the ones the database makes by itself through ondelete = "cascade", which run no unlink override. follow_deletes = [("_keys_follow", cache = "actions", key_table = "ir_actions")] puts a statement-level AFTER DELETE trigger on the model's table that deletes the key table's rows with the deleted ids and bumps the named cache's generation once per transaction (every process drops its cached values at its next transaction); relation = "<many2many field>" puts one that only bumps the generation on that field's relation table (its rows go when either side is deleted). The ORM's unlink follows the cascades of the registry into such tables and invalidates the cache in the deleting transaction too. cache and key_table may name &str constants; the cache name is [a-z0-9_], at most 40 bytes, and the key table the table of another model of the registry, checked when the registry is built; the key table needs a stored char field type naming each key row's model (only the trigger's own model's key rows are deleted). TRUNCATE of a followed table is refused (it cannot be followed), and a DELETE your transaction sends as SQL on one invalidates the cache in that transaction too.

A field's default is a literal (default = <literal>) or a function (default_fn = path). The ORM asks for defaults through the model's default_get method: create for every field the values leave out, the web client's forms and onchange for a new record (CRUD §4.5, SPEC-CRUD-005 to SPEC-CRUD-008). A default function has the signature fn(&DefaultContext) -> Value: it receives the current user id (ctx.uid) and returns a dynamic value, which is normalized like any other default (below).
use erp_sdk::prelude::*; use erp_sdk::{DefaultContext, ValueMap}; fn current_user(ctx: &DefaultContext) -> Value { Value::Int(ctx.uid) }

pub struct Book { #[field(char, required)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(integer, default = 1)] pub copies: i32, #[field(selection, selection = [("draft", "Draft"), ("done", "Done")], default = "draft")] pub state: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "res.users", default_fn = current_user)] pub user_id: Many2one<ResUsers>, }

let books = tx.env().model::<Book>()?; // What a new record would get: let defaults: ValueMap = books.default_get(&mut tx, &["copies", "state", "user_id"]).await?; assert_eq!(defaults.get("state"), Some(&Value::from("draft"))); // A default_<field> context key wins over the declaration: let with_ctx = books.with_context([("default_state", Value::from("done"))]); let custom = with_ctx.default_get(&mut tx, &["state"]).await?; assert_eq!(custom.get("state"), Some(&Value::from("done")));

For each requested name, the first matching rule wins: 1. **Context key default_<name>** (SPEC-CRUD-006), set with `with_context([("default_state", Value::from("done"))])`. Returned even when the name is not a field of the model. 2. Other names that are not fields of the model are skipped (never an error). 3. **Stored overrides from ir.default** for non-company-dependent fields, when that model is installed. Applicable user, company and global scopes are resolved by the ORM. 4. **The field's declared default** (SPEC-CRUD-005): default = <literal>, or default_fn = path (fn(&DefaultContext) -> Value). default = none in an extension drops an inherited default. 5. **Company-dependent fallbacks from ir.default**, when that model is installed and the environment has a current company. 6. **Fields delegated to an _inherits parent** (SPEC-CRUD-007): the parent model's own default_get (its overrides included), unless the field is Odoo's NO_ACCESS (groups = ".") outside superuser mode.

- **Normalization**: scalar values are converted to the field's type (a value of the wrong shape is a Validation error naming the field). x2many defaults become command triples: one SET of the linked records followed by one CREATE per new line (False gives [[6, 0, []]]). - **Overriding default_get**: an addon can override default_get like any model method; create and the web client go through the override too: # erp_sdk::addon!(name = "library"); # use erp_sdk::prelude::*; # use erp_sdk::ValueMap; # #[model(name = "library.book", description = "Book")] # pub struct Book { #     #[field(integer)] #     pub copies: i32, # } #[methods(Book)] impl Book { #[method(override)] async fn default_get( this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, names: Vec<String>, sup: Super, ) -> Result<ValueMap> { let asked_copies = names.iter().any(|n| n == "copies"); let mut defaults: ValueMap = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), (names,)).await?; if asked_copies && !defaults.contains_key("copies") { defaults.insert("copies".into(), Value::from(5)); } Ok(defaults) } } # fn main() -> std::result::Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { #     erp_testkit::Harness::builder([&ADDON]).check()?; #     Ok(()) # } Only add names that were asked for: create writes every field of the result that its values leave out, and a returned name that is not a field is a Programming error.

Native addon code can derive env.without_default_overrides() after admitting the source records and inputs of an internal workflow. Use that environment for the generated recordsets, for example records.with_env(records.env().without_default_overrides()). The ordinary create and default_get lifecycle still runs. The derived environment removes context default_* keys and suppresses the base default_get lookup of stored ir.default overrides at global, company and user scope, including company-dependent creation fallbacks. Declared field defaults still apply, and explicit creation values retain their normal precedence. The policy survives with_user, sudo, with_company, context updates and context replacement; new default_* keys supplied to those context operations are removed. It participates in Env equality and hashing. Calling it again is idempotent, and the original environment keeps its ordinary default behavior. Use the original environment for source-record admission and ordinary interactive creation. A JSON/RPC context key cannot enable or disable this native policy. This is a default-resolution choice, not an access grant: it does not change the principal, permissions or company restrictions, and it does not alter property reads on existing records. It does not bypass addon default_get overrides or sanitize explicitly supplied creation values. Addon overrides and internal workflow code remain responsible for their own input validation and authorization. See ADR 0262.

ORM columns have no database default: the ORM applies defaults before the INSERT (ADR 0017 §5). A row written with plain SQL (bootstrap statements, migrations, an operator's script, a test fixture) therefore gets NULL in a column it leaves out, and a required column refuses it. For a boolean that must fail closed whoever writes the row, such as the share flag the company restriction of res.users escapes through, declare db_default (ERPForAll only, ADR 0171):
pub struct Member { /// External member until computed otherwise; a raw INSERT without the column stores true. #[field(boolean, required, default = true, db_default)] pub external: bool, }

- Schema sync keeps the static default as the column's DEFAULT: on a new table, on a new column (the fast default is not dropped) and on an existing column that lacks it or has another value (ALTER COLUMN … SET DEFAULT, catalog-only). An extension that declares db_default = false makes the next sync drop it again. - Only a stored, required boolean with default = true or default = false, not company-dependent and not generated; anything else is a Programming error at registry build that names the field and the missing condition. Models declared in models/*.toml and WebAssembly addons cannot set it. - The ORM still writes the column in every create (the static default when the caller leaves it out), so ORM and SQL writers store the same value. Use it for fail-closed flags only, not to move ordinary defaults into the database.
Domains are Odoo's: build them in Rust or parse list syntax sent by a client.
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

let books = tx.env().model::<Book>()?; let dune = Domain::field("name")?.ilike("dune") & Domain::field("copies")?.gt(0); let found = books.search(&mut tx, &dune).await?;                   // the model's order let page = books .search_with(&mut tx, &dune, &SearchOptions::new().order("name desc").limit(20).offset(40)) .await?; let n = books.search_count(&mut tx, &dune, None).await?; let fetched = books                                                  // ids + columns, one query .search_with(&mut tx, &dune, &SearchOptions::new().fetch_fields(["name", "copies"])) .await?;                                                         // Odoo's search_fetch let pairs = books.name_search(&mut tx, "du").await?;                 // ilike, 100 results let pairs = books .name_search_with(&mut tx, "du", &NameSearch::new().operator(Operator::EqILike).limit(None)) .await?; let rows = books.search_read(&mut tx, &dune, &["name"], &SearchOptions::new()).await?; let from_client = Domain::from_json(&body["domain"])?;              // 422 on malformed input books.fetch(&mut tx, Some(&["name"])).await?;                       // prefetch missing columns

- Archived records (active/x_active false) are left out unless the domain mentions the active field, the context sets active_test to false, or SearchOptions::active_test(false) is given. - The access policy's record rules are added to the domain and evaluated in SQL; nothing is filtered in memory. - Relative dates ('today', 'now -1d', '=1d' …) are resolved in the user's timezone (context tz). =week_start uses Sunday until languages arrive. - Every operator on stored fields, paths (partner_id.country_id.code), any/not any, child_of/parent_of, display_name through rec_names_search, and order on columns, selections (declaration order) and many2one fields (by the comodel's order). Field search= methods are refused with a "not supported until" error. - records.fetch(&mut tx, Some(&["name"])) loads what is missing for a recordset in one query per batch; read leaves out records that were deleted. Outside superuser mode both evaluate the record rules in SQL even when every value is already cached. - **Order of ties.** Unless the order already contains id, id is added as the last sort key, so records with equal keys come back in the same order on every page. Odoo leaves ties to PostgreSQL (undefined and possibly different between pages); this only fixes what Odoo leaves open. - **Negations are not index-friendly.** !=, not in, not like and not ilike on a nullable column compile to (… OR col IS NULL) so that records without a value match, as in Odoo; such conditions usually scan. Prefer a positive condition when a selective index matters. - **like patterns.** like/ilike wrap the value in %…%; % and _ inside the value are wildcards and \ escapes them (name like '50\%' finds a literal 50%). =like/=ilike use the pattern exactly as given. Escape user input before using it as a literal. - **Accents.** With OrmConfig::unaccent on, ilike ignores accents. Schema sync then creates an immutable erp_unaccent() over the unaccent extension (it must be installed) and trigram indexes use the same expression, so they serve those searches. - **Plans.** A search whose domain has values runs as an unnamed statement that PostgreSQL plans for those values (as it plans Odoo's literal SQL); reads by id and searches without values are prepared once per connection and reused (ADR 0017 §3). Nothing to do in addon code. - **"queries overflow the depth limit".** An addon crate that awaits a search deep inside its own async code (several layers of async fn around search, search_with or search_read) can stop compiling with rustc's error: queries overflow the depth limit! while rustc lays out the nested future. Until a boxed boundary is put at the search entry (planned), raise the limit at the top of the addon crate's lib.rs (#![recursion_limit = "256"], as the base addon's res_users doctest does), or box the awaited call in your own code (Box::pin(books.search(&mut tx, &dune)).await?). Neither changes what runs.

OFFSET 40000 makes PostgreSQL read and throw away 40,000 rows; search_after continues from the last record of the previous page instead, so page 1,000 costs what page 1 costs (measured on 1,000,000 rows: 0.12 ms instead of 307 ms, docs/bench/m1-s7-orm-perf.md §4), and records created or deleted before the cursor do not shift the pages.

let opts = SearchOptions::new().order("date_order desc, name").limit(80); let mut page = orders.as_records().search_after(&mut tx, &domain, &opts, None).await?; while let Some(cursor) = page.next.take() { // … show page.records …; a client sends back cursor.order() and cursor.values() page = orders.as_records().search_after(&mut tx, &domain, &opts, Some(&cursor)).await?; } let resumed = Cursor::new(order_from_client, values_from_client);   // checked when used

- next is None on the last page (a page shorter than the limit). The cursor holds the order and the last record's key (one value per order term, id last); a cursor of another order, or whose values do not fit, is a Validation error. offset must be 0 and limit positive. - Order terms: the model's stored columns (text, numbers, dates, booleans, selections) and many2one fields by id (partner_id.id, or a comodel whose order is id). Ordering through a comodel's order (partner_id when partners are ordered by name) is refused: order by a field of the model instead. - Index use: give the leading order term an index. When every term has the same direction the next page is one range scan ((a, id) > ($1, $2)); a nullable leading term whose NULLs come last adds a second, IS NULL query on the one page that reaches them. Orders mixing directions are bounded by their leading term and filtered within it.

search_with and read_rows keep every record they read in the transaction's cache until it ends: right for a page or a form, wrong for an export, a report over a year of lines or a batch job over a whole table. stream reads the records of a domain window by window instead. Each window is a Rows batch equal to read_rows of its records; before the next window is read, the window's records leave the cache and its buffers are reused, so a stream holds one window whatever the result size (measured: the same peak for 20,000 and 40,000 lines, docs/design/perf-stream-window.md §5).

let books = tx.env().model::<Book>()?; let opts = erp_sdk::StreamOptions::new().order("id").load(erp_sdk::Load::Raw); let mut stream = books.as_records().stream(&mut tx, &domain, &["name", "copies"], &opts).await?; let mut copies = 0i64; while let Some(window) = stream.next(&mut tx).await? { for i in window.indices() { copies += window.i64(i, "copies")?.unwrap_or(0); let _name: Option<&str> = window.str(i, "name")?; } } // explicit records, in their order, by id chunks (no cursor; no order or active test option) let picked = books.as_records().browse([3, 1, 2])?; let chunk_opts = erp_sdk::StreamOptions::new().load(erp_sdk::Load::Raw); let mut chunks = picked.stream_records(&["name"], &chunk_opts)?; while let Some(window) = chunks.next(&mut tx).await? { let _ = window.len(); } // raw SQL without collecting the answer: each row is lent, nothing is kept let mut total = 0i64; let n = tx .query_each("SELECT copies FROM library_book WHERE copies > $1", &[&0i32], |row| { total += i64::from(row.try_get::<i32>(0)?); Ok(()) }) .await?;

- **What a domain stream sends.** The first window rides one flight: DECLARE erp_cN NO SCROLL CURSOR WITHOUT HOLD FOR <the search> and FETCH, with SET LOCAL cursor_tuple_fraction = 1 in front for the transaction's first stream (the setting lasts until the transaction ends, so it is sent once per transaction, and again only after a rollback to a savepoint opened before it undid it; it steers the planner of every later cursor of the transaction too, DECLAREs only, plain queries are not affected). Every further window is one FETCH, one round trip. The search is search_with's: record rules, the active test and the order (the model's unless StreamOptions::order is given). Pending writes are flushed before the cursor is declared. stream_records reads its recordset as it is and refuses order and active_test(false). - **Snapshot.** The cursor reads the transaction's snapshot: rows other transactions commit while you read are not seen, rows this transaction wrote before stream are. - **Writes inside the loop.** A cursor keeps the rows of its DECLARE, also for what the transaction itself writes later. So once the transaction changed the streamed model after the DECLARE (an ORM write or unlink once flushed, a stored compute written back, a raw UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT or MERGE of its table or of a many2many link table it is a side of, a DELETE of a table whose rows its many2one points at with ondelete cascade or set null, followed through further cascades, a data statement on a table the registry does not know, any other raw statement the ORM cannot attribute, an invalidation, a rollback to a savepoint), each later window takes only the ids from the cursor and reads its values fresh by id, exactly as stream_records does: one more statement per window, values current. What happens to the rows the writes touch, on both sources: a record changed so that it no longer matches the domain still arrives, with its new values (the record list is the one of the DECLARE; stream_records has no domain); a record deleted is left out (like read_rows of a deleted record); a record created is not in a domain stream (it was not in the DECLARE's result) and is in stream_records only if it is in the recordset. For a restricted user, once the policy or a row its record rule reads changed (the streamed model or a model the rule reads), each window's ids are checked against the rule again (one statement) before it is lent: a record the rule no longer lets the user read is refused with the Access error read_rows gives, the same on both sources. A window whose every record was deleted is skipped: the next one is read. - **What the ORM does not see.** The ORM knows what a statement may change from the statement itself. Two kinds of writes do not show in it: a function called from a SELECT that writes (SELECT my_function(...)), and a database trigger that writes other tables. After such a statement the cursor would lend the rows of its DECLARE for the tables written behind the ORM's back. Code that runs one inside a stream loop, and an addon that installs such a trigger, must call Records::modified_external for affected stored scalar columns after settling prior ORM work, so source caches and dependents update. When no dependency notification is needed, Transaction::invalidate_model (or invalidate_records) remains available. These operations move the model's tick and the next window reads fresh values. - **Raw SQL the ORM cannot read with certainty.** The ORM reads raw SQL with PostgreSQL's own lexical rules. What it is not certain about it treats as a statement that may change anything (every stream reads fresh afterwards, an onchange scope opens its savepoint), and a read-intent transaction refuses it with an error saying so: a U&'…' string or U&"…" name, a backslash outside an E'…' string (write E'a\\b', as the ORM's own literals do), a stray $, and unterminated text. The ORM reads statements as a connection with standard_conforming_strings = on and client_encoding = UTF8 does: the pool refuses a connection that opens with other values, with an error naming the setting (for standard_conforming_strings a role or database default; client_encoding always opens as UTF8, since the driver asks for it at connect, which outranks role and database defaults, and the server applies it after the connection's options). When the server reports a new value of either setting on the connection (whatever caused it: SET, set_config, RESET, a function, dynamic SQL in a DO block; also before the transaction got the connection, by code that used a pooled connection directly), every later raw statement of the transaction object is treated as one that may change anything, a read-intent transaction refuses raw SQL from then on, and the connection is closed instead of going back to the pool. Code that takes a connection from the pool directly (outside a transaction object) may get such a connection before a transaction closes it: write text in its SQL as E'…' (as erp_sql::literal does) or bind it as a parameter, never as a plain '…' string with a backslash. - **Functions a read-intent transaction refuses by name.** pg_notify, set_config, the advisory lock and unlock functions, pg_terminate_backend, pg_cancel_backend and the dblink functions: READ ONLY allows them, but their effect outlives the call or reaches past the transaction. A function of your own that calls one of them inside is not seen; declare effect = write for an entry point that calls it. - **Savepoints.** A rollback to a savepoint ends the cursors declared under it (using the stream then is a Programming error). A FETCH made inside a savepoint that is rolled back is not undone by the server: a cursor does not rewind, so the next next refuses (fetch outside the savepoint, or start a new stream). A FETCH inside a savepoint that is released is kept. - **Window size.** By default 2,000 rows first (1,000 when a field is text, html or json), then about 1 MiB of rows per window, between 1,000 rows and OrmConfig::prefetch_chunk. StreamOptions::fixed_window(n) takes 1,000 ≤ n ≤ 10,000 (never 0 = unlimited, never below Odoo's export batch of 1,000) and is refused when above prefetch_chunk. The bound is in rows, not bytes: the 1 MiB aim follows the bytes of the window before, so a window that follows narrow rows can hold up to prefetch_chunk (at most 10,000) wide ones; the worst case is that row count times the widest row. - **The window is lent.** It is valid until the next next call. Keep values you need by copying them out; a clone of the batch stays valid too (the stream then makes new buffers for the next window, counted by buffers_renewed). Writing to records inside the loop is fine: the writes are flushed before the next window (see "Writes inside the loop"). Creating a new (in-memory) record inside the loop is refused, because the window is dropped from the cache and a new record cannot be. A call to next dropped before it finished (a cancelled task, a timeout) while its FETCH was in flight leaves the cursor's position unknown: the stream stops and the next call says so. - **Several streams.** Streams of one transaction may be read in turns (two exports, a stream inside another's loop); each equals read_rows of its records. A transaction holds at most 32 open cursors (Transaction::set_cursor_limit changes it for that transaction object); one more stream is refused with a Programming error naming the setting. The cursor names erp_c1, erp_c2, ... are reserved: raw SQL must not declare cursors with the erp_c prefix. - **Closing.** A stream that is finished, closed (close) or dropped asks the transaction to close its cursor; the CLOSE goes out with the transaction's next statement (no round trip of its own), and nothing is sent when the transaction ends first. A stream belongs to its transaction: using it with another one, after a commit, rollback or lost connection, or after a rollback to a savepoint it was declared under is a Programming error. Streams are refused inside an onchange. - **The transaction stays open between windows.** Between two FETCHes the transaction is idle but open, and holds its snapshot: PostgreSQL's idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (if the server sets one) ends a stream whose consumer is slower than it; the snapshot holds back VACUUM (dead rows of every table stay until the transaction ends: bloat on a busy database); on a hot standby, a long stream can be cancelled by a replication conflict (max_standby_streaming_delay). Keep the work per window short and the transaction no longer than the stream; long exports belong in the export service (planned). - **query_each** runs raw SQL like Transaction::query (prepared, counted, no access rules, the read-only guard applies) and lends each row as an SqlRow (len, column_name, column_type_name, try_get into an SqlValue type: integers, floats, bool, text, bytes, JSON, Decimal, Date, DateTime, each also as an Option). The memory of a large answer is one received batch, whatever the row count. An error returned by the closure stops the rows; the transaction goes on.

Recordsets are immutable collections of record ids sharing an environment and a prefetch set. Typed (RecordSet<M>) and dynamic (Records) recordsets offer the same operations as Odoo's recordsets; a RecordSet<M> also gives access to every Records method.
use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

// 1. Browsing (no query): let book_model = tx.env().model::<Book>()?; let books = book_model.browse([1, 2, 3])?; let one = books.browse([1])?; let single = one.ensure_one()?; // Programming error unless exactly one record assert_eq!(books.len(), 3); assert_eq!(books.ids(), vec![1, 2, 3]); // 2. Python-style indexing and slicing: let first = books.at(0)?;                      // id 1 let last = books.at(-1)?;                      // id 3 (negative index from the end) let slice = books.slice(Some(0), Some(2), 1)?; // ids 1 and 2 let reversed = books.slice(None, None, -1)?;   // ids 3, 2, 1 // 3. Set operations (order and prefetch preserved): let more_books = book_model.browse([3, 4])?; let combined = books.concat(&more_books)?;      // [1, 2, 3, 3, 4] (duplicates kept) let united = books.union(&more_books)?;         // [1, 2, 3, 4] (de-duplicated) let common = books.intersection(&more_books)?;  // [3] let diff = books.difference(&more_books)?;      // [1, 2] assert!(books.contains(&first)?); assert!(diff.is_subset(&books)?); // 4. Other environments (same ids): let sudo_books = books.sudo(true);              // superuser mode: no access checks let user_books = books.with_user(user_id);      // another user's rights (who may switch: below) let ctx_books = books.with_context([("tz", Value::from("UTC")), ("active_test", Value::Bool(false))]); // 5. Filtering, mapping, sorting and grouping on field values: let in_stock = books.filtered(&mut tx, Book::COPIES, |c| *c > 0).await?;      // one column read let named = books.as_records().filtered_path(&mut tx, "name").await?;         // truthy name let shelved = books.as_records().filtered_path(&mut tx, "shelf_id.name").await?; // through a many2one let shelves = books.as_records().mapped_path(&mut tx, "shelf_id").await?;     // Mapped::Records(union) let by_shelf = books.as_records().grouped_records(&mut tx, "shelf_id").await?; // recordset keys let few = books.filtered_domain(&mut tx, &Domain::field("copies")?.lt(3)).await?; let titles = books.mapped(&mut tx, Book::NAME).await?;                         // Vec<Option<Arc<str>>> let ordered = books.sorted(&mut tx, Some("copies desc, name"), false).await?; // None: model order let by_copies = books.grouped(&mut tx, Book::COPIES).await?;                   // Vec<(i32, RecordSet<Book>)> let still_there = books.exists(&mut tx).await?; books.lock_for_update(&mut tx, false).await?;                                  // Lock error (409) if taken let mine = books.try_lock_for_update(&mut tx, false, Some(10)).await?;         // skips locked rows // 6. Closures that need no database access: let nonempty = books.filtered_by(|b| !b.is_empty()); let by_id = books.sorted_by_key(|b| b.ids(), false);

- **Set operations**: - concat(&other) (+): both recordsets in order, duplicates kept (SPEC-RSET-016). - union(&other) (|): union in first-occurrence order, de-duplicated (SPEC-RSET-017). - intersection(&other) (&): ids of self that are in other, de-duplicated, in self's order (SPEC-RSET-018). - difference(&other) (-): ids of self that are not in other, self's duplicates kept (SPEC-RSET-018). - concat_all(sets) / union_all(sets): the same over an iterable of recordsets (SPEC-RSET-020). - is_subset(&other) (<=) / is_strict_subset(&other) (<) (SPEC-RSET-013). - Operands of different models are an error (SPEC-RSET-019). - **Environments** (each returns the same ids on a new environment; the transaction's cache is shared): - records.sudo(flag): superuser mode on or off, same user id. Turning it on removes the default_* keys from the context (SPEC-ENV-004). - records.with_user(uid): another user; superuser mode only when uid is the superuser (SPEC-ENV-005). Who may switch is decided on the principal of the environment you call it on (ADR 0164 A4, SPEC-PRIN-029): the System principal switches to anyone, any principal to its own user, and another user only when it holds the capability principal.impersonate (base maps it to Settings administrators); otherwise the first use of the new environment (a read, a write, a model check, a scoped block, a job enqueue, a capability question) fails with Access "user A may not act as user B: with_user needs the capability 'principal.impersonate'". A switch to the superuser id from any principal but System is always refused ("only the system principal may act as the superuser …"), also from sudo(true); the refused environment stays the caller's own user and never reports su(). To ask whether another user is in a group, call tx.user_has_group(&env, user, "module.group") instead of switching; to open a transaction or an environment for a caller, use orm.begin_caller(user) / orm.env_caller(user, context) (or BeginOptions::caller, PrincipalHint::caller), which refuse the superuser id. - records.with_context(pairs): the context updated with (key, Value) pairs (tz, lang, active_test, default_* …) (SPEC-ENV-006). - records.with_env(env): the same ids on a given environment. - records.with_prefetch(ids): another prefetch set (None: the recordset's own ids) (SPEC-ENV-028). - Results keep the input's order and duplicates and share its prefetch set, so a field read through one result (or one group) is loaded for all of them. Each operation reads a field once for the whole recordset: at most one query per field group when the values are not cached, none when they are. Write loops over recordsets with these operations instead of reading records one by one. - filtered_domain evaluates the domain on the values in memory with the same rules as search (NULLs, 0/'' treated as "not set", negations): search(D) and search([]).filtered_domain(D) agree. It also works on non-stored computed fields and display_name, and follows relational conditions (any, paths, x2many in, child_of): the targets are filtered in memory on the comodel, once for all records; any! and bypass_search_access fields look at the targets as superuser. Text follows the C collation of ERPForAll databases: code-point order, and ilike folds ASCII letters only (É does not match é unless OrmConfig::unaccent is on). - sorted takes the same order syntax as search and places NULLs the same way (last ascending, first descending, unless nulls first/nulls last). It is stable, also with reverse. Like Odoo's in-memory sort it differs from search in three ways: selections sort by key text, not declaration order; NULL integers/floats/amounts count as 0; a many2one is ordered by its comodel's order read with your rights. Text compares by code point (the C collation of Odoo databases). - Closures that need no database access have _by variants: filtered_by, sorted_by_key, grouped_by. To filter or sort on field values, use the field forms above. - exists() always asks the database (one query per batch of ids); it ignores record rules and active and never touches the cache. New records always exist. - Locks use SKIP LOCKED: they never wait. lock_for_update fails with a Lock error when any row is held by another transaction or deleted (rows locked before the error stay locked until the transaction ends); try_lock_for_update returns what it could lock, in recordset order, at most limit records (new records count as locked and come first). allow_referencing = true takes the weaker FOR NO KEY UPDATE lock, which still lets others insert rows pointing at these records.
In an addon that depends on library:

pub struct BookIsbn { #[field(char, size = 13)] pub isbn: Option<Arc<str>>, // redefining a field merges attributes: this one becomes required with a new default #[field(integer, required, default = 2)] pub copies: i32, }

The new field handles are constants of the extension type with the extended model as their model: BookIsbn::ISBN: Field<Book, Option<Arc<str>>>. The extended model may live in another addon crate: depend on that crate and list its addon in depends. See [Extending other addons, data-only models and custom fields](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md), which also covers models declared in models/*.toml and custom x_ fields.

A model can protect its table: with owner_only_stored_fields on the declaration that creates it, only that addon (the owner) and the co-owner addons it names may add a column to the model or change the storage, type, relation or generated expression of one (ADR 0166 decision 7). Integrity code that compares or guards the table's columns can then rely on them. The policy is native only: model files, WebAssembly descriptions and overlays cannot set it, and an extension cannot set, replace or widen it. A co-owner must be a known addon (installed, or linked into the build) and, when installed, depend on the owner; one that is linked but not installed has no effect. #[extend] refuses the attribute.
name = "ledger.entry", description = "Entry", addon = "ledger", owner_only_stored_fields = ["ledger_audit"] )] pub struct Entry { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, }
// in ledger_audit, the named co-owner: a new column is admitted
pub struct EntryAudit { #[field(char)] pub audit_ref: Option<Arc<str>>, }

Any other addon still extends the model with fields that have no column of their own: nonstored computed or related fields, VIRTUAL generated fields (ADR 0062), one2many fields, and many2many fields on a relation table of its own; it keeps its data in a companion model of its own. A stored column from it (ordinary, stored computed or related, STORED generated, translated, row_version) is refused with Programming, naming the addon, the model and field, the owner and the declaration (with its source file and line when it has them), in this form: addon 'audit_x' cannot add or change stored field 'ledger.entry.note'; owner is 'ledger'; declared by model definition 'ledger.entry' of addon 'audit_x' The same holds when the column arrives through a mixin that addon adds or extends, through its model files, or as a custom x_ field (dropped and reported under DropBroken). store = true alone is not the test: a VIRTUAL generated field has it and stores nothing. A relation table of the model belongs to whoever created it; another field naming that table needs the same owner group. Another model cannot take the protected model's table or one of its relation tables with table = "…", and a many2many cannot name it as its relation, unless the declaring addon is in the owner group.

Adding an indexed field, a many2one, a stored computed field or making a field required changes the table of a model that may already hold millions of rows.
