Schema sync keeps the install transaction short on such tables (ADR 0009 §2): when the table has more rows than the host's threshold (100,000 by default), the work that would scan it runs after the install commits, as post-commit steps: | Your change | In the install transaction | After the commit | |---|---|---| | #[field(..., index)], a many2one (indexed by default), indexes/unique_indexes | nothing | CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY | | a many2one (foreign key) | the key, added NOT VALID (new writes are checked) | VALIDATE CONSTRAINT | | a field becomes required without a default | the not-null constraint, added NOT VALID | VALIDATE CONSTRAINT | | a field becomes required with a default | nothing | NULLs filled with the default in batches, then the constraint added and validated | | a new stored computed field (compute = …, store) | the column | the computation for every existing record, in batches | On smaller tables everything runs in the install transaction, as in Odoo, and a new stored computed field is computed for every existing record before the install commits. Until a step has run, its index is missing (a unique_indexes entry does not reject duplicates yet) and records not reached by a backfill read an empty value for the new field. Write a computation that does not depend on the order in which records are computed, since the batches follow record ids. A step does not keep your users waiting: when it would wait for a lock while holding readers or writers up, it gives up after a short wait (10 seconds by default), and the next schema sync plans the unfinished work again.
The addon that owns the model defines a method:

impl Book { #[method] async fn label(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<String> { let name = this.ensure_one()?.get(tx, Book::NAME).await?; Ok(name.as_deref().unwrap_or_default().to_owned()) } }
Another addon overrides it, and callers use the generated BookMethods trait:

impl BookIsbn { #[method(override)] async fn label(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, sup: Super) -> Result<String> { let base: String = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), ()).await?; Ok(format!("{base} (ISBN)")) } }
let label = book.label(&mut tx).await?;   // runs BookIsbn's override, which calls Book's

- #[method] introduces a method; #[method(override)] overrides it and receives sup: Super as its last parameter (super() in Odoo). Arguments after tx must be owned types. - The newest addon in load order runs first; sup.call reaches the previous one. - #[methods(Book)] impl Book generates a trait BookMethods for typed calls (books.label(&mut tx).await?), available on recordsets of Book and of models inheriting it. - A method defined by an addon you do not depend on can still be called by name: this.call::<(), i64>(tx, "bar", ()).await?. - create and write are overridable the same way: create takes Vec<RawVals> (one entry per record to create) and returns Records; write takes RawVals. Overrides receive whole recordsets and value lists: never assume a single record. - copy, copy_data, name_create, action_archive and action_unarchive are overridable model methods through the same dispatch chain: - copy takes default: Option<ValueMap> and returns Records (the newly created duplicate records); - copy_data takes default: Option<ValueMap> and returns Vec<Option<ValueMap>> (field mappings ready for create); - name_create takes name: String and returns (i64, Arc<str>) (the id and display name of the created record; requires _rec_name); - action_archive and action_unarchive take no arguments and return () (writing active = False or active = True on active or inactive records; requires an active field). Copy traversal has fixed limits of 16 nested one2many levels and 10,000 distinct records; exceeding them returns a validation error. Group-restricted copyable fields require read access and otherwise refuse the copy. Stored translations are not yet copied as translation maps. The override below gives copied books a naming convention while respecting an explicit name. Archive methods can be called directly; an override is unnecessary unless the addon adds behavior. # erp_sdk::addon!(name = "library"); # use erp_sdk::prelude::*; # use erp_sdk::ValueMap; # #[model(name = "library.book", description = "Book")] # pub struct Book { #     #[field(char)] #     pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #     #[field(boolean, default = true)] #     pub active: bool, # } #[methods(Book)] impl Book { #[method(override)] async fn copy( this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, default: Option<ValueMap>, sup: Super, ) -> Result<Records> { let mut d = default.unwrap_or_default(); if !d.contains_key("name") { let orig = this.get(tx, Book::NAME).await?; if let Some(name) = orig { d.insert("name".into(), Value::str(format!("{name} (custom copy)"))); } } sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), (Some(d),)).await } } # async fn example(mut tx: Transaction, book: RecordSet<Book>) -> Result<()> { # let copied = book.copy(&mut tx, None).await?; # Ok(()) # } # fn main() -> std::result::Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { #     erp_testkit::Harness::builder([&ADDON]).check()?; #     Ok(()) # } - Of the recordset operations, only exists (no arguments, returns Records) and filtered_domain (takes a Domain, returns Records) can be overridden, as Odoo addons do (for example to answer exists from a cached id set, or to rewrite a condition before calling sup). filtered, mapped, sorted, grouped, the set operators and ensure_one are final. These are reported at startup with the file and line of the implementations involved: - two implementations of one method with different signatures; - an override with no definition below it; - two plain #[method] definitions in one chain (the later one must be #[method(override)]); - a #[methods(Model)] block in an addon that has no #[model]/#[extend] of that model; - one addon implementing a method twice.

The order in which declarations of a model are applied (field attribute merges, method chains) is: 1. addon load order: dependency depth, then addon name (identical after install, upgrade and restart, ADR 0009 §3); 2. inside one addon: source file path, then line. Link-time registration has no order of its own, so an addon that declares one model in several files gets the file-path order, not Odoo's import order; keep each model's declarations of one addon in one file when their order matters.

Trusted native code that changes a model's stored scalar columns with SQL must notify the ORM about the affected records and fields. This includes columns maintained by a database trigger. Settle pending ORM work **before** the SQL, then call modified_external:

let books = tx.env().model::<Book>()?; let book = books.create(&mut tx, vec![books.vals().set(Book::COPIES, 2)]).await?; tx.flush().await?; // settle ORM work before SQL, never after it to resolve a conflict let id = book.ids()[0]; tx.execute("UPDATE library_book SET copies = copies + 1 WHERE id = $1", &[&id]).await?; book.modified_external(&mut tx, &["copies"]).await?; let copies = book.get(&mut tx, Book::COPIES).await?; assert_eq!(copies, 3);

The notification drops the named source values from cache and runs the same dependency walk as an ORM write. Stored computed dependents become pending; non-stored dependents lose their cached values in every context, including dependents reached through unchanged relations. Normal reads and commit settle the computed values. The call itself neither flushes nor writes; relation traversal may issue SELECTs. It also advances the affected model's stream generation, so an already-open cursor cannot put an earlier value back in cache. This method performs no access authorization and grants no read or write right. The SQL writer must authorize its operation, identify all affected rows and columns, and record any required source audit or business events. Notification creates no source audit or event record. Normal later dependent recomputation retains its existing provenance requirements. An error after partial notification leaves the transaction rollback-only; rollback before continuing. Only physical stored scalar columns owned by the recordset's model are admitted. Unknown fields, delegated projections, non-stored fields and x2many fields fail by name. Relationship source columns are not supported yet: changing a parent link requires information about its previous owner. Notification still follows dependencies through links that did not change. Draft records and notified fields with dirty values or pending computations are refused; settle them before running external SQL. Resolve any principal switch before that SQL too: notification validates provenance without a flushing resolution step. Read-only generated-input callbacks also refuse notification. Catching that refusal does not let the callback finish successfully. The method is final and native-only; it has no RPC, script or WASM route. Duplicate names/ids are coalesced, and empty admitted input does nothing. Field names are validated even when the recordset is empty. invalidate_records remains a flushing cache-invalidation operation; it does not replace dependency notification after an external change.
A computed field names its compute method; the method lives in a #[methods] block and declares what it depends on:

pub struct Book { #[field(char)] pub title: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(integer)] pub pages: i32, #[field(many2one, comodel = "library.shelf")] pub shelf_id: Many2one<Shelf>, /// stored: persisted, recomputed when pages changes #[field(float, compute = "_compute_weight", store)] pub weight: f64, /// not stored: computed when read, dropped from the cache when title changes #[field(char, compute = "_compute_label", inverse = "_inverse_label")] pub label: Option<Arc<str>>, /// related field: follows a relation path (as superuser by default) #[field(char, related = "shelf_id.name")] pub shelf_name: Option<Arc<str>>, /// writable related field: writing it writes the shelf's name #[field(char, related = "shelf_id.name", readonly = false)] pub editable_shelf_name: Option<Arc<str>>, }

impl Book { #[compute(depends = ["pages"])] fn _compute_weight(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Book>) -> Result<()> { for i in batch.indices() { let pages = batch.get(i, Book::PAGES)?; batch.set(i, Book::WEIGHT, f64::from(pages) * 2.5)?; } Ok(()) } #[compute(depends = ["title"])] fn _compute_label(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Book>) -> Result<()> { for i in batch.indices() { let title = batch.get(i, Book::TITLE)?; batch.set(i, Book::LABEL, format!("«{}»", title.as_deref().unwrap_or("")))?; } Ok(()) } #[method] async fn _inverse_label(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<()> { for book in this.iter() { let label = book.get(tx, Book::LABEL).await?; let title: Option<Arc<str>> = label .as_deref() .map(|s| Arc::from(s.trim_matches('«').trim_matches('»'))); book.set(tx, Book::TITLE, title).await?; } Ok(()) } }

- **Sync computes** (plain fn) run once per batch of records over values the ORM loaded first. They may read only their depends, the fields listed in reads = [...] (read without triggering a recompute) and the fields computed by the same method; anything else is an error. batch.set_all(field, value) assigns every record. - **Async computes** (async fn) are for computes that search, aggregate or create records. They receive the whole batch as a recordset and assign through out: # erp_sdk::addon!(name = "library"); # use erp_sdk::prelude::*; # #[model(name = "library.book", description = "Book")] # pub struct Book { #     #[field(char)] #     pub title: Option<Arc<str>>, #     #[field(char, compute = "_compute_summary")] #     pub summary: Option<Arc<str>>, # } # #[methods(Book)] # impl Book { #[compute(depends = ["title"])] async fn _compute_summary( this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, out: &mut Assign<'_, Book>, ) -> Result<()> { // one query for the whole batch, not one per record let total = this.search_count(tx, &Domain::TRUE, None).await?; let titles = this.mapped(tx, Book::TITLE).await?; for (i, title) in titles.iter().enumerate() { out.set(i, Book::SUMMARY, format!("{} (1 of {total})", title.as_deref().unwrap_or("")))?; } Ok(()) } # } # fn main() -> std::result::Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { #     erp_testkit::Harness::builder([&ADDON]).check()?; #     Ok(()) # } They also run once per batch, never per record. - Several fields may share one compute method (they must all be stored or all non-stored). - depends lists fields of the record, or paths through relational fields ("line_ids.price_subtotal", "partner_id.country_id.code"). A sync compute reads the values its paths reach with batch.value_of(Field, id) (or values_of for several ids); the ORM loads them for the whole batch first, one query per step at most: # erp_sdk::addon!(name = "sale"); # use erp_sdk::prelude::*; # #[model(name = "sale.order", description = "Order")] # pub struct Order { #     #[field(one2many, comodel = "sale.order.line", inverse_name = "order_id")] #     pub line_ids: X2many<Line>, #     #[field(float, compute = "_compute_amount_total", store)] #     pub amount_total: f64, # } # #[model(name = "sale.order.line", description = "Order Line")] # pub struct Line { #     #[field(many2one, comodel = "sale.order", required, ondelete = "cascade")] #     pub order_id: Many2one<Order>, #     #[field(float)] #     pub price_subtotal: f64, # } # #[methods(Order)] # impl Order { #[compute(depends = ["line_ids.price_subtotal"])] fn _compute_amount_total(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Order>) -> Result<()> { for i in batch.indices() { let lines = batch.get(i, Order::LINE_IDS)?;              // X2many<Line> let total: f64 = batch.values_of(Line::PRICE_SUBTOTAL, lines.ids())?.iter().sum(); batch.set(i, Order::AMOUNT_TOTAL, total)?; } Ok(()) } # } # fn main() -> std::result::Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { #     erp_testkit::Harness::builder([&ADDON]).check()?; #     Ok(()) # } Every prefix of a path is a dependency: changing a line's price, moving a line to another order (both orders) or creating a line marks the order. A record's x2many reads like the record would see it (archived lines left out). Reading a field that no path reaches is an error, as for the record's own fields; reads = [...] takes paths too. - A field that depends on itself through a relation ("parent_id.display_name") is recursive: it is computed level by level, parents first, and a whole hierarchy settles in one flush. - Changes on regular models never mark fields of transient models (a wizard's path stops where it enters a regular model). - Marking dependents through relations reads the relation from the cache when it can (the inverse field of a one2many, a mirror many2many), otherwise one query per relation step, for all the changed records at once; nothing is read when every dependent behind a step is non-stored and not cached. - Override a compute in another addon with #[compute(override, depends = [...])] and a last parameter sup: ComputeSuper, sync or async (an async compute receives the async variant, AsyncComputeSuper); call sup.call(batch)? (sync) or sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), out).await? (async) for the inherited value. The dependencies of every implementation add up. A depends = [...] on the field itself replaces them: # mod library { #     erp_sdk::addon!(name = "library"); #     use erp_sdk::prelude::*; #     #[model(name = "library.book", description = "Book", addon = "library")] #     pub struct Book { #         #[field(char)] #         pub title: Option<Arc<str>>, #         #[field(integer)] #         pub pages: i32, #         #[field(float, compute = "_compute_weight", store)] #         pub weight: f64, #         #[field(char, compute = "_compute_summary")] #         pub summary: Option<Arc<str>>, #     } #     #[methods(Book, addon = "library")] #     impl Book { #         #[compute(depends = ["pages"])] #         fn _compute_weight(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Book>) -> Result<()> { #             for i in batch.indices() { #                 let pages = batch.get(i, Book::PAGES)?; #                 batch.set(i, Book::WEIGHT, f64::from(pages) * 2.5)?; #             } #             Ok(()) #         } #         #[compute(depends = ["title"])] #         async fn _compute_summary( #             this: &RecordSet<Book>, #             tx: &mut Transaction, #             out: &mut Assign<'_, Book>, #         ) -> Result<()> { #             let titles = this.mapped(tx, Book::TITLE).await?; #             for (i, title) in titles.iter().enumerate() { #                 out.set(i, Book::SUMMARY, title.clone())?; #             } #             Ok(()) #         } #     } # } # erp_sdk::addon!(name = "library_isbn", depends = ["library"]); # use erp_sdk::prelude::*; # use library::Book; # #[extend(Book)] # pub struct BookIsbn {} #[methods(Book)] impl BookIsbn { #[compute(override, depends = ["pages"])] fn _compute_weight(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Book>, sup: ComputeSuper) -> Result<()> { sup.call(batch)?; for i in batch.indices() { let w: f64 = batch.get(i, Book::WEIGHT)?; batch.set(i, Book::WEIGHT, w + 0.1)?; } Ok(()) } #[compute(override, depends = ["title"])] async fn _compute_summary( this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, out: &mut Assign<'_, Book>, sup: ComputeSuper, ) -> Result<()> { sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), out).await?; // then adjust or complete the inherited values with out.set(...) Ok(()) } } # fn main() -> std::result::Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { #     erp_testkit::Harness::builder([&ADDON, &library::ADDON]).check()?; #     Ok(()) # } - Field options: store, readonly = false (a written value is kept until a dependency changes), inverse = "_method" (an async #[method] with no arguments that writes the dependencies back), compute_sudo, depends_context = ["key", "uid", ...] (non-stored values cached per context), related = "partner_id.country_id.code" (a path, or a field of the same record; computed as superuser by default, writable with readonly = false: writing it writes the target record, when both records are database records or both are new). Non-stored related fields are searchable (partner_name = 'x' searches partner_id.name; a condition matching empty values also matches records without a partner). - Sensitive display-name inputs can use Env::label_reader() to obtain the original consumer of an internally elevated label read, or the current environment for an ordinary read. Check permissions and read those inputs through this environment. Declare depends_context = ["label_reader", ...] to separate cached values by its principal binding, policy snapshot, resolution/groups and validated companies. This reserved key is derived by the engine; a context dictionary cannot impersonate a different reader. It does not replace ordinary data dependencies or authorization checks (ADR 0195). - Stored computes are computed **before** the INSERT of create (one statement per batch of records), unless the field was given and is editable. Through relations, only paths of many2one fields qualify (partner_id.name: the partners are read for the whole batch); a dependency through an x2many (line_ids.price) is computed after the lines exist, at the next flush or read. Async stored computes are computed at the next flush or read. The full rules, and what precompute = false and precompute = true mean, are in [Stored computes at create](#stored-computes-at-create). - Writing a value equal to the cached one triggers nothing. Recomputation happens lazily: when the field is read, or at flush (before commit, before savepoints, or tx.flush_fields(...)). - A flush that keeps finding new work (computes creating records that need computing, and so on) fails after OrmConfig::max_flush_rounds rounds instead of committing a half-computed state. - When a compute does not assign a **stored** field, the record keeps its current value (as in Odoo), an in-memory record the value it holds (a form's value); only a record with no value at all gets an empty one. A non-stored, readonly field must be assigned for every record: otherwise reading it is an error. - Computations triggered by a flush run in the transaction's environment (tx.env()), not in the environment that changed the dependencies; rows written only by such a recompute get that environment's user as write_uid. Computes triggered by a read run in the reader's environment. compute_sudo fields always compute as superuser, keeping the uid. - Dependencies may include display_name; it follows the model's rec-name field. - precompute = false on a stored computed field keeps it out of the INSERT; a compute that reads (or depends on) a field computed after the INSERT is computed after it too.

A stored computed or related field is written by the INSERT of create, not by an UPDATE after it, whenever its inputs are known when the row is inserted. No declaration is needed: this is the default (ADR 0053). Odoo does it only for fields declared precompute=True and writes every other stored compute of a new row a second time at the flush. **Known at the INSERT** are the row's own fields (given or defaulted), the stored computes of the row that are themselves computed before the INSERT, and fields reached through many2one fields only (partner_id.country_id.code: the partners and countries exist; they are read once for the whole batch, nothing when they are cached). **Computed after the INSERT** (at the next flush or read, one UPDATE per batch) are: - async computes (they may query); - computes that read display_name; - computes with a dependency through a one2many or a many2many (line_ids.price_subtotal: the lines of a new record are created after it); - fields declared precompute = false; - every field that reads one of those. The fields of one compute method decide together: if one of them is computed after the INSERT, all of them are. At create, a **readonly** precomputed field ignores a given or default value and is always computed; an **editable** one keeps a given or default value, and giving one editable field of a compute method leaves the method's other fields empty (as in Odoo). **Inverses and related writes in the same create.** A field computed before the INSERT without a declaration is recomputed at the flush when an inverse method or an editable related field given in the same create changes one of its inputs, so the stored value is the one Odoo computes at the flush; only that case costs an UPDATE. A field declared precompute = true keeps the value it was given before the INSERT for the rest of the create, as in Odoo. precompute = false opts out: the field is computed after the INSERT, together with everything that reads it. It is rarely needed; use it when the value must be computed on the stored row, for example by an async compute that queries it. precompute = true is an assertion, not a switch. It does two things: the value computed before the INSERT is kept for the rest of the create (inverses and related writes do not recompute it, as in Odoo), and the ORM refuses to build (ErrorKind::Programming) when the graph cannot honour it, naming the field and the first input that blocks it. Declare it where you rely on the value being in the INSERT, for example a field that a record rule on create reads: a later change that moves the field after the INSERT (a new dependency through a one2many, say) then fails the build instead of passing unnoticed. It is not needed for a field to be precomputed:
pub struct Author { #[field(char)] pub country_code: Option<Arc<str>>, }

pub struct Book { #[field(integer)] pub pages: i32, #[field(many2one, comodel = "library.author", required)] pub author_id: Many2one<Author>, /// in the INSERT without any declaration #[field(float, compute = "_compute_weight", store)] pub weight: f64, /// asserted (a create rule reads it): through a many2one, its input is known at the INSERT #[field(char, related = "author_id.country_code", store, precompute)] pub origin: Option<Arc<str>>, /// computed after the INSERT, at the next flush or read #[field(char, compute = "_compute_label", store, precompute = false)] pub label: Option<Arc<str>>, }

impl Book { #[compute(depends = ["pages"])] fn _compute_weight(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Book>) -> Result<()> { for i in batch.indices() { let pages = batch.get(i, Book::PAGES)?; batch.set(i, Book::WEIGHT, f64::from(pages) * 2.5)?; } Ok(()) } #[compute(depends = ["pages"])] fn _compute_label(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Book>) -> Result<()> { for i in batch.indices() { let pages = batch.get(i, Book::PAGES)?; batch.set(i, Book::LABEL, format!("{pages} pages"))?; } Ok(()) } }

Declaring precompute on a field that reads label, or on a total over line_ids, fails at build with a one-line error that names the field, says it cannot be computed before the INSERT, names the dependency it reads (here line_ids.price through the one2many library.book.line_ids, whose lines are created after the INSERT) and says that precompute over one2many lines is not supported yet. Odoo only warns there and turns precompute off, so the field is silently written twice; when moving such a field from Odoo, drop the declaration (or the dependency that blocks it). Separately from any declaration, a **required** stored compute that is computed after the INSERT and not given would fail on the column's NOT NULL. create refuses the call before sending anything, with the same ErrorKind::Validation and text as that violation plus the reason (one line): The database refused the change: Missing required field 'Code' (code) for model 'Book' (library.book): it is computed after the INSERT because it is declared precompute = false

- A Validation error raised by create, write, a recompute or a flush (a constraint, a value the converter rejects, a database constraint) leaves the transaction unable to commit: commit() returns that error until rollback(). A savepoint whose block failed is rolled back with its errors, and the transaction can commit again. - Cancelling an ORM future half-way (dropping it, a select! branch losing, a timeout) also poisons the transaction: every later call fails until rollback().

impl Book { #[constrains("pages")] async fn _check_pages(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<()> { for book in this.iter() { if book.get(tx, Book::PAGES).await? < 0 { return Err(Error::validation("A book cannot have a negative number of pages")); } } Ok(()) } }
Constraints run as superuser, once per create/write call on the whole recordset, and after a stored computed field they name is recomputed. In-memory records (new_record) never run them.

pub struct Shelf { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(one2many, comodel = "library.book", inverse_name = "shelf_id")] pub book_ids: X2many<Book>,                       // typed by its comodel #[field(many2many, comodel = "library.tag")]      // table library_shelf_library_tag_rel pub tag_ids: Vec<RecId>,                          // untyped ids } /// Delegation inheritance: every field of library.item is also a field of Book

pub struct Book { #[field(many2one, comodel = "library.item", required, ondelete = "cascade")] pub item_id: Many2one<Item>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "library.shelf", ondelete = "set null")] pub shelf_id: Many2one<Shelf>, #[field(char)] pub title: Option<Arc<str>>, }

// Add a new book, rename one, take a book from another shelf, delete a worn-out one: shelf.write(&mut tx, Vals::<Shelf>::new().commands(Shelf::BOOK_IDS, [ Cmd::create(Vals::<Book>::new().set(Book::TITLE, "Rust in Action")), Cmd::update(dune, Vals::<Book>::new().set(Book::TITLE, "Dune (2nd ed.)")), Cmd::link(stray), Cmd::delete(worn_out), ])).await?; // Keep exactly these books on the shelf: shelf.write(&mut tx, Vals::<Shelf>::new().commands(Shelf::BOOK_IDS, [Cmd::set([dune, stray])])).await?; // Following a typed relation gives a typed recordset: let books: RecordSet<Book> = shelf.related(&mut tx, Shelf::BOOK_IDS).await?;

- Declare relational fields with Many2one<C> / X2many<C> to carry the comodel in the type: shelf.related(&mut tx, Shelf::BOOK_IDS) then returns a RecordSet<Book>, and vals.commands(Shelf::BOOK_IDS, [Cmd::create(Vals::<Book>::new().set(Book::TITLE, "x"))]) only accepts Book values (anything else does not compile). Option<RecId> / Vec<RecId> remain available, with untyped Commands. On the dynamic surface `records.related(&mut tx, "book_ids") returns a Records, records.assign(&mut tx, "shelf_id", &shelf)` writes one, and read returns many2one values as [id, display_name] (read_with(.., Load::Raw) gives the bare id); a written many2one list must be exactly [id, name or False].

| Operation | Typed Cmd | Dynamic Command | Python triple (code, id, vals) | Effect | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Create** | Cmd::create(vals) | Command::Create(raw_vals) | (0, 0, vals) | Creates a comodel record and links it | | **Update** | Cmd::update(id, vals) | Command::Update(id, raw_vals) | (1, id, vals) | Writes values on the record (does not link it) | | **Delete** | Cmd::delete(id) | Command::Delete(id) | (2, id, 0) | Deletes the record and so removes the link | | **Unlink** | Cmd::unlink(id) | Command::Unlink(id) | (3, id, 0) | Removes the link (one2many: deletes the line when its many2one is ondelete = "cascade", else empties the many2one) | | **Link** | Cmd::link(id) | Command::Link(id) | (4, id, 0) | Links an existing record | | **Clear** | Cmd::clear() | Command::Clear | (5, 0, 0) | Removes all links | | **Set** | Cmd::set(ids) | Command::Set(ids) | (6, 0, ids) | Replaces all links with the given ids | - x2many fields are written with commands, as in Odoo: create(vals), update(id, vals), delete(id), unlink(id), link(id), clear(), set(ids), or as Odoo's [(0, 0, {...})] triples in write_values (exactly three elements; SET takes a list of ids). A plain id list written to an x2many field means set. Commands in a create run after the record exists; updates, unlinks and links are batched per record, many2many pairs of a batch are written in one statement. - **Fail-loud ownership** (ADR 0014 F3): update, delete and unlink on a one2many only accept the record's own lines (a Validation error otherwise; Odoo would modify any record). - **One2many full-delete guard** (SPEC-REL-050): on a one2many, once a CREATE or LINK was seen in the command list (and always in create), CLEAR is ignored and SET only links, so lines created or linked in the same list are never wiped. Many2many commands have no such guard. - **New records in memory**: New (in-memory) records named by link/set on a database record are created (or, with an origin, linked and updated), so `order.assign(&mut tx, "line_ids", &lines_with_new_ones)` saves them. Commands on new records only change the cache (see below). Commands on a non-stored x2many apply to its current value in the cache; its inverse method then saves it. - A one2many may also be the inverse of a many2one_reference (res_model + res_id): only the rows naming the owner's model belong to it, and lines created through it get the model name. An integer inverse is refused when the registry is built. - A reference value must name a model the field declares and a record that exists (a Missing error otherwise; Odoo stores an empty value). - Ids of a multi-row create ascend in input order. When all rows give the same fields (the usual case), each batch of rows is one INSERT … RETURNING; rows giving different fields first reserve their ids (one extra statement). - ondelete of a many2one is set null by default (cascade/restrict available; a required field must say which). unlink deletes cascaded rows in the database and only forgets cached values that point at the deleted records; other cached values stay valid. Stored computed fields depending on a many2one that a deletion empties, or on a one2many/many2many that loses records, are recomputed. - An error raised by create, write or unlink after it changed data (rows inserted, parents written, lines created) makes commit() refuse until you roll back or the savepoint it ran in is rolled back. - inherits = [("library.item", "item_id")] gives the model every field of library.item: creating a record creates its parent, writing a delegated field writes the parent, and the child's constraints on delegated fields are checked after the parent is written. - With check_company_auto, create and write check the check_company fields: their targets must belong to no company or to the record's company, else a user error lists the conflicts. - Differences from Odoo in the SQL (the rows are the same): a negated condition on a many2one path (partner_id.name != 'x') compiles to NOT EXISTS (…) instead of IS NULL OR … NOT IN (…), and without a parent store child_of/parent_of become a recursive sub-query of the same statement (id IN (WITH RECURSIVE …)) instead of one query per level.

pub struct Category { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "library.category", ondelete = "cascade")] pub parent_id: Many2one<Category>, #[field(char, index)] pub parent_path: Option<Arc<str>>, }

let categories = tx.env().model::<Category>()?; // the category and everything below it let subtree = categories .search(&mut tx, &Domain::field("parent_id")?.child_of(parent_cat_id)) .await?; // the category and everything above it let ancestors = categories .search(&mut tx, &Domain::field("parent_id")?.parent_of(sub_cat_id)) .await?;

- parent_store = true needs a many2one to the model itself (parent_name, default parent_id) and an indexed parent_path char field; otherwise the registry does not build. - The ORM keeps parent_path ("1/4/9/", the ids from the root) up to date in SQL, at once: one extra statement after create, one per new parent when records move. Values given for parent_path are ignored. Moving a record under itself or one of its descendants is a UserError, raised before anything is written. - child_of and parent_of on the parent field use the paths (parent_path =like '1/4/%'), in SQL and in memory. - Adding parent_store to a model whose table has rows fills every path at the next schema update.

let books = tx.env().model::<Book>()?; // An in-memory record: never written to the table let draft = books .new_record(&mut tx, Vals::<Book>::new().set(Book::TITLE, "Draft Volume")) .await?; // Assignments change the in-memory record only: draft.set(&mut tx, Book::PAGES, 120).await?; // A shelf form with a new line, turned back into commands for a database record: let shelves = tx.env().model::<Shelf>()?; let form = shelves .new_record( &mut tx, Vals::<Shelf>::new().commands( Shelf::BOOK_IDS, [Cmd::create(Vals::<Book>::new().set(Book::TITLE, "New"))], ), ) .await?; let commands: Vec<Command> = form.as_records().x2many_commands(&mut tx, "book_ids").await?; // Work on database records inside a savepoint: tx.savepoint(async |tx| { book.set(tx, Book::PAGES, 200).await?; // returning Err here rolls the database back to the savepoint // and empties the transaction's record cache Ok(()) }) .await?;

- model.new_record(&mut tx, vals).await and `model.new_with(&mut tx, vals, origin, reference).await` build records that are never written; their computed fields compute on read, stored fields come from the origin, other fields from their defaults. - A new record's x2many holds new records: with an origin, the origin's lines as new records of those origins (line.new_with(.., origin = line) is the same record), so the value's origin() is the origin's value; a many2one may point at a database record or at a new record. Reading these for several new records reads the origins once. - x2many commands on new records only change the cache: create makes a new line, update changes a line's values, delete/unlink drop the line from the value (nothing is deleted), link/set add database records as new records of those origins. The lines' inverse fields follow (a one2many line's many2one points at the new record). Database records never see new records in their cached values. - record.x2many_commands(&mut tx, "line_ids") turns a value back into commands for a database record (Odoo's convert_to_write): set of the database lines (origins included), then create for each new line without origin and update with the changed values for each new line that differs from its origin; the inverse field is left out. - tx.savepoint(async |tx| { … }).await flushes, runs the block in a database savepoint and releases it; when the block fails, the database rolls back to the savepoint and the transaction's cache is emptied, so later reads see the database again.
use erp_sdk::prelude::*; use erp_sdk::ReadGroupingSets;

let books = tx.env().records("library.book")?; let groups = books ._read_group( &mut tx, ReadGroup::new(Domain::field("state")?.eq("done")) .groupby(["shelf_id", "create_date:month"]) .aggregates(["pages:sum", "__count"]) .order("pages:sum desc") .limit(10), ) .await?; for row in groups.rows() { // [shelf, month start, sum of pages, count]; the shelf is a one-record recordset, // or an empty one for the "no shelf" group let shelf: Option<&Records> = row[0].as_records(); } let tuples = books.read_group(&mut tx, ReadGroup::new(Domain::TRUE).groupby(["state"])).await?; // GROUPING SETS: several groupings in a single SQL statement let sets = [vec!["shelf_id", "state"], vec!["shelf_id"], vec![]]; let per_grouping = books ._read_grouping_sets( &mut tx, ReadGroupingSets::new(Domain::field("state")?.eq("done"), sets) .aggregates(["pages:sum", "__count"]), ) .await?; for groups in per_grouping { for row in groups.rows() { // [group values..., aggregates...] } }

- Group-by specs: a field, date_field:granularity (hour, day, week, month, quarter, year, or a number part: year_number, quarter_number, month_number, iso_week_number, day_of_year, day_of_month, day_of_week, hour_number, minute_number, second_number), or a many2one path partner_id.country_id[:granularity]. Aggregates: __count, `field:sum|avg|min|max|count|count_distinct|bool_and|bool_or|array_agg| array_agg_distinct|recordset. having` takes domain-like items over aggregate specs. - **Group count and pagination**: ReadGroup::new(domain).limit(10).offset(20).count_groups(true) also counts all groups, before limit/offset, in the same SQL statement (COUNT(*) OVER ()); groups.group_count() then returns Some(total). - **Group values**: groups.rows() returns rows of GroupValue cells: Null (a NULL item of an array_agg list), False (an empty group value, or an aggregate without values), Bool, Int, Float, Decimal (exact, for numeric columns and their sums), Str, Date, DateTime, Json, Records (a relational group value: one record or empty; also a recordset aggregate) and List (an array_agg list). - Datetimes are bucketed in the context timezone (tz); weeks start on Sunday until languages arrive (M3). Selection groups follow the declaration order; a boolean groups NULL with False. Without an order, groups are sorted by the group-by values (many2one by id); with an explicit order, a many2one term follows the comodel's own order. - Everything is one SQL statement, the search predicate included: record rules restrict the grouped rows, the many2many relation joined for a many2many group-by, and a many2one path's comodel (hidden targets fall into the empty group). Pending writes of the fields involved are flushed first; a domain known to be empty runs nothing. - _read_group and _read_grouping_sets are overridable (#[method(override)] async fn _read_group(this, tx, args: ReadGroup, sup: Super) -> Result<Groups>); every caller, the web client's included, goes through them. read_group is final and returns ids instead of recordsets. - _read_grouping_sets(ReadGroupingSets::new(domain, [vec!["a", "b"], vec!["a"], vec![]])) computes several groupings in one statement (GROUPING SETS). - numeric sums stay exact decimals; sum_currency needs currency rates and is refused until M3.

The always-installed web addon puts the web client's model methods on base: web_read, web_search_read, web_name_search, web_save, web_save_multi, web_resequence, web_unlink, formatted_read_group, formatted_read_grouping_sets, web_read_group, read_progress_bar, search_panel_select_range, search_panel_select_multi_range, onchange and onchange_batch. They take Odoo's arguments (a *specification* {field: {fields, context, limit, order}} instead of a field list) and return Odoo's shapes. Override them per model like any method:

impl Book { #[method(override)] async fn web_read( this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, spec: erp_sdk::web::Spec, sup: Super, ) -> Result<Vec<Value>> { let rows: Vec<Value> = sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), (spec,)).await?; // adjust the rows sent to the client here Ok(rows) } }

// Calling a web method with keyword arguments (the JSON-2 body as dynamic values): let map = |pairs: Vec<(&str, Value)>| { Value::Map(Arc::new(pairs.into_iter().map(|(k, v)| (k.to_owned(), v)).collect::<ValueMap>())) }; let kwargs = map(vec![( "specification", map(vec![("name", map(vec![])), ("pages", map(vec![]))]), )]); let result: Value = books.as_records().web_call(&mut tx, "web_read", &kwargs).await?;

- records.web_call(&mut tx, "web_search_read", &kwargs) runs a method with keyword arguments given as dynamic values (the JSON-2 body): unknown or malformed arguments, unknown fields in a specification and lossy values are Validation errors (422). - web_read_group reads the records of every opened group in one statement and takes the length of a limited level from the grouped statement itself: a kanban with ten open columns costs a few statements, not one per column. web_save_multi writes records sharing the same values together, and per-record values are flushed in one UPDATE per field set. - web_unlink raises a UserError with Odoo's UnlinkBlockedError context (Error::context()) when a restrict reference blocks the deletion, directly or through a cascade; nothing is deleted and no table or constraint name reaches the client. - Ordering grouped lists by a numeric field orders by its sum (Odoo's default aggregator). - search_panel_select_range and search_panel_select_multi_range compute range and filter categories/tags for the web search panel, supporting hierarchical categories, counter badges via grouped counts, and custom domains. Omit limit, or send false or 0, for an unlimited display range. A positive limit reaching the display boundary returns {"error_msg": "Too many items to display."}; counters remain complete. Hierarchical category reads apply the limit to comodel records before retaining only closed parent chains. Use hierarchize=false for a flat category list; comodel_domain restricts visible choices. Selection filters ignore group_by and return no group keys. For many2many filters, group_domain is a map from JSON-encoded group IDs to domains: integer ID 7 uses key "7", an unset group uses "false", and a string group ID uses its full JSON string encoding (including quotes and escapes). Keys are parsed as JSON scalars and canonicalized: escaped Unicode and literal UTF-8 keys for the same group ID are equivalent. Missing entries and {} add no restriction; malformed maps, keys or domains raise typed validation errors. For many2one filters, group_domain is instead a domain applied to counters. Relational group_by accepts many2one, selection and other valid scalar fields; compound and binary group values raise an explicit typed error. Counter execution uses one grouped statement per field, including custom per-group predicates; it does not count each choice separately. The returned values use Value::Rows internally, with a shared column layout, while JSON callers still receive an array of choice objects. Relational choices are filtered through comodel search_with and read with read_rows, preserving comodel visibility and display labels. - Not yet: group_expand and fill_temporal (M4), other field aggregators (M4), pending attachments in web_save (M3).

impl Order { #[onchange("partner_id")] async fn _onchange_partner(this: &RecordSet<Order>, tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<OnchangeResult> { let partner = this.as_records().related(tx, "partner_id").await?; if partner.is_empty() { return Ok(OnchangeResult::warning("No customer", "Pick a customer first.")); } this.set(tx, Order::NOTE, "Customer set").await?; Ok(OnchangeResult::none()) } }

- An #[onchange] method runs on the in-memory record of the form when one of its fields changes; it assigns fields with set/write and may return values and a warning. The whole onchange is isolated (ADR 0017 §2): nothing it writes, even to database records, persists, and the transaction's cache is left as it was before the call. An onchange that only reads costs no extra statement; the first statement that would change data opens a savepoint that is always rolled back. A database error on a read inside an onchange aborts the transaction like anywhere else (roll back). A SELECT that calls a function which writes is not recognised as a change: do not call such functions from an onchange. Methods of every addon run in method-name order, each at most once per pass; passes repeat while fields of the form keep changing (unless the context sets recursive_onchanges to false). - The record starts from the edited record's values (computed ones included), so only the dependents of what changed are recomputed. The response contains only what differs from the form, x2many fields as command lists. - **Return values and warnings**: - OnchangeResult::none(): nothing besides the assignments made with set/write. - OnchangeResult::warning(title, message): a warning the client shows in a dialog. - OnchangeWarning::with_options(class_name, sticky) validates optional notification presentation (ADR 0123). Class text is at most 512 UTF-8 bytes, eight distinct CSS identifier tokens of at most 64 bytes, separated only by ASCII spaces. Tokens match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*; malformed/duplicate values return Validation. The wire spelling is className; sticky is optional boolean. A single warning preserves these options, including explicit empty class text or sticky false. Complete normalized warnings deduplicate; several distinct warnings combine in method order into the existing dialog, without notification-only options. The default dialog ignores notification presentation. - .value(field, value): also assign field (Odoo's {'value': …}). id is ignored; a name that is not a field of the model is a Programming error (Odoo ignores it). - **Calling onchange**: the web client calls records.web_call(&mut tx, "onchange", &kwargs); Rust code can call records.onchange(&mut tx, values, field_names, spec) directly.

pub struct Move { #[field(integer)] pub copies: i32, #[field(one2many, comodel = "account.payment", inverse_name = "move_id")] pub payment_ids: X2many<Payment>, /// sees the amounts of unsaved payments in a form #[field(integer, compute = "_compute_total")] pub total: i32, }

impl Move { #[compute(depends = ["payment_ids.amount"])] fn _compute_total(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Move>) -> Result<()> { for i in batch.indices() { let payments = batch.get(i, Move::PAYMENT_IDS)?; let mut total: i32 = 0; for amount in batch.values_of(Payment::AMOUNT, payments.ids())? { total = total .checked_add(amount) .ok_or_else(|| Error::validation("the total of the payments overflows"))?; } batch.set(i, Move::TOTAL, total)?; } Ok(()) } } /// A payment is a move: copies and total are fields of Payment too
pub struct Payment { #[field(many2one, comodel = "account.move", required, ondelete = "cascade")] pub move_id: Many2one<Move>, #[field(integer)] pub amount: i32, }

impl Payment { #[onchange("amount")] async fn _onchange_amount(this: &RecordSet<Payment>, tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<OnchangeResult> { // a delegated field: assigned on the form's in-memory move, never in the database this.as_records().set_value(tx, "copies", Value::Int(2)).await?; Ok(OnchangeResult::none()) } }

- Delegated fields work in onchange like the model's own: the in-memory record gets an in-memory parent (the edited record's parent, or a new one), the form's values and first-call defaults of delegated fields go to it, and the parent's computed fields follow. A payment form changing amount gets the move's recomputed total back, unsaved amount included; changing a field the move's computed fields depend on returns those fields too. An onchange method may assign a delegated field (set_value above): it is written on the in-memory parent only. - In a one2many whose inverse is the delegate (payment_ids of a move), a line's delegated values go to the form's record. Every in-memory line of a one2many points at the form's record (as in Odoo), so a line's computed fields see the form's values; a line or record moved to another parent leaves the old one, so the old parent's aggregates no longer count it. The cost does not grow with the number of lines: their parents are read together. - A delegate pointing at a record that does not exist, or that the user may not read, is a Missing / Access error. A many2one value given as a map is read as the record its id names (its other keys are not applied); without id it is a Validation error (Odoo builds an in-memory record from the map; see docs/design/m1-onchg.md). - Outside onchange, a new record takes values of delegated fields only when its delegate is a new record: new with delegated values, or a write on a new record whose delegate is empty or a database record, is a Programming error (Odoo writes them on a new parent). So is a write of delegated values on database records that sets a new record as delegate, or that empties the delegate. - Not yet: change_default with ir.default (M3).

pub struct Post { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field( many2many, comodel = "blog.tag", relation = "blog_post_tag_rel", column1 = "post_id", column2 = "tag_id" )] pub tag_ids: X2many<Tag>, } /// post_ids is the mirror of blog.post.tag_ids: the same table, the columns swapped

pub struct Tag { #[field(char)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field( many2many, comodel = "blog.post", relation = "blog_post_tag_rel", column1 = "tag_id", column2 = "post_id" )] pub post_ids: X2many<Post>, /// in a post's form, a tag of the form counts the unsaved post too #[field(integer, compute = "_compute_post_count")] pub post_count: i32, }

impl Tag { #[compute(depends = ["post_ids"])] fn _compute_post_count(batch: &mut Batch<'_, Tag>) -> Result<()> { for i in batch.indices() { let posts = batch.get(i, Tag::POST_IDS)?; let count = i32::try_from(posts.len()) .map_err(|_| Error::validation("too many posts to count"))?; batch.set(i, Tag::POST_COUNT, count)?; } Ok(()) } }

- Every line of a many2many in a form lists the form's in-memory record in the comodel's mirror many2many (the field on the same table with the columns swapped), as in Odoo: a tag created in a post's form has post_count 1, and a computed field of the post over tag_ids.post_ids counts the post on every tag. An edited post is listed once on the tags it already has. It costs no statement per line. - Tags linked from the database keep the stored values of the fields the form shows for them (Odoo copies them before building the form's record), so a post_count in the tag list shows the stored count for them; their mirror lists the post all the same. - A tag the form removes still lists the post in its mirror until the onchange ends (as in Odoo; it is not part of the response). Nothing outlives the onchange. - A delegated many2many (_inherits) lists the form's in-memory parent on its lines the same way, also for changed values, where Odoo lists it only on lines whose mirror was already read (docs/design/m1-onchg-m2m.md, candidate divergence D6 of the GRP spec).

pub struct Order { #[field(one2many, comodel = "sale.order.line", inverse_name = "order_id")] pub line_ids: Vec<RecId>, #[field( many2many, comodel = "account.tax", relation = "sale_order_tax_rel", column1 = "order_id", column2 = "tax_id" )] pub tax_ids: Vec<RecId>, }

pub struct OrderLine { #[field(many2one, comodel = "sale.order", ondelete = "cascade")] pub order_id: Option<RecId>, #[field( many2many, comodel = "account.tax", relation = "sale_order_line_tax_rel", column1 = "line_id", column2 = "tax_id" )] pub tax_ids: Vec<RecId>, }

impl Order { /// The order's taxes are added to every line's taxes. #[onchange("tax_ids")] async fn _onchange_taxes(this: &RecordSet<Order>, tx: &mut Transaction) -> Result<OnchangeResult> { let taxes = this.as_records().related(tx, "tax_ids").await?; let lines = this.as_records().related(tx, "line_ids").await?; for line in lines.iter() { let all = line.related(tx, "tax_ids").await?.union(&taxes)?; line.assign(tx, "tax_ids", &all).await?; } Ok(OnchangeResult::none()) } }

- The values of a line command may hold the line's own x2many values, command lists again, at any depth: [0, "virtual_7", {"tax_ids": [[4, 3, 0]]}]. They apply like the form's own values, on the line's current value (a saved line starts from its stored lines, a new line from none); the new lines of a one2many inside a line point at that in-memory line, so computed fields over any level (an order total over the lines' sub-lines) see them. - With the lines' x2many fields in the specification (`{"line_ids": {"fields": {"tax_ids": {"fields": {"name": {}}}}}}`), their changes come back as nested command lists inside the line's command: the method above returns `[1, line, {"tax_ids": [[4, tax, {"id": tax, "name": …}]]}] for every line. A saved line linked into the form (LINK`) comes back with its stored values and an UPDATE whose nested commands compare its lines with the stored ones. - A line's value of a delegated x2many field goes to the line's in-memory parent, like its other delegated values. - Limits: command lists nested deeper than 16 levels, or more than 100,000 line commands in one call (all levels together, a SET counting its ids), are Validation errors.

A named cache (tx.ormcache(name, key, compute), tx.invalidate_ormcache(name)) is shared by the transactions of one process. When the server runs with cross-process signals (set up by the server, not by addons), an invalidation is also seen by every other process serving the database: - Committing a transaction that called invalidate_ormcache(name) records a change of cache:<name> in the same transaction. Other processes clear that cache before their next transaction runs; no notification is sent for caches, the start of every transaction reads the change. - A value your method computes is published at commit only if no other process invalidated the cache after your transaction started. Otherwise it is dropped (it may come from data that is already out of date) and the next call computes it again. Nothing to do in addon code: compute from the transaction you are given. - Cache names are 1 to 64 characters of [a-z0-9_.]; committing an invalidation of a cache with any other name fails with a Programming error.

Append-mostly tables (an outbox, an audit trail, job history, logs) grow by millions of rows a day and are cleaned up by age. Declare them **partitioned**: the rows live in one table per hour, day, week or month, the ORM creates the coming partitions ahead of time, and old rows go away by dropping whole partitions (constant time, no DELETE, no vacuum debt). Odoo has no partitioning; the rules below are ERPForAll's (ADR 0040 D6, docs/design/m3-ormx.md §7).
use erp_sdk::prelude::*; /// One table per day of create_date, 7 days created ahead, 30 days kept.

name = "audit.event", description = "Audit Event", partition = partition(interval = "day", premake = 7, retain = 30) )] pub struct AuditEvent { #[field(json)] pub payload: Option<erp_sdk::serde_json::Value>, } /// One table per month of recorded_at, which the server fills; every partition is kept.

name = "audit.entry", description = "Audit Entry", partition = partition(by = "recorded_at", interval = "month", premake = 2, retain = "all") )] pub struct AuditEntry { #[field(datetime, required, server_set)] pub recorded_at: Option<DateTime>, #[field(char)] pub what: Option<Arc<str>>, }

partition(...) takes interval ("hour", "day", "week" from Monday, or "month", all in UTC), premake (intervals created after the current one, 1 to 1000; at least 2 for "hour", because partition upkeep may run up to one hour apart), retain (intervals kept before the current one, 1 to 1000, or "all") and, optionally, by. None of them has a default. **The partition key is always server time.** It is create_date unless by names another field, which must be a stored, required datetime field declared server_set. The ORM fills a server_set field at insert with the transaction timestamp, exactly as it fills create_date; the field is readonly in fields_get, never copied, and a value for it in create, write or a data file fails with Programming 'audit.entry.recorded_at' is set by the server and cannot be written. The same error answers a value for create_date on a partitioned model (Odoo drops it silently on other models and still does for write_date; a partitioned model refuses it, whichever column is its key). So no caller can steer a row into a partition, and a row never moves between partitions. server_set is allowed on any stored datetime field without a compute, related path or default, partitioned model or not. **Only leaf models can be partitioned.** The table's primary key is (id, key): id alone is not unique across partitions, so nothing may reference the model. The registry refuses, when it is built: - a many2one (an _inherits delegate is one) or a many2many pointing to the model, and a many2many on the model itself: model 'audit.event' is partitioned, so no field may reference it; 'sale.order.event_id' does; - partition on an #[extend]: only the declaration that creates the model decides (partitioning of 'audit.event' can only be declared by its owner (audit_trail)), and a model inheriting a partitioned one under a new name is not partitioned; - the access engine's policy tables (ir.access, res.groups, res.users, …: ADR 0035 D4), abstract and transient models, a fill factor, a table name longer than 51 bytes (partition names append _p and up to 10 digits), and a key that is not server time; - partition in models/*.toml: partitioning is declared by native addons only; - a business key (keys = [key(...)], the arbiter of upsert): a unique constraint of a partitioned table must contain the partition key, which the server sets on every insert, so no row could ever match it (`business key '_k' of partitioned model 'audit.event' cannot be an upsert key: ...; rows of a partitioned model are inserted with create, not upserted), and upsert on a partitioned model is a Programming` error too; - an exclusion or a WITHOUT OVERLAPS key that does not compare the partition key with = (exclusion '_no_overlap' of partitioned model 'audit.slot' must include the partition key 'recorded_at'): list it in equal (or the key's fields). Soft references (res_model/res_id, reference fields) and a one2many listing the model's rows from another model are fine. **Schema sync** creates the table PARTITION BY RANGE (<key>) with the partitions of the declared window, named <table>_p<YYYYMMDDHH> (hour), <table>_p<YYYYMMDD> (day, week) or <table>_p<YYYYMM> (month), each covering [start, next start). There is never a default partition. An existing partitioned table that matches the declaration (range on the key, a timestamp key column, primary key (id, key), every partition named and bounded for the interval, no default partition) is **adopted** as it is, whoever created it: a module that wrote its own partition DDL in this convention moves to the declaration without a rewrite. A table whose partitioning would change (regular to partitioned, back, or a different interval) is created again when it was never written, and refused when it has rows: `table 'audit_event' has rows; changing its partitioning is not supported (ADR 0040 D6; business tables: M5 partitioning ADR)`. **Upkeep** keeps the window. Until the job scheduler runs it for you, call it yourself, from a loop that runs once per interval for example; each call runs on the **owner** pool (the request role has no DDL right), outside any request transaction:

// create what is missing up to premake intervals ahead (cheap when nothing is missing) let report = orm.ensure_partitions(owner, "audit.event", Horizon::Declared).await?; for entry in report.entries() { println!("{} {}: {}", entry.model(), entry.partition(), entry.action()); } // detach (concurrently: writers keep inserting) and drop what is older than retain let retired = orm.retire_partitions(owner, "audit.event", KeepAfter::Declared).await?; retired.into_result()?; // a failed step becomes an error listing it

- ensure_partitions first finishes any detach an interruption left pending, then creates every missing partition of the window; it is safe to call from several processes at once (a partition created meanwhile is reported existed). retire_partitions marks each old partition, detaches it with DETACH PARTITION … CONCURRENTLY and drops it; a table an interrupted retirement left behind is dropped by the next call. maintain_partitions(owner, now) does both for every partitioned model. - The native server calls generic upkeep at startup and periodically with the current installed registry and an owner pool. Addons only declare their partition policy; they do not register an upkeep job. base.partition_upkeep_interval_secs is a database-wide Technical parameter (default 3600 seconds, allowed 60 through 3600). Closed audit/outbox event-table upkeep is separate. This timer is independent of ordinary queue enablement; queue-based execution history for it is not available yet. - The returned PartitionReport lists every partition created, existed, finalized, detached, dropped or failed with the database's reason; a failed step never stops the others, and nothing is skipped silently. It is #[must_use]: check is_complete() or call into_result(). - Every lock wait of the upkeep is bounded by OrmConfig::partition_lock_timeout (5 s by default, 100 ms to 1 h); a concurrent detach that waits longer for older transactions gives up and leaves the partition pending, and the next call finishes it. - Removing a retired partition takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the tables its foreign keys point to (the create_uid and write_uid keys point to res_users), and readers of those tables queue behind a waiting removal. The removal therefore gives up after 300 ms (PARTITION_SHORT_LOCK_TIMEOUT, not the longer partition_lock_timeout): the table stays detached and marked, the report lists it as drop deferred (drops_deferred(), not a failure; also logged as a tracing warning) and the next retire_partitions or maintain_partitions removes it. Attaching a new partition, detaching a retired one and finishing a pending detach take SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on those tables, which queues their *writers* (a login updating res_users) behind a waiting statement; they run under the same 300 ms. A wait that is cut is a failed entry whose PartitionEntry::is_lock_timeout() is true (SQLSTATE 55P03, error kind Lock): not a fault, the next run repeats it (a cut detach leaves the partition attached, or pending, which the next run finishes; the marker erp:retired is taken back from a partition that stayed attached). - The 300 ms bound also cuts the wait of a detach or finalize for older transactions (it is database-wide: any transaction open longer than that, in any session, counts). With a long transaction around, a detach stays pending run after run and old partitions are not retired. Watch partition_health: PartitionWindow::pending_detaches() counts the detaches left pending and oldest_pending_end() gives the end of the oldest such partition's range; a count above 0 over several runs means look for a long-running or prepared transaction. - A failed entry carries its structure, not only text: PartitionEntry::step(), reason(), sqlstate() and error_kind(). A scheduler retries is_lock_timeout() entries quietly and raises the others. - ensure_partitions(…, Horizon::Through(t)) with t before the interval holding the current time is a Programming error. A step that finds its lock held by another upkeep fails with a Lock error naming the table. - maintain_partitions(owner, now) places the window and the retention cutoff by now, one clock; the database's clock only guards (a cutoff after it is refused, so a clock running ahead cannot retire live partitions). Pass the database's time, or your own when it is within an interval of it. - A partition whose bounds are not a pair of timestamps cannot be compared with the cutoff: every retirement lists it as failed until someone detaches it by hand. - Upkeep bumps no cross-process generation: attaching or detaching a partition changes no result shape, and PostgreSQL re-plans the statements that read the table, in every process. **When upkeep falls behind**, inserts fail loudly instead of landing in a catch-all partition: `no partition of 'audit.event' accepts create_date = 2026-10-19 10:00:00.123456: partition upkeep has not created it yet (window: 7 days; see the health check) (Database, SQLSTATE 23514`). Orm::partition_health(pool) reports, per partitioned model, how many consecutive intervals from the current one have a partition; fewer than 2 is short. It also counts the partitions it cannot place in time (PartitionWindow::unreadable_bounds(): a MINVALUE, MAXVALUE or infinity bound, a default partition); anything above 0 wants a look. A model whose table is missing or not partitioned in the database is a Database error, not a window of 0. **A partitioned table that already holds rows** follows the large-table rule of schema sync (SchemaSyncOptions::large_table_rows). PostgreSQL refuses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a partitioned parent, so an index on a large partitioned table becomes one SchemaStep (SchemaStepKind::CreatePartitionedIndex): CREATE INDEX ... ON ONLY the parent (a catalog entry, invalid for now), one CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY per partition, and ALTER INDEX ... ATTACH PARTITION, after which the parent index is valid. A step that stopped half-way continues with the partitions that have no index attached yet (a parent index left by another declaration, or without a comment to tell, is dropped with the partition indexes attached to it and built again). Each partition's build holds the table's partition upkeep lock, so a retirement cannot detach it meanwhile; a run that cannot take the lock within the step's lock timeout fails with a Lock error and resumes at the next sync. A UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint object has no online form (ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX is refused on a partitioned table), so the install fails before any DDL naming the constraint, the table and the threshold; declare a unique index (it must include the key) instead. An exclusion is refused like on any large table. Reads and writes need nothing special: create, read, search, write and unlink work as on any model, with the same statement counts (a read by id probes each partition's primary key index; the retention keeps their number bounded). Search-panel many2many group_domain maps accept at most 64 entries per call; larger maps fail with Validation. This input-shape bound does not limit returned choices or truncate counters. For example, construct typed panel options and pass them to a model recordset: use erp_orm::{Records, SearchPanelSelectMultiRange, SearchPanelSelectRange, Transaction}; use erp_fields::{Result, Value}; async fn panel_values(tx: &mut Transaction, model: &Records) -> Result<(Value, Value)> { let mut category = SearchPanelSelectRange::new("category_id"); category.enable_counters = true; let mut tags = SearchPanelSelectMultiRange::new("tag_ids"); tags.enable_counters = true; tags.group_by = Some("category_id".to_owned()); let categories = model.search_panel_select_range(tx, category).await?; let filters = model.search_panel_select_multi_range(tx, tags).await?; Ok((categories, filters)) }

A native selection_method uses #[selection] inside #[methods]. Its second parameter is &mut SelectionContext, and it returns Result<()>. Emit each pair through the checked sink, or read an authorized stored-text catalog: erp_sdk::addon!(name = "selection_guide"); use erp_sdk::prelude::*; use erp_sdk::{SelectionContext, SelectionLimits};
pub struct Catalog { #[field(char)] pub code: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(text)] pub label: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(boolean, default = true)] pub active: bool, }
pub struct Item { #[field(selection, selection_method = "_choices")] pub choice: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(selection, selection_method = "_priority")] pub priority: Option<Arc<str>>, }

impl Item { #[selection] async fn _choices(_this: &RecordSet<Item>, ctx: &mut SelectionContext<'_>) -> Result<()> { ctx.catalog("selection_guide.catalog", &Domain::TRUE, "code", "label", "code").await } #[selection] async fn _priority(_this: &RecordSet<Item>, ctx: &mut SelectionContext<'_>) -> Result<()> { ctx.emit("normal", "Normal")?; ctx.emit("high", "High") } }
let limits = SelectionLimits::new(100, 16_384, 4, 512)?; let config = erp_sdk::OrmConfig { selection_limits: limits, ..Default::default() };

Use #[selection(override)] and a final sup: erp_sdk::SelectionSuper for an inherited provider; sup.call(ctx, this.as_records()).await reaches the next native implementation. Ordinary #[method] signatures are refused before execution. Provider names can remain owned registry strings; no 'static conversion is needed. emit checks duplicate keys and admission before copying. One metadata operation, including sibling fields and ctx.resolve(model, field) re-entry, shares at most 4096 pairs, 1 MiB owned UTF-8 key/label bytes, depth 16 and 8192 work units. Limits are positive and can only tighten. Pair emission, catalog rows, provider entries, catalog domain/value nodes (including policy predicates) and explicit ctx.charge(work) each consume work. Charge native calculations before performing them or copying their results. A caught failure still refuses the outer metadata operation. Empty catalogs are valid; duplicate keys and NULL keys or labels are errors. Static selections and callable field-value conversion keep their existing behavior: a callable catalog is not a generic membership constraint. catalog retains the caller's model/field/record rights, company and active context, and database snapshot. It supports stored text projections and direct stored scalar domains/orders with literal or principal-parameter operands. Custom nodes, opaque SQL/query operands and nested domain values refuse before optimization. Relational traversal, hierarchy/access operators and nonstored projection fields refuse; they do not trigger arbitrary computed callbacks. Pending writes are prepared before capability entry. SQL limits candidates and suppresses oversized strings before the driver receives them. There is no cross-transaction catalog cache. The capability exposes environment inspection, emit, catalog, resolve and charge. It exposes no mutable transaction, raw SQL, create/write/unlink, flush, commit-hook registration or transaction control. Native Rust is trusted executable code: cooperative charging does not sandbox arbitrary CPU, allocation, files or network access. Untrusted executable providers require a separate script/Wasm budget; #[selection] is currently native-only.

A nonstored compute can declare search_method and a synchronous #[search_method] provider. The provider receives a validated operator/value request and a read-only context, and returns a bounded domain instead of loading and filtering records. The ordinary addon MRO supports an explicit FieldSearchSuper continuation. ADR 0086 is accepted in substance and remains Proposed until the designated lead merges it. See [search-method contracts and examples](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/search-methods.md).

Stored-compute backfills that can change eventful physical fields are not supported yet. Schema planning refuses them before applying planned DDL or backfill writes, including a non-eventful source whose computed dependencies reach an eventful model. A previously queued backfill is checked against the current registry on resume. The error says that capture of the stored-compute backfill is not available yet. No request identity is substituted for a system upgrade origin. Keep affected addons from opting into events until this system-origin boundary and the lead's other pre-opt-in follow-ups are delivered. Fresh creation of a table without a backfill is separate. An existing table that holds no row is admitted: the new column is added, nothing is backfilled and no event is written, because there is no record to report. A table whose rows were deleted but not yet vacuumed away is still refused, because the check after the column is added looks at the table's physical size; a VACUUM of the table normally gives those pages back (it skips that step when it cannot take the lock), after which the sync is admitted. An eventful model may have at most 128 fields with a column of its own table (id not counted), because one event lists at most 128 changed field names. A model above that limit, including one an extension makes eventful or one a custom field pushes over it, is refused when the registry is built, with an error naming the model, the addon that opted it in, the count and the limit. Whether wide models such as journal entries get a larger bound is an open lead decision. Frozen ABI1 generic guest create/write calls are subject to the same native-field refusal as direct guest CRUD, even when the called model has only native methods. Host/RPC calls to entirely native chains still accept the native scalar types. When a WASM override is present in a create/write chain, explicit native-field writes are refused for every caller before native hooks or lossy argument conversion. Ordinary neighboring fields remain usable; no whole-model activation ban applies. See also: [Tracked fields](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/tracking.md) (tracking = true | <sequence> and the change capture).

audit_reads = true selects successful RPC reads of the invoked model for independent auditing (ADR 0167 D4). Use it on native models or extensions, ModelDecl::audit_reads(true), ModelDef::audit_reads(true), data-only model TOML, or described WASM model arguments. The default is false. Composition ORs every declaration in the model's MRO: a false extension cannot disable a true declaration. Abstract mixins contribute to concrete descendants, and transient models may opt in. Delegation alone does not transfer the flag. A registry rebuild recomputes it from the currently loaded declarations. A selected read remains READ ONLY. Its result is buffered until an independent read_ok attempt commits; audit failure withholds the result with erp.audit_unavailable and does not rerun the successful method. Operator policy can widen selection, and request context cannot disable it. This flag does not grant read access or admit additional principal kinds to RPC.
A stored Char or Text field can select byte ordering explicitly: use erp_sdk::prelude::*; erp_sdk::addon!(name = "collation_example", depends = ["base"]);
pub struct Item { #[field(char, collation = "C")] pub code: Option<String>, }

The closed choices are "C" and "default". Omission inherits an earlier declaration; otherwise it uses the database default. An extending addon can select collation = "default" to reset an inherited C. Native FieldDecl::collation and owned FieldDef::collation use the same names; data-only model fields accept a string collation property. Unknown names and nontext, translated, company-dependent or nonstored storage are refused at registration. Locale and ICU collations are not available. C compares bytes in the database encoding. In UTF-8 this agrees with code-point ordering, not natural-language order. It does not normalize Unicode or make equality case-insensitive. PostgreSQL case conversion and character classification also use collation; selecting C is not a promise of Unicode case folding. Ordinary column indexes inherit the column's collation. Schema sync compares catalog identities, including when the database itself defaults to C. Changing an ordinary stored column's choice runs transactional DDL and can rebuild indexes; use a maintenance window when the normal schema admission requires one. It preserves existing varchar width when a narrower declaration would otherwise be ignored. Dependent database objects can refuse an alteration, and the operation must then roll back. Existing generated outputs require explicit migration for collation changes; fresh outputs support the declaration. A view's explicitly declared output collation must match its installed output. Only the owning addon and admitted co-owners can change a protected stored field's collation. For an existing generated output without an explicit collation declaration, its recorded installed provenance remains authoritative, including a trusted owner migration. An explicit declaration is checked against that identity before automatic sync; catalog-only drift still refuses.

Status: the addon platform is complete. The rules that schedule installs, upgrades, and uninstalls, the one-transaction runner, hooks, init() and _register_hook(), the post-commit phase, data and view loaders (erp-data), CLI operations (erp module), and authorized uninstalls are in place (erp_modules::system::ModuleSystem). Administrator groups are planned (until then only the superuser may run module operations).

Lifecycle callers use the ordinary async methods directly. The module engine owns heap indirection for its large inner lifecycle future, so initialization, immediate installation and upgrade do not require caller-side Box::pin workarounds. SPEC-MOD-059 exercises those operations on an explicit 2 MiB thread with stored model/data assertions. This bounded framework fixture does not guarantee the stack requirements of arbitrary addon hooks or recursive callbacks. Transaction and post-commit semantics remain those documented below; returned errors and post-commit reports must still be checked. Future-layout diagnostics are covered by the module tests.

The native ModuleSystem engine has a separate two-call uninstall seam under ADR 0083. It requires a trusted InstallAuthorizer backed by current primary session authority. A fingerprint acknowledges the described effect; it is never an authorization credential or an idempotency key. Call preview_uninstall_authorized(names, authorizer), present the complete returned UninstallImpact, then pass its fingerprint().as_str() unchanged with the same requested names to uninstall_authorized(names, fingerprint, authorizer). The executor rechecks authority, rebuilds the shared plan under transaction locks and compares the new fingerprint before effects. A changed plan returns Conflict: Uninstall impact changed; preview again before confirming. Obtain another preview and confirmation instead of automatically replaying the destructive call. Preview rolls its transaction back and changes no catalog, data, schema, audit or registry generation. The supported subset admits the built-in ErpDataLoader or no loader in bounded callback-free compositions. Survivor record deletions requiring any unlink implementation remain refused, including the built-in base implementation. The full base addon composition is currently refused by the native-schema admission (currently ir_dated_parameter index support), and its ir.actions.actions register hook is also outside the described plan. This is not yet a full-base/browser uninstall capability. Within that subset it removes complete ordinary model tables and their explicit reflection, XML-identity and queued post-commit metadata.
