Reverse dependents are included. Counts, including aggregate target cardinality, are decimal strings, and the public impact contains no raw record IDs or values. The identity bound includes metadata rows and dropped schema objects: 10,000 total identities, 65,536 serialized impact bytes and at most 512 current-schema tables. Planner SQL statements have a 5,000 ms deadline, lowered further when the active operation already has a shorter limit. This planner cap does not cover the pre-BEGIN opening probe or the earlier lifecycle/authority opening. Preview takes ACCESS SHARE relation locks and describes a repeatable-read snapshot, allowing ordinary reads and writes. Confirmation independently recomputes under broad ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks on current-schema ordinary tables and retains those locks through commit. Changes after preview therefore require a fresh confirmation fingerprint. An id-less metadata relation is checked for matching references without selecting a fictional id. Matching references refuse as an unsupported survivor foreign-key effect; references only to retained metadata do not imply a deletion or cascade. Unsupported paths refuse before effects. Registered host lifecycle services also refuse: their required asset or other publication work is neither executed outside the described plan nor silently skipped. An empty configured package runtime remains an opaque callback provider. In particular, this seam does not run custom data-loader purges, uninstall hooks, package callbacks, non-base register hooks, selection policies, survivor-model extensions or deletions requiring unlink behavior, many2many removal or copied-view cascades. It refuses unsafe database triggers/rules, view and FK dependencies, partitioned/foreign tables, inherited-table removal, row-security membership sources and generated company-restriction cleanup. The one trigger exception is an exactly attested, registry-declared built-in policy signal trigger: its structure, owner/signature, complete native function body and pinned configuration must match. The ORM helper checks the exact native body; catalog SQL checks the sole expected configuration entry using PostgreSQL's quote_ident schema representation. Reordered or extra search-path entries refuse. A matching name alone is insufficient. Its policy bump is included as an explicit bump_policy impact effect; the registry bump is described as bump_registry. Arbitrary callbacks remain refused. Catalog planning sources are independently limited to 10,000 rows and 1,048,576 serialized row bytes per source, before they are fetched. Relevant trigger definitions also have count and function-body byte admission limits. Dropped-table columns, defaults, constraints, indexes, triggers and owned sequences are counted and bound by their catalog identities/definitions; public drop_schema_objects metadata reports their count without exposing the definitions. Each dropped table's schema definitions must fit 1,048,576 bytes both per table and in aggregate, and the shared target-identity cap. Private canonical serialization is bounded to 8,388,608 bytes by a capped writer before extending its buffer; the public impact still has its independent 65,536-byte admission limit. Application schema/function DDL must honor the existing SCHEMA_LOCK protocol, and the runtime role must have no DDL ownership or schema CREATE authority. Privileged operator DDL outside that protocol is outside this admission guarantee. Authorized preview and confirmation require a clean connection lookup state. Before any lazy BEGIN or automatic Signal read, a metadata-only probe runs on the same held, fully elevated System connection while its transaction is still Idle. pg_catalog must be the **first effective schema**, including any temporary namespace. An implicit temporary namespace ahead of it refuses even when empty; the engine does not silently normalize the path. A configured Signal store must be an ordinary persistent table that is not a partition, has no row-level security and takes no part in inheritance; its key is native text and its weight int8, with no generated columns, no enabled user triggers, no rewrite rules and no non-catalog sum overload on the search path. Any other shape refuses while Idle, before the automatic generation read; a store that passes admits that read, which is never suppressed. The pre-BEGIN probe leaves a check-then-use window against concurrent privileged DDL (ADR 0186, decision 3). The unconfigured minimal native composition retains direct durable generation reads/bumps under the operation locks. The probe obtains no second pool connection and issues no explicit table locks; its catalog SELECT naturally takes implicit catalog read locks. This conservative precondition grants no authority and is rechecked inside the lifecycle transaction after each authorizer. Before planner data scans, the engine requires this catalog precedence and native scalar/array column types across current-schema ordinary tables. Custom/domain column types, custom table/index access-method or operator-class provenance, generated columns refuse. Expression/partial indexes refuse on actual planner scan tables: core metadata sources, dropped targets, dynamic FK sources and both counterpart tables of incoming/outgoing FKs incident to writes. Cross-schema FK counterparts refuse. Unrelated native login-throttle partial age indexes are allowed when their tables do not enter that scan inventory. Present CHECKs and INSERT defaults on the core writable tables must match the exact native allowlist, after native dependency checks performed before expression deparsing. All ordinary-table CHECK/default/trigger-condition dependency admission also runs before dropped-schema deparsing, with separate count/byte bounds. Native column types include inet. Application overloads of used planner operators and routines named like native built-ins refuse even with pg_catalog first; unrelated unused extension operators are outside that symbol fence. The native audit sequence/time and signal defaults remain supported; an addon callback hidden in a CHECK/default is refused rather than executed. Metadata FKs with live SET NULL/SET DEFAULT references refuse. A CASCADE reference is admitted only when every source row is explicitly planned and its table is deleted before the referenced target table; unordered cascades refuse. base, web and their required dependencies are protected, including indirect removal. Pending lifecycle work must be resolved first; a refused confirmation preserves that pending state. Shadowed SQL sources and a changed schema after trusted authorization refuse admission. Unsupported effect categories return an explicit error before any uninstall effect; callers must not treat a refusal as an empty plan. Durable registry signal and lifecycle audit storage must already exist. The engine binds confirmation to the database, actor/session, durable generation, available addon content and exact target identities, so replacing rows while retaining their count still requires a fresh preview. Installed artifact attestation remains a separate prerequisite (planned); available catalog/source content alone does not establish it. This package enables no browser uninstall route. Successful removal and its insert-only lifecycle audit commit atomically. Use OperationOutcome::orm afterward and inspect OperationOutcome::post_commit: a post-commit failure is reported after the uninstall has committed and cannot be treated as a rollback. The existing install audit history is preserved. Remote validation and browser delivery status are recorded in the engine design; this guide is not a claim that broader browser/multi-node acceptance has passed. The proposed native SQL-object contract does not add callable lifecycle APIs yet. In particular, SQL-object guards are not an exemption from the current confirmed-uninstall restrictions on hooks. Do not declare SQL bodies, grant policies or SQLSTATE registrations in a manifest or model file.

A served node (erp server) and the lifecycle commands (erp module install | upgrade | uninstall) offer two kinds of addon from their addon directory: data-only addons (manifest, model files, data; see [the data-only guide](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/data-only-addon.md)) and the native addons compiled into the erp binary. A folder of the addon directory that holds a Rust crate (Cargo.toml, src/) but is not compiled in is not offered: the Addons page does not list it, and every install route refuses it by name, the browser, erp module install and an install that would pull it in as a dependency alike. The refusal ends with this binary does not link the addon's native code: <reason>. The native addons the binary compiles in are one list, crates/erp-cli/src/native_addons/names.rs: - LINKED: the addons linked into erp, in dependency order. crates/erp-cli/src/native_addons.rs holds their descriptors (DESCRIPTORS, same order), which every composition site passes to ModuleSystem::builder(..).code(..); crates/erp-cli/build.rs reads the same names for the per-addon identity receipts, so the linked code and the receipts cannot drift apart. - NOT_LINKED: the addon crates of addons/ that are left out on purpose, each with its reason. Today these are the declared bridge addons that have a manifest and a dependency declaration but no model and no data yet (delivery, product_expiry, purchase_stock, sale_stock, stock_account, stock_delivery, stock_dropshipping, stock_landed_costs, stock_sms): offering one would install an application that promises features it does not have. To make a new native addon installable on a served node: 1. Add its crate to [dependencies] of crates/erp-cli/Cargo.toml (not [dev-dependencies]: a test binary links dev-dependencies, the served binary does not). 2. Add its name to LINKED and its ADDON descriptor to DESCRIPTORS, at the same position. 3. If it is not ready to be offered, add it to NOT_LINKED with the reason instead. The test every_addon_crate_is_linked_or_excluded_with_a_reason (crates/erp-cli/tests/served_account_stock.rs) fails when a crate under addons/ is in neither list, in both, or when the descriptors and names differ, so a new addon cannot be left out silently. The addon catalogue writes one server log line per addon it does not offer, addon catalogue: <name> is not offered for installation: <reason>; for the declared bridges the reason starts with declared, no behaviour yet and then says what the addon holds (only its manifest and dependency declaration, or storage models without access rows, data or operations), for a folder with a crate the binary does not link it says the folder holds a Rust crate (Cargo.toml or src/) of a native addon that this binary does not link. A folder named in NOT_LINKED that holds no crate gets its own refusal, never the NOT_LINKED reason.

| Key | Effect on the lifecycle | |---|---| | depends | Installing your addon installs these first; uninstalling one of them uninstalls your addon. Your addon always loads after them, and only the order of dependencies is guaranteed: an addon that overrides another must depend on it. | | auto_install | true: installed as soon as all depends are installed or being installed, and at least one of them is being installed now. A list (['sale', 'stock']) restricts the triggers: the other dependencies are installed with it, not required. This is how glue addons work. | | icon | The addon's icon where the web client lists addons: the Settings sidebar (for an addon whose settings have no root menu of their own) and its tile on the Apps page. "lucide:<name>", the same form as a menu's web_icon (for example icon = "lucide:palette"); any other value refuses the manifest when it is read. A name the client does not ship shows the default icon with a console warning. Without it the addon shows its first letter. An addon that appears in any menu or sidebar should declare one. | | countries | Two-letter ISO 3166-1 country codes ("BE"; any case, stored upper case); anything else ("BEL", "B1", a path) is refused when the manifest is read. With auto_install: only when a company is in one of these countries. Company countries arrive with res.company in M3; until then an operation that would auto-install such an addon fails with "Module "x" auto-installs only for companies in BE, but the companies' countries are not known until res.company arrives (M3); install "x" by name in the same operation to include it" instead of skipping it silently. Naming the module works with every entry point (button_immediate_install takes no options); code driving a Catalog directly can also pass InstallOptions::with_company_countries (a list of CountryCode). | | excludes | Installing your addon while one of these is installed (or the reverse) is refused: Modules "A" and "B" are incompatible. | | category | "Sales & CRM/Tools" creates the categories Sales & CRM and its child Tools (external IDs base.module_category_sales_and_crm and …_tools). In a category flagged exclusive, the installed modules must all be dependencies of one of them. Empty segments ("A//B") and segments with leading or trailing whitespace ("Sales / Tools") are refused when the manifest is read. Two categories whose external IDs would be the same ("A/B" and "A B" both give module_category_a_b, as in Odoo, where they silently merge into one category with the wrong parent) are refused by update_list with a message naming both: rename one of them. | | installable | false: the module is listed as uninstallable. Asking to install it, or a module that depends on it, is an error (Odoo silently drops it later). | | version | Stored as the installed version after install and upgrade; 20.0.1.2 becomes 1.2.0 (ADR 0009 §5). | | data, demo | Loaded in this order on install (init mode) and upgrade (update mode). Demo files load only when every dependency has demo data (base takes the database's demo flag). | | pre_init_hook, post_init_hook, uninstall_hook | Functions of your addon, see below. |

The transaction guarantee below covers failure before the lifecycle commit. Restoring an older executable after a successful upgrade does not undo its committed schema or data migration. Manifest versions select migration steps; they do not certify that an older binary can serve the upgraded database. The separate schema compatibility admission proposal is planned; it adds no manifest key or active runtime check yet. An install, upgrade or uninstall is **one PostgreSQL transaction** (ADR 0009 §2): when anything fails (a hook, a data file, a schema change), nothing of the operation is kept, not even the modules that were processed before the failure. Odoo commits each module on its own; ERPForAll does not. The error names the module and the step that failed (Error::StepFailed); the step's own error is its source, so print the whole chain (std::error::Error::source, or anyhow's {:#}) to see both: Module "library": post_init_hook 'fill_shelves' failed caused by: <your hook's error> Module "library": data file 'data/books.xml' failed caused by: <the loader's or parser's error> Module "library": init() of library.book failed caused by: <your init's error> Module "library": _register_hook() of library.book failed caused by: <the override's error> _register_hook() failures name the module that declares the model, whichever override failed. When the data loader's purge fails on uninstall, the error names every module being removed ("Modules a, b: the data loader's purge before uninstall failed"): the loader purges them together. After a successful operation, use the returned ORM (outcome.orm) and drop the one you called with: the old ORM still has the registry from before (no models of the installed modules, the models of uninstalled ones still there). The outcome is #[must_use]; ...await? alone does not look at outcome.post_commit, which is where post-commit failures are reported. Each operation runs with a lock_timeout (default 30 s) and a statement_timeout (default 30 min), set right after the operation lock; the host can lower them (ModuleSystemBuilder::lock_timeout, ::statement_timeout), never raise them: until a planned change moves the schema sync's own index builds and backfills out of the operation transaction, these limits are what bounds the locks it holds (ADR 0022 §10): until then module operations run the ORM's schema step inline (Transaction::init_models, whatever the size of the tables) and not the large-table form init_models_with; a session that already has lower limits keeps them. The ORM's own schema bounds (10 s / 5 min) never raise them either, and apply to each schema statement of an install or upgrade. A statement that cannot get a lock fails the operation with "A statement of a module operation could not get a database lock (SQLSTATE 55P03; lock_timeout is … ms)" (Error::LockNotAvailable); one that is canceled with "… was canceled (SQLSTATE 57014; statement_timeout is … ms)" (Error::StatementCanceled). The same codes come from a NOWAIT lock or from an administrator's pg_cancel_backend, so the message names the limit without claiming it was the cause; PostgreSQL's own message, the source, says which. The errors carry the limit that was in force for the failed statement as a Duration (zero for no statement_timeout). Index builds and backfills on large tables belong in the post-commit phase (below); creating them inside a hook runs into these limits on big tables. Hooks, data loaders and init() / _register_hook() methods run in the operation's transaction but cannot end it: tx.commit(), tx.rollback(), tx.commit_pipelined() and tx.switch_orm() return a Programming error ("this transaction belongs to a module operation, which commits or rolls it back itself"). A raw COMMIT or BEGIN sent as a statement cannot be refused; the operation notices right after the hook, stops with Error::OperationTransactionEnded and resets the transient module states. What the hook had already committed stays in the database, so the error says it may hold a partial change. Inside the transaction, each module you install gets its own registry step, so your code sees what it would see in Odoo: 1. pre_init_hook runs on the registry **without** your addon: your models and tables do not exist yet. Use raw SQL (tx.execute, tx.query), for example to pre-create a column so that a new computed column does not have to be filled row by row. 2. Your models are added; their tables are created or altered, then init() runs on every model your addon declares or extends (also for models of other addons that you extend). 3. data files in manifest order, then demo files. 4. post_init_hook runs: your models, tables and data exist. 5. The module is marked installed with its version. Upgrades run steps 2, 3 and 5 for each upgraded module (data in update mode). After the last module, _register_hook() runs once on every model of the final registry, never on the intermediate ones. So a hook may check rows that a data file of the same operation creates, such as a group your release adds: erp module install | upgrade | uninstall loads the installed set first without the hooks, and the operation runs them at its end. A server start runs them on its load: started on a database its release was not upgraded on, the server stops at the hook that finds the rows missing, instead of serving. When an installed module gains a new dependency in an upgrade, the dependency is installed first in the same transaction. Uninstalling runs every uninstall_hook in reverse load order (dependents first) while the modules' models and data are still there, then the data loader's purge (it deletes the records the modules' external IDs name in models that stay installed), then drops the columns the modules' fields added to other models, the tables of models that disappear and their many2many relation tables, and removes the modules' external IDs and post-commit steps. Nothing is dropped with CASCADE: if a view, foreign key or index of another module (or of the administrator) uses a table or column being removed, the uninstall fails and names it ("Cannot remove the schema of modules x: cannot drop table x_thing because other objects depend on it (view y_report depends on table x_thing); remove the objects that use it first"). PostgreSQL's DROP COLUMN would silently remove an index or constraint of the same table that uses the column together with other columns; those are refused too ("… cannot drop columns that other objects use together with columns that stay (index y_mixed_idx on x_thing (name, x_note)) …"), unless the removed modules declared them. An index or constraint on removed columns only goes with them. A table to drop that no longer exists (removed by hand) fails the uninstall with its name ("Cannot remove the schema of modules x: table x_thing_y_tag_rel does not exist (it was removed outside ERPForAll)"). A table that a model or relation that stays still maps to is never dropped: if a removed model and a kept one (or one of the module system's own models) share a _table, the uninstall fails naming the table and both models ("… table x_shared is used by model a.old, which is removed, and also by model b.keep, which stays"). The column of a custom field (x_…, ADR 0036) that the uninstall breaks (for example a stored related field through a removed field) stays: custom fields are the database owner's, and a dropped custom field keeps its column. Refused as well: - a module that still owns records (external IDs) in a model that stays installed, for example a partner your data file created. Without a data loader the uninstall is refused with an error saying that the module owns records of models that stay installed (for example res.partner: 3) and that no data loader is installed to remove them — delete those records in your uninstall_hook (and their external IDs) to uninstall now. With a loader whose purge left some: "… after the data loader's purge it still owns records …"; - a module whose source is gone, or whose manifest says installable = false: ERPForAll finds the tables to drop from the module's declarations, so restore the source first (Odoo uses its ir.model metadata instead). Only one operation runs at a time per database: a second one, and any scheduling call (button_install, button_upgrade, button_uninstall, button_reset_state, update_list), is refused at once with "ERPForAll is currently processing another module operation." A plain load (ModuleSystem::load, server start) that finds scheduled modules runs them first; it waits for an operation in progress (up to 30 min, ModuleSystemBuilder::operation_wait_timeout) instead of failing. Only the superuser (uid 1, the System principal with full elevation) may run module operations until M3 adds administrator groups; sudo() of another user is not enough, and the environment must come from the ORM of the same module system (ModuleSystem::load()/initialize outcomes): an environment made by another ORM, even on the same database, is refused with "Access denied to module.<method>: the environment does not belong to this module system's ORM". An installed module whose dependency is not installed (a database edited by hand, a restored dump) stops the load and every operation with "Inconsistent module states in the database" listing the pairs, instead of loading without the module. If a failure leaves modules scheduled (to install, to upgrade, to remove), they are reset to uninstalled / installed; when another operation started in between, the reset is skipped and both errors are returned (button_reset_state resets later). A scheduled module whose source disappeared, or that the dependency graph leaves out, fails the next operation with the list of such modules and why.

Data and demo files are read from the addon folder: regular files only (a symbolic link, a path under one, or a file with several hard links is refused), at most 64 MiB each (the host can lower the limit with ModuleSystemBuilder::max_data_file_bytes). A module may list at most 512 data and demo files and one operation reads at most 1 GiB of them in total; the host can lower both (max_data_files, max_operation_data_bytes), and a module over them fails its operation naming the limit. manifest.toml is read the same way (a regular file with one link, at most 256 KiB), on the blocking pool. XML files are handed to the data loader one operation at a time; CSV files are read whole first (a known limit until the CSV reader streams). The loader must consume every operation of a file: if it returns early, or drops a parse error, the operation fails anyway.

Name the hook in manifest.toml and give one implementation per name: name = "Library" depends = ["base"] post_init_hook = "fill_shelves" use erp_modules::hooks::{HookImpl, HookKind}; use erp_orm::{BoxFuture, Transaction}; fn fill_shelves(tx: &mut Transaction) -> BoxFuture<'_, erp_fields::Result<()>> { Box::pin(async move { tx.execute("UPDATE library_book SET shelf = 'A' WHERE shelf IS NULL", &[]).await?; Ok(()) }) }

static FILL_SHELVES: HookImpl = HookImpl::new("library", HookKind::PostInit, "fill_shelves", fill_shelves).at(file!(), line!()); (Write it exactly like this: HookImpl::new(addon, kind, name, function) and .at(file!(), line!()), which error messages point at; a #[hook] attribute in erp-sdk will generate it later. The same form is compiled in crates/erp-modules/tests/system_specs.rs, linked_hooks_run.) The pairing is checked when the module system starts: a hook named in a manifest without an implementation, two implementations of one hook, or an implementation the manifest does not name is an error naming the addon, the hook kind and the source location. Hooks run as the superuser, inside the operation's transaction; returning an error aborts the operation. Odoo's post_load does not exist (no runtime patching, ADR 0009 §6).

An upgrade runs the addon's migrations for the versions between the installed one and the manifest's: #[erp_sdk::migration(addon, version, stage)] functions and migrations/<version>/<stage>-*.sql files, in the stages pre, post and end, inside the operation's transaction. See [migrations.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/migrations.md).
Every model has both as no-op methods of base; override them like any method and call super:

impl Book { #[method(override)] async fn init(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, sup: Super) -> Result<()> { tx.batch( "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW library_book_titles AS \ SELECT id, upper(name) AS name FROM library_book", ) .await?; sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), ()).await } #[method(override)] async fn _register_hook(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, sup: Super) -> Result<()> { // registry-wide setup; runs once per registry build, after all modules are loaded sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), ()).await } } init() creates SQL views, indexes or functions after the table exists; it runs on install and upgrade of any addon that touches the model. (Tested in crates/erp-test-models/tests/model_hooks.rs.)

Work that cannot run in a transaction (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) or would hold locks too long is scheduled from a hook and runs after the operation commits, each step on its own. A step is a structured **action**, not SQL text: the queue (ir_module_post_commit) is read back and run with the module system's database rights, so there is nothing to inject into. Two actions exist: PostCommitAction::create_index and PostCommitAction::analyze. use erp_modules::{ CreateIndex, IndexColumn, IndexMethod, IndexName, ModuleName, PostCommitAction, PostCommitKey, TableName, schedule_post_commit, }; let library = ModuleName::new("library") .map_err(|e| erp_fields::Error::programming(e.to_string()))?; let table = TableName::parse("library_book")?; let index = CreateIndex::new( table.clone(), IndexName::parse("library_book_name_trgm")?, vec![IndexColumn::new("name")?.with_opclass("gin_trgm_ops")?], )? .method(IndexMethod::Gin); let trgm = PostCommitKey::parse("book_name_trgm")?; let analyze = PostCommitKey::parse("analyze_books")?; schedule_post_commit(tx, &library, &trgm, &PostCommitAction::create_index(index)).await?; schedule_post_commit(tx, &library, &analyze, &PostCommitAction::analyze(table)).await?; schedule_post_commit only works from the transaction of a module operation (a hook or data loader the module system runs) acting as the System principal: any other transaction is refused (Programming for an unmanaged one, Access for another principal). Rules: - Table, column, operator class and index names are 1 to 63 bytes of a-z, 0-9, _, not starting with a digit (table and index names also not with pg_, PostgreSQL's catalogs); they are validated when the value is made, stored in columns (kind, table_name, index_name, spec as strict JSON of at most 4 KiB) and quoted when the statement is built. An index has 1 to 32 columns, an optional operator class per column, an access method (btree, hash, gin, gist, brin) and may be unique(). **A step must be idempotent and may run more than once**: a failed step runs again in every later phase until it succeeds or has failed three times (MAX_POST_COMMIT_ATTEMPTS), when it is parked (see below), and a phase that was interrupted may have run a statement whose result was never recorded. Both actions are (CREATE INDEX ... IF NOT EXISTS, ANALYZE). The key is 1 to 64 bytes of a-z, 0-9, _, ., -, unique per module; scheduling the same key again replaces the step (and makes it run again, also when a phase is running the old one: that run is not recorded and shows in outcome.post_commit.superseded). The runner reads each row again before running it: a row changed in the table directly that no longer parses (a table name that is SQL, an unknown kind, a spec with an unknown key) is never run; it is marked failed with the reason and reported in outcome.post_commit.invalid. - The queue is closed to everything but the module system. Only the module system writes ir.module.post_commit: creating, changing or deleting its rows through the ORM is refused, for the superuser too. Database initialization revokes every privilege on the table from PUBLIC, and the server setup calls erp_modules::revoke_post_commit_access(tx, role) for the role that serves requests, next to Transaction::grant_signal_request_role. - A failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY leaves an invalid index that IF NOT EXISTS would accept; an index step drops an invalid index of that name before the retry, but only when it is on the step's table (an index of that name on another table fails the step and is left alone), and after the statement checks that the index exists, is valid and is on the table (otherwise the step is failed). The index is looked up in the current schema, where the ORM's tables are. - A concurrent index build holds SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on its table for as long as it runs: a module operation that alters that table meanwhile waits up to its lock_timeout and fails with Error::LockNotAvailable; run it again once the build is done. - Each step runs with a statement_timeout (default 6 h, ModuleSystemBuilder::post_commit_statement_timeout), and waits for locks for as long as that (an index build waits for old transactions); the statements between steps use the short lock_timeout (30 s). A step runs on a connection of its own that is closed afterwards: what it changes in its session (SET ROLE, search_path, an open BEGIN) never reaches another user of the pool. - Steps run in scheduling order. A failed step is reported in the operation's outcome (outcome.post_commit.failed, with the SQLSTATE) and logged, stays failed and runs again in the next phase; ModuleSystem::pending_post_commit() shows it as `PendingState::Failed { step, error, sqlstate } with attempts`, the number of runs since it was scheduled. After the third failure the step is **parked** (PendingState::Parked, PostCommitFailure::parked in the report): it stays failed and no phase runs it until an operation schedules it again, so a step that can never succeed does not run after every operation for ever. A row of the queue that no longer passes the checks of scheduling is listed as PendingState::Invalid (a load does not refuse to start for it, and the table's own CHECK constraints refuse most such rows) and a phase marks it failed, counts the attempt (it parks the same way) and reports it in outcome.post_commit.invalid. A row another transaction holds locked when the phase wants it (an operation scheduling or removing the step) is reported in outcome.post_commit.skipped_row_locked, not as superseded. When two phases run together, one runs the steps and the other reports PostCommitStop::Busy: the running phase reads the queue again until no new step is left (and once more after it releases its lock), so steps an operation commits while another phase runs are not left behind. A phase makes at most 8 passes over the queue (MAX_POST_COMMIT_PASSES) and then stops with PostCommitStop::PassLimit when steps keep being scheduled; the rest stay pending. Uninstalling a module removes its steps, and the steps of other modules on a table the uninstall drops. - Work of an install or upgrade that would scan or rewrite a large table (an index build, validating a foreign key or a not-null constraint, filling a column that becomes required, computing a new stored computed field) is queued by the operation as schema steps, one row per step, when the table has more rows than ModuleSystemBuilder::schema_sync_options says (SchemaSyncOptions::large_table_rows, 100,000 by default); smaller tables get the same work inside the operation. The phase plans each step again from the ORM you pass to run_post_commit and the database, so pass the ORM of the current module set. A failed step stays queued and runs again; a batched one resumes after the last batch it committed. - A plain load (ModuleSystem::load, server start) never runs post-commit steps, also not those its forced update scheduled, so startup never waits for an index build. It lists the steps waiting (LoadOutcome::post_commit_pending: left by an interrupted or skipped phase, failed earlier, or new) and logs a warning with their number; run them with ModuleSystem::run_post_commit(&orm), typically in a background task once the server serves. ModuleSystem::pending_post_commit() gives the same list at any time (a health check). Dropping the future of a running phase closes its connection: the statement running there keeps running on the server until it ends (or reaches its timeout), stays pending, and keeps the phase lock until then; a phase started meanwhile reports PostCommitStop::Busy { holder_pid } naming the backend (pg_stat_activity, pg_cancel_backend). If the dropped future was an operation's, its outcome is lost although the operation committed: read the module states and pending_post_commit(), and take the ORM from ModuleSystem::load(). let loaded = system.load().await?; if !loaded.post_commit_pending.is_empty() { let system = Arc::clone(&system); tokio::spawn(async move { let report = system.run_post_commit(&loaded.orm).await; if !report.is_clean() { // failed steps and the reason the phase stopped are in the report } }); }

The database keeps one ir.module.module row per known addon, with its dependencies (ir.module.module.dependency), exclusions, category (ir.module.category) and the external ID base.module_<name>. A row of an installed or scheduled module cannot be deleted ("You are trying to remove a module that is installed or will be installed."), and categories cannot form cycles. A module installed in the database but present in no addon source is reported as unavailable: the registry loads without it.

exact_only = true in manifest.toml opts an addon into exact numeric column admission. Native addons declare the same value with erp_sdk::addon!(name = "my_addon", exact_only = true); package describe metadata must agree with the manifest. An absent flag defaults to false for ordinary addons. Names starting with account or stock, and exact names product and uom, are always protected; explicitly disabling their flag is an error. The registry checks the final physical columns after inheritance and related-field composition. Delegated values are checked at their owning parent column, including a chain of delegates. A model defined by an exact-only addon is protected model-wide, including columns added later by ordinary addons or runtime overlays. On an existing model that the addon only extends, protection applies to fields it declares or redeclares and survives later redeclarations. Unrelated base columns retain their original policy; a method-only extension does not protect the whole base model. Exact calculations using an inherited ordinary float require an explicit conversion rule in the addon's own spec. Native macro declarations support fixed/named digits or digits = 0 for unrounded exact decimals. Data-only models/*.toml declarations currently support fixed numeric digits = [precision, scale]; named and unrounded digit syntax is not available through that route. Booked monetary amounts keep their Monetary contract. A nonstored field or a JSON column is not a Float8 column; this admission check does not prove that arbitrary addon code uses no binary arithmetic. An admission failure names the protecting addon and declaration, the declaring definition with its source location, and the physical owning column (including delegated parents). Installation/upgrade stops; there is no automatic float-to-decimal data conversion. Under ManualFieldPolicy::DropBroken, an eligible broken manual field is instead omitted and returned in the typed dropped-field report with DropReason::Refused; its physical column and data remain intact (ADR 0036). Addon-declared violations still fail under both policies. Review an explicit migration before redeclaring a populated float column. Shared registry and descriptor identities include the policy, so enabling it cannot reuse an ordinary-policy registry. The stock SQL constraints and precision-reduction guard are separate integration obligations.

A native addon registers a count-only uninstall guard through erp_sdk::sql_uninstall, with its declared read tables, static error message and independent manifest. The ORM owns the shared collector/runtime; ModuleSystem retains owner filtering, lock-first execution and rollback (ADR0249). The legacy framework namespace remains a reexport for host code. A declaration does not grant request-time System authority. The module engine locks those tables before taking the destructive transaction's data snapshot. A protected row committed while that lock was waiting therefore prevents removal. Positive counts stop uninstall before its hooks, purge or schema removal; failures leave the installed addon and its data intact. The same protection applies when a previously scheduled uninstall is consumed during loading. Guards use the ordinary RepeatableRead ORM lifecycle. Native host composition configures their registration and bounded admission policy; runtime model files cannot introduce guard callbacks or arbitrary SQL. Table locks remain held until commit or rollback. Cancelling a guarded operation closes its held connection so session locks cannot leak into subsequent operations. Lock and statement waits obey the configured module operation timeouts and lower caller limits. Native SQL functions, triggers and foreign keys are removed restrictively in dependency order, preserving surviving ownership. Unexpected dependencies refuse removal and roll back the complete lifecycle. The confirmed-uninstall planner currently refuses addons with these SQL-object effects or native guards; it does not authorize their removal from a stale preview. Its existing supported ordinary effects retain their confirmation and authorization checks.

docs.title: Money, currency rates and dated parameters

sections.text: base supplies the money services of hook H41 and the dated parameter table of hook H35. Everything below is exact decimal arithmetic: no f64 appears on any path. Design and decisions: docs/design/m3-base-c-money.md; contract: ADR 0046 D1-D3.

erp_sdk::money holds the pure primitives (no database, also built for WASM). A quotient stays an exact ratio until you name a rounding boundary; the mode is always explicit. use erp_sdk::Decimal; use erp_sdk::money::{ExactRatio, Increment, RoundingMode, canonical_string, parse_decimal};

// 24,000,000 x 11/12 is 22,000,000 before any rounding; 1/3 never becomes a finite decimal. let share = ExactRatio::quotient(Decimal::from(11), Decimal::from(12))?; let wages = ExactRatio::from_decimal(parse_decimal("24000000")?)?; let owed = wages.checked_mul(&share)?; assert_eq!(owed.to_string(), "22000000"); let third = ExactRatio::quotient(Decimal::ONE, Decimal::from(3))?; assert_eq!(third.to_string(), "1/3"); // Currency rounding: half away from zero to an increment (a cash increment works too). let cent = Increment::new(parse_decimal("0.01")?)?; let rounded = cent.quantize(parse_decimal("2.675")?, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero)?; assert_eq!(canonical_string(rounded), "2.68"); let nickel = Increment::new(parse_decimal("0.05")?)?; assert_eq!(canonical_string(nickel.quantize(parse_decimal("1.03")?, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero)?), "1.05"); // is_zero rounds the amount you give it; compare rounds both sides first. They differ: let (a, b) = (parse_decimal("0.006")?, parse_decimal("0.002")?); assert!(cent.is_zero(a - b, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero)?); assert_ne!(cent.compare(a, b, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero)?, std::cmp::Ordering::Equal);

Refused, never rounded to fit: a numerator or denominator over 4096 bits, a zero denominator, a zero or negative increment, a quantized result outside the decimal range (coefficient below 2^96, at most 28 decimals), a decimal text with an exponent, whitespace, +, more than 64 bytes or more than 28 decimals. Money errors convert to Validation errors.

res.currency.rate stores, per currency, root company (or none: shared) and day, the rate as units of the currency per unit of the company currency (numeric, exact, strictly positive). Rules of RateBook: 1. Rates belong to the **root company** of the company you pass; a root company rate wins over a shared one. 2. The candidate is the latest rate **strictly before** the date (Odoo 20; SPEC-BASE-061), or on or before it with RateDateRule::OnOrBefore. 3. With no earlier rate, the earliest later one is used and marked RateOrigin::LaterFallback. 4. The company's own currency needs no row (rate one, RateOrigin::ReferenceCurrency). 5. Any other currency without a rate is a UserError naming currency, company and date. There is no rate of one. use erp_addon_base::money::{self, RateBook, RoundingTable}; use erp_sdk::money::RateDateRule; use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

// One call: exact product, rounded once to the target currency (half away from zero). let eur_amount = money::convert(env, tx, Decimal::from(100), usd, eur, company, day).await?; // Many pairs: one book (two statements), then pure lookups. The snapshot names the rates used. let book = RateBook::load(env, tx, company, day, RateDateRule::StrictlyBefore, &[usd, eur]).await?; let snapshot = book.snapshot(usd, eur)?; let exact = snapshot.convert_exact(Decimal::from(100))?; // Per-currency rounding helpers. let table = RoundingTable::load(env, tx, &[eur]).await?; let eur_rounding = table.get(eur)?; assert_eq!(eur_rounding.round(eur_amount)?, eur_amount); let _ = (exact, eur_rounding.is_zero(eur_amount)?);

The caller needs read access to res.currency and res.currency.rate and the company must be one of the caller's companies; the rate statement itself reads the root company's rows directly, as Odoo's sudo() read does. convert_with returns the amount, the unrounded ExactRatio and the FxSnapshot to store with a booking.

Every rate belongs to a **rate type** (res.currency.rate.type, ADR 0140 D2): spot, monthly_average, closing, historical, budget and tax are seeded, with a stable unique code. A rate is unique per currency, company, type and day; a rate created without a type is a spot rate, and a type that still has rates cannot be deleted. Each type carries its date rule (strictly_before for spot, historical and budget; on_or_before for tax, monthly_average and closing) and a later_fallback flag (only spot). The default spot type cannot be deleted, assigned a different code (or cleared), or archived, even before it has rates. These operations return a UserError naming spot; a mixed-recordset operation is refused as a whole. Its label and sequence remain editable, and writing the same code or setting it active is allowed. Other types retain their ordinary lifecycle rules. RateBook::load is unchanged: it reads spot rows under the rule you pass and keeps the earliest-later fallback. RateBook::load_typed reads one named type under that type's rule and fallback: use erp_addon_base::money::RateBook; use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

let book = RateBook::load_typed(env, tx, company, day, "tax", &[usd, idr]).await?; assert_eq!(book.rate_type().code(), "tax"); let snapshot = book.snapshot(usd, idr)?; // a missing tax rate is a UserError naming "Rate type: tax."

Lookups never leave their type: a missing tax rate is an error, never a spot rate. An unknown type code is Missing; an archived type is still read. FxSnapshot does not carry the type; the booking that freezes evidence records book.rate_type().id() itself. Upgrading a database that predates rate types gives every existing rate the spot type (base 1.6 pre-migration). A forced re-initialisation (reinit) of a populated rate table skips that migration and is refused by the schema step, and a rate table above the large-table threshold needs the manual key change the schema step names. Per-company date-rule overrides and rate coverage certificates belong to later slices.

decimal.precision rows name a usage (unique) with 0 to 28 digits. precision_get answers Odoo's default 2 for an unconfigured usage; precision_defined returns None instead, for callers that must not accept the default. The lookup reads the table as the system (administrator-only table, public digits), so any user can resolve a usage. field_scale(env, tx, "model", "field") resolves one field: Places(n) for fixed or named digits, Unrounded for digits = 0, Currency { currency_field } for a monetary field. Native field descriptions now resolve named precision from the table too. fields_get is async: pass a mutable transaction and await the description. Only selected readable fields whose digits attribute is requested trigger this metadata lookup. Cached digits live only in that transaction; creating, changing or deleting precision rows invalidates them, and rollback discards them. Missing usages still resolve to (16, 2); lookup failures are returned to the caller. Named-digit writes follow the [scale rejection policy](#named-digits-on-writes) below; fixed-digit rounding remains unchanged. use erp_sdk::{Records, Result, Transaction};
let fields = items.fields_get(tx, Some(&["price"]), Some(&["digits"])).await?; if let Some(price) = fields.get("price") { let _digits = price.get("digits"); }

A monetary field uses its resolved currency_field to round amounts through the base addon's exact increment service, half away from zero. Create inputs and computed outputs are normalized before dependent computations consume them; typed set, dynamic set_value, and write share this conversion path. Default, related and delegated currencies are resolved from the same call's final values. Without a currency, the Decimal keeps its precision. A currency-only write keeps the current amount; assign the amount again when it needs rounding in the new currency. The resolved currency field must be a many2one to res.currency, including when inherited or related; a different field kind or comodel is rejected during registry composition. Related currency paths may traverse many2one hops only; a one2many or many2many hop is rejected even if the path ends in res.currency. A shared write of zero or null skips currency admission and rounding, so it can clear amounts across different currencies. For a shared nonzero amount, only non-null currency ids count: no currency preserves precision, one real currency rounds the value for the whole set (including rows without a currency), and distinct real currencies return Validation. A same-call currency replacement for the whole recordset can resolve that ambiguity. Independent create rows and compute outputs may use different currencies. Currency identity and rounding-data lookup use narrowly scoped sudo, so a hidden currency field or denied currency read alone does not block amount normalization. The amount mutation still needs the caller's model/field write access, record rules and company admission; currency lookup grants no amount-write rights. Computed output publication retains its declared compute_sudo environment and company bounds, including related/delegated native currency computes. If that compute needs a denied input, normalization returns Access; result-lookup sudo does not grant input access. Parity: divergent — ADR 0087. This intentionally differs from upstream sudo currency access. Supplied in-memory new-record amounts and monetary defaults are also normalized before cache publication and dependent consumption, a stronger contract than upstream new() with validation disabled (Parity: divergent — ADR 0087). Rounding is not cached across operations or rollback. These r1 requirements are recorded in ADR 0087; implementation validation is tracked in the monetary design/readiness note. Explicit/default zero or null amounts do not force currency precomputation solely for rounding; ordinary declared dependencies still apply. Onchange normalizes scalar amounts before cache publication and dependent computation, including same-call currencies and staged relation links in root, persisted-origin and nested forms. First calls for new forms use staged native currency inputs, including non-triggering reads; later calls preserve the existing currency unless a declared dependency changes. No-currency values keep their precision; failures preserve form isolation. When a declared dependency changes, synchronous currency computes use staged scalar inputs before rounding. Non-triggering reads alone keep the stored currency; comparison uses normalized dependency values and only affected records are projected. Initial in-memory fills evaluate staged inputs without caching provisional defaults. An async currency compute joins same-call monetary admission only when it is registered candidate (see [Candidate currency computes](#candidate-currency-computes)). For a nonzero, non-null amount, a same-call dependency change to an async currency compute without candidate, or an explicit create amount needing such a late currency, returns Programming before amount publication; the message names the candidate flag as the fix. Async currency values already computed from unchanged inputs remain readable.

async fn _currency( this: &RecordSet<Invoice>, tx: &mut ReadTx<'_>, out: &mut Assign<'_, Invoice>, ) -> Result<()> { let selected = tx.mapped(this, Invoice::SELECTED_CURRENCY_ID).await?; for (i, currency) in selected.into_iter().enumerate() { out.set(i, Invoice::CURRENCY_ID, currency)?; } Ok(()) } A candidate compute is an async compute that receives ReadTx, a read-only view of the transaction, instead of &mut Transaction. The view offers get / mapped (ORM reads) and query (guarded SQL, see below). It has no write, no extension<T>(), no after_commit and no way back to the mutable transaction, so none of those compile. Rules: - **Visibility.** ORM reads of the compute's own batch show the *staged* values of its declared depends and reads. Reading another field of the batch is a Programming error: declare it. ORM reads of other records see the transaction as it is before the mutation. **SQL sees the database as it was before the mutation**: it never sees the staged inputs or cache writes not yet flushed. Compute from the declared fields; use SQL only for other rows. - **SQL guard.** query is meant for SELECT statements and refuses, with Programming, data-changing keywords, SELECT ... INTO, locking clauses (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE), set_config, the advisory-lock and dblink families, nextval, setval, pg_sleep, lo_* functions, and text that cannot be read with certainty. This is a lexical deny-list, not a proof that a statement is read-only: a SELECT that calls a volatile function of your own, or one the list does not name, is not caught. Keep candidate SQL to plain reads. - **Direct fields only.** A candidate may not declare dependencies or reads through a relation (a_id.b); the registry refuses it when it is built. - **Reads of other records.** get/mapped of records outside the batch read through the transaction under the usual rules, so they can trigger those records' own computes. Reads of the compute's own batch from the staged values skip the field read checks that the lazy recompute path applies. Both points are pending lead confirmation (ADR 0087). - **Registration.** candidate needs an async fn, cannot be an override and has no super(), and its second parameter is &mut ReadTx<'_>; each is a compile error. A candidate and a non-candidate implementation of one method, or two implementations of a candidate method, are a registry-build error. - **Execution.** On create the candidate runs on the precompute synthetic ids, so no INSERT precedes admission. It runs once per accepted mutation: its result is used for admission and then published with the write, with no rollback or replay. Recompute chunks (recompute_batch) each run it once; admission is over the whole recordset, and amounts are published only after every currency is admitted. A provider error leaves nothing published or inserted. Onchange runs it for the preview only and memoizes nothing, so a later lazy read may run it again (an exception to "once per accepted mutation", pending lead confirmation). - **Access.** compute_sudo, the caller's access checks and the narrow currency-lookup elevation are unchanged: with compute_sudo = false an input the caller may not read is an Access error; amount-write rights are not elevated. In-memory amounts accept persisted currencies. An in-memory currency is refused with Programming before publication (support for new in-memory currencies is planned). A present currency requires the private native res.currency._round_monetary adapter; absence is an error rather than unrounded success. **Upsert compatibility:** all typed and dynamic business-key upserts on models containing a monetary field are refused before key planning or SQL, including empty calls and operations which omit the monetary field. Use ordinary create/write until rounding is integrated with atomic conflict updates and accumulation. This restriction is accepted in ADR 0087.

One write, create, default fill, new-record or onchange call that stages monetary values, and every create on a model with a monetary field (its own or through _inherits), is bounded: at most **200,000 target records** and at most **2,000,000 staged monetary cells**. A cell is one monetary field of one record that the operation actually stages (the fields you write or supply, plus the computed monetary outputs of a create or recompute and the monetary inputs a same-call currency projection stages again); a model with many monetary fields only counts the ones present. An operation over either bound is refused with Validation, naming the limit, before anything is published: the database and the written fields are untouched, and the cache and pending recomputes are as they were, with one documented exception: a refusal caused only by cells that a same-call currency projection adds can come after a stored sibling's pending recompute (of an editable computed monetary field) was brought up to date in the cache. Split a bulk import or a mass update into several calls (the JSON-2 API already accepts at most 100,000 create documents per call). The bound includes reads that fill monetary defaults of more than 200,000 uncached in-memory records. The numbers are internal constants, not part of the Rust API. Odoo has no such bound (Parity: divergent, lead decision 2026-10-31); operations of that size that were admitted before are refused now.

ir.dated.parameter rows give a key (lower-case words joined by dots), an optional company, date_from, an optional date_to (both ends inclusive, empty is unbounded) and a typed value (decimal, integer, boolean, text). Periods of one key in one scope cannot overlap; the database enforces it. The nearest scope wins: the company's own value, then its parent's up to the root company (a branch inherits from its root and may override it), then the shared one; a date with nothing in force is a UserError. use erp_addon_base::dated_parameter::resolve_many; use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

// One search for all keys the rule or report needs; bind entries() as variables. let rates = resolve_many(env, tx, &["payroll.pension_rate", "payroll.max_lines"], company, day).await?; let pension: Decimal = rates.decimal("payroll.pension_rate")?; let max_lines: i64 = rates.integer("payroll.max_lines")?; for (key, value) in rates.entries() { let _ = (key, value); } let _ = (pension, max_lines);
The reader goes through the ORM search of the model, so access rights and record rules apply, and the company must be one of the caller's.

A numeric field declared with digits = "Product Price" uses the transaction-visible decimal.precision value as a write limit. Excess significant fractional digits raise a Validation error naming the model, field, usage and permitted digits. The ORM does not round such values. 1.2300 fits a two-place usage because trailing zeroes are lossless. Apply the appropriate explicit rounding rule before writing values produced by a conversion. Typed/dynamic mutations, defaults, stored computed outputs and upserts obey this admission boundary. Fixed-digit fields retain their existing rounding contract; unrounded numeric fields retain exact values. The metadata cache's Transaction::set_precision override does not alter authoritative write policy. Unknown usages and an absent precision model retain the documented two-place default; an installed adapter that fails is an error rather than a fallback. Precision lookups remain a private base service. Applications do not gain access to the precision table through writing a field. The write cache belongs to one transaction and is cleared by precision mutations, invalidation and rollback. Existing transactions retain their PostgreSQL isolation snapshot; a new transaction sees committed configuration. A database-wide guard against lowering a setting over historical rows remains an outstanding ADR 0079 D6 obligation.

A carrying value can need a coefficient larger than Decimal's 96-bit range. GridValue keeps a signed coefficient below 2^256 and an explicitly selected scale from 0 through 28. It is distinct from booked money. GridValue::quantize uses HalfAwayFromZero and returns both the finite value and the exact signed precision remainder: use erp_sdk::money::{CanonicalFraction, ExactNumericError, GridValue};

let third = CanonicalFraction::parse("1", "3")?; let result = GridValue::quantize(third.as_ratio(), 18)?; assert_eq!(result.value().to_string(), "0.333333333333333333"); assert_eq!(result.remainder().as_ratio().to_string(), "1/3000000000000000000");

The chosen scale is part of the numerical policy. Parsing and rescale refuse nonzero finer digits and coefficient overflow; they never round to fit. Canonical output removes trailing zeroes, and negative-zero input is refused. checked_add and checked_sub retain the left operand's grid and require the right operand to rescale exactly. CanonicalFraction::parse admits canonical signed integer text for the numerator and positive denominator, each below 2^4096. It rejects non-reduced pairs and accepts zero only as 0/1. from_ratio retains an already validated arithmetic result. The representation has no unchecked raw constructor or direct deserialization. With the database feature enabled, bind GridValue and the fraction's numerator() and denominator() directly as numeric parameters. Decode both fraction components as CanonicalInteger and call CanonicalFraction::new on the complete pair. A component alone is not a valid fraction. Numeric decoding returns minimal significant scale; rescale a decoded grid value to its frozen policy before using it. Admit a decoded carry with validate_carry(&increment): it uses the larger of scale 18 and the normalized increment scale, enforces the 256-bit coefficient bound, and admits signed values up to half the increment. An odd increment at the finest grid may have an unrepresentable half-increment endpoint, which is refused rather than rounded. erp_sql::exact_numeric supplies grid_check, carry_check, and fraction_check for unconstrained numeric columns. They quote validated column names and reject invalid required values explicitly, including NULL and non-finite values. Grid checks take an explicit nullable-column flag. These definitions do not install constraints or authorize writes; the owning addon must install them and protect complete-pair writes. SQL sees normalized numeric values, so lexical negative zero must be rejected at text admission.

How concepts from Odoo Community and Enterprise correspond to ERPForAll's native Rust crates and data-only addons, and where ERPForAll behaves differently. ERPForAll is an ERP framework rebuilt in Rust, modeled on Odoo: a faster, leaner ORM, a clean and reactive web client, and modular addons that declare and extend models, views, menus, actions, security, and UI. While the mental model closely mirrors Odoo's architectural concepts, ERPForAll replaces dynamic Python runtime patching with Rust's compile-time type safety, memory safety, explicit contracts, and strict "fail loudly" error handling. ---

| Odoo Concept | ERPForAll Equivalent | Mechanism / Crate | Guide Reference | |---|---|---|---| | __manifest__.py | manifest.toml (and Cargo.toml for native crates) | Declarative TOML manifest read by erp-modules (ADR 0009, ADR 0018). Strict schema: unknown keys rejected unless under [extra]. | [cli.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cli.md), [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md) | | models.Model, _name | #[model(name = "...")] struct | Rust struct decorated with #[model] (or [[model]] in models/*.toml for data-only addons). Associated constants for field handles. | [models.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md) | | _inherit (in-place extension) | #[extend(TargetModel)] struct | Extension struct decorated with #[extend] in an extending crate (or [[extend]] in models/*.toml). Zero runtime cost. | [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md) | | _inherits (delegation) | #[model(inherits = [("model", "field")])] | Compositional delegation inheritance where parent fields are exposed transparently. | [models.md#relational-fields](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md#relational-fields) | | Mixins (e.g., mail.thread) | Composable Rust traits & extension models | Explicit trait bounds or cross-addon extension structs rather than dynamic Python multiple inheritance. | [models.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md) | | Fields (fields.Char, Integer, Many2one, ...) | #[field(char)], #[field(integer)], #[field(many2one, comodel = "...")] | Strongly typed struct fields using erp-fields / erp-sdk. Fields are handles with associated metadata. | [models.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md) | | @api.depends(...) | #[field(..., compute = "_method")] + #[compute(depends = [...])] | Compute methods declared in #[methods(Model)] with explicit dependency paths. | [models.md#computed-fields](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md#computed-fields) | | @api.onchange(...) | #[onchange("field")] | Form onchange handlers returning modified field values in a ValueMap. | [models.md#onchange-methods](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md#onchange-methods) | | @api.constrains(...) | #[constrains("field")] | Validation functions returning Result<()>. Invariants checked before transaction commit. | [models.md#constraints](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md#constraints) | | super().method(...) | #[method(override)] with sup: Super | Explicit method override chain using the Super dispatcher. Evaluated in deterministic dependency order. | [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md), [models.md#methods-and-overrides](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md#methods-and-overrides) | | ir.model.access.csv + ir.rule | ir.access (security/ir.access.csv) | Unified access model (ADR 0035). Groups provide permissions (ORed); rules without groups restrict (ANDed). | [security.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/security.md), [access.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/access.md) | | Field security (groups="...") | #[field(..., groups = "...")] | Field-level read/write permissions declared in the model and enforced by the access engine. | [field-access.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/field-access.md), [security.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/security.md) | | XML views + XPath inheritance | erp-views arch DOM & combine_view | In-memory DOM tree (ArchNode) combining parent and extension views using XPath locators and positions. | [views.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/views.md) | | Data files (XML / CSV) | erp-data reader (ConvertMode) | Streaming XML and CSV reader (ADR 0019). Strict element and attribute validation with file and line diagnostics. | [data-files.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/data-files.md) | | Python server actions (state='code') | Sandboxed Luau scripts | Secure execution via crates/erp-script (ADR 0001, ADR 0009 §6/§10). Runs with caller's rights and tight memory/step limits. | [luau-scripts.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/luau-scripts.md) | | QWeb reports (wkhtmltopdf) | Native Typst report engine | High-performance PDF generation directly via Typst (ADR 0031). PDF/A-3 e-invoices, no headless browser. | ADR 0031 | | JSON-RPC (/web/dataset/call_kw) | JSON-2 (POST /json/2/<model>/<method>) | Explicit #[rpc(effect = ...)] methods (ADR 0038). Effect classes (read, write, destructive, external), idempotency keys. | [rpc.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/rpc.md) | | res.users._check_credentials, ir.config_parameter.get_param, _post_logout | _check_credentials(Arc<Credential>, CheckEnv) -> AuthInfo override with super; typed get_str/int/float/bool; session_end_hook! | Password login, sessions and the database settings. A malformed setting is an error, not a default; database.secret is unreadable without full elevation. | [auth.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/auth.md) | ---

In Odoo, an addon is identified by __manifest__.py. In ERPForAll: - **Native Addon**: A Rust crate with a Cargo.toml and a manifest.toml. The crate root calls erp_sdk::addon!(name = "sale_stock", depends = ["sale", "stock"]); as documented in [models.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md) ("Declaring an addon"). Notice that base is always an implicit dependency in erp_sdk::addon!, so depends lists only explicit non-base addon dependencies. In manifest.toml, depends = ["base", "other_addon"]. - **Data-Only Addon**: A plain directory containing manifest.toml, models/*.toml, and data files (XML/CSV) without Rust compilation (see [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md)).
name = "Library Extension" summary = "Extend library book with borrowing features" version = "1.0.0" depends = ["base", "test_ext_a"] data = [ "security/ir.access.csv", "views/book_views.xml", ]

In Odoo, models.Model classes are dynamically instantiated and monkey-patched at runtime via _inherit. In ERPForAll: - A new model is defined with #[model(name = "tech.name", description = "Label")] pub struct ModelName;. - Extending an existing model from another addon is defined in the extending crate using #[extend(ParentModel)] pub struct ExtensionStruct;. - The Rust struct acts as a compile-time declaration tag. Record operations use RecordSet<ModelName>, and fields are accessed via generated typed associated constants (such as Book::NAME or BookPages::PAGES).
In Odoo, method inheritance uses Python's cooperative super() and method resolution order (MRO):

class Book(models.Model): _inherit = "library.book" def describe(self): res = super().describe() return f"{res}, {self.pages} pages" In ERPForAll, method overrides are declared explicitly with #[method(override)] and accept a sup: Super parameter: // ERPForAll Rust (from crates/erp-test-models/addons/test_ext_b)

impl BookPages { #[method(override)] async fn describe(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, sup: Super) -> Result<String> { let pages = this.get(tx, BookPages::PAGES).await?; Ok(format!( "{}, {pages} pages", sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), ()).await? )) } } The override order is strictly deterministic: (depth, order_name) based on the dependency graph, identical after install, upgrade, or server restart (ADR 0009 §3).

Odoo historically splits access into ir.model.access.csv (table-level CRUD permissions) and ir.rule XML records (row-level domain filters). In ERPForAll (ADR 0035), both permissions and restrictions are unified into the ir.access format (matching Odoo 20's consolidated design): id,name,model_id,group_id/id,operation,domain access_rental_user,Rental User,test_ext.rental,base.group_user,r, access_rental_manager,Rental Manager,test_ext.rental,base.group_system,crud, rental_own_branch,Rentals in own branch,test_ext.rental,,crud,"[('company_id', 'in', company_ids)]" - Rows **with a group** grant permissions (ORed across all groups held by the user). - Rows **without a group** impose restrictions (ANDed across all users). - Operation spelling follows Odoo 20's 15 non-empty subsets of crud in strict c, r, u, d order (c create, r read, u update/write, d delete/unlink). Any unrecognized character (such as w) or out-of-order string fails parsing loudly with RowError::InvalidOperation. - Access domains compile directly into PostgreSQL SQL parameters ($uid, $company_ids, $now), evaluated once by the query planner rather than record-by-record in memory. ---

This worked example demonstrates extending an addon using the exact crate structure, workspace conventions, and compiled patterns from crates/erp-test-models/addons/test_ext_a and test_ext_b (documented in [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md)). The extending addon (test_ext_b, package erp-addon-test_ext_b) extends the base addon (test_ext_a, package erp-addon-test_ext_a): 1. **Manifest and Cargo configuration**: Declares workspace package dependencies and metadata. 2. **New model (test_ext.rental)**: Declares a new model with relational and scalar fields. 3. **Model extension (BookPages)**: Adds fields (pages, isbn) to test_ext_a::Book. 4. **Method override**: Overrides Book::describe to include page count via sup: Super. 5. **View extension**: Injects the new fields into the book form view via XPath. 6. **Access rules**: Grants permissions in security/ir.access.csv.

Reference documentation: [cli.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cli.md), [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md). Declare crate dependencies in Cargo.toml using workspace inheritance (edition 2024):

[package] name = "erp-addon-test_ext_b" description = "ERPForAll fixture addon test_ext_b: cross-crate model extension" version.workspace = true edition.workspace = true rust-version.workspace = true license.workspace = true repository.workspace = true publish.workspace = true [dependencies] erp-sdk = { workspace = true } erp-addon-test_ext_a = { workspace = true } [lints] workspace = true Declare module metadata in manifest.toml:
name = "Test Ext B" summary = "Fixture: extends test_ext.book from a separate crate" depends = ["base", "test_ext_a"] data = [ "security/ir.access.csv", "views/book_views.xml", ]

Reference documentation: [models.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md). The new model uses strongly typed fields with types that implement ValueFor<K> from erp-fields / erp-orm (Option<Arc<str>> for char, Option<Date> for date, Many2one<Book> for many2one): // addons/test_ext_b/src/rental.rs use erp_addon_test_ext_a::Book; use erp_sdk::prelude::*;

pub struct Rental { #[field(char, required = true)] pub name: Option<Arc<str>>, #[field(many2one, comodel = "test_ext.book", required = true, ondelete = "cascade")] pub book_id: Many2one<Book>, #[field(date)] pub rental_date: Option<Date>, #[field(selection, selection = [("active", "Active"), ("returned", "Returned")], default = "active")] pub state: Option<Arc<str>>, }

Reference documentation: [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md), [models.md#computed-fields](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md#computed-fields). The following snippet is taken verbatim from crates/erp-test-models/addons/test_ext_b/src/lib.rs (which builds and runs in CI): // addons/test_ext_b/src/lib.rs use erp_addon_test_ext_a::Book; use erp_sdk::prelude::*; /// B's extension of test_ext.book.

pub struct BookPages { /// Number of pages. #[field(integer)] pub pages: i32, /// ISBN, with an explicit label. #[field(char, string = "ISBN")] pub isbn: Option<Arc<str>>, } If a computed field is needed on an extension (e.g. is_rented), declare on the struct the fields it needs — #[field(one2many, comodel = "test_ext.rental", inverse_name = "book_id")] pub rental_ids: Vec<RecId> and #[field(boolean, compute = "_compute_is_rented", store)] pub is_rented: bool — and implement #[compute(depends = [...])] in #[methods(Book)] using Assign<'_, Book> (illustrative; not part of the fixture crate):

impl BookPages { #[compute(depends = ["rental_ids.state"])] async fn _compute_is_rented( this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, out: &mut Assign<'_, Book>, ) -> Result<()> { let rentals = this.mapped(tx, BookPages::RENTAL_IDS).await?; for (i, book_rentals) in rentals.iter().enumerate() { let states = book_rentals.mapped(tx, Rental::STATE).await?; let active = states.iter().any(|s| s.as_deref() == Some("active")); out.set(i, BookPages::IS_RENTED, active)?; } Ok(()) } }

Reference documentation: [cross-addon-extension.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/cross-addon-extension.md), [models.md#methods-and-overrides](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/models.md#methods-and-overrides). Taken verbatim from crates/erp-test-models/addons/test_ext_b/src/lib.rs: // addons/test_ext_b/src/lib.rs (continued)

impl BookPages { /// Appends the page count to the result of the next implementation. #[method(override)] async fn describe(this: &RecordSet<Book>, tx: &mut Transaction, sup: Super) -> Result<String> { let pages = this.get(tx, BookPages::PAGES).await?; Ok(format!( "{}, {pages} pages", sup.call(tx, this.as_records(), ()).await? )) } } Declare the addon at the top of src/lib.rs (the fixture keeps everything in one file; a larger addon splits models into modules): // addons/test_ext_b/src/lib.rs use erp_sdk::prelude::*; erp_sdk::addon!(name = "test_ext_b", depends = ["test_ext_a"]);

Reference documentation: [views.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/views.md). Extend the book form view using XPath to inject pages and isbn after name: <!-- addons/test_ext_b/views/book_views.xml --> <erp> <record id="view_book_form_ext" model="ir.ui.view"> <field name="name">test_ext.book.form.inherit</field> <field name="model">test_ext.book</field> <field name="inherit_id" ref="test_ext_a.view_book_form"/> <field name="arch" type="xml"> <xpath expr="//field[@name='name']" position="after"> <field name="pages"/> <field name="isbn"/> </xpath> </field> </record> </erp>

Reference documentation: [security.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/security.md), [access.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/access.md). Define access grants in security/ir.access.csv: id,name,model_id,group_id/id,operation,domain access_rental_user,Rental User,test_ext.rental,base.group_user,r, access_rental_manager,Rental Manager,test_ext.rental,base.group_system,crud, rental_own_branch,Rentals in own branch,test_ext.rental,,crud,"[('company_id', 'in', company_ids)]" ---

Odoo's company flags map one to one: _check_company_auto, check_company=True, _check_company_domain (here company_match) and with_company keep their meaning. What differs is the default and a few guarantees, all recorded in ADR 0044; the details are in [company-consistency.md](/en/next/developer/addon-guide/company-consistency.md). | Area | Odoo | ERPForAll | |---|---|---| | **Check on by default** | A link is checked only when the model sets _check_company_auto and the field sets check_company=True; a forgotten flag is a silent cross-company link. | Every stored many2one/many2many of a company-scoped model whose comodel is company-scoped is checked. Opt out with check_company_auto = false on the model or check_company = false on the field (Odoo's behaviour exactly). A flag on a model without company_id/company_ids fails the registry build instead of being logged and skipped. | | **Related reads** | A related field is read as superuser (related_sudo), so a user in company A reads a value through a record of company B. | A related field that does not declare compute_sudo is read as superuser for permissions but only through records of the active companies (or of none), including the record its last relational field points to; a hop outside fails with Access. compute_sudo = true is the opt-out, compute_sudo = false the read as the caller. An explicit sudo() read keeps Odoo's value. | | **Validation under sudo()** | sudo() takes the ids of allowed_company_ids as given, so a company the user is not in is accepted. | Company membership is validated under every elevation (One of the selected companies does not exist or is not one of yours.); the same check as for an unelevated environment. | | **Duplicate ids** | allowed_company_ids=[1, 1] is accepted. | A duplicated id is a Validation error naming it. | | **Names in errors** | Display names in the inconsistency error and in the debug listing of an access error are read as superuser. | Names are read as the caller; an unreadable record is written <model>(<id>,). The debug listing shows a name only for records without company or in one of the principal's active companies, and never names a company the user is not in. The hint texts and suggested_company are Odoo's. | | **System principal** | The superuser takes any company list as given. | Kept for the System principal the core creates. with_user(SUPERUSER_ID) from any other principal is refused (ADR 0164 A4, SPEC-PRIN-029): the environment stays the caller's own user, with that user's companies. | Checklist: a link across companies on purpose gets check_company = false; a related field that must show a value across companies (a partner's country on a document of another company) gets compute_sudo = true; a sudo().with_company(other) that relied on other being unchecked must be a company the user belongs to. ---

res.company exposes street, street2, zip, city, email, phone, website and vat as writable related fields of partner_id (related = "partner_id.street", readonly = false, compute_sudo = true, so whoever may read the company reads these values, as in Odoo), so a read returns the company partner's value and a write changes the partner. Known limit: a value the partner normalises on write (a bare website gets http://) reads back as written on the company until the next transaction.
